A group of around 40 men allegedly ambushed a house church in Rayan village in West Bengal’s Purba Bardhaman district on November 1, and physically assaulted the pastor and several Christian worshippers during a Sunday prayer service. The attackers accused the congregation of converting Hindus by luring them with incentives, and also accused them of running a ‘honey trap’.
Survivors told Alt News that they were forced to chant ‘Jai Sri Ram’, and were told, “This is a Hindu area; worshipping Jesus will not be tolerated”.
Several worshippers sustained severe injuries after the attack. Survivors said they were left traumatised without administrative protection or assurance. A written complaint was submitted at Burdwan police station. However, the survivors alleged that they were forced into withdrawing the complaint as attackers entered the police station and threatened to kill the complainant.
Alt News spoke to pastor Chottu Ruidas, who was leading the Sunday prayer service, and other survivors of the attack. Recounting the incident, Ruidas said the congregation had assembled at Sushanta Majila’s house around 10 am, and the service was nearing its conclusion, with the worshippers participating in communion, when a group of approximately 40 men descended on the house church, raising ‘Jai Sri Ram’ slogans.
According to Ruidas, Bisweshwar Choudhury, an influential and wealthy resident of the village who is known for helping people in need, was part of the group. He approached Ruidas during the prayer service and allegedly slapped him.
“Thereafter, the goons accompanying Choudhury started beating us mercilessly,” Ruidas told Alt News. “They slapped us, kicked us and beat us with the bamboo sticks they were carrying. They even took off their belts and whipped us.”
Ruidas said a 17-year-old boy sustained a severe head injury, leaving him bleeding profusely. “The goons told him, ‘We have treated you. Now go to a doctor and get it fixed,” he recounted.
The attackers allegedly dragged worshippers out of the house and beaten up. Those who attempted to seek refuge in neighbouring homes were pursued and assaulted, Ruidas said.
“After the goons beat us, the other attendees locked me inside a kitchen to keep me safe. But they broke open the door and dragged me out. My elder sister hugged me and fell to the ground while trying to protect me. But they continued kicking us. My sister eventually fell unconscious, and I had to take her to a nearby dispensary,” he said.
Ruidas told Alt News that he had attempted to contact police while hiding inside the kitchen but could not get through. He subsequently informed Pastor Jose Bernard, who then contacted the cops.
Bernard told Alt News that he called the Burdwan police station two to three times, but the police allegedly did not take the matter seriously. He eventually dialled the emergency helpline, 112, following which police personnel reached the village.
Bernard said his wife and minor daughter were also among the worshippers present at the congregation. By the time police reached the location, several miscreants had fled the scene. He claimed that when police entered the premises, the remaining miscreants accused the worshippers of having picked a fight with them.
Then, according to the pastor, instead of taking action against the attackers, police detained 20 women, three minors, and eight men from the Christian congregation.
Bernard categorically denied allegations of forceful conversion or conversion through inducement.
Worshippers Detained, Threatened by Accused inside Police Station
The detainees were first taken to Bardhaman Medical College and Hospital, where a doctor examined them inside the vehicle. Then, they were taken to the police station and kept in two separate rooms.
Pastor Jose Bernard subsequently submitted a written complaint at the police station. However, shortly afterwards, a group of alleged attackers entered the police station, grabbed him by the collar and threatened him with dire consequences unless he withdrew the complaint. He alleged that this happened in the presence of police personnel.
“They entered the police station, grabbed me by the collar, physically intimidated me and threatened to kill me if I did not withdraw my complaint. And all of this happened in front of the police,” Bernard told Alt News.
According to Bernard, police merely told the men, “There are CCTV cameras here; leave the premises’. That’s all.”
Bernard said that the threats and intimidation eventually compelled him to withdraw the complaint. He told Alt News that he had pleaded with the miscreants and police to at least ensure that Christians in Rayan village would not be subjected to further harassment. “This is our government. A Hindu government. A Hindu country. Worshipping Jesus is not allowed. They have to bathe in the Ganga, and we will perform ‘ghar wapsi’,” Bernard recalled them saying.
Bernard further alleged that the inspector in-charge, Debabrata Mukherjee, questioned the congregation about why they had assembled to pray in the first place. When the attendees and Bernard attempted to reason, Mukherjee allegedly asked why they were taking such risks when people were being assaulted for doing so in several places.
Eventually, the women were released from the police station around 11 pm, while the men were released around 1 am.
Speaking to Alt News, Burdwan IC Debabrata Mukherjee denied the allegation that the attackers entered the police station and threatened Pastor Jose Bernard to withdraw the complaint.
He said, “They submitted a complaint and, after some time, retracted it. No one threatened them inside the police station,” adding that “Counter-complaints have been filed against them by locals.”
Asked why the injured were detained at police station for long hours, Mukherjee claimed their families hadn’t turned up to take them home.
The officer refused to answer further questions over phone.
Elderly Woman Assaulted at Home
Another attendee, Sagari Konai, managed to escape the initial attack and returned to her home. However, a group of men allegedly went to her residence and assaulted her. She sustained a fracture in her finger due to the assault, the pastors added.
Ruidas alleged that the men forced Konai to perform sit-ups while holding her ears and apologise for practising Christianity. She was also allegedly coerced into participating in Hindu rituals at a nearby temple.
Konai is an elderly widow who lives with her daughter.
The attack has left the survivors deeply shaken. Ruidas said that he was still in pain from the injuries he sustained and that he was afraid to return to his home in Rayan village. He is currently staying with Bernerd.
Bernerd, meanwhile, said the incident had a profound impact on his young daughter, who witnessed the violence firsthand.
“She has never been exposed to such brutal hatred unfolding before her eyes. I wonder whether these people are animals,” he said.

She lost her sight - now she is fighting to make history for Africa
- Published
Rukayat Taiwo Suleimon only took up sambo this year, but the Nigerian has already secured her place in the history of the martial art.
The sport shares strong roots with judo and wrestling, combining techniques such as hip and leg throws to take opponents to the mat, where they can be pinned.
Originally developed by the Soviet Union's Red Army in the 1920s, it was officially recognised as a combat sport by USSR officials in 1938.
Competing at the 2026 World Sambo Cup in Armenia, Suleimon defeated Uzbekistan's Charos Ortikova in the final of the women's 54kg category to claim victory on her international debut.
It was the first time that women with visual impairments had been included at the competition.
"Being the first female blind sambist in the world to win the gold medal makes me great," the 32-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"This is my first time in sambo and God crowned my efforts."
Suleimon's achievement was part of a breakthrough moment for African women in the sport. She and compatriot Elizabeth Aseso, who competed in the 59kg category, were among the pioneering sambists representing the continent in Yerevan.
For Suleimon, her gold medal is a reward for the hard work over many years which has seen her move from athletics to judo and now to the top of the international sambo podium.
"I really benefit a lot from sports and, despite my blindness, I achieve a lot," she said.
"If I [were] not blind, I don't think I would be at this level. I believe I will achieve even more."
From darkness to double glory
Suleimon's journey to becoming a champion has been marked by hardship and a determination to rebuild her life.
After failed surgeries she lost her sight in 2009 because of glaucoma, an eye condition that damages the optic nerve and can lead to permanent loss of vision.
The change in her circumstances affected her relationships, leaving her feeling isolated at a time when she needed support the most.
"People looked down on me. I would just stay indoors and cry," she explained.
"So many friends left me. They stopped communicating with me."
Her life began to take a different direction after she attended a vocational training centre for blind people in Lagos.
Through a friend, she was introduced to a para-athletics coach who helped her discover her potential in sport.
Since 2011, Suleimon has won more than 20 national medals across sprint events (alongside guide runner Stephen Oyelakin), discus and shot put.
She then began practicing judo and sambo.
"Since I [started] sports I have seen that where there is life, there is hope," she said.
"What sighted people can do, a blind person can do even better.
"I'm proud of myself because it's not easy to be a champion in athletics and in sambo. I don't want to lose the glory."
Her achievements have also become a source of pride for her family. Her twin sister Ganiyat Kehinde Suleimon says her sibling's disability has never defined her worth.
"She is someone we are all proud of. She is now a champion," Ganiyat told BBC Sport Africa.
"Her disability did not make her a liability to us."
For Nigerian sambo coach Olugbenga Adekahunsi, Suleimon's performance in Yerevan offered a glimpse of what she can accomplish with the right support and continued development.
"I see a lot of quality in her because she is very strong and the confidence is there," he told BBC Sport Africa.
"I believe she will become a great sambist."
'No support' for para-athletes
Suleimon says the recognition she has earned internationally has not been matched by adequate "support" at home.
However, her victory is the latest milestone in Nigeria's growing presence in the discipline.
Two years ago Samuel Oladele Kekere became the first blind African to compete at the World Sambo Championships in Kazakhstan, and Sodiq Ajibade followed that with a bronze medal at last year's edition in Kyrgyzstan.
"Despite making Nigeria and the whole of Africa proud, there is nothing to show for it," Suleimon said.
Her concerns reflect wider complaints from Nigerian para-athletes about limited funding, inadequate specialist facilities and insufficient institutional backing, despite their achievements.
Sherif Hammed, vice-president of the Sambo Association of Nigeria, says a lack of resources can prevent talented athletes from reaching their full potential.
"When athletes do not have facilities to train, they cannot compete at the world level," he said.
"It is quite disheartening and heartbreaking.
"People with disabilities, particularly visually impaired athletes, sometimes feel that because of their challenges, they have no purpose in life."
For Suleimon, a Lagos State judo champion, the journey to training is also an issue. Travelling across the city and covering transport costs make maintaining a demanding schedule difficult.
"I leave home at 5.30am to make it to training on time," she explained.
"It takes a lot of money and sacrifice."
Suleimon was unable to follow up her World Cup success at the World Sambo Championships in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, where blind women were again scheduled to compete for the first time.
Beaten in Friday's opening round by Moldova's Ina Cernei, she still hopes her exploits on the global stage can inspire others.
"I want to encourage my fellow blind Africans to believe they can do it," said Suleimon. "And I want to make my country proud again."

Madurai Corporation cleared a total of 331 tonnes of garbage, till 6 p.m. on Monday, which was generated across the city on Deepavali day.
Along with the corporation cleanliness workers, volunteers from the Democratic Youth Federation of India, joined the mass cleaning drive early on Monday morning.
Mayor (in-charge), T. Nagarajan, and Corporation Commissioner, Gaurav Kumar, inaugurated the cleanliness drive.
The drive started on the Chithrai Streets, Aavani Moola Streets, Masi Streets, Veli Streets and Vilakkuthoon junction around Sri Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple where commercial establishments, especially textile showrooms, are located.
Besides, the workers focussed on spots at Teppakulam, Mattuthavani bus stand and Vaigai Bank Roads where garbage accumulation is higher.
Besides the usual vehicles used for transporting garbage, 11 earth movers, five bobcat machinery, nine tipper trucks and 42 tractors were involved in the exercise.
The work was expedited in the early hours so much so that 128.40 tonnes of garbage was cleared in the city by 12 noon. This was 33.32 tonnes of additional festival-time garbage removed when compared to 95.08 tonnes cleared during the same time in the last Deepavali season.
The workers had already removed 137 tonnes of garbage on Deepavali day (Sunday).
City Health Officer, Aravind Jothi, Assistant Health Officer, Abishek, DYFI district president, Selva, and secretary, Vel Deva, were present.

Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
- Published
Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.
"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."
Addressing reporters from the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.
Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict.
This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.
The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.
Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict.
Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.
"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.
Global oil prices, which have fallen sharply since the midterms, dipped further after Trump's comments.
On Tuesday afternoon in Asia, Brent crude was more than 1% lower at $91.50 (£52) while US-traded was down by 1.2% at $85.82.
Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.
In a post on X, the Qatari leader said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".
Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to the threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.
Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.
Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.
Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".
While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.

Quick Answer
To optimize WhatsApp privacy, hide your Last Seen, Online status, profile info, and status sharing under Settings > Privacy. Turn off read receipts, silence unknown callers, restrict group invites, disable link previews, and enable disappearing messages, passkeys, two-step verification, biometric locks, and end-to-end encrypted backups.
I don’t need to specifically tell you about WhatsApp’s popularity. It has billions of users worldwide, and it is the go-to messaging app for many people. Thanks to the network effect, most popular messaging apps haven’t replaced WhatsApp, even with better features and privacy.
One of the biggest reasons most people use WhatsApp, besides the fact that their friends or family are already on it, is that it is free to use. And since Meta owns it, free usually comes with a caveat. And that’s your data and how Meta tracks your WhatsApp chats. Although your chats are encrypted and Meta openly says it won’t use your data for advertising, you can talk to a friend on WhatsApp and still see relevant ads on other Meta platforms like Instagram instantly. Don’t you believe me? Just try it once.
Fortunately, WhatsApp also offers various privacy settings to keep your conversations private, prevent scams, and more. In this ultimate guide, we’ll cover all the privacy settings you need to enable on WhatsApp for maximum privacy. This guide includes all the methods, and I update it frequently and make changes if the features or flow change. Bookmark this page and revisit it anytime to keep your WhatsApp privacy settings up to date.
Table of Contents
WhatsApp Privacy Settings You Should Enable
Hide your Last Seen and Online status
If you care about your privacy and don’t want your people to know when you were online and when you last used the app, WhatsApp allows you to hide the last seen and online status completely
By default, WhatsApp shows the exact time when you last used the app and shows users when you are actually using the app
While these two features let others know when you use WhatsApp, they can also be a downside, especially if others are expecting an immediate reply when they see you online
Fortunately, WhatsApp lets you disable your last seen and completely hide your status. It also gives you more flexibility by letting you hide these from specific contacts, from your contacts, or disable them entirely for everyone.
Here is how to hide your last seen and online status on WhatsApp:
Open WhatsApp on your Android or iPhone and tap the You tab in the bottom-right corner, then tap Privacy.
Now scroll down and, under Who can see your personal info, tap Last seen and online. To hide it from everyone, select Nobody. To show it only to my contacts, select My contacts; to show it only to specific contacts, tap My contacts except.
Hide your profile photo, About, and Links from strangers
Like Last Seen and online status, WhatsApp also shows your profile picture and About to contacts. This also applies to contacts you have outside your network.
Fortunately, like Last Seen and Online Status, WhatsApp also lets you hide your profile photo and About info from strangers, specific contacts, or no one.
How to hide your profile and About from strangers
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, then tap on Privacy, and then tap on the Profile Picture option
Now you can hide your profile picture, About, and links. To hide it from everyone, set it to Nobody.
If you want to share with all your contacts, select My contacts. To share your profile picture only with specific contacts, tap My contacts except and select the contacts you want to hide your profile picture, About, and links from.
Control who can see and reshare your Status
WhatsApp’s status feature is slowly turning into Instagram Stories. You can now also reshare statuses on WhatsApp. However, unlike Last Seen, this feature is disabled by default.
If you accidentally enabled it and don’t want others to share your status, you can turn off sharing in the status privacy settings. From there, you can also turn off Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your WhatsApp status from being shared on other platforms.
How to turn off status sharing on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, and from here tap on the privacy option
Scroll down, tap Status, then turn off Allow sharing and set your status to be visible only to my contacts. You can also remove specific people by setting up exceptions for contacts, or you can share only with specific contacts. From the bottom, also disable Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your status from automatically sharing to Facebook and Instagram Stories.
Turn off read receipts
Even if you hide your online status and last seen on WhatsApp, read receipts can still show blue checkmarks when you read their messages. However, if you don’t want them to know you have read their messages and feel pressured to reply instantly, or if you want better privacy and to balance work and personal WhatsApp chats, you can disable read receipts.
Remember, if you disable it, you also cannot see whether they have read your messages. WhatsApp only shows grey ticks even if you read their messages.
Here is how to turn off read receipts on WhatsApp
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture. Scroll down and tap Privacy. Scroll down again and turn off Read Receipts.
Stop strangers from adding you to groups
Another feature that WhatsApp turns on by default is the ability to let your contacts add you to any groups. This includes the number you have temporarily shared with users you don’t know, and once you add it to the group, your number will be shared with everyone in that group, which is a total privacy nightmare.
Fortunately, WhatsApp allows you to stop random people from adding you to groups.
How to stop people from adding you to random groups
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, then tap on the privacy option
Scroll down and tap on Groups, then select who can add you to groups. However, WhatsApp doesn’t let you set nobody as an option, but you can still do it by selecting My contacts except and selecting all contacts.
Silence calls from unknown numbers
Since WhatsApp primarily requires your phone number to create an account, once your number is exposed, anyone can contact you on WhatsApp. This is why many of us often receive spam business calls.
However, you can silence unknown calls so that you won’t get notified of random spam calls.
How to silence unknown callers on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp, tap on your profile picture, and tap on the privacy option
Now scroll down, tap on Calls, and enable the Silence unknown callers option
Make new chats disappear automatically
WhatsApp now supports disappearing messages, which deletes chats from both the sender and receiver after a set time. WhatsApp allows you to enable disappearing messages for individual chats or for the entire WhatsApp for up to 90 days
This is especially useful if you don’t want the other person to save your chats.
Since WhatsApp keeps your messages forever even if you delete your own copy, the other person’s phone still has everything.
When you turn on disappearing messages, WhatsApp also prevents the other person from taking a screenshot and reminds you when they try to save a specific chat.
How to enable disappearing messages on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, then tap Privacy. From here, tap on Default message timer and select how many days you want to set for WhatsApp. You can select up to 90 days or even 24 hours.
If you want to turn on disappearing messages for individual chats, open the new chat and tap on the three-dot menu on the top right corner of the screen, select disappearing messages, and select the timer
Keep WhatsApp photos out of your gallery
By default, WhatsApp saves all photos you receive to your media gallery, including sensitive and personal ones. Even if you lock WhatsApp, anyone can see the photos you received by opening your phone gallery. This also uses your data to automatically download them and increases your storage usage.
WhatsApp allows you to turn off automatic media download and also lets you stop showing media directly from your photos app
How to stop WhatsApp from automatically saving media
First, you can turn off automatic media downloads. To do that, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then scroll down and tap Storage and data.
From there, scroll down and tap Media auto-download, then select all three: when you are using mobile data, when you are connected to Wi-Fi, and when roaming. Then disable all download options, including photos, audio, video, and documents. This prevents files from auto-downloading on Wi-Fi, mobile data, or while roaming.
How to stop WhatsApp from showing media in your device gallery
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, scroll down, tap Chats, then under Chat settings, disable Media visibility.
Turn on two-step verification with a password
WhatsApp also supports two-step verification to prevent your account from getting hacked. While WhatsApp sends a six-digit SMS code for verification, someone with access to that code can log in to your WhatsApp account. However, you can set a second verification method, such as a password, to prevent anyone from accessing your WhatsApp.
Here is how having two-factor authentication adds better security for your WhatsApp account.
Here is how to set two-step verification with a password on WhatsApp
First, open your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, tap on account option, and tap on Password
Now create a new password. Tap Create password and create a new password.
Once you add two-factor authentication, remember to add a recovery email. This is especially useful if you lose your network; your email acts as a secondary verification method, where WhatsApp sends a code to your email instead of sending a verification SMS.
Create a passkey for phishing-proof login
WhatsApp also added support for passkeys; if you’re not sure what a passkey is, we have explained it in a detailed guide.
Passkeys use your fingerprint or Face ID for authentication instead of depending on SMS or passwords. Setting up passkeys lets you log in to your WhatsApp account using your device ID, which is unique to you.
But it also comes with downsides: if someone else has registered a Face ID or fingerprint, they can also log in to your WhatsApp account, so keep note of it.
How to enable passkeys for your WhatsApp account
To enable passkeys, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then tap Account. From here, under the Login and Security section, tap on Passkeys. Then follow the on-screen instructions to create a passkey.
Turn on security notifications
Next, enable security notifications on your WhatsApp account so WhatsApp notifies you if someone switches phones, reinstalls WhatsApp, or changes linked devices. This could also mean someone else accessed their WhatsApp account and signed in on a new device. Turn on security notifications and confirm with the other person why the security key changed.
How to enable security notifications on WhatsApp

In an aside in the New York Times Cooking video I watched recently, where Melissa Clark made her lemony white bean soup with turkey and greens, the food reporter and recipe columnist invited viewers to leave a comment telling her what they do with the kale stems. It highlighted this sweet, funny relationship between a media brand’s personalities and its audience, a warm-casual vibe.
I am not among the multitudes in the Cooking section's commenter army, but a few days later I was very surprised to see some of them in open revolt. I was even more surprised to see why: In an iOS-only beta, the Times is now using AI to allow subscribers to modify recipes.
Below the article announcing the change on October 23, commenters loudly aired their grievances, threatening to cancel subscriptions, asking who wanted this, and how to turn it off.
After four days and 172 almost exclusively angry comments, commenting for the story was turned off.
The Times doesn't share Cooking's subscriber numbers, but NYT executive communications director Jordan Cohen said the site and app were visited 514 million times in 2025, and its YouTube channel has over 1.4 million subscribers. Reading over the section's AI plans and thinking about how many bungled attempts I'd seen to mush technology into places where it doesn't need to be in the kitchen, I guessed that I would side with the commenters. Then I tried the new AI feature, and found that it worked surprisingly well.
My writing for WIRED over the past decade has shown me again and again that adding tech to a kitchen product is risky at best. I've repeatedly watched companies try and fail: Bluetooth connections for all the appliances, apps that lean too heavily on crummy recipes, toasters with optical sensors or touchscreens that still couldn't toast particularly well. Just about anything that was part of the "smart kitchen" tended not to be very smart at all.
Developing dependable, delicious recipes is hard, expensive work that can require a whole staff. Yet skimping can hurt the brand. Two notable companies with a deep bench—The New York Times Cooking and America's Test Kitchen—are cooking content makers. Recipes, which is to say delicious, high-quality, tested recipes, are what they do.
Since AI is often a lousy chef, giving it a role in the presentation of NYT's gold mine of content is a big risk.
Earlier this year, the Times allowed AI to help with a recipe-scaling feature (modifying ingredient quantities so "serves 4" turns into "serves 6") and converting from imperial measurements to metric—cups, tablespoons, and Fahrenheit to grams, milliliters, and Celsius. Now, in the iOS-only beta, a "customize this recipe" field appears just above the ingredient list.
If you want to make banana bread but tell it you don't have a loaf pan, it'll ask you what kind of pans you do have, then modify the recipe to suit. All the changes throughout the recipe are noted in a visible red-orange text. Over several days of testing, I saw how you can do relatively simple things like swap ground pork for ground beef, or make more complicated demands like asking it to tailor things to your dietary needs. The modifications it makes are very visible throughout the recipe. If you ask it for something too out there—like turning Eric Kim's gochujang buttered noodles into a cookie—it gives you a "hard redirect" and points you to a better-suited recipe, which in this case is Kim's gochujang caramel cookies.
"We put a lot of effort into trying to tell you when not to do something if it's no longer in the spirit of the recipe," says Camilla Velasquez, the general manager of NYT Cooking.
For its recommendations, the LLM looks at the recipe itself, the Times’ ingredient substitution guide, user comments, and then what it calls AI "drawing on our expertise," in that order. Velasquez says the AI should be a helper, not the main act, noting, "You shouldn't be chatting with it."
She explains that when the Times built the AI functionality, recipe editors helped create the original rule set, then evaluated how it worked at the end.
When I ask what this means for the jobs of 60 editors, writers, video journalists, and other employees—the team that creates the recipes people use and curates the vibe readers relate to—Velasquez stresses that NYT Cooking has been "hiring more than ever" and that it has "zero intention of publishing fewer recipes."
So far, she says people are mainly using it for ingredient and equipment substitutions, along with adjusting recipes for dietary needs. "Some people use the chatbot to scale, or they'll scale to match an ingredient," giving the example of someone who had only one cup of oil for a recipe that needed more.
As a food writer whose career has taken some substantial turns due to AI recently, I wouldn't say I've been clamoring for this, but I find the Times’ measured approach works pretty well.
I started testing it out by making chicken and dumplings using a five-star Alison Roman recipe with more than 6,000 ratings. I asked the AI tool to swap out bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs for boneless, skinless breasts. It thought about it for a moment—"simmering" in AI Cooking patois—and then offered up "Chicken Breast and Dumplings," with the "breast" in the title rendered in the red-orange color that indicates a modification. Just below the title, it said it was "Joseph's version made with AI. Not tested or endorsed by the original recipe's creators." Along with those visible changes, I could also toggle back and forth between my version and the original.
Once I started cooking, things went smoothly. I'm a recipe follower, not an improviser, and the Times’ recipes are easy to follow. The modifications were too. I was also impressed by how the app flagged that the chicken breast simmering time would be reduced because it cooks faster than thighs, and since they don't render as much fat as skin-on thighs do, it added some butter to the roux. These changes were incorporated into the right places in the recipe.
It all made sense except for one bit. It suggested the shredded, cooked breast go back into the pot for about another 30 minutes while the sauce thickens and the dumplings cook. I saw this coming and, well, I wasn't going to do that to my dinner. I put a handful of shredded meat in as directed so I could see what happened and reserved the rest. The shredded bits that were in for that extra half hour weren’t bad per se, but their texture was notably less succulent than what I'd reserved and way less than thighs would be.
This was the largest issue I encountered in all of my testing. If I had been the creator of the Times' original recipe, I'm not sure how I'd feel about the option to use a breast instead of thighs, which is not unheard of, but not very common in classic chicken and dumpling recipes. Perhaps it's something that could be fine-tuned or simply not offered as an option.
From there, it was fairly smooth sailing. I had it turn a Francis Lam roasted mushroom and broccoli grain bowl into a roasted mushroom, cauliflower, and squash grain bowl. The crucifer crisscross was an easy one-to-one, but I also told it to add a pound of delicata squash. It had me slice the squash into half moons so everything would finish at the same time, then upped the total amount of olive oil. Lam's poetic voice was preserved in both versions of the recipe, telling you to heat the olive oil "until it slips around the pan like water" before adding beaten eggs for festive dish-topping egg ribbons. My buddy Dave had come by for cribbage night, and this made for an enjoyable, healthy, pregame dinner before he went on to skunk me twice.
I'd been curious how it would handle batters, and it capably transformed Yewande Komolafe’s Toasted Sesame and Scallion Waffles into a yeasted version, which, unlike the original, gets an overnight in the fridge, letting the active dry yeast get bubbly and add an appealing tang.
A friend suggested Colu Henry's pasta and chickpea stew. I swapped canned diced tomatoes I had in my pantry for whole, and asked it to "add more vegetables." It gave options in line with the recipe—carrots, celery, onion, zucchini, mushrooms, and extra greens—then put what I chose into the right spots throughout the procedure so everything went in at the right time. It made for a healthy, hearty dinner.
Having been to the Portland Fermentation Festival recently and wanting guidance on incorporating a few extra ingredients, particularly garlic, into my sauerkraut, I used the AI to modify Lidey Heuck's original, saying "add carrots, garlic, and kale," which it suggested grating, thin slicing, and mincing, respectively, all in the right-feeling proportions. It also added more salt, since I was making more kraut. The big jar is sitting next to me as I type, and while it's several days from being ready, a sniff test tells me it's on its way to being a good batch.
Finally, I turned Sue Li's peanut noodles with spicy tofu into peanut udon with tofu, whitefish, and cucumber. I started by asking it to make the original less spicy, add veggies, and "keep the tofu," but add some good-looking rockfish I found at the grocery store. Impressively, since the fish was an add-on, it had me cook it, then set it aside and wipe out the pan (!) before cooking the tofu. Since I swapped udon for the original bucatini, it customized the noodle-cooking guidance, too.
It seems pretty natural that the Cooking section ran into some resistance when launching this feature. The NYT employs some of the best recipe creators in the business. Using AI to help us make substitutions is helpful, and the way the app integrates those changes into the recipes is impressive, but this tinkering with the original is essentially a subtractive process. How many of us are going to make substitutions and land on something better than Melissa Clark, Yewande Komolafe, or Francis Lam set out to make by design?
Instead, it's saving us a trip to the store, or helping us use something we have on hand, or making it gluten-free, serving as a good and rare example of how you can use technology to make a product incrementally better.
It also sounds like the commenters’ concerns have been heard. Velasquez let me know right away when we spoke that people will be able to hide the AI feature in the app if they want. The Times is also keeping the whole thing in iOS-only beta for now, and not saying when it would be available on other platforms.
That bond that you can see between the Cooking team and its users is a pretty sweet thing. Deep down, I'm guessing the upset Cooking commenters felt worried they were going to lose some of that human connection. I hope it never goes away.

Two of the top lawmakers backing the Pentagon’s Golden Dome missile defense shield are among the wave of Republicans leaving Congress in the coming Democratic takeover, raising questions about the future of President Donald Trump’s signature second-term defense initiative.
The shakeup on Capitol Hill comes after military officials signaled in recent months that they might backpedal from one element Trump asked for in Golden Dome: the capability to shoot down missiles in their initial boost phase shortly after launch.
The Golden Dome has escaped serious congressional scrutiny since Trump announced the program in January 2025, one week into his second term in the White House. That lack of scrutiny will change as Democrats take responsibility for writing the Pentagon’s budget, introduce limits on funding, and put forth bills to strip out Golden Dome’s most controversial component and give the program a new name.
That’s the opinion of a half-dozen current and former officials in industry and government. Ars spoke with sources before and after last week’s congressional elections to get a sense of how a new Democratic Congress might make its imprint on missile defense.
It’s important to know that much of what the Trump administration calls “Golden Dome” was already in development (or in some cases, operational) when Trump signed the executive order outlining the initiative 22 months ago. Trump’s order created a new program to consolidate the Pentagon’s existing missile defense efforts, accelerate work already underway on new Ground-Based Interceptors (GBIs), and deploy a new layer of orbiting sensors and Space-Based Interceptors (SBIs) to defend the US homeland against both traditional ballistic missiles and new emerging threats like drones and hypersonic weapons.
Ramming it through
The Golden Dome was immediately politicized. The first tranche of its funding—approximately $24 billion—was part of Trump’s so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill,” along with some of the White House’s other contentious policy priorities. The bill passed Congress on a party-line vote. This meant the budget for Golden Dome was not part of the normal military budgeting process in Congress, which usually involves both parties. Instead, it passed Congress through a controversial shortcut known as reconciliation.
Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said in a September hearing that the White House’s decision to link Golden Dome’s first tranche of funding to a partisan reconciliation bill was unnecessary. “This should have been on a bipartisan basis,” Rounds said. Indeed, Capitol Hill Republicans refused the Trump administration’s effort to add $350 billion to the Pentagon’s budget this year through a similar reconciliation mechanism.
Lawmakers also formed an all-Republican “Golden Dome Caucus” soon after the unveiling of Golden Dome. Seven House members of the caucus either lost their reelection bids or did not run for reelection at all in the 2026 midterms. These include the caucus’s co-chair, Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colo.), and the chair of the House subcommittee overseeing Golden Dome, Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.). Both are among the Golden Dome’s biggest cheerleaders in Congress.
The Democratic ranking member of the House Subcommittee on Strategic Forces, Rep. Scott Moulton (D-Mass.), is retiring from Congress. That leaves Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) as the next-senior Democrat on the subcommittee, with a path to becoming chairman when the new Congress convenes in January. In remarks earlier this year, he called Golden Dome a “massive, extraordinarily expensive, and ultimately inadequate defensive system.”
John Plumb, then-assistant secretary of defense for space policy, testifies before a subcommittee of the House Armed Services Committee on March 30, 2023.
Credit:
Alex Wong/Getty Images
John Plumb, then-assistant secretary of defense for space policy, testifies before a subcommittee of the House Armed Services Committee on March 30, 2023.
Credit:
Alex Wong/Getty Images
“When you use the words Golden Dome, now it’s political, and when you politicize national security, you get a political response, so it is damaging,” said John Plumb, who supervised military space policy for the Biden administration, in a panel discussion at the CyberSat conference this week.
The Trump administration projects Golden Dome will cost $185 billion over the next 10 years, a figure that’s hard to verify with the scarce information military officials have released about how the system will work.
Other cost estimates are significantly higher. The Congressional Budget Office concluded that a national missile defense system meeting the requirements set out in Trump’s executive order would cost about $1.2 trillion. The American Enterprise Institute released a report last year with a menu of potential Golden Dome architectures, ranging from a quarter-trillion dollars (without SBIs) to $3.6 trillion at the high end.
Pentagon officials chafe at these numbers, claiming they do not take into account the military’s assumptions for low-cost launches and mass-produced satellite networks.
The shiny new thing
The military envisions at least hundreds, and perhaps thousands, of Space-Based Interceptors in the uppermost layer of Golden Dome. These interceptors would loiter in orbit to wait for a missile attack. SBIs have never been placed into orbit before, despite decades of research and development. The idea has been around at least since the 1980s, when former President Ronald Reagan pushed the Strategic Defense Initiative, or “Star Wars,” weapons program.
“The most ambitious element of Golden Dome is the Space-Based Interceptor layer, and that is going to face significant technical challenges,” said Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), in a congressional hearing earlier this year.
“The cost, the physics, the likely reliability, in my view, do not support a full-scale space-based intercept architecture,” said Kelly, a former Navy combat pilot and astronaut. “This means that we could spend more than a trillion dollars and end up with a system that’s not going to work, and it’s not going to meaningfully improve our security.”
Some critics call out Golden Dome’s potential negative impact on global stability, fearing it could spark an arms race driving the world’s other nuclear powers to expand their arsenals. “It motivates the other side to just build more missiles because the easiest way to overcome a defense like that is just to buy more,” said Frank Kendall, who served as secretary of the Air Force in the Biden administration.
Others point to the risks of weaponizing space—a similar argument used against the Reagan-era Star Wars program. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink lifted that taboo in September with the first public disclosure that the US Space Force already has weapons in orbit.
A ground-based Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptor is launched from the Reagan Test Site, Kwajalein Atoll in the Republic of the Marshall Islands, on a flight test on August 30, 2019. THAAD interceptors are currently operational, but they’re expensive, estimated to cost about $13 million per shot.
Credit:
Missile Defense Agency
A ground-based Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptor is launched from the Reagan Test Site, Kwajalein Atoll in the Republic of the Marshall Islands, on a flight test on August 30, 2019. THAAD interceptors are currently operational, but they’re expensive, estimated to cost about $13 million per shot.
Credit:
Missile Defense Agency
But there’s more to the story than SBIs. The satellites and radars that detect and track missile launches are either in use today or were already in development during previous administrations. The same goes for Ground-Based Interceptors, which have been deployed for decades to take out missiles as they approach their targets. Under President Biden, the Pentagon’s Missile Defense Agency awarded Lockheed Martin a $17 billion contract to develop a next-generation Ground-Based Interceptor to defend against more sophisticated missile threats.
Optimism meets skepticism
The $24 billion Congress approved for Golden Dome last year was a one-time allocation for fiscal year 2026, which ended on October 1. The program’s funding dried up last month because the government is currently operating under a continuing resolution—an extension of last year’s regular military budget, which, of course, did not include the $24 billion Golden Dome infusion routed through reconciliation. The preliminary funding bills in the House and Senate for fiscal year 2027, if passed as-is, would provide only a fraction of the more than $17 billion the Trump administration requested for Golden Dome in this budget cycle.
That’s because the Trump administration again separated a significant part of its record $1.5 trillion topline military budget request into a reconciliation package outside of the normal congressional appropriations process. The supplemental $350 billion funding request—which included funds for Golden Dome—went nowhere in the Republican-controlled Congress. And it won’t happen when Democrats take the gavels next year, either.
It’s impossible to judge the realism of the Pentagon’s aim to get a first draft of Golden Dome up and running by the end 0f 2028, before the end of Trump’s presidency, because so much of the system is classified—but skepticism is the safer bet. Military officials have said little about Golden Dome’s design, architecture, or concept of operations, citing a national security imperative for secrecy.
One thing we do know is that a homeland defense shield like Golden Dome will need international partners to host radar sensors, ground stations, and missile batteries. Canada is an obvious target for such a partnership, and a fully deployed Golden Dome would notionally provide protection over all of North America.
However, this part of the program is off to a slow start. Michael Guetlein, the four-star Space Force general in charge of Golden Dome development, said earlier this year that tariffs—a core Trump administration policy—were limiting his interactions with foreign governments.
Gen. Michael Guetlein, direct report program manager for Golden Dome for America in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, appears before the House Armed Services Strategic Forces subcommittee on April 15, 2026, in Washington, DC.
Credit:
Luke Johnson/Getty Images
Gen. Michael Guetlein, direct report program manager for Golden Dome for America in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, appears before the House Armed Services Strategic Forces subcommittee on April 15, 2026, in Washington, DC.
Credit:
Luke Johnson/Getty Images
The hardest problem
So what can we expect when the next Congress convenes with Democratic majorities in January? The consensus among the experts Ars interviewed is that military leaders will still push for new options in missile defense, a need they say is underscored by their experience during the US war with Iran and Russia’s persistent missile strikes on Ukraine.
Modern missiles and drones can easily dodge existing defense systems. The stark expense of existing Western interceptors compared to the cost of Iranian missiles and drones can make defenders think twice about whether to shoot or keep their powder dry for a future attack.
“I feel like the entire effort would benefit from a better problem statement,” one former military space official told Ars. “Why do we think we need something that we don’t currently have? What’s changed? What’s different? What is it?”
This official offered some answers to these questions: “We are not in the 1970s or 1980s anymore, where it was us and the Soviet Union. The vast share of strategic threats to us were strategic ballistic missiles that we could see coming. That’s how things used to be.”
“Today’s environment is different,” he continued. “You have a host of strategic threats that are making classic ballistic missiles shrink in share. You’ve got hypersonic weapons. You’ve got endo-atmospheric hypersonic vehicles. You have increasingly accurate and harder to detect cruise missiles. It’s no longer just Russia. It’s China now, and to a lesser extent, North Korea and Iran.”
These new missile threats and the ubiquity of one-way attack drones make US and allied bases more susceptible to attack, the official said.
“What do we do about it? Do we just build more Mutually Assured Destruction platforms, or is there something else we can do? I think that’s what gets you to maybe we should look at ways to at least interfere with a potential attack against us.”
But some parts of Golden Dome, if followed to the letter of Trump’s executive order, simply may not work, at least at the scale required for global coverage, the official told Ars. One of them is a requirement to develop SBIs that can destroy enemy missiles during their boost phase soon after launch. This is in contrast to midcourse intercept in space or terminal intercept as the missile homes in on its target.
“The boost-phase intercept is a much bigger challenge,” the former military official said. “I’m probably going to have to have an interceptor that can survive reentry, track through reentry, and hit something while it’s still in the atmosphere. Hitting something in midcourse, as it’s left the atmosphere and is in space is just an easier problem… The original executive order talked about boost-phase intercept, and I was always skeptical about that one.”
An SBI aimed at a boost-phase ballistic missile would have to look down toward the Earth, not up toward space. The interceptor would have to distinguish the missile it’s tracking against the background of Earth, with clouds, cities, land, and water. It’s much easier to do that against the cold blackness of space. There are some benefits to a boost-phase intercept. For example, the ballistic missile is traveling slower soon after launch, and you might have another shot to intercept it if you miss.
The window for intercepting a missile in boost phase is also exceptionally narrow. The time from a launch detection to a shoot-down decision might be less than a minute, and a commander charged with making a “kill decision” would likely want more time to understand what’s happening before pulling the trigger on an interceptor.
“When does the person who has the authority for weapons engagement release the weapon? If your answer is it’s all automated, that’s interesting, but it’s also a little scary,” the former military official said. “Now I’m going to explain to the president why you just killed three taikonauts (Chinese astronauts) coming off a launch pad because no human was there. If you do need a human to say, ‘OK, I authorize release of the weapon,’ then that’s a time gap.”
Guetlein, the man in charge of Golden Dome, has acknowledged this challenge.
“I do believe that the technology exists to get after that threat today, and we believe we can solve it, but… can I do it at scale, and can I do it affordably? That’s going to be the huge challenge for boost-phase intercept,” Guetlein told lawmakers in an April hearing. “I will tell you, because we are so focused on affordability, if we cannot do it affordably, we will not go into production.”

Credit:
German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), 2025/CC BY 4.0
This infographic produced by the German Institute for International and Security Affairs illustrates the elements of a space-based missile defense system.
Credit:
German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), 2025/CC BY 4.0
There are other ways to take down missiles if engineers can’t close the case for boost-phase intercept, Guetlein said. “If boost-phase intercept from space is not affordable and [doesn’t] scale well, we will not produce it because we have other options to get after it.”
If proven feasible, directed-energy weapons using microwave or laser beams would provide US forces near-endless “magazine depth” in responding to massive salvos of missiles and drones, eschewing the need for “kinetic” SBIs for missile defense. Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said in a hearing earlier this year that the Space Force should spend more on directed-energy research than on space-based kinetic kill vehicles.
Plumb, the former Biden military space policy chief, pointed to bipartisan support for the Pentagon’s existing missile defense programs, along with new initiatives to improve tracking hypersonic missiles. “I think any administration, Republican or Democrat, is going to continue to improve missile defenses for the US, 100 percent,” he said, adding that it is “probably unlikely” that SBIs survive the coming cull.
So what do the people actually building Golden Dome think? Their answer is similar. Some missile defense priorities will survive, but maybe with a new name.
The name Golden Dome is a “brand,” said Dylan Taylor, chairman and CEO of Voyager Technologies, which works with Anduril on SBIs. “It’s a proxy for layers of a protective onion, if you will, and there are elements of what is being called Golden Dome, where the technology is very advanced, and it works. The systems work. They’re more functional than I think people have reported on or have indicated.”
“Golden Dome is a lot more than SBIs,” said another executive at a space company working on the project. “It’s one layer and element. We believe that there’s bipartisan support for this capability because it is a required capability for national security. The question is whether it can be achieved at a price that makes it executable and palatable. The technical aspect of this closes, and there’s just a question about scalability and cost.”
The executive told Ars that newer, smaller space companies can do the job for less money than the Pentagon’s legacy contractors. Many companies are spending private capital on Golden Dome-related research and development with the promise of future Pentagon business. Military leaders have added stops on Wall Street and with venture capital firms to their usual tours of bases, command centers, and test ranges.
“There’s real hardware being built by all the players,” the official said, suggesting optimism about fielding a working preliminary version of Golden Dome by 2028. “From us, on our execution to date, we’ve conducted engine tests and thermal tests and communications tests.
“My fiduciary responsibility is to turn our investment into these critical technologies into future value, and I wouldn’t have made that call had I not been comfortable with the survivability of the program, assuming we can achieve the technical and financial targets, which we’ve convinced ourselves we can,” the official said.
Rocket Lab is another company with business ties to Golden Dome. The company’s founder and CEO, Peter Beck, told Ars he was convinced missile defense will remain a priority no matter who controls Congress or the White House.
“Is it a national security imperative that we go to the Moon? Probably not. Is it a national security imperative that we can protect the nation from incoming missile threats? Yes,” Beck said. “With these sorts of things, I’d say it’s what shape and scale they are, not whether they survive.”
“There are elements of Golden Dome that I don’t think are going to be politically vulnerable, and there will be other parts of Golden Dome that, of course, will be,” Taylor said. “The point I want to emphasize is people who say, ‘Well, Golden Dome is dead; the whole thing is dead,’ they don’t necessarily understand that there are four or five or six layers to the system, and some are vulnerable and some are not.”
Voyager’s expertise for missile defense is in advanced propulsion, and Taylor said those technologies are relevant for a range of systems, not just Golden Dome.
“There’s no doubt that whatever it’s going to be called, it won’t be called Golden Dome, and there will definitely be machinations in the system, but it won’t be a ‘throw the baby out with the bath water’ approach,” Taylor said. “Given the risk profile, I don’t see that happening.”

In a Senate hearing in September, Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, proposed the idea of a name change as one option to “depoliticize” the missile defense issue.
“It is no secret that the ‘Golden Dome’ moniker has contributed to political polarization around the effort,” Karako said in his testimony. “Several options exist to depolarize and depoliticize the effort. It belongs to Congress to name or rename executive departments—witness the pending proposal to rename the Department of Defense as the Department of War. Congress likewise has legislative power to rename the Golden Dome initiative in a future national defense authorization act.”
“There are things in the program that make sense,” said Sen. Kelly, who serves on the Senate Subcommittee for Strategic Forces. These include new capabilities for “detecting launches,” he said. “The Space-Based Interceptor part is really, really hard, and the physics clearly favors the offense,” Kelly said. “We could go down this road, spend hundreds of billions of dollars, and not get any return on that investment, and missile defense is too important to pursue this just based on aspiration alone.”
Kathy Warden, the CEO of Northrop Grumman, acknowledged last year that with SBIs, “more invention is required than other parts of the [Golden Dome] architecture.”
The most recent trends in warfare, as seen in the Middle East and Ukraine, highlight the need for cheaper, mass-produced countermeasures to use against massive drone and missile attacks. In other words, it requires magazine depth, as some military commanders like to say. Democrats seem likely to conclude that the path to magazine depth does not include SBIs.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

అమెరికాలోని న్యూయార్క్ ఎయిర్పోర్ట్లో ఇమ్మిగ్రేషన్ అధికారులకు ఒక మహిళ పట్టుబడిందని, ఆమె తన దేశం పేరు “టొరెంజో” అని చెప్పిందని, అసలు ఉనికిలో లేని ఈ దేశం పేరుతోనే ఆమె పాస్పోర్ట్ కూడా కలిగి ఉందని పేర్కొంటూ ఒక వీడియో సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారమవుతోంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: న్యూయార్క్ ఎయిర్పోర్ట్లో ప్రపంచంలో ఉనికిలోనే లేని “టొరెంజో” అనే దేశం నుండి వచ్చిన ఒక ప్రయాణికురాలిని చూపుతున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ ప్రచారం పూర్తిగా కల్పితం, అసలు ఇలాంటి ఘటన జరిగినట్లు ఆధారాలు లేవు. వైరల్ వీడియో వాస్తవానికి 2004లో ప్రసారమైన ‘ఎయిర్లైన్’ అనే అమెరికన్ రియాలిటీ టీవీ సిరీస్లోని ఒక దృశ్యం. ఫుటేజ్లో లాస్ ఏంజెలెస్కు ప్రయాణించిన ఒక అరబిక్ మాట్లాడే వృద్ధురాలిని చూపించారు తప్ప, “టొరెంజో” అనే ప్రస్తావన ఎక్కడా లేదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, ఈ విషయం గురించి ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతకగా, ఇటువంటి ఘటన జరిగినట్లు ఎటువంటి విశ్వసనీయ వార్తా కథనాలు లభించలేదు. ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దీనికి సంబంధించిన పూర్తి వీడియోను (ఆర్కైవ్ 1, ఆర్కైవ్ 2) A&E యూట్యూబ్ ఛానెల్లో 08 నవంబర్ 2024న “Airline: Best Full Episodes of 2024 MARATHON | A&E” అనే శీర్షికతో అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాము.ప్రస్తుతం ఈ వీడియో ప్రైవేట్ చేయబడింది.
దీని గురించి మరింత పరిశోధించగా, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియో వాస్తవానికి 2004-2005 మధ్య A&Eలో ప్రసారమైన ‘ఎయిర్లైన్’ అనే అమెరికన్ రియాలిటీ టీవీ సిరీస్లోని ఒక దృశ్యమని తేలింది. ఇది ప్రయాణికులతో సౌత్వెస్ట్ ఎయిర్లైన్స్ సిబ్బంది జరిపే రోజువారీ సంభాషణలను చూపుతుంది. వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఉన్న దృశ్యాలు, ఈ యూట్యూబ్ వీడియోలోని మొదటి ఎపిసోడ్లో 22వ నిమిషం వద్ద ప్రారంభమవుతాయి. ఈ దృశ్యాలు బాల్టిమోర్ నుండి లాస్ ఏంజెలెస్కు ప్రయాణించిన, ఆంగ్లం రాని ఒక వృద్ధురాలిని చూపుతాయి.
ఈ వీడియోలో, ఆమె పాస్పోర్ట్ ఇంగ్లీషులో లేదని గమనించిన ఒక ఎయిర్లైన్ ఉద్యోగి, “సౌదీ అరేబియా, వాళ్ళు అరబిక్ మాట్లాడతారు కదా?” అని చెబుతూ ఆమెను అరబిక్ మాట్లాడే వ్యక్తిగా గుర్తిస్తారు. ఇందులో ఎక్కడా కూడా “టొరెంజో” అనే ప్రదేశం ప్రస్తావనే లేదు. ఆ తర్వాత సిబ్బంది ఆమెను అరబిక్ మాట్లాడే మరో ఉద్యోగితో మాట్లాడిస్తారు, చివరకు ఆమెను తీసుకెళ్లడానికి ఆమె మేనల్లుడు ఎయిర్పోర్ట్కు వస్తారు.
దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియోలో చెప్పిన విషయాలు నిజం కాదని, వాస్తవానికి ఆ ఫుటేజ్ ఒక టెలివిజన్ సిరీస్కు చెందినదని నిర్ధారించవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, ఉనికిలో లేని “టొరెంజో” దేశం నుండి ఒక మహిళ వచ్చిందంటూ, ఒక అమెరికన్ టెలివిజన్ సిరీస్కు చెందిన దృశ్యాలను తప్పుగా ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారు.

After Michigan voters elected Democrat Abdul El-Sayed as senator in November 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that he had failed the background check required for classified Senate briefings.
One X user named Jonathan Gregory who shared the claim wrote that El-Sayed's alleged failure would exclude him from some meetings as a senator. The user wrote:
Abdul El Sayed has failed the background check required for classified Senate briefings. The denial blocks him from any session that involves sensitive national security information. Officials who conduct the clearances reported that the review did not meet the standards necessary for access to restricted materials. The failure leaves open the question of what specific issues prevented approval.
Senators who receive classified briefings must clear the same process before they can attend. El Sayed's rejection means he cannot participate in those meetings. The decision places him outside the normal flow of information that other members receive. Americans who expect every senator to qualify for the same briefings now see one individual excluded by the clearance system.
(@TrumpNews_Baby, accessed via X)
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to verify whether it was true.
The claim was false. El-Sayed could not have "failed" a background check "required for classified Senate briefings" because no such background check exists.
Congress members, including senators, are not required to pass a background check to gain security clearance and access classified material, according to a Congressional Research Service "Frequently Asked Questions" report about security clearances from 2023.
The U.S. Constitution, which lays out the requirements for senators, does not include a requirement for them to pass a background check to access classified information. According to Constitution Annotated, the Library of Congress' legal analysis and interpretation of the Constitution, the document has never allowed for changes to the requirements for a senator because that would undermine the legislative branch's investigative powers.
Additionally, federal law exempts members of Congress, including senators, from legislation that governs background checks and security clearances.
The false rumor may have originated as satire. Snopes previously linked another false claim about election fraud to Jonathan Gregory, who shared the first instance of the rumor about El-Sayed that we identified on X. Gregory labels himself as a comedian on his Facebook page, though his Instagram and X accounts don't display such a label. None of Gregory's profiles specifically mention the word "satire," though he has previously used the term near the very end of some of his posts — potentially as a way of hinting at the truth about his content.
We've published fact checks about other matters originating from Gregory's social media accounts, all of which involved false claims.
We contacted El-Sayed's campaign to ask if he had ever applied for, been granted or denied government security clearance before becoming a senator-elect. We also asked the national intelligence director's office whether it had ever granted or denied security clearance to El-Sayed in the past. We await replies to our questions.
Congress investigative powers allow members access to classified information
Members of Congress are implicitly allowed to access classified information because the U.S. Constitution gives the legislative branch investigative powers to inform laws and ensure they are being carried out. In practice, carrying out these investigations can mean that members of Congress need to access classified material, and the Information Security Oversight Office, which is responsible for the policy and oversight of the U.S. government's security classification system, wrote in 2001 that this is generally allowed (PDF Page 66).
It is important to note, however, that though El-Sayed and any other member of Congress bypass the normal procedure for getting security clearance, that does not give them unlimited access to classified information.
For example, the ISOO wrote in 2001 that though members of Congress were exempt from background checks and filling out the government's classified information nondisclosure agreement, they were not exempt from the "'need-to-know' requirement" (PDF Page 66).
For example, the office wrote (PDF Page 66) that members of Congress, "are not inherently authorized to receive all classified information, but agencies provide access as is necessary for Congress to perform its legislative functions."
Subject to election certification by state officials, the 120th Congress, which will include El-Sayed as one of two senators from Michigan, will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027.
For further reading, Snopes frequently investigates rumors relating to El-Sayed.

A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.
The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.
"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen, a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."
The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.
"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.
Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.
"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.
Researchers have been searching for a drug to lower Lp(a)
Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).
So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).
The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.
"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence.
Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.
In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.
What went wrong?
The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.
"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz, a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."
Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.
It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.
There could be other reasons for why the study failed.
"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal, a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.
"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron, a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.
The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.
Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.
It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.
Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.
"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson, a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."

Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.
The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.
This isn’t really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user’s local machine (assuming that machine doesn’t become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore list, which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.
But that .gitignore setting isn’t reflected at the repo level, meaning the sensitive file can be uploaded accidentally if a repo is cloned to another machine or a folder becomes a repo later, for instance. In many cases, Claude Code itself will commit changes to the settings file without the user’s input, Apiiro writes.
Apiiro’s researchers found over 100,000 cases where Claude Code’s local settings file had been uploaded to a public GitHub repository. Of these, only about 1,100 from 63 different organizations contained secrets such as public API tokens, database passwords, or private keys. Even after these files are discovered and removed from a repository, the secrets can persist in forks of the original project if a GitHub user isn’t careful.

NASA has unveiled a new experimental vehicle, the X-70 Fractal, although many of its features remain a mystery. The agency describes it as a research platform designed to conduct advanced aeronautical tests, but so far it has released only computer-generated images and some technical specifications regarding its capabilities.
Despite the secrecy, it is possible to get some idea of what the new vehicle is like. First of all, it’s not a spacecraft, meaning it is not designed to reach Earth’s orbit or operate outside the atmosphere. However, this crewed, subsonic aircraft is capable of flying far above commercial jets, reaching altitudes over 45,000 feet, well into the stratosphere. Other specs released include the plane’s max speed of Mach 0.75—about 575 miles per hour—and that it can travel nearly 1,700 miles in a single flight.
According to NASA, the X-70 Fractal will enable research into maneuver capabilities never before demonstrated in crewed aircraft, although the agency has not specified what types of maneuvers it intends to perform. The plane will also be capable of carrying up to one ton of experimental equipment and is expected to make its first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years.
One of the key features of the craft will be its modular design, allowing for the rapid installation and replacement of experimental equipment both inside and outside the aircraft. This is largely why it is referred to as an “experimental platform.” It will also feature reconfigurable flight control systems so that NASA can study different ways of steering an aircraft without having to develop a separate platform for each research project.
Although NASA is best known for its space missions, it’s long been dedicated to aeronautical research. That’s what the first A stands for. The agency also traces its origins to the creation of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, which was founded in 1915 and was folded into the newly formed NASA in 1958.
Since then, the space agency has developed numerous experimental aircraft to test technologies that range from supersonic flight and propulsion systems to new aerodynamic configurations. Not all of these prototypes go on to become operational aircraft, but the knowledge gained contributes to the development of future commercial and military aircraft as well as space vehicles.
Among its most recent projects is the X-59, developed in collaboration with aerospace and defense company Lockheed Martin to investigate ways to reduce the noise produced by supersonic aircraft. The X-70 Fractal will join this tradition of pioneers in the sky.
The development of these technologies also has a strategic dimension. In its budget documents for 2027, NASA identifies aeronautical research as a tool for maintaining US technological leadership in the face of growing international competition. The agency also plans to collaborate with the Department of Defense to advance new flight capabilities, although it has not yet announced any military applications for the X-70 Fractal.
During the unveiling of the new aircraft, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman noted that the project represents only one part of a new era for federal aeronautical research and hinted that more announcements are coming. For now, the agency has not provided details on what those initiatives might be, nor has it specified when it will release more information about the X-70 Fractal.
