US President Donald Trump on Monday (local time) said that the Iran war is "effectively over" militarily, but added that he would maintain the "status quo" of economically isolating Tehran, including through a naval blockade and a newly announced initiative to sever its overland trade routes. He made these remarks at a press briefing alongside UFC CEO Dana White, the New York Post reported. The US President said, "Iran, militarily, is effectively over. We're just keeping it the status quo. And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbors. It’s got 301% inflation. It’s got problems like you don’t even want to think about.” Quoting Trump, CBS News reported, "Look, Iran, I hope we're going to be able to make a deal with them." He added, "But nothing's going to happen. And if we have to, we'll take it very seriously. We are so loaded." Continuing his warning, Trump said that the US was "fully locked and loaded with the best equipment ever made" if the situation were to change. However, he added, "We don't think there's going to be any reason to use it, however." The US President, who has renewed threats of fresh strikes against Iran in recent weeks, has reportedly deferred a decision to attack the country following a conversation with Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani. This came after he announced the new "Operation Iron Gate" to sever Tehran's land connections with other countries. Trump said, "Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others would prefer the status quo that we remain as is. In other words, a continuation of the greatest naval blockade in the history of our country, probably in the history of the world,” in addition to Operation Iron Gate. He added, "So you have land and sea, total lockdown. I’ve agreed that Iran cannot have, and everybody’s agreed, Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, and that’s a non-negotiable point. They understand that. They accept that. They don’t admit that they accept it, and they will tell you that they don’t accept it, but they accept it 100%." Trump's remarks signalling restraint towards Iran also appeared to ease concerns in the oil market, with crude prices falling sharply in post-settlement trading, Reuters reported. Brent crude futures extended their losses in post-settlement trading on Monday, falling by more than $7 a barrel to their lowest level since late August. The decline came after Trump played down the possibility of fresh military strikes against Iran. Brent crude ended the session $5.75 lower, down 5.85%, at $92.57 a barrel. It continued to slide after settlement and was last trading more than $7 below its previous close. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures settled at $86.85 a barrel, down $3.98, or 4.38%. The US benchmark also extended its decline after settlement, falling by more than $5. Brent crude had already dropped 16% last week, marking its sharpest weekly decline since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. However, it remains to be seen whether the two sides will be able to negotiate an agreement to end the war or whether Trump will order fresh strikes. The Union Health Ministry has proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, to immediately suspend the manufacturing licences of drugs declared Not of Standard Quality (NSQ) on specified critical quality parameters.
The government said on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) that the proposed amendments seek to enable prompt regulatory intervention upon detection of substandard medicines, prevent their continued manufacture and distribution, and strengthen the mechanism for ensuring compliance with prescribed quality standards, in the interest of patient safety and public health.
Under the existing provisions of the Drugs Rules, 1945, suspension or cancellation of a manufacturing licence is preceded by the prescribed regulatory procedure, including issuance of a show-cause notice. This may result in a time gap between the declaration of a drug as NSQ and the initiation of regulatory action. During this period, the drug may remain in circulation, posing potential risks to public health and making effective recall more challenging.
To address this regulatory concern, the Ministry has proposed a provision for immediate suspension of the manufacturing licence of the drug by the Central Licensing Approving Authority or the State Licensing Authority upon receipt of a government analyst’s report declaring the drug as NSQ with respect to assay, dissolution, related substances, impurities or sterility.
“These parameters are critical to determining the quality of medicines. The proposed provision aims to ensure that instances of non-compliance involving these specified parameters are met with prompt regulatory action, thereby minimising potential risks to patients,’’ the Ministry said.
The proposed amendment provides for mandatory corrective measures before revocation of the suspension. The suspension shall continue until the manufacturer undertakes an effective root cause analysis to identify the reasons for the quality failure and implements appropriate Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) to the satisfaction of the licensing authority.
Suspension can be revoked after the requisite corrective and preventive measures are implemented and then verified by the licensing authority. This mechanism will ensure that identified quality deficiencies are adequately addressed and necessary safeguards are put in place to prevent their recurrence.
“To further strengthen regulatory coordination and facilitate timely action, consequential amendments have also been proposed to Form 13, relating to the test report of the Government Analyst. Under the proposed mechanism, the Government Analyst’s report would be endorsed to the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), the concerned State/UT Licensing Authority under whose jurisdiction the manufacturing site is located, as well as the manufacturer and marketer of the concerned drug,’’ the government said.
It added that the proposed arrangement is aimed at ensuring timely communication of NSQ findings to the relevant authorities and stakeholders, thereby facilitating coordinated regulatory action and strengthening accountability across the drug manufacturing and marketing chain.
The proposed amendments follow deliberations at the 65th meeting of the Drugs Consultative Committee, held on December 20, 2024, and recommendations of the 92nd meeting of the Drugs Technical Advisory Board, held on April 24, 2025.
The amendments are expected to strengthen post-marketing regulatory surveillance, facilitate timely action against substandard medicines, promote greater accountability among manufacturers and marketers, and reinforce public confidence in the quality of medicines available in the country.
The draft amendments have been notified for public consultation, inviting objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days from the date on which copies of the Gazette of India containing the draft rules are made available to the public.

At least 34 dead after Europe-bound migrant boat sinks off Senegal
- Published
At least 34 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports, citing an official source.
The Interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.
The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.
Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.
Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told AFP that all the bodies recovered so far were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.
In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.
"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.
The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.
Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.
Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.
Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.
Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.
More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.
The Canary Islands have become a major entry point into Europe for migrants and refugees making the dangerous Atlantic crossing from West Africa.
The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.
Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.
Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.
The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.
In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

A former Eli Lilly sales rep filed a lawsuit alleging that she was fired after complaining the company was promoting its Mounjaro diabetes drug to combat weight loss before receiving regulatory approval to do so.
Jennifer Mansion, who was hired as a senior territory manager in Dallas four years ago, claimed that she observed other Lilly sales reps promoting the diabetes drug as a salve for obesity. Mansion also contended that a physician touted Mounjaro as a weight loss option during a luncheon sponsored by the drugmaker, according to the suit filed in federal court in Texas.
Such promotions are known as off-label marketing in the pharmaceutical industry. The phrase refers to promoting a medicine for a usage that was not approved by the Food and Drug Administration. A physician may prescribe a medicine for an unapproved use, but a drugmaker is not permitted to market its drug for that purpose.

It’s definitely an upgrade to the typical indoor basketball experience. Plenty of play modes (perhaps too many), plus lots of streaming options.
TIRED
The hard included ball makes for a very noisy experience. Battery drains quickly, even when not in use. Some app modes didn’t work at all. Buggy remote. Weak speakers. No Netflix. Eventually it all gets a bit stale.
If your mom was one of those who always said, “Don’t play ball in the house,” well, she’s going to absolutely hate the Huupe Mini 2.
Huupe manufactures smart basketball hoops and add-on kits for existing setups that track shots, light up the board when a point is registered, and include social features like global challenges and leaderboards. The Huupe Mini 2 is the pint-sized, indoor version of that idea, clipping over the top of a door so you can shoot hoops without ever having to leave the room.
I’ve been testing one out for weeks, and while it’s a fun diversion, some of its features overreach beyond its core functionality, resulting in an experience that bricks as much as it dunks.
Season Tickets
The Huupe Mini 2 is, effectively, a smart television with a basketball hoop mounted to it. Or rather, a smart TV that comes with a basketball hoop that you have to mount yourself, courtesy of four screws and a little elbow grease. The LCD screen measures 19 inches diagonally, plus a hefty border that includes stereo speakers and a camera used to track you and your b-ball prowess. (Total size of the backboard is 25 inches diagonally, which fits comfortably within a door frame.)
A 5-inch inflatable rubber basketball is included, along with a small hand pump and needle. Also in the box are a small but otherwise traditional remote control—required to do anything with the Huupe—and a USB-C charger and lengthy cable so you can top up the battery without removing it from the door.
After a quick charge, the unit is ready to set up. I was surprised to discover there’s no app for the device; while larger Huupe hardware works with one, the Mini 2 is completely self-contained and web-based. Just connect the backboard to your Wi-Fi network through a process that you step through with the remote, just like you would on any modern television.
What’s new vs. the original Huupe Mini? According to the company, most of the upgrades are behind the scenes: a faster CPU, a larger battery (rated lifespan is now four hours), better display quality, and “significantly” better shot tracking. New games are also included, which I’ll cover in the sections to come.
Dunkin’
Once connected to the web, the Huupe Mini 2 opens up a world of entertainment to you, and, to my great surprise, not all of it is basketball-related. At first blush, the options available are actually quite daunting. It’s all arranged into traditional tiles on the home screen, which you scroll through with the remote.
Just Huupe is the board’s most basic scoring system, tracking shots and recording your shooting percentage in an untimed session. If you want to get competitive, Huupe Live and the Daily Prize Challenge are social games where you challenge players worldwide to score the most points in a given time frame. The winner gets a nominal prize—10 bucks for the daily challenge, a “cozy sweatsuit” for a monthlong challenge. Other games are fairly self-explanatory, like Most 3 Pointers in 90 Seconds and Family Mode (basically Horse).
Many of the games require online friends to play against; if you don’t have pals with their own Huupe Minis, you’ll probably be locked out of these modes—not that they add much beyond their multiplayer features.
Things get a little kookier—and buggier—from there. For example, Huupe Flyers is designed to be played without a ball. It’s a gesture-based version of Flappy Bird, wherein you literally flap your arms around to keep a basketball in the air, tracking your movements via the camera much like an Xbox Kinect. Unfortunately, unlike the ball-based games, I was never able to play it, as it failed the calibration process every time I tried to fire it up.
The system also works as a fairly straightforward streaming platform. Included are apps for YouTube, HBO Max, ESPN, Disney+, Prime Video, Hulu, Spotify, and more. There’s one glaring omission in that list, of course, and I’m not talking about Paramount+ but rather Netflix. Without Netflix support, can you even call yourself a streaming device? It’s also worth noting that the built-in speakers are surprisingly weak. On some apps the audio is OK; on others it’s nearly inaudible.
The Fade Away
The Huupe Mini 2 includes not just a sensor that can detect when a basket is successfully made; it also includes a camera to track how far the shooter is from the backboard. This is used to assign point values to various shots (depending on the specific game you’re playing), with more points earned the farther away you are from the hoop.
The good news is that in weeks of playing on the Huupe Mini 2, I never noticed a time when a successful basket was recorded as a miss or vice versa. The distance calculation, however, is another thing. I’ve shot from across the room and had it count as 1 point, while some shots from just a few feet away ring up as 3 points. I could never figure out much rhyme or reason for this variability, except that shots straight-on to the backboard generally registered as lower point values, even if they were distant, while shots from the wings earned more. Of course, navigating all of this is highly dependent on the geometry of your room. Unless you have the Huupe Mini 2 set up in an empty garage, you are probably, like me, going to have plenty of obstacles that get in the way of a lot of your shots—and plenty of crawling under furniture to retrieve wayward balls.
Out of Bounds
I can say with authority that it is harder to make a basket on the Huupe Mini 2 than on a regulation basketball goal, even at a very close distance. The hoop is small, and the ball tends to rebound wildly off the springy backboard. It’s quite unforgiving, and it didn’t really make me want to spend a lot of time playing, chasing balls that bounced into the corner or rolled under the bed.
The other big problem: When the included inflatable ball hits the Huupe Mini 2, the impact is extremely loud, to the point where I was promptly informed by my wife that it was not appropriate for use when anyone else was in the house. While Huupe says the device is intended solely for use with the included ball, I found a workaround by purchasing a 5-inch foam basketball from Amazon, which makes a bit less noise on impact and also softens the rebound a bit. It has had zero trouble registering baskets.
Battery life is another issue. While four hours is plenty of playing time, the battery continues to drain when the Huupe is in standby mode, which meant I would play a few games in the morning, ostensibly shut the Huupe off, then come back in the afternoon to a completely dead device. The Huupe can run with the power cord attached, but only once the battery has charged to at least about 5 percent.
Unfortunately, even turning the power off is puzzlingly difficult. The power button on my remote control did nothing; I ultimately had to turn the system on and off with the physical button on the bottom of the backboard.
At $429 (on deep discount from a hefty list price of $799), the Huupe Mini 2 sits perhaps just over the edge of what might pass for a quirky holiday gift—and I think it’s safe to say no one is buying this device for themselves. You’d have to be a huge basketball nut to get enough mileage out of the device to make it worthwhile. I expect you would also have to loathe leaving your room. With today’s kids, who knows.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

I love my old iPhone 14, but I’m starting to face the facts: It’s going to die. The battery is about to go; apps take longer to load than they used to. Some of it I can fix. I can go to the Genius Bar and swap the battery. Maybe I could even do it myself; that’d buy me some time. But eventually, Apple won’t support this wildly expensive device at all, and there’s not much I can do about it.
Apple did start offering self-repair services a few years ago, but it involves renting nearly 80 pounds of equipment and requires you to use official parts. When all is said and done, it doesn’t save you that much money versus just going to the Apple Store. But if I buy a screen or a camera component from a third party, there's a chance my iPhone is gonna lock me out of certain features because it doesn't recognize it.
This problem goes far beyond iPhones. Manufacturers have put similar locks on all kinds of gadgets, from video game consoles to cars to smart home devices, making them hard to modify and even harder to restore after some firmware update renders a certain feature unusable.
Not surprisingly, a lot of people think this isn't fair, that there should be a better way to do it. I think at this point it's safe to say it qualifies as a movement, one that unites under the banner of “right to repair.” Built around the radical idea that when you buy something you should be able to truly own it, right-to-repair advocates believe consumers have the right to maintain, fix, or modify any piece of hardware they’ve purchased. The movement has gained even more traction now that AI makes it even easier to hack the software powering consumers’ devices.
To find out what’s next for the right-to-repair movement, I went straight to the source: Louis Rossmann, a YouTuber and consumer rights advocate who recently organized the Own Your Shit tour, which went around the US earlier this year to call for the death of Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, which prohibits users from bypassing digital restrictions put on devices by manufacturers.
Rossmann and I talked about more than just Section 1201. We also discussed the US midterm elections, putting out bounties to find product fixes, and what will happen as the right-to-repair movement collides with the rise of AI.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
BRIAN BARRETT: Louis, thank you so much for being here. You're someone who spends a lot of time not just evangelizing over “right to repair,’ but I would imagine introducing it to people who don't know what it is. How do you do that?
LOUIS ROSSMANN: I try to avoid talking about it, and I try to show people. So instead of telling people, “Here’s why you should care about this issue,” which sounds like lecturing, what I’ll do is if I’m done fixing something for a customer and they say, “The Apple Store told me $2,000," and we could do it for $200, when they’re giving me the hug and saying, “Thank you for getting back all of our baby pictures” or something, I’ll say, “Here’s how close you were to this never happening.”
I like to tell them, “This is the document that I used to fix your device.” When they ask me what was wrong with it, I’ll tell them, “By the way, you should know that Apple tells the company that makes this chip not to sell it to me, and if everybody in that chain listened, I would not be able to fix this, and you wouldn’t have any of your data back.” So I always try to show people and get them excited about what it is I’m doing.
Got it.
I have over 1,000 repair videos on YouTube where I show people how to do what I do, and there are people that say, “I was working at Walmart for seven bucks an hour, and I picked up a soldering iron and started fixing boards on eBay, and now I make triple what I did before.”
There are people that fix their own things, so not just making careers for people, but maybe somebody saved themselves some money by doing a repair themself. Or when I fix something for somebody that otherwise wouldn't have been fixed or that they were told couldn’t be fixed. I always try to get people personally invested because lecturing people about it just doesn’t make it very fun.
Your organization has a wall of shame, almost, of examples of things that companies have done to take away the ownership of a product. Because that’s really what it is, right? It's like you buy something, you expect to be able to own it and do what you want with it, but that's not always how it plays out. To your mind, what are some of the more egregious instances of companies not letting you know what you want?
Some of my favorites are some of these thermostat companies. One of them sent out a firmware update after the company went bankrupt that required that you pay $117 a year to get some of the functionality that you had beforehand. So it’s not even necessarily when a company has a device that has a specific date when it’s gonna turn off.
It’s when they realize, “We need to make more money, so we’re gonna change what it is we’re offering you after the sale.”
When I started doing this, I was just talking about right to repair for Apple devices, which is what my small shop worked on. I saw it from my small lens. I focused on the items where I knew exactly what was going on, and I really thought, “This is a problem that only affects me.”
It wasn’t until about 2017 when I went to Nebraska for this legislative hearing that I realized that it really is not just something that affects my small field. I was in a room filled with farmers that were talking about all the problems they were having with their tractors, and I remember going, “Where’s the right-to-repair?” And someone says, “This is the right-to-repair room. Everybody has this problem now.” And that’s when I started opening my field of view up to everybody who has this issue.
As time went on, my channel stopped just discussing right to repair, and it started discussing how right to repair is a small element under this umbrella of ownership. And ownership being taken away is, in my opinion, the real problem. Your inability to fix what you own is one thing, but also the fact that everything is turning into a subscription, that the things that you buy must connect to the manufacturer’s server in order to work, which means that they can disable your product at any time.
It’s all small things under this large umbrella of ownership, and that’s slowly being taken away from people over the past 10 to 20 years.
I wanna go back to the farmers because they have been on the vanguard of this. They have been in a years-long struggle with John Deere specifically, trying to get the right to repair their own tractors. But there have been some breakthroughs recently. Do you mind talking through wins like that, like how either that movement or other movements have actually been able to make changes happen?
I think a lot of the change so far has been change that occurs at the cultural level more than the legislative level. Some of these changes have been memorandums of understanding where the company says, “OK, we won’t do this particular thing.”
When I speak to farmers, it’s very much the same version of what I deal with in my business, where you’ll see a headline where a company says they’re supporting repair, and then you actually look into the details of it, and it’s really very surface level.
One of the examples I have of this is with Samsung. They had released this independent repair program, and they made screens and batteries available, so you could buy a battery. But the battery cost over $200 because they glued the battery to the screen, and if you wanted to buy it, you had to buy both of them together.
A $200 to $250 battery is pretty useless to a lot of people who have a phone that’s worth $200 when it works. And one of the issues that I’ve found when I'm speaking to farmers is, at the end of the day, they still have the same problem that they did. They’re still using cracked Ukrainian software to be able to work on their tractor themselves without having to take it back to the dealer. So there’s still a lot of work to be done.
Right to repair is in the news more frequently than it used to be. Some outlets, like WIRED, have covered it for a while. Our writer Boone Ashworth has talked to you before and covered it quite a bit. But it seems to have reached national prominence in the last year or so. Is there an inflection point that you can point to?
I think it’s been a slow burn for the past 12 years. CBC News did a piece on Apple in 2018. That was a really fun one for me. I remember the producer came to me and said they wanted to do a piece on how Apple is bad with upgrades. I remember saying, “Upgrades are not very fun, but also the piece is starting with the conclusion. You’re starting with doing a piece on Apple being bad, and there’s no fun in that. What if you do this: Find a broken machine, take it to Apple, record what they say, take it to me, record what I say, and let the story write itself.” And they said, “Well, what if they give a good answer?” I’m just smirking like, “Just let the story write itself. Have faith.”
They took it to Apple. They said, “We gotta do the motherboard,” all this other stuff. I see that it’s a bent pin in a screen cable because whoever had worked on it before had likely tried to misroute the screen cable when they were plugging it into the board, so they were stretching it, and they shorted pin one to ground, which caused the backlight to go out. So I take a tweezer, bend it back, and it works. It was featured on national news.
There’s some other inflection points, like in 2016 when Apple had asked if I would take down one of my videos showing where a fuse was. There was a video I did showing you how to fix a MacBook Air if you get some liquid around the trackpad, and your trackpad and keyboard stop working. There’s a zero-ohm resistor. It’s kinda like a fuse that will blow in that area so that the entire machine doesn’t die.
So I showed how to replace this thing. At 55 seconds in the video, I’m showing where the fuse is in the motherboard, and they asked me to take the video down, and I’m like, “I don’t want to. File a DMCA claim.” That got some attention. I started a nonprofit to try and do this more professionally and push this forward in a more organized manner.
I think a lot of people might say, “That sounds good, and I’m behind it,” but the idea of a fuse, a motherboard, those are things people aren’t always comfortable messing with. It sounds intimidating to someone who’s not steeped in tech. Is that so in practice? Has it become easier to fix stuff even as companies make it harder?
The right to repair doesn’t mean that you have to fix something, nor does it mean that you have to go incredibly deep to fix the issue. If you’re the type of person that wants to pay somebody else to fix it, I respect that. If you wanna replace the entire display assembly, meaning the entire lid on the laptop because that’s easier for you, and you’re willing to pay an extra $100 or $200 to buy the screen preassembled, go for it.
If you wanna replace the LCD cell, which is just the front layer that makes the picture, which is absolutely miserably difficult to do—but you can buy that part sometimes for 30 to 50 bucks—do that too. I am not telling people that they should have to fix anything, and I’ll never shame somebody because they decide to buy something new or have somebody else fix it.
Right to repair simply means that you have the right to fix it if you want, or send it to the manufacturer, send it to a third party, or buy something new if you don’t want to fix it. Ironically, most of the devices in my house that don't work, I don't wind up fixing them. I wind up buying something new, because after 12 or 15 hours a day of fixing other people’s stuff, I just don’t have it in me to fix my own.
The wall of laptops I see behind you are a testament to that.
So recently, for instance, my air conditioner broke, and I was willing to pay somebody to fix it, and he ghosted me three times. And the company said, “We don't fix them. We can give you a new one for $10,000.” And I look at the cost of the unit that I have and it’s $2,500, and I’m just like, “What?” So I opened it up and I realized the contactor, which is a relay, it’s the thing that every time your thermostat says “turn on the AC” it sends 24 volts to this thing, and then that turns on the 240 volts going to the AC. It was filled, absolutely filled, with fire ants. I don’t know why fire ants love 240 volts. They really love it even though it’s not good for them. And that was kind of fun for me. So at that moment, I wanted to fix it because I was boiling hot, and it was taking forever for somebody else to.
Now in this case, there was not a lot that was stopping me. My unit is so old that I was actually able to find the schematics for it online, so if I wanted to buy parts for it, I could. And that's really all most people are asking for. I'm not saying that you have to do a motherboard repair yourself, but it would be nice if somebody who's qualified to do so is not blocked from being able to do so.
Now, it’s not Apple’s job to make it easy for me. It’s not their job to design their product in a way where I have a more luxurious experience while I’m doing the job. My job is gonna be difficult, and that's part of the game. Technology is consistently evolving.
Where right to repair comes in is when I try to talk to the electronics distributor that sells all these chips, and I say, “I wanna buy this,” and they say, “You’re not on the list. We can’t sell to you.” That’s where right to repair comes in and says that’s not OK.
Companies will say—and I know this because they say it to us all the time when we go to them with stories about this—that, fundamentally, a lot of this is about quality control. If we let you use an unauthorized part, we’re not gonna guarantee that the device is gonna perform up to our standards. If we let you tinker around with this, you might break it. We want to guarantee a certain level of quality with the experience of our devices. How does that reasoning sit with you?
If the issue is quality control, then why does my store have a better rating on Google Maps than every single Apple Store in the country?
What is right to repair asking for? Right to repair very often asks for the ability to buy the same part that they are using. I want to be able to buy the parts that go into the device.
We’ve seen stories in recent weeks where now that people have Claude Code they can use it to check their smart TVs and get rid of all the bloatware and all the adware and have a more streamlined smart TV experience. I think those tools also give them access to guides to figure out how to replace all kinds of things, how to fix software in all kinds of ways. Is part of the future of owning our things also making it easier to not just tinker with the hardware aspect of it, but to get into the software and make it more in line with what we want out of our experiences and give companies less control over the advertising, the spyware, whatever it is?
I love it. I love seeing people being able to use AI in that way. I love the idea of it being used to break digital locks, that you could just get access to what the company has taken away from you. I think that that is a great use of AI. The only issue there is when you’re talking about ownership, when people are using these frontier models, when they’re using Claude Code or Codex you’re using a model that runs on somebody else’s computer, and if you type the wrong thing, it’s easy to get around some of Claude Code’s guardrails, and sometimes I’ve done some experiments to have fun with it. But there are a lot of guardrails on it, and I wouldn’t be surprised if at some point in the future, enough of these companies started saying, “Hey, people are using Claude Code to actually free themselves from our bullshit. Can you stop that?” And them stopping it.
This is where it’s nice to see that it’s not just the US leading in this. Many other countries are creating their own AI models that can run on your system. I’m very excited to see what happens, as time goes on, when models that can run on a standard laptop like this have the ability to actually do this.
You know, when people are remaking Adobe Suite with Claude Code, I wouldn’t be surprised if one or two years from now they can’t do that at all because it’s able to detect, “Hey, you’re actually trying to free yourself from Adobe.”
But what I’m hoping to see happen is that there are enough local models that run on your system that you don’t have to worry about some company that gets to tell you what you can do, being able to help people get around all these types of digital locks and bullshit. I don’t think that that’s gonna happen in the next year or two, but I think it’s coming, and I’m excited to see it.
This does lead us to the fact those digital locks and bullshit are in legally murky territory sometimes, right? Or at least companies can claim legal defenses. I’m talking specifically about Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, something that you do not like, and I think it’s fair to say you want to see it gone for good.
Do you mind telling us a little bit about what Section 1201 of the DMCA is and how it ties into this conversation and makes it a little bit more fraught to do that unlocking?
Section 1201 of the DMCA makes it illegal to bypass a technical protection measure, otherwise known as a digital lock, to gain access to a protected work, even if it’s for the purpose of repair. It was put in place to try and stop piracy, and it was put together in one of the most corrupt ways possible.
Congress repeatedly said no to this law. No, this is way too restrictive. So the architect of it, Bruce Lehman, decided to try and get it negotiated into an international treaty. Then he came back to the United States and said, “Look, we signed this treaty, so now you have to pass this law. We’re going to be out of step with our obligations to the international community.” So he’s potentially sidestepped Congress in order to get this law passed that says that you cannot bypass a digital lock, even if it’s on something that you own.
Now, I can’t go to your house and break into your home. That’s illegal. I should not be allowed to do that. But if I spend $600,000 on a house, and I notice that there’s a locked closet in the house, once I’ve paid $600,000 for the house, I should be able to break that lock to get into that closet, because I own the house.
The problem with this law is that it allows companies to lock you out of things that you have already paid for. And the way that you see this being abused now is when you see companies taking away features from you or sending out firmware updates that stop features from working on the device after the company has gone bankrupt and they figure out, “Oh, wait, we need more money.”
I’ve had companies that failed before, and I really wish I had the ability to say, “You know what? I realize that I sold it at a price that’s a little too low. I’m gonna need to take $5 from every customer I had in the past year.” I’m not allowed to do that. I can’t stop my customers’ products from working.
But because I was selling a physical good that did not have any sort of firmware on it that connects to the internet, I’m not able to do that. Section 1201 of the DMCA is a law that came out in the late 1990s. This was before most normal people even had the internet, much less had their washing machine, their television, their dryer attached to the internet like they are now.
That law was, in my opinion, horribly put together for the world of the mid- to late-1990s, and it is way worse built for today. The architect of the law also said that the purpose of it was to try and fight piracy, and he admitted in 2007 and 2013 when he was looking back on it that it didn’t do that at all.
It’s very easy right now. I was able to show my 79-year-old father how to pirate television, movies, music, and it took me less than 10 minutes to show him how to use something like SoulSeek or Usenet to be able to get whatever he wants. These laws fundamentally have not worked, but what they’ve done a very good job of is making it much more difficult for people who wanna follow the law to be able to use their media.
Right.
If I want to rip my legally purchased Blu-ray and be able to play it on my legally purchased phone, I have to break the digital lock inside the Blu-ray disc to do that, which is illegal. What I’m actually supposed to do is I’m supposed to buy another version of it that’s only gonna work on here, and it makes it much more difficult for people who actually want to obey the law.
I think people are now waking up to this, but software is copyrightable. So when you buy a book on Amazon Kindle, say, and you have a Kindle book, what you’re actually doing is you’re signing an end-user licensing agreement that gives you the right to access that book.
You don’t own that book in a technical way, even though it feels like you should and feels like you do. So we’ve had cases where Amazon has actually removed books from Kindles after you bought them, and there’s no recourse for that. I think the idea of ownership in the digital age is informed by so much of Section 1201 and the way that we approach copyright and software.
Do you see any progress towards changing that?
Instead of every single year going back and asking for an exemption, what we’d really like to do is we’d like to pass durable legislation that doesn’t require that we ask for an exemption. We’re starting with the area that is the most reasonable, which is repair. If you want to be able to fix what you bought and paid for, that should not be a crime.
You should be able to repair what you own, and you should be able to show other people how to repair what they own without that being considered a copyright crime. We’re not even saying, “Can I please rip my legally purchased Blu-ray so that I could watch it on my legally purchased portable media player?” Right now, we’re simply saying, “I would like to fix what I bought and paid for.”
The problem that I’ve experienced throughout this process is there’s always an issue that people find more exciting, that’s more accessible, because you can only focus on so many things at once. If people are concerned about the economy, culture-war issues, if somebody’s concerned about immigration or Covid or policing—there’re so many issues that resonate far more with the voting public than this. The right to repair is this really abstract issue, and when you start talking about digital locks—my job, as I see it, is to get ordinary people to understand why this acronym and set of numbers directly ties into your thermostat saying it’s not gonna work anymore unless you give them $10 a month.
I don’t think that I’ve done a good enough job of that over the past 12 years to get it on par with all these other issues that people face every day. Admittedly, if you’re paying like $5, $6 a gallon for gas, you’re probably gonna care about that before you care about this.
So we’re talking not long after the midterms, and Democrats have won control over the Senate and the House. You do have a couple of politicians who actually have been speaking out about the right to repair who are in office now: Josh Turek in Iowa; Jake Johnson in Minnesota looks like he’s gonna get a seat. Is it encouraging that it’s even an issue people are talking about, or is that still not enough?
It’s encouraging to see that they’re talking about it, but I also realize that, especially going into this next Congress, there is going to be so much work and so many things that they’re going to want to do. I remember somebody asking me, “Like, no offense Louis, but I’d rather see them spend time on, I don't know, getting rid of Pete Hegseth.” I never tell people my issue is more important than your issue, and everybody votes according to what is important to them.
But there’s so many things that I imagine this Congress is going to want to do when they get elected that my job is gonna be making sure that there’s enough of a base of support and showing that there’s enough people that care about this, that if you spend the 20 minutes to do something about this, that it will actually work in your favor.
And that’s part of what we’ve been trying to do with the FULU [Freedom from Unethical Limitations on Users] Own Your Shit tour over the past few months. We’ve traveled around the country to 13 different cities, and in every one of these cities, we are trying to bring people together.
We had one of the ex-FTC commissioners show up, which was really cool. He gave an inspiring speech in San Jose. We’re also inviting their congresspeople to say, “Yeah, this is an issue that I will actually be more likely to vote for. This is as important to me as the other issues.” And our job is showing the people that are elected that we care about this. Because what’s their job? Their job is to represent us. If people are not talking about this issue or it's only being talked about on a couple of subreddits or on the fringes of the internet, I almost don't blame the representative for not prioritizing it. But our job is to show them that if they prioritize it, they'll be rewarded for it.
So I am happy to see that there are people talking about it. I remember when right to repair was put into an executive order by Biden in summer of 2021. I was excited, but there wasn’t a lot that came from it. I’m hoping for something different here.
So FULU is your organization that supports right to repair. You also have bounties that you pay out for people who can disable these digital locks. How is that going? Have you successfully paid out bounties yet? Can you talk about that program a little bit and why you're sort of taking matters into your own hands here?
That program came out about 2:00 or 3:00 in the morning. I was doing a video on Futurehome after somebody who works there, or used to work there, sent me information on what they were doing. He was talking about this thermostat that when it got a firmware update after the company went bankrupt, it stopped you from being able to use some of the features you could use before.
I did the video going over it, and I’m just sitting there at, like, 2 am editing this and thinking, “This is not enough.” And I said, “I'll give $5,000 or $10,000 to whoever makes this thing work again.” I was thinking back to what I was doing when I was doing all these repair videos showing the schematics.
Now you have hundreds of people doing repair videos that are way better than mine every single day on YouTube, and I love it. But back in 2013 and 2014, I didn’t see anything like that, and that’s because at the bottom right corner of the screen, it has this little message on the schematic. It says, “Proprietary property of Apple Inc. Keep confidential. Do not share.” Most people don’t like getting sued or having their livelihoods destroyed. For me, that’s like a Tuesday. I find it fun. I enjoy going to court. I encourage my employees to go to court.
Got it.
So I was thinking, “How do I get more people to start poking at these things? How do I get more people to start saying, ‘No, this is not enough. You can’t do that.’” So we came up with this bounty, and you could see in that video that most of it was done during the day, and the part with the bounty was done at 3:00 in the morning in some corner of my house when I’m dead tired.
I said, “5,000 bucks to whoever makes this work again.” And there was an employee that emailed me with a solution shortly thereafter, and he said, “Louis, I appreciate this. I would’ve done this for free, but here I made a Home Assistant integration,” and people were able to use the thermostat again.
So what we’re trying to do with the bounty program is we’re trying to show people that, A, this is a problem, and B, we’re trying to incentivize people to start making things work again so that we can point to how bad this law is. We can also point to things that tangibly work again. The reason that the right-to-repair stuff with Apple that I was doing was successful is because I wasn’t just saying, “Here’s why you should care about this.”
Millions of people probably have working MacBooks again because of those videos that I was doing back in the day. So when somebody personally saves $1,000, when they personally get their data back, they are now invested in my cause in a way that no Twitter hashtag and no bumper sticker is ever gonna make happen.
What’s a gateway drug into right to repair? If you want to get into repairing your own stuff, what is an easy thing? Is it an iPhone battery replacement or a trackpad upgrade? What do you point people to and say, “This is something that you can actually do. This is something you can manage. It’s gonna make your life better. It’s gonna make your experience better”?
I don't have a very well-packaged answer for that. For me, it it has to be something fun. It has to be, It's 103 degrees in Texas this week, and my asshole air conditioning technician has stiffed me three times. Let me open it up and, oh, I just used compressed air on the contactor and I blew out the fire ants, so now it works again. That’s what’s gonna get people excited about this. I get excited about repair not because of the repair that’s being done, and admittedly not even the money, it’s the story that’s involved in it.
So anytime you’re fixing something because I need this to work right now, or I don't have the money to make this work again, anytime there’s some sort of story attached to it, it’s going to be something that gets you excited.
Some people may feel incredibly excited about replacing the battery in their phone. Some people are really just gonna hate it. But I think there has to be some sort of story behind it that makes it worth it. I actually don’t find repair fun. I don't think that putting 96 solder balls back onto a chip that's the size of my pinky fingernail is fun.
I don’t do it for that. I do it for the hug that the customer gives you when you get back all their baby pictures, or when you do this for the police and they're able to catch the murderer because of it. I don’t find taking a battery out of a phone, using a heat gun, and using a little spudger to get all this off, but not breaking the screen—that’s not fun.
It’s fun if you can’t afford a new one. That makes it a lot of fun. It’s fun if you’re doing it to get something back. But there has to be a story. There has to be a reason that makes that particular repair exciting to you, and that's gonna be different for everybody, and it’s usually gonna be based on whatever your circumstances are at the time.

Ramayana – Part I, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, continues its phenomenal run at the Indian box office. After creating history with a staggering Rs. 103.47 crore nett collection on Monday, November 9, the Nitesh Tiwari-directed mythological epic is heading towards another extraordinary day. As of 8:30 PM on Tuesday, November 10, the film has collected Rs. 84.15 crores nett across all languages, putting it on course for a massive sixth-day total.
The latest trends suggest that Ramayana could finish Tuesday in the Rs. 90–100 crore nett range, depending on the performance of the remaining night shows.
What makes the development particularly remarkable is that Tuesday marks the film's sixth day in cinemas. Despite the initial opening-weekend rush being over, the mythological epic continues to attract substantial audiences.
Earlier in the afternoon, Ramayana had registered collections of Rs. 31.66 crores nett across 10,952 shows. At that point, the film was running approximately 11.83% below Monday's collections at the corresponding reporting time. However, the latest figures indicate a substantial improvement as the day progressed.
By 8:30 PM, collections had climbed to Rs. 84.15 crores, an increase of Rs. 52.49 crores over the afternoon update. The sharp rise suggests that evening screenings have played an important role in strengthening Tuesday's business.
Morning shows recorded an occupancy of 34%, which increased considerably to 59.2% during afternoon screenings. The evening witnessed an even stronger response, with occupancy reaching 63.6%, the highest among the reported show periods. Night occupancy currently stands at 48.1%, although this figure could change as the remaining screenings progress.
The biggest question now is whether Ramayana can achieve the extraordinary feat of collecting Rs. 100 crores nett on two consecutive days.

Delhi Metro has found a new fan in British travel vlogger Jack Heaton.
During his ongoing trip to India, Heaton documented his first ride on New Delhi's sprawling rapid transit network, declaring it cleaner, cheaper, and noticeably more modern than several European systems, including London's iconic Tube.
Adding to his surprise was the highly affordable ticket price, with the vlogger noting he paid just ₹32 ($0.34) for his journey.
Taking to Instagram, Heaton shared his experience of navigating the transport network. Although his first metro ride coincided with recent protests that caused some delays, he remained highly appreciative of the overall infrastructure.
"But besides that it is a HUGE metro system, kept pretty clean, way more modern than say the London but that's because it's underground, so obviously all the technological improvements that have come with time,” he said in the viral video.
The viral video quickly sparked a debate in the comments section, with some Indians beaming with pride and others offering a reality check regarding European transport.
“Thank you for showing the good side of India to the world. Have a great time while you are here,” one user commented. Another regular metro commuter agreed, saying, “Been using the Delhi Metro service for years and I can vouch for its excellence.”
However, not everyone agreed with the European comparison.
“I don't think so. Europe's transport system is robust and unmatched. Trams give you last door connectivity, metros are seamless and buses are the cherry on top," one comment read. “Delhi Metro is good but it needs new cross lines, it needs support of other transport system, its over burdened. But no, it definitely doesn't mock European public - city transportation systems.”
Defending the Indian network, another individual commented, “Many European cities have excellent metro systems, but the Delhi Metro is also considered one of the world's top five metro systems in terms of reliability.”
Pointing out the city's massive population, one user mentioned, “It's still not enough for the size.” Meanwhile, a local offered a helpful tip on pricing: “Bro, you bought a ticket from counter, try online apps. There you can get cheap tickets for $0.06 and sometimes even for free.”
New Delhi boasts one of the largest metro networks in India.
The Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) currently operates nine main routes—Red, Yellow, Blue, Green, Violet, Pink, Magenta, and Grey lines—along with the Airport Express line. Together, these cover a massive 374.46 km across 271 stations.
When combined with other NCR transit services such as Noida's Aqua Line, Gurugram's Rapid Metro, Namo Bharat, and the Meerut Metro, the entire regional network spans an impressive 519.50 km and includes 330 stations.

On Nov. 3, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. In the days that followed, a claim circulated that El-Sayed had said that "Michigan is the capital of Arab America," sparking vitriol from opponents.
The alleged quote played into a trope — commonly used against Muslims, immigrants and other communities — that institutions such as the U.S. government are being "infiltrated" by foreigners. For example, the caption of one Facebook post sharing a purported clip of El-Sayed saying the quote began: "WE'VE BEEN INVADED" (archived).
Other social media users, including Turning Point USA CEO Erika Kirk, shared the clip (archived). "There is no 'Arab America.' There is only the United States of America," she wrote. Readers also wrote in to Snopes, looking for answers.
The quote was correctly attributed to El-Sayed, and the clip of him saying it was authentic. He made the comment during a speech at the CONNECT Empowerment Summit, also known as the Arab American Leadership and Empowerment Summit, in the Washington, D.C., suburb of Chantilly, Virginia, on Nov. 6.
The video clip is available on multiple platforms, including C-SPAN.
"Ahlan wa sahlan," he opened his comments — "welcome" in Arabic. He then introduced himself as "Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed," his full name, before saying:
I'm honored to be the next United States senator from the great state of Michigan. Which of course — I know we're here in D.C., which of course is the capital of the United States of America, but Michigan is the capital of Arab America.
His remarks were met with cheers.
Michigan has a rich Arab American history, with the highest-concentrated Arab population in the country, according to World Population Review. In cities such as Dearborn, Arab Americans make up more than half the population.
For further reading on El-Sayed, we've previously covered a claim that he would force Michigan students to learn Arabic numerals (they already do) and a false rumor that he said it was acceptable for young girls to see male genitals in their locker rooms because "they are going to see them on the internet anyway."

Wenger considers standing against Infantino
- Published
Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger is considering standing against Gianni Infantino as a candidate in Fifa's presidential election.
For weeks, senior figures in European football have been hoping the Frenchman would run for the job, and he is now giving it serious thought.
Wenger is 77, leading to questions over whether he could provide long-term leadership for the sport.
But some of his supporters have told BBC Sport that they would be happy for him to win the election, then stand down before serving a full four-year term.
Infantino's position was plunged into crisis by a backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors.
But he retains support in South America, Africa and Asia, and recently insisted he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.
However, that support could be tested if Wenger stands.
Fifa's head of global development would have the backing of Uefa, which has spearheaded opposition to Infantino, and he has credibility throughout the footballing world.
Sources close to Wenger say he is yet to decide whether to stand, and they still believe Infantino is favourite to win a fourth and final term in next year's election.
The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November.
Former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega was the first person to put his name forward in October.
Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima has also announced his intention to stand.
This month Fifa said "key documents" relating to Infantino's plan to sell stakes in the World Cup would be made available to members of its council, but they will have to travel to its Zurich base, and access will be under "strict protocols".
Last month Uefa gave football's world governing body until 2 November to release details about the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and to answer questions relating to its decision-making.
That followed a council meeting at which Infantino apologised for the abandoned sell-off plot but failed to explain how the proposal was devised, asking that questions be submitted in writing.
Amid the fallout over FFE, Wenger, who has traditionally been loyal to Infantino, distanced himself from the aborted plot.
"I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports," Wenger said at the time.
"The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity."
Wenger has caused controversy at times in his Fifa role, notably for proposals such as biennial World Cups and a "daylight" offside law.
But he also has a global profile, including in Africa, where Infantino recently received a major re-election boost when receiving the backing of all 54 member national associations after promising an increase in funding.
Known as a champion of African players when in charge at Arsenal, Wenger's support of an expanded 48-team World Cup in order to drive development in countries beyond the game's traditional powers has been well received in the continent.

Oxford museum returns ancestral Naga skulls to India
- Published
The University of Oxford has returned the remains of 39 people taken from the Naga community during British colonial rule in India.
A delegation of around 30 people from Nagaland, a mountainous state in north-eastern India, attended a ceremony at Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum on Monday to mark the handover.
The remains, most of which are skulls, will be taken back to India and given what Naga tribal leaders have described as a "respectful rest". There are plans to bury them under a joint memorial in a park in Nagaland.
Museum director Laura Van Broekhoven described it as "a historic moment that will be part of stories told to next generations".
She said the remains were finally on their way home after overcoming "so much red tape everywhere".
The human remains were displayed at the Oxford museum for decades before being removed from public view in 2020 as part of what it described as a "decolonisation process".
The Pitt Rivers Museum holds more than 6,000 objects associated with Naga culture, believed to be the largest such collection in the world. Most were acquired during British colonial rule in India and Myanmar (the former Burma).
The museum's website lists 219 items as human remains.
These were added to the museum's collection between 1910 and 1940 and mostly collected by two colonial administrators who were anthropologists.
The museum's website, external mentions that the objects collected during this period were "frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given".
During their visit to Oxford, the Naga delegation also met descendants of one of the anthropologists involved in collecting the remains.
"The manner in which these human remains were taken away from our land leaves much for us to speculate," one of the tribal leaders, Thejao Vihienuo, told AFP.
"I suspect that nobody would have given the skull of his father or his grandfather as a gift to another person."
Anthropologists say that the Naga people once practised head hunting, severing the heads of enemies as trophies. But they also kept the heads of their own chiefs at the centre of villages.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, founded in the 19th Century, has previously returned human remains to indigenous communities in Australia, New Zealand and the US.
The latest handover to India concerns only the 39 ancestral remains and comes after a visit by a Naga delegation to Oxford in 2025, when it formally requested their return.
The museum had announced in September that the remains would be returned to India.
