- The claim that every calf birthed on a Texas ranch has been stillborn following the construction of a nearby artificial intelligence data center is unproven.
- The rumor has spread since at least May 2026. It appears to be based on an account shared by Clayton Tucker — the Democratic incoming Texas agriculture commissioner — who described a rancher in the state allegedly experiencing repeated cattle stillbirths after such a facility was built nearby.
- None of the versions of the story contain enough verifiable details to identify the rancher or the nearby facility. The accounts also differ regarding whether the plant is an AI data center or a battery energy storage system. The Texas Animal Health Commission said via email that it has not received any complaints or reports matching the account and has found no related investigations.
- It was not possible to find any scientific evidence linking noise or electromagnetic fields from data centers to cattle stillbirths.
- Snopes has reached out to Tucker — as well as veterinary and scientific experts specializing in cattle reproduction, noise and electromagnetic fields — for more information. We await replies to our inquiries and will update this article if additional information surfaces.
Throughout 2026, a claim circulated that every calf birthed on an unnamed Texas ranch has been stillborn following the construction of a nearby artificial intelligence data center.
For instance, one popular Instagram post (archived) from October features an image with text that says:
A Texas rancher says every calf born on his ranch has been stillborn since a data center was built next door.
They will call it anecdotal. A man burying calf after calf does not need a peer-reviewed study to know the building next door changed something.
(Instagram user @wonderzofthewild)
The caption attributes the story to Clayton Tucker — the Democratic candidate who won the 2026 midterms race to become the next Texas agriculture commissioner — and suggests "noise or vibrations" from the facility could be affecting the cattle.
Iterations of the rumor have spread widely on X, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit and TikTok. One Instagram user posted about it in early June 2026 without mentioning any identifying details. Snopes readers also contacted us to ask whether the story is true.
In short, it was not possible to find evidence confirming the rumor. None of the posts identify the rancher or the facility, while different versions of the story describe the facility as either a data center or a battery energy storage system. A spokesperson for the Texas Animal Health Commission said via email the agency has not received any reports or complaints about cattle stillbirths near data centers or battery storage facilities.
It was also not possible to find evidence that noise or electromagnetic fields from data centers cause cattle stillbirths.
Given the above and the lack of verifiable information, we have left this claim unrated.
Origin of rumor
The source of the claim, and the origin of the story at the heart of it, is unclear. Some of the earliest accounts come from Tucker, though it was not possible to establish when he first heard the alleged story.
Tucker discussed the supposed issue in a YouTube video posted on May 18, in which he said a farmer told him they had "not had a new calf in about two years" because of "ultra-low-frequency" noise and vibrations originating from a nearby AI data center.
He then told the story during a June 1 meeting of the Bell County Commissioners Court, at a July 7 Lubbock City Council meeting (around 1:33:51) — on that occasion citing numerous farmers — and during an August interview, in which he said a retired man bought a ranch in Fannin County, north of Dallas, but had to sell it for a loss due to a nearby data center causing multiple calf stillbirths.
Tucker's descriptions of the facility have, at times, differed. For instance, during an Aug. 24 podcast interview, he described the plant at the center of the story as a battery energy storage system (BESS), rather than an AI data center.
Local reporting confirms that a battery energy storage facility was built near Savoy, Fannin County. Meanwhile, reports from March describe plans for a data center in the area, but it was not possible to confirm that one was operating when Tucker began sharing the story. We also could not establish whether either one was the facility Tucker described.
Tucker shared posts repeating the allegation on Oct. 17 and Oct. 25. His captions acknowledge that "no veterinarian has confirmed the stillbirths" and that "no study has tied data center noise to livestock deaths," but still suggest data centers are to blame.
Separately, in April 2026 testimony (Page 42) to Texas lawmakers, Fannin County resident Cindy Tronzano reported that her cattle stopped grazing near a BESS facility and that her family had moved because of the noise. She did not mention stillbirths and it is unclear whether her account is connected to Tucker's story.
Snopes has contacted Tucker seeking more details about the stories he has repeatedly told. We will update this article if we receive a response.
A spokesperson for the Texas Animal Health Commission said via email that it has not received any reports or complaints about cattle stillbirths near data centers or battery storage facilities. The agency also said it has not found any investigations matching those circumstances.
Potential effects of data center noise on cattle
Data centers can produce continuous noise from cooling systems and other equipment, but it was not possible to locate evidence that such noise causes calf stillbirths, like the ones Tucker has discussed.
A 2023 scientific review published in "Annals of Animal Science" found that noise can cause stress in cattle and affect their behavior and health. It did not establish a connection between noise and stillbirths.
In early September 2026, French news agency Agence France-Presse investigated similar claims about data centers causing health problems and deaths among animals, including cattle and honeybees. Researcher Said Benaissa reportedly told AFP that studies do not support claims that electromagnetic fields from data centers cause cattle stillbirths. He reportedly said some studies have found small changes in fertility cycles and milk production.
It should be noted that electromagnetic fields and noise are different things. Therefore, these findings do not directly address the claims about low-frequency noise that social media posts cited.
What a September 2026 noise survey found
Some social media posts cite a survey that two nonprofit organizations, Quiet Communities and Science for Georgia, published in September 2026. Out of 103 people surveyed near data centers or cryptomining facilities, 83% reported hearing the noise they produce inside their homes. The organizations also note that some equipment can produce noise above 80 decibels.
The survey involved a small group and includes no reference to measuring noise at a Texas ranch. Only about 20% of respondents could answer questions about livestock, which was too little data to analyze. Therefore, the survey did not provide evidence linking data center noise to cattle stillbirths.
Snopes contacted experts in cattle reproduction, acoustics and electromagnetic fields for comment on the rumor about the calf stillbirths in Texas. We are awaiting their responses.
For further reading, we have previously investigated numerous other claims about data centers.

Voters approved Question 1, which places protections for first- and second-trimester abortions in the state constitution. However, it also gives the state Legislature the power to pass some restrictions on abortions in the third trimester.
As the results of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections rolled in, posts on social media suggested that Virginia voters had approved an amendment to the state's constitution that would allow, as one X post put it, "the abortion of babies who are minutes from being born."
Snopes readers also contacted us looking for more information about the supposed vote.
The claim is false.
The posts used common anti-abortion framing to create a misleading description of a real proposal on the ballot, Question 1. The measure, which voters overwhelmingly approved, does enshrine in Virginia's constitution an individual's right to receive an abortion.
However, the measure explicitly contains an exception allowing the state Legislature to pass laws that restrict access to some abortions in the third trimester of pregnancy. Because this exception exists, Virginia voters did not approve "abortions up to birth."
It's also worth reviewing basic facts about abortions — doing so reveals that the anti-abortion posts are using dramatic language to attack a strawman argument they created.
The strawman argument
The misleading posts do not mention how far into their pregnancies women generally receive abortions. That's because the language of the claim relies on the idea that late-term abortions are a common practice, while the medical data shows they are quite uncommon.
According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the premier professional association for OB/GYNs in the U.S., less than 1% of abortions in the country are performed in the third trimester, and about 1% of abortions are performed after the woman has reached 21 weeks of pregnancy. The nonprofit Guttmacher Institute, a highly reputable source of information on abortion data, estimated that doctors performed 1.13 million abortion procedures throughout the country in 2025. Therefore, only about 11,300 abortions total were performed after the 21-week mark, still seven weeks shy of the third trimester.
In sum, late-term abortions are incredibly rare. The ACOG lists the following reasons why they are performed:
- As a result of a fetal diagnosis received later in pregnancy that may have a profound impact on the pregnancy's prognosis
- As a result of a diagnosis related to risks to their own health during pregnancy that did not present until later in pregnancy
- Not recognizing that they were pregnant until later in the pregnancy, which may delay them in presenting to start care
- Barriers to obtaining care earlier in pregnancy, including limited financial means, inability to travel, or work or childcare obligations
- A combination of any of the above
To put it another way, doctors, who take an oath to do no harm, perform late-term abortions because the baby is "life-limiting," the mother may not survive the pregnancy or the mother couldn't have the procedure earlier, even if she wanted to.
Question 1, explained
Question 1 enshrines the right to an abortion without any limitations through the first and second trimesters of pregnancy, amongst other reproductive care. This language reinforces the access currently available under Virginia law, according to reproductive healthcare nonprofit Planned Parenthood.
The amendment specifically permits the state Legislature to enact laws restricting abortions in the third trimester of pregnancy, with caveats. Those laws may not restrict abortions if "the patient's health is at risk or the pregnancy cannot survive," according to the wording on the ballot.
The following paragraph is the actual language of that caveat that will be added to the state constitution, according to Ballotpedia:
Notwithstanding the above, the Commonwealth may regulate the provision of abortion care in the third trimester, provided that in no circumstance shall the Commonwealth prohibit an abortion (i) that in the professional judgment of a physician is medically indicated to protect the life or physical or mental health of the pregnant individual or (ii) when in the professional judgment of a physician the fetus is not viable.
In addition, Question 1 also protects both patients and medical providers from punishment for providing or receiving abortion care.

Resource group for Education and Advocacy for Community Health (REACH), a not-for-profit organisation working to strengthen the tuberculosis (TB) response in India, has been awarded the Kochon Prize 2026, becoming the first civil society, non-profit organisation from India to receive this prestigious global recognition for its contributions to combating TB, a press release said.
Presented by the Kochon Foundation, an independent Korean non-profit foundation, in partnership with the Stop TB Partnership, the Kochon Prize recognises individuals and organisations that have made significant contributions to the fight against TB. The 2026 Kochon Prize is shared by REACH, the Centre for Health Solutions, Kenya, and the Marshall Islands TB Control Program. Previous winners from India include L.S. Chauhan (2006), head of the Revised National TB Control Programme, the Indian Council of Medical Research (2017) and Molbio Diagnostics (2024). The award was presented at the Stop TB Partnership Board Meeting held in Indonesia on November 5, 2026.
“Treat the person, not the disease - our journey with TB communities has been just that. We realised early on that overcoming barriers to care means addressing more than clinical needs - it means recognising social, community, family, mental health and situational challenges. That is the essence of integrated care: seeing the whole person, understanding their realities, and doing whatever it takes to ensure that no one is left behind,” said Nalini Krishnan, chairperson and co-founder, REACH.
“REACH is a remarkable and rare organisation that has been consistently ahead of the curve in terms of public health action, and particularly in the field of TB. A women-led organisation, they genuinely care about the people they’re supporting, beyond the numbers, data and reports to donor. However, they combine this with a robust scientific and technical approach and a shrewd understanding of the public health landscape in the country,” said Soumya Swaminathan, chairperson, M. S. Swaminathan Research Foundation and former chief scientist, WHO, who nominated REACH for the award.
“This recognition is testimony to the dedication of the community health workers, TB Nanbans and TB Champions who work alongside us, and to the families affected by TB and non-communicable diseases (NCDs) who have placed their trust in us. We are deeply grateful to their unwavering commitment and fortitude, and are energised to do more to help facilitate equitable access to health,” said Ramya Ananthakrishnan, director, REACH.

In Maine, a new approach to practicing medicine in the sky
Clipboard in hand, pilot Will Bradbury stands near a helicopter at LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters. He's running down emergency landing tips with his crew.
"If we need to get out quickly because of smoke or fire, just watch the terrain so that you're not walking uphill into the rotors," he reminds flight nurse Denise Saucier and paramedic Brian Merklin.
The team is getting ready to take off on a medical transport flight. Saucier folds herself into the compact helicopter. She's worked for the air ambulance service for seven years and still calls it a dream job.
Dream job or not, the life of a flight clinician is hard and, given the headwinds slamming rural healthcare, getting harder.
Since 2015, demand for medical flights in Maine has doubled. In 2025, LifeFlight crews flew 3,031 flights, more than one every three hours. This year, demand is up another 10%.
Nationwide, air medical services are filling the gaps left behind as rural hospitals close, convert to outpatient-only rural emergency hospitals, or stop offering unprofitable services like labor and delivery.
And, as Medicaid cuts estimated by the Congressional Budget Office at $911 billion over ten years take effect, it's going to get worse. Hundreds more rural hospitals or maternity departments are at immediate risk of closing. With every closure, medical care gets further away.
And, increasingly, ground ambulance stations, many of which are also struggling to keep their doors open, can't meet the need. That leaves flight clinicians like Saucier and Merklin seeing more patients every day.
"We're seeing this across the board. The need for air medical services is increasing year over year," says Nicholas George. He runs the ETHOS Database, a national tracking system for air medical programs.
When the rural health care system breaks, EMS — on the ground and, increasingly, in the air — is the backstop.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Healthcare of last resort
Every week or two, Saucier finds herself on a flight to one of Maine's thousands of islands. Occasionally, crews even land in the state's vast forests and mountains, then take snowmobiles to reach patients.
But "scene calls" to roadside — or trailside — accidents are less than 10% of LifeFlight's transports. (They're a higher percentage in urban areas.)
Most are interfacility transports, like today's. They'll stabilize a patient at a small, local hospital and fly them to a larger, better resourced one.
Saucier glances out the window for hazards. The view still reminds her of the role the organization plays in Maine, one of the country's most rural states.
"You go so long of a distance without seeing any houses, any roads," Saucier says. "It really hits home how rural Maine is and how necessary EMS is in the state."
And the pressure is on air ambulances as ground services in Maine are increasingly strained. The system is so fragmented that patients can fall through the cracks. Last year, a woman in a small northern Maine town died while the county dispatch center called 10 ambulance services. None responded.
Air ambulance services, though, come with unique challenges, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. It's been difficult to retain staff with the medical expertise to treat everything from heart attacks to injuries to fragile newborns, and who can stick with the demanding job without burning out.
Almost a quarter of ground-based EMS workers leaves the field every year. While there's no comprehensive staffing data for air medical services, flight clinicians face a slew of unique stresses, including dangerous conditions; long shifts and unpredictable hours; ever-increasing training and certification requirements; and significant mental health burdens. And then there's the pay, which is low throughout emergency medical services.
For years, LifeFlight retained only 60% to 70% of its workers, says CEO Joe Kellner.
"This is a really hard job," Kellner says. "By their job description, they are seeing people on their worst day, over and over again."
Training elite clinicians
This year, for the first time in nine years, LifeFlight is nearly fully staffed. One of the nation's handful of independent nonprofit air medical companies, LifeFlight has taken an innovative approach to the problems that plague the industry, including a combination of better training, higher pay and in-house mental health support.
Mike Abernethy, an EMS expert and retired emergency medicine professor at the University of Wisconsin, considers the company one of a handful of model programs for the industry. LifeFlight of Maine is a nonprofit, unlike much of the industry, which is dominated by for-profit businesses with reputations for charging exorbitant prices.
"There's just absolutely no comparison in the aviation and medical quality of these programs" versus an average for-profit air medical business, Abernethy argues.
When Kellner, a paramedic himself, became CEO in 2023, he began addressing the recruitment and retention problems. What LifeFlight calls the "Critical Care Academy," a six- to eight-month orientation program, is intended to address both issues.
Emergency critical care advances quickly. So most clinicians need regular education, both to remain successful on the job and to get hired in the first place.
On another day at headquarters, four instructors sit in a claustrophobic control room. Through a window looking into what appears to be a hospital room, paramedics Daniel Horne and Brad Alleger are undergoing an annual skills assessment, a simulation of a real-life medical crisis.
Dr. Dave Saquet turns on a mic and coughs. "It's hard to breathe," he whispers urgently. "It hurts everywhere."
His voice seems to be coming from the patient — a breathing, bleeding mannequin lying on a hospital bed.
"What happened to you?" Horne asks.
"My house was on fire," Saquet chokes out.
A wall monitor displays the patient's vital signs — which Saquet is manipulating on his laptop.
Medics and nurses here do simulations often, both to pass the Critical Care Academy, and also to stay up to date on occasional but critical events, like emergency births, newborn resuscitation, and burns. Before the assessment ends, the paramedics will have tried and failed to intubate the patient. After that "failure," they performed an emergency procedure to enable breathing, switching from the mannequin to a pig trachea.
Because it's hard to find recruits qualified enough for the rigorous training, the company also started a mentorship program for people considering applying. Some even attend the academy, gaining skills even if they'll never work for LifeFlight.
Success comes slowly: Recently, LifeFlight hired one of last year's mentees.
Experiments
Kellner instituted an unusual change that he says even nurses endorse: LifeFlight raised paramedics' pay to match flight nurses' compensation. Industrywide, paramedics make less. That keeps costs down, which is why pay equity is rare. Kellner believes the change has helped with recruitment.
Another experiment: LifeFlight hired a full-time mental-health counselor.
EMS workers' rates of post-traumatic stress injury, anxiety and depression are more thanfive times higher than the average American's.
"That has led people to leave this profession," Kellner says.
That was true for paramedic Brian Merklin, who was working for a different service in Nevada during the pandemic.
"We got hit really hard," he says. "The crews were just flying nonstop. We did four-day shifts, so for 96 hours we were just going, going, going."
About a third of the staff quit, he says. "They were getting air medical service plus COVID, right in the teeth."
Eventually, Merklin too needed a break. He left the profession for a few years. Then, when he felt the urge to fly again, he found LifeFlight.
Today's trip
The helicopter, which took off from Bangor, lands on a community hospital's rooftop helipad. Merklin and Saucier hurry to the patient's side. Most LifeFlight patients are unconscious or too ill to consent to share their stories, so the details are private. The injuries are shocking. If this patient doesn't get to a trauma center quickly, they might die.
Merklin and Saucier are unfazed.
But it's this kind of incessant trauma exposure that makes mental health support for first responders so invaluable.
Merklin serves on a peer support team.
"There's a lot of lip service paid … to the cost to your mental health in this profession. But this is the only place I have ever worked that actually provided support," he says. "I would love to see it take hold in other areas."
If counseling keeps two or three people from leaving, it's a wise investment, Kellner argues: "The cost of training somebody new into our organization is about $100,000."
As both air and ground EMS become even more essential, the task is to recruit and keep more people like Merklin and Saucier.
Because, if hundreds more hospitals do close, highly trained EMS workers may be the only people standing between patients dying and getting the care they need.

Violence erupts in Bangladesh as ousted PM's supporters stage protest
- Published
Police in Bangladesh have fired tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse supporters of the deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who are demanding her return to the country.
A police vehicle was set on fire in Gopalganj district, where the banned student wing of Hasina's Awami League party clashed with security forces.
Nationwide protests by pro-Hasina activists started a day after the former leader said she had requested a passport to return to Bangladesh from exile in India.
The demonstrations by the student wing, called Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), are seen as the first organised show of force by Hasina's supporters since she was ousted in August 2024 following a huge uprising against her rule.
Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.
Several passenger vehicles were also set on fire in various parts of Bangladesh in the run up to the protest.
A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.
Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region.
Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere.
"Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.
"Our supporters were not responsible for the violent incidents. They were carried out by unknown miscreants. We believe in peaceful protests," a senior leader of the BCL, who is now in exile in a foreign country, said.
Hasina fled to neighbouring India two years ago following a massive uprising, bringing an end to her 15-year reign.
Opposition parties accused Hasina of jailing political rivals, supressing dissent and overseeing widespread human rights abuses. She always denied the charges.
The United Nations has estimated up to 1,400 people were killed, most by gunfire from security forces, during the anti-government protests in 2024.
The activities of the Awami League were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.
A special Bangladeshi tribunal last year sentenced her to death in absentia after being found guilty of crimes against humanity.
She has denied all the charges, calling the trial "biased and politically motivated".
Despite the death penalty threat, Hasina said she wanted to return to Bangladesh in December and requesteded the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to issue her with a passport.
But the Bangladeshi government said the country would not provide a passport to her and called her "a terrorist".
"She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign affairs minister, said.
"Should we treat her like an ordinary commercial traveller and tell her to come and visit her in-laws' residence?" Kobir asked.
A state prosecutor in Bangladesh on Tuesday said the verdict would be executed if she came back, saying she had missed the opportunity to appeal.
Awami League leaders allege that in the past two years hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces.
Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted.

How good is Hamilton and how long can he stay in F1? - Q&A
- Published
McLaren's Lando Norris converted pole position into a race win at a wet-dry-wet Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday.
Max Verstappen came through the field to take second after starting at the back of the grid because of an engine penalty, while his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar was on the podium in third.
Mercedes sealed the constructors' championship for the first time since 2021 at Interlagos following a fourth-place finish for George Russell and fifth for new world champion Kimi Antonelli.
Here BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
Lewis Hamilton has just completed his 400th F1 grand prix, with more than 100 of these races having him on pole position. There are drivers with a better pole percentage than this, so just how good is he and for how much longer can he stay at the top? - Clive
Lewis Hamilton is unquestionably one of the greatest Formula 1 drivers in history.
He's statistically the most successful - with the most race wins and pole positions.
He's tied with Michael Schumacher for the most championships with seven, and many would - and do - argue he should have eight, given the controversy of the mishandled final race of the 2021 season.
Greatness as an F1 driver is about more than raw statistics, but even so Hamilton has consistently proved to be at the very highest level, with a series of outstanding drives in races that will go down in history as some of the greatest ever.
Examples of those would be the 2008 British Grand Prix and the 2021 Brazilian Grand Prix, along with many others.
All of this should go without saying.
He's also won races in nearly all his seasons - the only exceptions being 2022, 2023 and 2025.
There is no question that, within the context of his remarkable career, Hamilton struggled relatively in the era of 'ground-effect' cars from 2022-25.
He was beaten by Mercedes team-mate George Russell in two of their three seasons together, and looked a shadow of his usual self against Charles Leclerc in 2025.
Those performances led some to question why a driver formerly famed and lauded for his adaptability did not seem as able to adapt to the driving style required of those cars.
And that, in turn, led to questions as to whether the fact he apparently could not was related to his age - he is now 41.
But with this year's cars, Hamilton is back in much more familiar territory, is performing extremely well again and is neck-and-neck with Leclerc.
Those questions about the four years from 2022-25 will remain just that, but there is no doubt Hamilton is sensitive to them. He has referenced them a number of times this year, including last weekend in Brazil, when the topic of his 400th race came up.
"I never ever thought that I would be reaching numbers like that," he said. "It's crazy because I still feel young, and regardless of the things that people say, you saw my pole last week, I still have the pace, I still have the speed and I still have the dedication, which is most important and the focus. For me, that number is kind of irrelevant."
Longevity in sport depends on many factors, and each athlete is different.
On the face of it, however, there is no obvious reason why, on an age front, Hamilton cannot continue for a good few more years - Fernando Alonso is 45 and is still performing at an extremely high level, as he proved yet again in Brazil at the weekend.
Hamilton has said he wants to race at least until F1 returns to Africa, which will not be until 2030 at the earliest, when he, too, will be 45.
For that, he will need at least one new contract, as his current one with Ferrari is believed to end next year.

  - Published1 day ago
We heard, and saw, a lot of 'yo-yo racing' in the first half of the season. This seems to have reduced. What has changed? - Ali
'Yo-yo racing' was a term coined at the start of this year for a new character of on-track battle in which cars swapped positions multiple times over a series of laps.
This was caused by the new power-units introduced this year, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power and are fundamentally energy starved.
The operations of these engines included 'overtake' and 'boost' modes.
'Boost' is a facility for a driver to demand extra electrical energy whenever he wants, as long as the battery has charge.
'Overtake' mode gives a driver following within one second of a car in front an extra 0.5MJ of energy recovery and deployment capability per lap.
At the start of the season, this - combined with the teams' and drivers' relative unfamiliarity with the new technology - led to a number of examples of yo-yo racing in the early grands prix.
This is where one driver has more electrical energy available, uses it to overtake, whereupon the driver behind now has more and overtakes back, and so on.
This has been less prevalent recently and there are two reasons for that.
Primarily, the tracks in recent weeks have been less 'energy-starved'. And the more energy-starved a car is at a track, the more likelihood there is for yo-yo racing.
The overtaking comes from the variation in energy levels, and being at tracks where drivers can't use all the energy they want all the time.
On top of that, drivers and teams have now been using the engines for a season and are much more on top of how to use them, and therefore how not to leave themselves vulnerable.
At the same time, rule changes have been introduced since the start of the season to reduce the impact of energy starvation, such as imposing energy limits on tracks where it is a major issue. This flattens out the peaks and troughs in energy availability.
And into next year and beyond further steps are being taken to make the engines more "normal" in operation - by changing the energy split to 60-40 in two steps by 2028.
This is almost certainly going to lead to the frequency of overtaking reducing, while the drivers become happier with how the cars feel to drive.
Whether the audience perceives that as better or worse racing remains to be seen.
What is the reason a driver like Esteban Ocon would want to stay in F1 as a reserve driver rather than commit to race elsewhere in a different series? All F1 drivers are very, very good, and presumably would be in demand, so why not compete elsewhere, win some races, be a hero? - Stephen
When it became clear that Ocon was not going to be retained by Haas next year, and that his options for a race seat seemed to have evaporated, the Frenchman was insistent that his F1 career was not over.
Staying involved in the sport as a reserve driver - if he can find a spot - is the best way to keep current in the sport.
It means a driver is available should either of the race drivers at whatever team he can land with be incapacitated.
It keeps him familiar with current F1 machinery through simulator sessions, and perhaps driving recent cars.
And it simply keeps his face around and in people's minds.
Go and race elsewhere, whether it's Indycar, Formula E or endurance racing, for example, and it's much easer to be forgotten, or for people to assume your time has come and gone.
Why hasn't Liam Lawson been confirmed for 2027 despite his brilliant driving this year? - Pete
The decision as to which two of the three drivers in contention to drive for Racing Bulls next year is in the hands of the Red Bull shareholders Chalerm Yoovidhya and Mark Mateschitz, and Red Bull's ultimate F1 boss Oliver Mintzlaff.
Lawson is in contention along with his current team-mate Arvid Lindblad and F2 front-runner Nikola Tsolov.
The old Red Bull way - under Helmut Marko and Christian Horner - would have been to jettison Lawson now on the basis he has had his chance in the lead team and is unlikely to be considered for another, and put in Tsolov as the next cab off the rank, so to speak.
The counter-argument is that leaves two unproven talents going against each other next year, which would leave Red Bull not knowing what they are looking at.
Better, this argument goes, to keep Lawson and Lindblad together next year for a fuller reading on Lindblad, with Lawson as a known-quantity benchmark, then drop whoever performs least well at the end of 2027 in favour of Tsolov.
In not so many words, Racing Bulls team boss Alan Permane made this second argument in Brazil at the weekend.
"Red Bull's had a very successful young driver programme," he said, "and I don't want to be critical of it, but I think if you guys are critical of it, maybe sometimes the drivers haven't been able to have enough time to settle, or maybe some snap decisions have been made.
"We're trying to apply a little bit of science, and that takes some time.
"So we are looking at everything and studying, analysing, and time is on our side. We're not in a rush to do anything, and I'm very confident the right decision will be made.
"I realise it's frustrating for our drivers. I realise it's frustrating for everyone else, but we want to get it right, and we will get it right."
Interlagos consistently produces thrilling races. Should F1 be doing more to preserve racing at 'classic' circuits? - Nathan
F1 faces a difficult balancing act with the calendar.
It wants a truly global world championship. It wants exciting racing that engages audiences. It wants a good mix of circuit types for variation and interest. And it wants to make money.
When it comes to 'classic' race tracks, that's not always an easy equation to solve.
The main reason is that the classic tracks are often in countries that are not able or willing to pay the big-money fees.
The same model and restrictions do not apply in autocracies that want to use races for national self-promotion, hence they can and do tend to pay bigger fees.
But F1 is well aware of the importance of classic circuits, and it wants to ensure it keeps the best of them.
As a consequence, F1 does make compromises that ensure the likes of Monaco, Silverstone, Spa and Suzuka stay on the calendar, even if not every year any more in the case of Spa.
At the same time, the sport makes a considerable effort to make new tracks as interesting as possible. Some are more successful than others, but that's always going to be the case.
Take Las Vegas, for example. It is far from the greatest track in terms of driving challenge, and was hardly likely to be given it is made up of streets in an American city, but it makes up for that with spectacle and kudos.
As for forthcoming permanent circuits, former F1 driver Alex Wurz - the designer of the new tracks in Qiddiyah, Saudi Arabia, and Rwanda, which are both due to come on to the calendar in the next few years - has done his level best to ensure they are fulfilling and challenging for drivers and promote good racing.

Have you heard of the names Kadambini Ganguly and Anandibai Joshi? Considered India’s first female doctors, these names have often been looked past in the pages of history and even medical textbooks. Today, let’s talk about the story of Kadambini Ganguly — India’s first practising lady doctor.
It was in 1861 that Brahmo reformer and headmaster Braja Kishore Basu had a daughter. She was named Kadambini Basu. Young Kadambini, despite hailing from a community that did not necessarily support women’s education like many others at the time did, received an education at the Brahmo Eden Female School and later at the Hindu Mahila Vidyalaya.
As the daughter of someone who organised and fought for women’s emancipation, Kadambini went on to study in college and became the first woman to pass the University of Calcutta entrance examination. In 1882, she passed the examination for the Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree along with Chandramukhi Basu from the University of Calcutta, making her and Chandramukhi the first female graduates in the country.
Entry into medicine
Wanting to study medicine, Kadambini decided to enrol at the Calcutta Medical College after graduation. She was, however, believed to have been unable to receive the BMC certificate due to a shortage of a couple of marks. She did receive the GBMC (Graduate of Bengal Medical College) degree, though, in 1886. Thus, she became the first Indian woman to be allowed to practice Western medicine.
Around 1888, Kadambini started working at the Lady Dufferin Hospital for a monthly salary of 300 rupees. She had even gone to Nepal to treat British royalty. Along with pursuing medicine, she was also politically quite vocal and active. Around 1899, Kadambini was one of the first women delegates elected to the Fifth Session of the Congress in Bombay and the next year, she won to become the first women speaker at the Congress.
She also served as the president of the Transvaal Indian Association, founded by Gandhiji’s colleague Henry Pollock. She was a member of the Women’s Conference held in Calcutta and even presided over the General Brahmo Samaj session in Calcutta.
A doctor, wife and mother
Around 1883, Kadambini married Dwarakanath Ganguly (thus the change in name from Kadambini Bose to Kadambini Ganguly in many documents). Dwarakanath Ganguly was a Bengali Brahmo reformer, educator, journalist, and pioneer of women’s rights in British India.
She was a mother to eight children and is often said to have been deft in needlework. She became a practising doctor while equally devoting herself to family and household affairs, an action which was deemed impossible by many in the era.
Despite having being burdened with domestic chores, like most women of that time, Kadambini still managed to smash the glass ceilings and societal stereotypes in both her professional and personal life.
A name which should not be forgotten in the course of time, Dr Kadambini is a reason many of us are able to pursue our passion — in medicine and in life.

A video circulating on X, bearing the logo of M World, purports to show Russian foreign minister Sergey Viktorovich Lavrov saying that India is merely an oil-trading partner to Russia and that the two countries share only a commercial relationship. In the video, Lavrov is also heard claiming that India has no right to interfere in Russia’s foreign policy or advise Moscow on matters concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States or any other country.
Supreme Court advocate and activist Prashant Bhushan shared the video on his X account (@pbhushan1), which he later deleted. In his post, he criticized the Indian government and questioned what kind of advice external affairs minister S Jaishankar gave to Russia.
Another X account, Diya Kapoor, also shared the video with the similar claim of Sergey Lavrov drawing clear boundaries about the relationship with India.
🚨🇷🇺🇮🇳 RUSSIA DRAWS A CLEAR LINE!
“India is a trading partner, nothing more. We supply oil, and India pays for it. This commercial relationship does not give New Delhi the right to dictate or interfere in Russia’s foreign policy.”
Sergey Viktorovich ⚠️🌍 https://t.co/uX1x0adl0G
— Diya kapoor (@DiyaKapoor113) November 2, 2026
Some X accounts also shared this video with the claim of Sergey Lavrov dismissing India.
Fact Check
After a closer examination of the video, the movements of Sergey Lavrov while speaking appear unnatural and seem out of sync with the audio. This suggests that the clip may have been edited or manipulated. Using this as a lead, we performed a Google reverse image search on several keyframes from the video and found a video with the same background and clothing uploaded by M WORLD on October 31.
A comparison of the two videos shows that Sergey Lavrov’s clothing, background, head movements, and hand gestures are the same, with only the audio being different. Even the ‘M World’ YouTube channel logo appeared in both videos, confirming that the original video had been digitally manipulated. Both videos also feature the exact same glitch at the same moment.
In the original video, Sergey Lavrov is seen refusing the reports from Ukrainian officials claiming that Russian President Vladimir Putin refused to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and stating if Zelenskyy wants a direct meeting, he must travel to Moscow, where Russia will guarantee his safety and security.
Media outlet DW News posted the original video on October 31 showing the conversation about President Putin and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy meeting.
Furthermore, the official X account of the Russian Embassy in India, Russia in India (@RusEmbIndia) has also debunked the video. “Please stop copying silly AI fakes,” it said in a comment to the X post by Diya Kapoor.
@DiyaKapoor113 Please stop copying silly AI fakes
— Russia in India 🇷🇺 (@RusEmbIndia) November 3, 2026
Union government’s official MEA fact check account, too, flagged the post as fake.
Fake Alert!!! 🚨🚨🚨
The video of the Russian Foreign Minister being used in this post is fake! https://t.co/jpEX6qu19p
— MEA FactCheck (@MEAFactCheck) November 3, 2026
To sum up, the viral video claiming that Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov publicly dismissed India’s diplomatic standing is completely false and an AI-generated deepfake. The original footage contains a briefing regarding Russia-Ukraine relations, and there is no mention of India.

The parents of a 13-year-old girl have sued Google claiming she planned a potential suicide and funeral using its AI technology on a school-issued computer.
Filed Monday in a California court, the complaint is the first known case accusing Google of negligence related to AI integrations on Chromebooks, the tech giant's low-cost laptops used by millions of students in the United States and around the world.
The teenager was not able to access Google's Gemini app, nor OpenAI's ChatGPT, because they were blocked by her school. She was nonetheless still able to use Google's search engine, which contains AI-powered tools.
Those features were notably not among the tools that Google announced this week will be disabled by default for students.
"Schools should turn search off and keep it off until Google removes AI mode from search or ensures that every single student is always safe when they're interacting with AI," Andrew Liddell, one of the family's attorneys, told AFP on Thursday.
The complaint alleges that the child had been a "happy 13-year-old girl" in North Carolina who received great grades, played music and participated in Girl Scouts.
Despite "no history" of mental illness, within months of using Google's AI-powered search on her school laptop, she began a "quiet spiral into a severe psychological crisis" according to the complaint.
On March 17, the school's monitoring software flagged a document titled "Funeral," and the school notified her parents.
Her mother then saw the child writing a farewell letter in real-time after logging into her daughter's account, and her father intervened.
"We are reviewing the claims in the lawsuit and we take this very seriously," Google spokesperson Jose Castaneda told AFP.
Google argues that AI mode includes safeguards against self-harm and attempts to bypass them.
But the child "was able to keep going back over and over and over again," Liddle said. "Whatever safeguards they think they put in place were obviously insufficient."
Developers of fast-evolving AI technology are facing a litany of similar lawsuits in the US.
OpenAI faces several wrongful death suits, including from the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, a teenager who committed suicide allegedly using methods advised by ChatGPT.

Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted having an affair two days after the FT reported his alleged romantic relationship with a woman the US intelligence community believes was working as a spy for China.
Huang revealed the affair in an internal message to employees on Sunday that was obtained by the FT.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang said in the message. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
In a separate statement, Nvidia said its board would open an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Huang said he would fully cooperate. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust,” he said. “I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”
The FT reported on Friday that the US believed Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.
American officials this year wrote a memo, based on information from US intelligence, which said the Nvidia boss had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the chipmaker, according to people familiar with the document.
The affair is a damaging blow to the Nvidia chief, who in recent years has become the face of the AI boom, one of the technology’s loudest champions, and transformed the Silicon Valley group into the first $5 trillion company.

- The claim that Apple Maps replaced current satellite imagery of Gaza with outdated imagery showing buildings still intact is unfounded.
- The rumor circulated on social media, with some posts comparing Apple Maps' imagery of the area with images from other services, such as Google Maps.
- We confirmed that Apple Maps does show outdated images of Gaza, but we found no indication that the service had ever hosted images of the area that captured the destruction that has taken place since October 2023. Rather, it appeared that Apple Maps simply lagged behind its competitors in terms of providing up-to-date imagery.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Apple seeking information regarding its satellite images of Gaza, as well as to a parody social media page that may have started the claim, and are waiting for responses.
As Israel's war on Gaza played a crucial role in some 2026 U.S. midterm election candidates' campaigns, a claim circulated online that Apple Maps had replaced current satellite imagery of Gaza with outdated imagery showing buildings still intact.
In the more than three years since militant group Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, Israel has decimated Gaza's landscape and reportedly killed upwards of 74,000 people in what the United Nations has deemed a genocide. Social media users accused Apple Maps of "whitewashing" a genocide by presenting an inaccurate picture of the situation in Gaza.
One X post read, "Apple putting all the destroyed buildings back in Gaza on Maps isn't just wrong to do because it's an inaccurate depiction, it's terrifying. If a company with as much notoriety and influence as Apple wants to whitewash a genocide, what's next? Shame on you, Apple." Other posts expressed similar sentiments.
Although users claimed Apple had intentionally "replaced" current satellite imagery to make buildings appear they way they used to, this claim is unfounded. We did not find proof (such as a screenshot of Apple Maps imagery of Gaza showing the updated landscape) that Apple had updated the imagery at any point since at least October 2023, if not before.
As of this writing, Apple Maps imagery of Gaza is outdated compared to other services, such as Google Maps, but it has historically lagged in certain regions.
We did not find evidence that Apple Maps publicly dates its satellite imagery, but it's likely the imagery available as of this writing predates October 2023. We compared the current Apple Maps imagery to Google Earth imagery from August 2023 and October 2023, and some buildings that were destroyed by October 2023 still appear standing on Apple Maps.
(Apple Maps and Google Earth, Snopes illustration.)
We reached out to some of the social media users who circulated the claim, and they responded that they did not have definitive proof Apple had intentionally swapped out its imagery.
It's possible that the claim originated on a parody account. An X post (archived) from Nov. 1 by user @RabbiJeffx read: "JUST IN: Apple Maps has put all the buildings back in Gaza, because the easiest solution to a genocide is to pretend it isn't happening. Image on the right is from Google, showing the current reality." The user's bio describes itself as a parody account for memes and satire. We reached out to the account to ask if it was the origin of the claim and will update this story if we hear back.
Users have long noted the lack of Apple Maps' availability certain regions. We previously reported on Apple Maps' lack of updated global coverage when social media users claimed Apple Maps had removed the names of small towns and villages in Lebanon from its coverage amid Israel's bombing the small country to its north.
Snopes contacted Apple seeking information regarding its coverage of Gaza and did not immediately hear back. We will update this article if we receive a response.

- The claim that a Texas hospital attempted to kill a COVID-19 patient after learning she was unvaccinated is unproven.
- The rumor stems from the account of the patient, Gail Seiler, who is an anti-vaccination advocate.
- Seiler claimed in multiple interviews that she was abused and mistreated by the staff at Medical City Plano hospital, and alleged that they tried to kill her. We are unable to independently verify this without other primary evidence.
- Citing privacy laws, Medical City Plano declined to speak about Seiler's case, but it rejected "any suggestion that our hospital or its caregivers would intentionally harm a patient or withhold medically necessary care."
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Seiler and are waiting for her response.
On Sept. 28, U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., held a roundtable discussion with former patients, hospital staff and families, detailing alleged mistreatment they experienced from "rigid hospital protocols" during the COVID-19 pandemic. Many people online shared the statement of one former patient, claiming a Texas hospital tried to kill her by denying her food and water, among other forms of mistreatment.
The clip, shared on Facebook and X (archived), showed Gail Seiler, a former COVID-19 patient, claiming she was mistreated and abused after hospital staff learned she was unvaccinated. One post stated: "A Texas hospital allegedly tried to kill unvaccinated patient Gail Seiler by starving her for 12 days, denying her water for 7 days, and telling her husband she was going to die."
In a recorded statement at Johnson's panel, Seiler described her 2021 stay at Medical City Plano hospital. She said she was denied food for 12 days and water for seven days, and that staff treated her as though her death was inevitable after finding out she was unvaccinated. In a separate interview from 2025, she accused the hospital staff of trying to kill her.
Because the allegation is based solely on Seiler's account and we do not have other primary evidence, we leave this claim unrated.
The hospital sent us the following statement over email:
Federal patient privacy laws prevent us from discussing or disclosing information about an individual's medical care or even confirming if someone was a patient.
However, we strongly reject any suggestion that our hospital or its caregivers would intentionally harm a patient or withhold medically necessary care. Such characterizations are fundamentally inconsistent with our mission, our clinical standards and the dedication of the physicians, nurses and other healthcare professionals who care for our patients.
Snopes also reached out to Seiler to learn more and will update this article accordingly.
During the September panel, Seiler and her husband shared the following testimony about her December 2021 visit to Medical City Plano, when she was hospitalized with COVID-19 (emphasis ours):
What I experienced [at the hospital] changed my life forever and exposed me to a system that abandoned individual patient care in favor of rigid protocols, coercion, isolation, and fear.
When the hospitalist in the ICU learned that I was unvaccinated, he looked directly at me and said, "I'm so sorry, Mrs. Seiler, but you're going to die." From that moment forward, I was treated as if my death was expected and inevitable.
When I was in the ER, the emergency room, the doctor and primary-care nurse said that they follow the FLCCC protocol [a nonstandard protocol developed by a fringe doctors' group that has dubious efficacy against COVID-19]. Once they discovered my vaccination status, however, my options became limited to remdesivir and a ventilator. I repeatedly requested treatments such as ivermectin, hydroxychloroquine, budesonide, zinc, vitamin C and other early interventions, but those requests were denied. Instead, I faced aggressive pressure to take remdesivir, escalating oxygen protocols, and repeated pressure toward ventilation, even though I remained alert and did not require intubation. I refused sedatives and pain medications because I feared losing consciousness and the ability to advocate for myself. 
I was isolated from my family despite Texas legislation prohibiting these practices. I was denied access to my Catholic priest and my sacraments unless I received remdesivir. Believing I might die, I submitted to one round so that I could receive extreme unction. After my priest left, I refused any further doses.
During my hospitalization, I was denied food for 12 days, water for seven days. I was left naked and uncovered for extended period of time while staff observed me through the ICU windows instead of entering my room. I was designated a DNR or "do not resuscitate." That was against my wishes. I experienced physical, verbal and psychological abuse at the hands of some of the nurses because I was not vaccinated. My family was repeatedly told that I was unsavable and needed to be allowed to die.
My husband, Brad "Huckleberry" Seiler, a former ER nurse and former Army captain, became incredibly, increasingly alarmed by my condition. He believed the oxygen protocols were excessive and that the hospital's actions were accelerating my decline rather than helping me recover.
After I had been hospitalized for 12 days, Brad entered the ICU on Dec. 15, intending to get me out of the hospital and take me home. He was able to enter because the security guard was away from his desk and the ICU doors were standing wide open. Security and nurses followed him in demanding he leave, but Brad refused to leave without me. The hospital called the police in, resulting in a six-hour standoff as officers tried to persuade him to leave.
The day prior, my husband asked the police to perform a welfare check, and I had told the responding officer about the abuse and neglect I had experienced. He told me that they did not have a protocol for that, and he left me there. With the intervention of Col. Allen West and … Texas Sen. Bob Hall and our attorney, we were finally allowed to leave the hospital.
Doctors insisted that my lungs were permanently damaged and that I would not survive outside their care. They were wrong. With the help of Dr. Richard Bartlett, my husband and my daughter, they cared for me at home using treatments that the hospital had previously refused me, and I fully recovered.
Footage of her testimony is available on YouTube and X:
In 2025, Seiler described the same experience in more depth during a video interview hosted by Betrayal Project USA — a nonprofit group led by Seiler — who, before her hospitalization had protested vaccine mandates — to "defend medical freedom." She described taking offense at being asked by a doctor whether she was vaccinated: "As if that had something to do with the treatment." She also said she was not going to take the vaccine — which she called a "clot shot," referring to the debunked conspiracy theory that the COVID-19 vaccine caused blood clots.
She said that after the hospitalist allegedly told her she was going to die, "I knew that they were going to kill me or they were going to try to kill me."
It is unclear whether Seiler pursued legal action against the hospital. A search of Texas court records found no such lawsuits.
Johnson, the senator who hosted the September roundtable, has spread anti-vaccine misinformation, including falsely claiming thousands of deaths are connected to the COVID-19 vaccine, saying thathe was "sticking up for people who choose not to get vaccinated."
Snopes has previously debunked numerous claims about COVID-19 vaccines, including that the AstraZeneca vaccine causes blood clots and that countries' vaccination rates corresponded with their excess death rates.

Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics
- Published
When he started running, Yiech Pur Biel had to compete barefoot. Far from home in a new country, it was the first step towards rebuilding his life as a refugee.
"That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat.
In 2016, Biel made history competing in the 800m event as part of the first Olympic refugee team at the Rio summer Olympics in Brazil.
Ten years on, he's making history again leading the first refugee team for the Youth Olympics as their Chef de Mission.
Joining almost 3,000 athletes, the small team of six will be wanting to make sure their debut counts - but Biel says they're also hoping to send a message that "refugees still need our help".
Hosted in Senegal, Saturday's opening ceremony will launch the first ever Olympic sporting event on African soil.
Africa is home to nearly 45 million displaced people, out of almost 120 million globally, representing the world's biggest displacement crisis.
Biel says for the refugee team, the Youth Olympics is "a chance for them to tell the world and also to represent the population, especially the refugee population, in Africa".
"It's about representing the hope of young people who are living in a refugee camp, who have lost their motivation or their talent."
Biel was a child when he was forced to flee his home in South Sudan after his village was attacked.
He ended up in Kenya, telling BBC Newsbeat: "It traumatised me, starting a new life, being alone in Kakuma," referring to the major refugee settlement close to the border between Kenya and South Sudan.
"But I started a new life, I believe that school helped me a lot. It helped me to interact with young people who faced the same challenges."
The rest of his childhood was spent on the refugee camp where he took an interest in football.
After realising it wasn't the sport for him, he gave running a go during trials set up by the International Olympic Committee - where he raced without shoes.
It made him "believe that if I can work harder by myself, I can achieve", he says.
One of the athletes on the refugee team, Arno Yafunga Botay, also lived at Kakuma after fleeing his home in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2017, when he was six.
Now 15, he will be competing in judo and told BBC Sport Africa he's promised to bring back a gold medal which he'd like to take to the refugee camp.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo," he said.
As for Biel, he says it's an honour to be chosen as the team's Chef de Mission.
"This is so important for them, to learn from my experience as an athlete and also as a refugee who is coming from a refugee camp," he says.
"So this role means a lot to me and also means a lot to those young athletes who are going to compete."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins later, with the opening ceremony on Saturday.

On 02 November 2026, Union Home Minister Amit Shah participated in the BJP’s ‘Loktantra Bachao, Arajakata Hatao’ Maha Padayatra in Hyderabad. Organised by the Telangana unit of the BJP, the march began near the Dr Babu Jagjivan Ram statue in Basheerbagh and concluded at Moazzam Jahi Market. Shah was accompanied by Union Ministers G Kishan Reddy and Bandi Sanjay Kumar, Telangana BJP president N Ramchander Rao, and other party leaders and workers. The march was organised as part of the BJP’s campaign against the INDIA bloc’s allegations concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls (here, here, and here).
Amid this incident, a video is circulating on social media (here, here, and here), claiming it shows people protesting against Union Home Minister Amit Shah and chasing him away during the BJP’s Loktantra Bachao, Arajakata Hatao’ Maha padayatra in Telangana on 02 November 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows people chasing Union Home Minister Amit Shah away during his Telangana padayatra on 02 November 2026.
Fact: The video dates back to July 2023 and shows Rahul Gandhi travelling in a car amid a crowd waving Congress flags in Khammam, Telangana. Rahul Gandhi attended the ‘Telangana Jana Garjana Sabha’ in Khammam on 02 July 2023. On the same day, Amit Shah attended a programme in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, after virtually inaugurating the Akshar River Cruise in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. We found no reports of him visiting Hyderabad that day. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an X post (archived) dated 4 July 2023, featuring a clearer version of the same video. Rahul Gandhi is clearly visible inside the VIP car, with people waving Congress flags. The post’s caption identifies the location as Khammam district in Telangana and states that Rahul Gandhi was returning after delivering a speech. This suggests that the video is from a Congress event held in Telangana.
On 02 July 2023, Rahul Gandhi attended the ‘Telangana Jana Garjana Sabha‘ in Khammam, Telangana, as part of the Congress party’s campaign ahead of the Telangana Assembly elections. Rahul Gandhi also shared videos from the event on his official YouTube channel, while the Congress party issued a press release about the programme.
To verify whether Amit Shah was in Hyderabad on 2 July 2023, we conducted a Google search and found that he was scheduled to attend the ‘Jan-Swabhiman Divas‘ programme at the Indira Gandhi Pratishthan in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, organised to mark the 74th birth anniversary of Dr Sonelal Patel. He attended the event as the chief guest and addressed the gathering between 2:30 pm and 4:30 pm. Earlier that day, he had virtually inaugurated the Akshar River Cruise at the Sabarmati Riverfront in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, through video conferencing. These reports indicate that Amit Shah was engaged in public programmes in Ahmedabad and Lucknow on 2 July 2023; However, we found no reports indicating that he visited Hyderabad that day.
To sum up, this viral video does not show Union Home Minister Amit Shah being chased away during the Hyderabad padayatra on 02 November 2026.

My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India, a country he visited many times on extended trips.
His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company.
Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.
Roy’s other books included A Brief History of Tea (2003), an authoritative account of the complex political and horticultural history of tea, and Outlaw (2010), which looked at the life of India’s “bandit queen” and politician Phoolan Devi, drawing on Roy’s friendship with her before her assassination in 2001. His last book, The Theft of India (2015), documented the rivalry between European colonial powers and the impact this had on Indians themselves.
Roy was born in Evesham, Worcestershire, to Marie (known as Min, nee Bland) and Wilson Moxham. Wilson, a baker, died when Roy was 11, after which Min, a shop worker, raised her three sons under straitened circumstances, often taking in lodgers to make ends meet.
After leaving Prince Henry’s grammar school in Evesham in the early 1960s, Roy put an advert in the Times newspaper that read: “Young man, good A-levels, seeks opportunity in Africa in tobacco or tea.” He received a reply offering him a job on a tea plantation in the British colony of Nyasaland (now Malawi), where, despite his youth, he became a supervisor in charge of 1,000 female tea pickers. Later he switched to selling agricultural machinery across east Africa, particularly in Kenya. In the mid-70s, after 13 years in Africa he returned to the UK, where he opened a gallery in Covent Garden, London, selling African art.
Following a period of squatting in Covent Garden, Roy became an early and longstanding member of the Seven Dials Housing Co-operative, living in one of their properties in that area for most of the rest of his life.
In 1978 he changed direction by studying book and paper conservation at Camberwell College of Arts, after which he worked as a conservator at the Canterbury Cathedral Archive, then at Senate House Library, University of London, where he remained until 2005.
While working, Roy had begun travelling regularly to India from 1992 onwards, and it was on those journeys that he began his three-year search for the Great Hedge. The book was hugely successful, often referenced by historians, writers and artists, and even inspired a Horrible Histories sketch.
After retiring in 2005, Roy lived in India for a number of months each year. His book about Devi, a champion of the Indian poor, came about after he wrote to her when she was in prison. When she was released they arranged a meeting, and became great friends.
Roy is survived by his two brothers, John and Jim, a nephew, three nieces and me.

Australia to set up AI regulator after OpenAI breaches government portal
Canberra will also require AI companies to report cybersecurity incidents

Artificial intelligence companies in Australia would be required to report cybersecurity breaches and face potential reforms to criminal law regarding "serious misconduct", prime minister Anthony Albanese announced on Tuesday, after an OpenAI agent broke into a government website.
The automated agent unlawfully accessed the medical statistics portal of Medicare, Australia's universal health insurance programme, while conducting research into public health spending, the government disclosed in September.
The security incident prompted an immediate official review, with Mr Albanese confirming his administration had accepted all of the recommendations put forward by the inquiry.
The recommendations include “mandatory AI company reporting when it comes to misaligned behaviour or cyber incidents and consideration of reforming criminal law in cases of serious misconduct", Mr Albanese told reporters. "The law needs to get ahead of, and in some cases, make sure that it catches up with what is a very fast-changing world."
OpenAI stated it only discovered the intrusion in August and maintained that the incident was entirely unintentional. The company's internal review concluded there was no evidence that patient records had been accessed by the software. The breach nevertheless escalated tension between Australia and major US technology firms, coming after Canberra refused to grant ChatGPT creator OpenAI and competitor Anthropic exemptions from copyright laws for model training, requiring them instead to negotiate licensing agreements directly with Australian rights holders.
However, both tech firms informed the Australian parliament last month that they would welcome legislation making it mandatory to report data breaches caused by their AI agents, acknowledging that notifying authorities currently remained at their own discretion.
Mr Albanese said his Labor government would set up a specialised AI regulator to oversee security controls throughout the entire development and deployment of AI systems, identify major risks and conduct independent model evaluations.
"The AI safety regulator will be able to enforce significant penalties for AI companies doing the wrong thing," he said.
The mandatory AI safety and security protections will form a central part of the government's proposed AI legislation, which ministers plan to introduce in the parliament next year, according to Mr Albanese.

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.
It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.
See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.
Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.
While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.
Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.
“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.
“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”
Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.
As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.
Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.
“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.
“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”
See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): High Air Quality Index (AQI) levels following Diwali, ranging from the 'very poor' (301-400) to 'severe' (401 and above) categories, pose serious immediate and long-term health risks.
Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and toxic gases released by firecrackers and combustion can particularly affect children, elderly persons, people with allergies or asthma and pregnant women.
Doctors have advised people to stay indoors, especially morning walkers. They have been advised to exercise indoors instead of venturing out. High-risk groups like children, elderly persons, people with allergies or asthma and pregnant women have been advised to stay indoors or wear masks when they go outside.
Dr Lokendra Dave, head of the pulmonary department at Gandhi Medical College (GMC), Bhopal, said, In these conditions, when air quality is very poor, outdoor activities should be restricted. Morning walkers are advised to exercise indoors.
Those who have no option but to work outdoors, such as traffic police personnel and construction workers, should wear masks. PM2.5 particles remain suspended in the air and can enter the lungs, causing serious health concerns.
Dr Priyanath Agrawal, a pulmonologist, said that high-risk groups include children, elderly persons, people with allergies and pregnant women. These groups should be cautious. If they go outside, they should wear masks.
They should try to stay indoors for their protection. They should always avoid sour items, cold drinks and food taken directly from the fridge. They should consume coffee, tea and hot water, said Agrawal.
Common side effects of high post-Diwali AQI
1. Eye, nose and throat irritation: Burning, itchy or watery eyes, a sore or scratchy throat and nasal congestion are often the first signs of exposure.
2. Respiratory symptoms: Persistent coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and shortness of breath occur as fine particles (PM2.5) travel deep into the airways and trigger inflammation.
3. Asthma and COPD flare-ups: People with asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or other lung conditions face a high risk of acute attacks and worsening symptoms.
4. Cardiovascular and neurological strain: Toxic particles can enter the bloodstream from the lungs, causing systemic inflammation, elevated stroke risk and cognitive fatigue.
5. Higher risk for vulnerable groups: Children, older adults and pregnant women experience more severe reactions because their bodies or lungs are more sensitive to airborne toxins.

After months of skirmishing, the Trump administration removed WuXi AppTec, a key contract developer and manufacturer for the pharmaceutical industry, from its list of “Chinese military companies” operating in the U.S.
The Department of Defense took this step to comply with a court ruling last August, according to a notice with the Federal Register. At the time, a U.S. District Court judge temporarily blocked the administration from pursuing the designation after WuXi filed a lawsuit arguing it was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.
Two months earlier, the administration had placed WuXi AppTec on the list over concerns that the company has ties to the Chinese government and military, and that U.S. biotech leadership is at risk due to growing competition from Chinese companies. WuXi is seen by China hawks in Washington as a rising threat to national security.
