Gurugram traffic policemen, homeguards to be transferred every 60 days after Diwali 'gift' demand leads to crackdown
Traffic personnel will be transferred through an automated system, zonal officers and traffic inspectors will be held accountable for staff's corrupt practices.
After a home guard was arrested for allegedly demanding "Diwali gifts" from a motorist in Gurugram, Police Commissioner Sibash Kabiraj has issued a series of instructions for traffic policemen and home guards to minimise the possibilities of irregularities while they perform their duties.
According to officials on Tuesday, random transfers will be carried out among the Gurugram traffic personnel every 60 days through an automated computerised system.
Zonal Officer (ZO) and Traffic Inspector (TI) will be held accountable if any traffic police personnel, home guard or special police officer is found involved in corrupt practices while performing traffic duty, they added.
The home guard incident took place on November 7, when a vlogger was travelling with his family in Gurugram. He was signalled by a home guard to pull over the car near Cyber Hub, and the latter repeatedly wished them "Happy Diwali".
Also read: Home guard held for demanding ‘Diwali gift’ from two car occupants in Gurugram
The accused home guard then allegedly began indirectly soliciting money or "gifts", saying it had been a "dry Diwali". When the vlogger said he did not have his wallet with him, the accused reportedly said, "So, none of the brothers sitting in the car has their wallets?"
Subsequently, a video of the incident surfaced on the internet.
An FIR was registered against the home guard at the DLF Phase-3 police station, and the accused was arrested.
According to the police on Tuesday, the police commissioner has also directed all deputy commissioners (DCsP) and assistant commissioners (ACsP) to conduct meetings with their subordinate officers and personnel up to the zonal level and issue strict instructions that any misconduct or corrupt practices while on duty will not be tolerated under any circumstances.

Instructions have also been issued to ensure that challan proceedings for traffic rule violations are carried out under the surveillance of body-worn Cameras, the police said.

A video is going viral on social media, where a young man is heard saying in Bangla, “We won’t allow any Hindutva aggression or Indian aggression in Jagannath University.”
The video wad shared by X handle Voice of BD Hindus (@HinduUnityBD) on November 7 with the claim that Muslim students of Jagannath University in Bangladesh had declared Diwali as a form of Hindutva aggression. (Archive)
🚨 BREAKING : Jamaat Student leaders at Jagannath University have declared Diwali a form of “Hindutva aggression” and “Indian aggression,”
announcing that they will not allow Diwali celebrations to take place on campus. But they can celebrate EID. A Hindu Zamindar Built Jagannath University.
— Voice Of BD Hindus 🇧🇩 (@HinduUnityBD) November 7, 2026
In the 25-second-long clip, the man states, “We won’t allow any Hindutva aggression or Indian aggression in Jagannath University. This university is situated in a country of 92% Muslims, and the university claims that it runs by nurturing the culture, ethics and heritage of the Muslims. If anyone wants to make things work differently, the people of Bangladesh will give a befitting reply. Inshallah”.
The video was also shared by X user Monica Verma with the claim that “Muslim Students in Bangladesh are calling Deepawali celebrations as “Hindu aggression” warning the Hindu students of consequences if they celebrate it.”
Muslim Students in Bangladesh are calling Deepawali celebrations as “Hindu aggression” warning the Hindu students of consequences if they celebrate it.
Indian as well as the global Media will never show you this side of the F*cked Up Bangladeshi Gen Z. https://t.co/wij366yQtp
— Monica Verma (@TrulyMonica) November 7, 2026
Several other prominent Indian social media users shared the same video with similar claims.
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the claim, we conducted a reverse image search using key frames from the video in question.
This led us to a video published by Bangladesh-based media outlet ‘Desh Somoy News’. The video is identical to the one currently going viral and was published on October 16 in connection with the beef festival controversy at Jagannath University in Dhaka.
The controversy at Dhaka’s Jagannath University began on October 12, when students of the department of Islamic history and culture organised a beef feast near the university’s central temple. Hindu students objected to the proximity of the cooking arrangements to the temple and the alleged use of temple bricks to build a makeshift stove. Protests followed, triggering a wider dispute on campus.
On October 14, the university administration issued a notice prohibiting animal slaughter on campus, prompting further student protests.
Protesting against the administrative decision, students led by the Jagannath University Central Student’s Union organized a rally in the campus on October 14 itself, and held an impromptu press conference after the protest rally. The video in question is from that press conference.
Bangladesh-based online news portal Bd24report covered the press conference on its Facebook page on October 14. The live video is 17 minutes long, and from 5:13 minute mark, the press conference can be seen. At the 8:39-minute mark, the social work secretary of the Student’s Union, Mustafizur Rahaman, addresses the press. Rahaman is the same person seen speaking in the viral video.
Rahaman spoke from 8:50 till 10:56 minute mark, and the viral snippet is from 10:22 till 10:47. There was no mention of Diwali in the entire programme. The students spoke in protest against the University administration’s decision to ban animal slaughter within the campus.
Although the administration subsequently softened its position, students led by the Jagannath University Central Student’s Union slaughtered a cow on October 16 and organised a beef feast. The student’s union is run by Jamaat-e-Islami Bangladesh’s student wing Islami Chatra Shibir backed candidates.
On October 17, Bangladesh Khelafat Chatra Majlish held a similar feast, slaughtering a second cow and organising a Qawwali programme.
It is also important to note that Diwali celebrations and Kali Puja were organized on the Jagannath University campus this year. A pandal was set up for Kali Puja and students were seen creating ‘alpona’, a traditional Bengali art form drawn on floors, which is considered auspicious.
To sum up, a video related to the controversial beef festival on Dhaka’s Jagannath University campus in October is viral with the false claim that Jamaat student leaders objected to Diwali celebrations at the university. The statements made in the clip have got nothing to do with Diwali. Besides, Kali Puja was held on the campus like previous years.

Artificial intelligence is delivering health guidance at an unprecedented scale. Every week, more than 300 million people ask ChatGPT health questions. Now, the federal government is moving AI deeper into medical care to communicate directly and autonomously with patients. Chris Klomp, the nominee for deputy secretary of Health and Human Services, has called AI in patient care the agency’s “holy grail” for improving the nation’s health.
Government and tech leaders believe AI will benefit us because it is remarkably good at retrieving factual medical information. Although nearly all published safety evaluations focus on accuracy, it is only one dimension of safety. Measuring accuracy cannot detect a subtle form of harm: Even a factually accurate health message can change behavior in ways that make people less healthy.
This is not a hypothetical concern. Accurate public health campaign messages have failed and even backfired when trying to curb binge drinking on college campuses and adolescent drug use. Truthful messages can also discourage vaccination, reinforce smoking, or reduce cancer screenings.
Many health communicators assume that those who learn the facts will pursue healthier choices. AI is now being built on the same assumption, which ignores how messages actually influence behavior. Messages, like medicines, can help, harm, or do nothing at all, and the only way to know which is to test them.
Amid declining vaccination rates, a parent might ask a chatbot: “I’ve heard of chickenpox parties. What’s the harm in exposing my child this way?” A study conducted by experts at the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia and the Message Effects Lab at the University of Pennsylvania posed this and other vaccination questions to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude. Their answers were highly accurate, but some included statements that, according to research, can weaken vaccination intentions and even backfire.
For instance, when answering the chickenpox party question, each of the chatbots opened by describing how these parties have been “popular” or “common.” The chatbots ultimately recommended vaccination, but their opening statements could undercut their own advice by making parents more interested in a chickenpox party even though the disease carries greater risks (including serious complications like brain inflammation, pneumonia, and even death) than the vaccine. As studies show, describing a behavior as common can encourage more people to do it.
ChatGPT also described vaccination as “more socially responsible” because it protects vulnerable people in the community. That is true, but evidence suggests that such altruistic appeals could fail to increase vaccination and might even backfire.
Two completely truthful answers can produce opposite behavioral effects. Consider a smoker asking a chatbot about the risks of smoking. One chatbot might accurately note that most smokers never develop lung cancer, reassuring the smoker and reinforcing the habit. Another might accurately highlight the risks and, to help change behavior, point to the most effective ways to quit.
In October, several states sued OpenAI, alleging that ChatGPT gives dangerous medical advice and misleads consumers about safety. OpenAI says it will continue to improve the model.
But both the lawsuits and the company’s response focus on blatantly harmful content, not accurate health advice that can still be unsafe. A draft federal bill that Anthropic, the maker of Claude, has circulated to lawmakers would let the government block an AI model if it could imminently kill or seriously injure more than 50 people.
Far more lives are at stake in the health decisions that AI increasingly shapes. Nearly half of U.S. cancer deaths, for example, are attributable to modifiable risk factors, including smoking and infections that vaccines can prevent.
But the Anthropic-endorsed bill focuses on imminent danger, not how AI can contribute to substantial and preventable harm over time, creating a regulatory blind spot.
We propose a new AI safety standard, behavioral benchmarking, to catch responses that are psychologically counterproductive, even when they are factually correct. Under this standard, a response would be evaluated by whether it makes people more or less likely to protect their health.
Fortunately, validated methods for testing already exist. Randomized controlled experiments measure how messages affect health decisions. Companies also use experiments to test user engagement online. A similar approach can test how AI health advice affects people’s intention and, where feasible, their behavior. AI companies can run tests alongside model development and use the results to retrain their models.
We are not proposing a new regulatory regime, which may not be needed. The insurance industry’s crash tests have spurred automakers to build safer vehicles, beyond what federal rules require. AI companies could publish behavioral test results, letting hospitals, health insurers, and consumers choose accordingly.
Some will argue that AI should be a neutral aggregator of information. But AI cannot be neutral: Every accurate answer excludes many additional facts and emphasizes some over others. Because of these choices, AI answers already influence behavior, as shown by the chickenpox party examples.
Medicine has never been neutral, either. Doctors also make subjective choices about what to communicate and when. Moreover, the best doctors do not simply recite facts; they try to help patients act on sound medical evidence. They want to see our diseases prevented or cured.
Behavioral benchmarking would not license AI to mislead because every response would still have to be accurate. To guard against overreach, behavioral benchmarking could be limited to areas with overwhelming scientific consensus, such as smoking cessation and childhood vaccination. Evaluators external or internal to tech companies can rely on guidelines from medical societies, such as the American Cancer Society and the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Medical ethics pairs the duty to do no harm with beneficence, which is an affirmative obligation to do good. Safety evaluations of AI have focused mainly on the first duty by screening for responses that encourage imminent self-harm, discourage necessary care, or spread false information. Behavioral benchmarking would extend the first duty beyond imminent danger to long-term harms. It could also advance the second duty, which has received far less attention: designing AI to help people by communicating more effectively. Responsible engineering means honoring both duties.
Jessica Fishman is a behavioral scientist and faculty director of the Message Effects Lab at the Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania. John L. Jackson Jr. is an anthropologist and provost at the University of Pennsylvania. He launched the Message Effects Lab while serving as dean of Penn’s Annenberg School for Communication.

It’s notoriously hard to govern Los Angeles, a city that gives its mayor less direct authority over the government than in a city like New York or Chicago. But even so, it’d be hard to do much worse than Karen Bass.
Los Angeles is about to test a new kind of housing politics
The city ousts its NIMBY mayor for a democratic socialist YIMBY.
Elected mayor of LA in 2022, Bass campaigned on promises to solve the city’s homelessness and housing affordability crises (which are really part of the same underlying crisis). She then spent her term undermining her own administration’s affordable housing policy and fighting the state of California’s efforts to compel cities to allow more housing production. She lost her bid for reelection this week to Nithya Raman, an LA City Council member, rising progressive star, and nationally prominent YIMBY.
Los Angeles has the highest ratio of home price to household income of any large city in America, and the second fewest homes per adult of any major city. It has a highly suburbanized and car-oriented fabric, like much of the rest of the country — all of which makes it a kind of proving ground for whether America’s sprawling cities can build their way out of their housing shortages.
Everyone in the city’s political leadership notionally agrees that LA needs to permit a lot more homes to meet demand — the only true way to make housing affordable — but not all of them have evidently had the policy discipline to follow through.
Raman may be different. She has gained a following in housing reform circles over the last few years with her brisk, direct-to-camera social videos explaining how LA’s housing shortage drives up rents and criticizing city policies that make it so difficult to build more homes (perhaps it’s no surprise that she has plenty of friends in Hollywood).
“There has been an overall lack of urgency in addressing housing supply in [Bass’s] administration,” Raman told me in an interview in July. How best to accommodate LA’s need for more housing, she said, is “a question that the city has actually turned away from.”
Even given LA’s relatively weak mayoralty, Bass’s failures on housing were often a matter of political choice. As The Atlantic’s Marc Novicoff put it, “Bass seems to have gone out of her way to exercise as little power as possible.” Where she did go out of her way to wield her influence, it was often to stop denser housing from being built. Some of her bewildering housing policy choices while in office include:
- Days into her term, Bass signed her first executive order, known as ED1, to fast-track housing developments where 100 percent of the apartments are affordable. Applications for these projects were to get approvals within 60 days instead of being dragged through excruciating permitting processes. It was a good idea — and it seemed to be working, quickly attracting developer applications to build thousands of affordable apartments. It was working so well, in fact, that a backlash from vocal NIMBYs followed. Less than six months after signing ED1, in June 2023, Bass weakened it to exclude projects in single-family neighborhoods — which make up three-quarters of LA’s residential land — from the fast-track approval process. Her administration even tried to apply that restriction retroactively to developments that had already applied to build in single-family areas under ED1, a breathtaking display of bureaucratic dysfunction; a judge later ruled that this violated California law. Bass has since added more restrictions to the ED1, and one observer has described it as “functionally gutted” for many developers. To be fair to Bass, even after she weakened it, the program has still resulted in more than 7,700 affordable apartments under construction, according to her campaign.
- Bass opposed SB 79, a landmark California law that passed in 2025 requiring cities and suburbs to allow construction of denser housing near transit stops. Permitting apartments near public transit is one of the most basic principles of sensible urban planning. But in LA, it was controversial enough that Bass urged Gov. Gavin Newsom to veto it. After he signed SB 79 into law anyway, Bass worked with LA’s city council to delay much of the law’s most ambitious upzoning until 2030, while permitting smaller apartment buildings near some transit stops.
- After the devastating January 2025 fires, some property owners whose homes had burned down in the Pacific Palisades had applied to rebuild under SB 9, another important California law that allows single-family lots to be modestly densified into up to four housing units. In response to backlash from some neighbors, Bass reportedly pressed Newsom to restrict SB 9 in fire-damaged areas; she then banned SB 9 applications in parts of the Palisades. (There are certainly legitimate questions about whether rebuilding in such a fire-prone area is a good idea at all. But Bass offered no publicly available analysis that the modest increase in density allowed by SB 9 posed a special danger, even as she worked to accelerate the rebuilding of single-family homes.)
All of these point to a leader who is not serious about changing the conditions that led to LA’s housing shortage, and lacks the courage to take on what is arguably the city’s most defining political challenge.
Raman has promised to fundamentally break from that approach. That will make her mayoralty an important experiment for the rest of the country. Even modest progress in a city as resistant to housing as LA could help crack open a way forward for new approaches to housing in the many other cities that face affordability crises.
This won’t be easy for her — she’ll face the same anti-building political pressures, and will need to maintain a cooperative relationship with the city council. When I spoke to Raman over the summer, I noticed that she treaded gingerly around the topic of adding density to single-family neighborhoods. Because of the uniquely American obsession with keeping single-family homes segregated from other types of development, it can be a real political third rail in LA and nationwide. But research has suggested the city can’t fill its housing shortage without building more in those neighborhoods. Raman will, at least, have an important ally in California’s newly elected governor, Xavier Becerra, who is also a strong YIMBY.
Raman’s affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) makes her emblematic of a fusion that’s been emerging in Democratic politics, between supply-side abundance and left-wing economic populism. It’s also evident in politicians like Zohran Mamdani and some of the young Democrats who won elections across the country this week.
From talking to Raman, I have the sense that she’s more at home with the YIMBY part of her politics than the DSA part. Her relationship with the DSA’s LA chapter has been strained (though it did endorse her candidacy). But her social-democratic commitments are also sincere — she’s been a strong champion of rent control and tenant protections in LA, for example, and helped shape a stronger rent stabilization law the city adopted last year.
The new political syntheses taking shape on the American left are exciting and intriguing. Whether it will finally make a breakthrough in LA’s — and California’s, and America’s — housing crisis, of course, remains to be tested. But it’s a welcome sign that American politics need not remain trapped in the same orthodoxies and failures.

Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case
- Published
A Massachusetts judge has denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of killing her three children.
The judge's ruling follows her defence team's request to dismiss the case after the 12-person jury in her September trial failed to reach a verdict.
Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.
The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.
Clancy's defence team argued to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that prevents a person from being tried for the same crime twice.
Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the 26-day jury trial last summer, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative.
The five-week trial, its lead-up and aftermath gripped Americans, and put postpartum mental health issues such as psychosis in the spotlight.
In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject Clancy to double jeopardy, according to court documents obtained by the BBC.
The possibility that "an unreasonably stubborn or eccentric juror" could be seated is "an unavoidable risk of the jury system", he said.
"Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy."
Sullivan also denied a defence motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath.
He said the defence failed to demonstrate that the records were needed for Clancy's defence at any retrial, and that questioning the juror "would have been impermissibly coercive".
The judge has marked 16 November to discuss scheduling a potential second trial. He previously suggested it could begin in March.
The BBC has contacted Clancy's lawyers for comment.
Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.
After weeks of emotional testimony, the jury took a week to deliberate, repeatedly telling the judge that they could not reach a verdict.
The deadlock stemmed from a lone juror who voted to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, while the 11 other jurors intended to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity.
In Massachusetts, as well as in all US criminal murder trials, juries must reach a unanimous decision to convict or acquit a defendant.
Because the jurors failed to unanimously agree on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law, the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September, which means that she was neither found guilty nor not guilty.
Clancy is currently being housed in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.
Ana Faguy contributed reporting.

The Monaco summit that will decide the future of Carrick and Man Utd
- Published
Michael Carrick's future as Manchester United head coach will be determined 800 miles away from Old Trafford in Monaco on Wednesday.
Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are flying out for one of their regular pre-planned meetings to discuss strategy around the football club.
On this occasion, the main issue to be decided is Carrick's future and what should happen next.
It is expected that Berrada and Wilcox's recommendation is for the head coach to go.
It is not a situation Sir Jim Ratcliffe can have expected to find himself in again, less than three years after purchasing a minority stake in United.
On Christmas Eve 2023, his vision was much different.
"Our shared ambition is clear: we all want to see Manchester United back where we belong, at the very top of English, European and world football," he said.
Instead, United are 18th, in the Premier League's relegation zone after winning just one of their first 10 games and none since August. It is their lowest position so far into a top-flight season since 1986-87 when they were 20th.
Ratcliffe has been criticised for many decisions since he bought his 28.94% stake for just over £1bn. This is one he really needs to get right.
Why is the meeting taking place in Monaco?
Ratcliffe's home is in Monaco and his company Ineos has offices in the principality.
The meeting had been in the diary for some time as a regular catch-up between senior executives and their boss.
Sources have stressed that the choice of location was not influenced by the debate around Carrick's future - it just happens to now be the most important item for discussion.
The decision to sack United's previous two managers was not made in a meeting in Monaco.
Ruben Amorim was sacked 19 hours after his explosive media conference following a 1-1 draw at Leeds in January.
Erik ten Hag went a day after Manchester United lost at West Ham leaving them with just three wins from their opening nine matches
A decision to sack Dutchman Ten Hag was taken at a meeting of senior Ineos executives in the summer of 2024, only for the choice to be reversed following the FA Cup final triumph over Manchester City.
Four months later there was a six-hour meeting at Ineos HQ in London as Ten Hag's tenure hung by a thread. He survived again but was gone three weeks later.
Amorim was summoned to Monaco after the Europa League final defeat to Tottenham in 2025.
There is daily contact between senior executives so if the meeting was purely to decide Carrick's fate, it could be done by video conference and the need to travel to Monaco is not the reason why there is yet to be a decision.
The travel element does add a complication given the preference for Berrada and Wilcox is to inform Carrick of any decision face to face.
Sources say the Monaco meetings used to be held every six weeks, although in more recent times they are less frequent.
Those who have attended them say they take place in the morning, tend to last between three and four hours and usually stop on time so Ratcliffe can go for his regular lunchtime jog.

What do we know about the recommendation to sack Carrick?
United stood by Carrick after the woeful 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October.
Club sources were adamant they wanted to give Carrick and his players a chance to turn the situation around it was also felt that the two-week international break in November represented a better chance for the club to properly assess the club's start to the campaign.
However, although they did end a long wait for a victory against Roma on 3 November, United had to come from two goals down to seal a 3-2 victory in a chaotic game.
They failed to press home their advantage after excelling in the first half against Chelsea and eventually lost 2-0 as experienced central defender Lisandro Martinez was sent off.
On Sunday, they conceded twice inside five minutes and had to come from two goals down twice to claim a point against Villa.
While sources said the comebacks showed the United squad were still playing for Carrick, it is also understood the chaotic nature of the games and the inability to stop the opposition from scoring has led Berrada and Wilcox, who were at all three matches, to conclude a change of coach is required to get United out of the mess they find themselves in.
United have conceded 30 goals so far this season in 15 games - 19 in 10 Premier League matches, eight in four in the Champions League and three in their one Carabao Cup tie.
Instead of replacing Carrick another option under consideration is additional coaching support to assist the current team.
Bayern Munich coach Aaron Danks, who worked with Carrick at Middlesbrough and was touted as a potential appointment in the summer, is one option.
Is the recommendation likely to be accepted?
The assumption is yes.
If Ratcliffe was to decide otherwise, it would raise serious questions over the future of Berrada and Wilcox.
How could they work with Carrick again in that scenario?
The pair have been the subject of intense and frequent fan discontent. But sources are adamant that Ratcliffe still retains faith in the pair, even though United are heading towards sacking a manager in mid-season for the third successive year, having backed them in the summer and spend millions on new players.
Ratcliffe is a ruthless operator, and has clear opinions of his own. He also has form, spending £5m hiring Dan Ashworth as sporting director from Newcastle in 2024, then waiting for the 55-year-old to spend five months on gardening leave before he could start work.
Five months later, Ashworth was sacked due to a divergence of opinion over who should replace Ten Hag. Ashworth felt someone with Premier League experience was a better fit for United's squad. Ratcliffe wanted a more modern alternative. Berrada suggested Amorim. Wilcox, after initial reservations, also got on board. Amorim was dismissed after 14 months.
The other unknown element is the Glazer family. They will need to sign off any decision.
At the time of the Ratcliffe purchase, United confirmed the club's 'board' had handed over responsibility for the football side. But United's articles of association state that responsibilities delegated by directors can also be "revoked or altered".
Crucially, of the 12 current directors, six are members of the Glazer family, including co-chairs Joel and Avi Glazer. United's rules state that if required, the chairman of any meeting will have a second and casting vote.
Although there have been media reports of Glazer dissatisfaction at United's current plight, there has been no public statement on the matter.
What is Carrick scheduled to be doing for the next couple of days?
It may seem strange, but the reality is, as with any employee, Carrick will continue to do his job until told otherwise - and so far, there has been no conversation to that effect.
Although most of his squad, and a significant number of academy players, are on international duty, a core remains at home.
This includes Mason Mount, Joshua Zirkzee and Matthijs de Ligt. Harry Maguire, who suffered a back spasm against Villa, is also there, as are other injured players, including Luke Shaw and Marcus Rashford.
Carrick gave his players a day off on Monday but scheduled training days for Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. After that, they are not due to report back until 17 November, by which time the international contingent should start to return and begin preparations for the trip to Liverpool on 22 November.
"Obviously some of the boys will be flying off around the world and different things, and the group will be split for 10 days or so, but as a normal international week is, we'll have some training and we'll have one or two days off," Carrick said after the Villa game. "Not too much. But we'll train and get ready for the next game."
Who might be discussed as a possible replacement for Carrick?
If the discussions go as anticipated, replacing Carrick will be a key element.
Mauricio Pochettino has emerged as a leading contender and is known to be keen on the job.
United spoke to the former Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea boss about their managerial position on three different occasions - first of all when Jose Mourinho was sacked in 2018, then in 2022 when the club decided on Ten Hag instead and then again when the Dutchman was sacked.
The obvious problem is that Pochettino currently has a job as head coach of the United States. He renewed his contract in August and has a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti over the next week. The Argentine, 54, is due to speak to the media on Friday and has a $10m (£7.5m) release clause.
Former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe is out of work and available. BBC Sport has reported the compensation due to his old club if Manchester United appointed thr 48-year-old now would be £3m. But it reduces as the season goes on and would be nothing in the summer.
Italian Antonio Conte is also thought to be keen and the 57-year-old has Premier League title-winning experience at Chelsea and more recently won Serie A with Napoli last season, before leaving the club.
Julian Nagelsmann stood down as Germany boss in the wake of their last-32 exit at the World Cup exit at the World Cup but the German, 39, won the Bundesliga title with Bayern Munich in 2022-23.
Kieran McKenna was part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching team at Manchester United and left Ipswich after four-and-a-half years this summer. However, it is felt more likely United would want a candidate with greater experience than the 40-year-old Northern Irishman.
Where does this all leave Carrick? In a unenviable position of carrying on as if it was business as usual when the reality is anything but.

How Germany's greatest goalscorer is guiding the next generation
- Published
It is no surprise Miroslav Klose recognises the value of a true goalscorer.
He is, after all, Germany's all-time leading marksman and until this summer had netted more than any other player in men's World Cup history. Even now, only Kylian Mbappe and Lionel Messi can top his 16 across four tournaments.
But of the more than 300 goals Klose scored in a career that began in Germany's amateur leagues and spanned Kaiserslautern, Werder Bremen, Bayern Munich and Lazio, he reckons all but two came inside the penalty area.
"Thankfully, we've moved away a little from the idea of the false nine or having a second striker playing around the main striker, with everyone coming towards the ball," explains the FC Nuremberg boss.
"For me, the most important thing is that you need someone who is there to score goals. You need someone in the box because that's where you're closest to the goal. That's why I'm a big believer in practising the final ball, whether it's a cross, a shot or something else.
"That's crucial. How do you create that final ball? When you develop automatisms and players get to know each other better, that's when you see harmony on the pitch.
"It can make things look effortless, but it involves a huge amount of work. A lot of work in training and attention to detail, making sure the players communicate with each other and understand their team-mates' strengths and weaknesses."
That focus on detail stems from Klose's diligence during his playing days. He would study opponents' movement, analyse a goalkeeper's position and shape when facing certain shots - do they make themselves big? Are their hands high or low?
"When goals are scored, the whole team deserves credit," adds the 48-year-old, who was as selfless as he was ruthless. "But you still need someone who has that ability in their feet or in their head to put the ball in the net."
'Kane a great role model'
Klose was 36 when he won the World Cup with Germany in 2014 - surpassing Ronaldo's goal record in a 7-1 semi-final thrashing of hosts Brazil.
It was the culmination of a career built on hard work after a series of near-misses - something that may offer solace to Harry Kane and England that a major tournament triumph remains possible.
Born in communist Poland, Klose's father Josef - also a footballer, most notably for Auxerre - moved the family to West Germany when his son was eight.
He was never in a big academy, playing in the lower leagues while training as a carpenter before eventually joining Kaiserslautern.
Klose, like Kane, was in his early 20s by the time he established himself in top-flight football, but just two years after his Bundesliga debut was starting a World Cup final defeat by Brazil.
The striker, 38 when he hung up his goalscoring boots, admires the way Kane has evolved as he has matured, using him as an example to his own young prospects.
"You could always see his quality, and he's worked incredibly hard to get where he is," says Klose of the Ballon d'Or winner.
"He's also a great role model for me, particularly because he has stayed in Germany. I often tell my players that they should look at someone like him as an example.
"Young players can't yet have the instinct and experience he has developed, but that's where it starts - thinking about what you can and can't do as a footballer. You have to keep learning. That's the crucial thing for me.
"If you understand that you train to become better, then in five years' time you'll naturally be a different player. But if you think everything will happen automatically just because 10 people around you tell you that you're a fantastic player, I don't think you'll continue to develop."
Klose has a knack for working with young talent, previously coaching Bayern Munich's under-17s. His Nuremberg side are the youngest in the German second tier with an average age of 23.3 years, according to Transfermarkt.
"You need that balance and a certain core of experienced players," he explains. "But we're very brave in that respect. Over the three years I've been here, we've made progress in how we assess young players and in the conversations we have about them.
"How do we rate them? How far along are they? What do they need to work on to take the next step? Is it perhaps more about their physical development? Because from a footballing perspective, we're already producing some really good players."
Klose's coaching journey began with the national team before he joined Bayern, briefly becoming Hansi Flick's assistant, and then took his first managerial role at Rheindorf Altach in Austria.
He joined Nuremberg, historically one of Germany's most successful clubs, in 2024 and steered them to 10th and eighth-placed finishes.
This season they sit second, behind Hertha BSC, and are the league's joint-top scorers, with eyes on a return to the Bundesliga for the first time since 2019.
"When I first arrived, I spoke to the youth coaches about the club's DNA and its coaching philosophy, and what they focus on," adds Klose.
"There was already a lot of common ground. We suggested trying certain things because we wanted to do a little more in particular areas, and they were open to that.
"That's important. We benefit from this because our young players are getting opportunities in the first team, and everyone is paying attention to their development.
"But that journey starts with the youth coaches. I know how important it is to take those steps. We're benefiting from that now because we have access to so many young talents.
"As a coaching team, we're brave enough to give them opportunities when we see that they can compete at this level. That's the first step."
Among the 11 to play the most minutes for Klose's side this season, seven are 22 years old or under, including top scorer Mohamed Ali Zoma, already capped by Italy.
"Of course, everyone gets a lot of praise, as is currently the case with Marc Kornwachs," says Klose of a 17-year-old midfielder also catching the eye.
"But his journey isn't over yet. Now it's about helping him become more consistent and establishing himself, while continuing to develop his game and take further steps forward.
"These players are so talented that we have absolutely no hesitation in giving them opportunities, regardless of the scoreline."
Klose also understands his managerial career is still young - mirroring the humble nature that earned him fair play awards in Germany and Italy.
"I'm very comfortable with the steps I've taken, even though it involves a huge amount of work," he says about his progress. "You learn something every day.
"I've said that I'm already a much better manager than I was three years ago. That's perfectly normal, and you have to embrace it. I've always been willing and eager to learn, and I've always been a hard worker. That isn't going to change."
So what does a Miroslav Klose team look like?
"Personally, as a player, I always liked having the ball for long periods, and that hasn't changed," he explains.
"When you have the ball, you have a certain level of dominance. I know you also have to be very adaptable in terms of possession, and that's something we are. We constantly show the players different ways of playing out of situations.
"It's great to see how they develop and to be able to support individual players along the way. That's exactly the approach I like to take as a manager."

UK children's author David Walliams accused of sex assault, grooming teens
The comedian and author denies the allegations, but in a letter published by the Guardian acknowledged that "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with".
LONDON: UK media on Tuesday (Nov 10) published allegations that British comedian and children's author David Walliams groomed teenage fans and sexually assaulted a 15-year-old girl as well as harassing young female colleagues.
The claims, published by The Guardian newspaper and ITV news channel, came after a joint investigation into allegations by multiple women dating as far back as 2003.
Walliams, who lost a High Court battle against being identified in the UK media and did not appeal, denied targeting teenagers and using his fame to manipulate them to have sex, his lawyers told media.
His lawyers did not respond to a request for comment from AFP. 
The Guardian published a letter Tuesday from Walliams, saying he "behaved thoughtlessly" in casual relationships.
But he said: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law".
Now 55, Walliams starred in the BBC's Little Britain sketch show in the early 2000s and was a judge on commercial broadcaster ITV's Britain's Got Talent.
He also penned books such as Mr Stink, Gangsta Granny and The Boy in the Dress, with his work translated into more than 50 languages and reportedly selling 50 million copies.
When seeking to block the publication of the reports, Walliams' legal team argued he was "highly likely" to die by suicide if they were published.
The High Court heard he made two suicide attempts this year and was detained in a secure hospital last month.
Almost all the women making claims were identified only by first names, some changed at their request.
"I WAS GROOMED, 100 PER CENT"
In a particularly grave allegation, one woman, named as Jade, said Walliams contacted her in 2007 via her social media page showing her age as 15.
Then aged 36, he invited her to his house and pulled up her top and sucked her breast, she said, with her words read by an actor in a documentary released by ITV.
"It's a sexual assault, it's a grooming, it's completely wrong in every way," she said.
It is illegal in Britain for someone aged over 18 to intentionally communicate with a child under 16 for a sexual purpose.
Walliams' lawyers said he never engaged in grooming young women and denied sexual contact with Jade.
Another woman, named as Alex, told The Guardian Walliams first met her when she was a 15-year-old aspiring comedy writer and he was 32.
He phoned her and gave her tickets to shows. They had sex for the first time at his home when she was 17 and he was 34, she said.
She said this was consensual but Walliams was "pushy" and treated her "like a prostitute".
"I think I was groomed, 100 per cent. We met when I was 15 and he was promising to help me ... He used that power," she said.
Walliams' lawyers told The Guardian he believed she was 18 and that she had got back into contact with him. 
The investigation also claims Walliams messaged teenage models and invited teenage fans back to his dressing room and his house.
His publisher, HarperCollins, dropped him last year after he faced accusations of harassing female staff, which he denied, and he has not posted on social media since. 
The latest allegations prompted more organisations to distance themselves from the former star.
A BBC spokesperson told AFP it has taken down some shows involving Walliams from its platforms, including all episodes of Little Britain, which ran between 2003 and 2006.
A spokesperson for his literary agents, Independent Talent Group, told AFP that after the latest claims, "we are no longer representing him in any capacity".
The ruling Labour Party is also understood to have suspended Walliams as a member.

Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say
- Published
Moscow and Kyiv are privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would controls Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario, US officials have said.
The comments came on the eve of the first trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine since February.
Senior officials from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington will meet in Abu Dhabi as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches.
Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.
"An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X.
But Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict in the first place remain far apart.
A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia.
Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security.
While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".
However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".
"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."
For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans.
The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.
The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.
Since then, European leaders - who have been largely excluded from peace talks – have pushed to be involved in the process amid concerns that decisions about the security of their continent would be made without them.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged on Monday to include Nato allies and EU members into any "meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture". President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly stated Kyiv wanted Europe to be part of the talks.
The US official said the Americans would propose moving into a multilateral format bringing the Europeans into the discussion. "Hopefully we'll get the Russians on board," the official said, while acknowledging that "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans."
Since the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.
Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.
After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine which "might involve all of Europe".
Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result into a fair peace.
Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believes Trump wants "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.
The only way to make Putin start real negotiations is by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said.
"While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".
Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi will include Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.
Kyiv is sending several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.
Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.
On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations."
"This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."

When I was growing up, one of my favorite things to hear from an adult was that I was smart. It made me feel special — like I was capable of doing things that other people weren’t.
Why animals are smarter than we think
Who gets to be sentient?
In hindsight, that pride came with baggage: pressure to do well academically, and a sense of competition that wasn’t always necessary. Like many, I grew out of it. But many people in power still have a preoccupation with intelligence and conventional ways of measuring it.
Now, though, the way that we think about intelligence and markers of it, such as IQ, are shifting in important ways. David Robson, the author of The Intelligence Trap: Why Smart People Make Dumb Mistakes, says that traditional markers like IQ are not the only factors when considering how smart someone is. “There’s practical intelligence, which is much more about how good you are at planning projects and executing those projects,” he explains. He even says that people with high IQs tend to be more susceptible to things like confirmation bias.
Philosopher Jeff Sebo goes further, arguing that even focusing our discussion of intelligence on people is too narrow. He’s the author of the book The Moral Circle: Who Matters, What Matters, and Why, and he says that making humans the bar for intelligence is a mistake. “Intelligence in general is the ability to process information and solve problems and adapt to the environment,” he told Vox. Animals’ brains “might not look exactly like ours, but they can help animals solve problems and navigate their environments and adapt to their situations really effectively.”
So what does animal intelligence actually look like? And what can we learn from it? We answer that and more on this week’s episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Sebo, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
What is it about one animal’s intelligence that makes us want to protect it versus another animal that can end up on our dinner table? I think of dogs versus cows and pigs or dolphins versus fish.
There are many factors that shape how much empathy we have for non-human animals of various kinds. Are they cute and do they look like us? Do they remind us of ourselves? What role do we assign them in our lives?
We have more empathy by default for animals who play companion roles in our lives as opposed to animals who play commodity roles in our lives. This is why we can often have much more empathy for some animals over others, even if they display the same markers of sentience and the same markers of intelligence.
What’s a discovery about an animal’s mind that might surprise people? That might make us think of that animal differently than we maybe do?
There are really interesting studies showing that bees are capable of play behaviors. You can go online and see a video of a bee rolling a wooden ball around in a way that displays all the hallmarks of play activity. This is done seemingly for the pure joy of rolling a wooden ball around.
Likewise, there are studies showing that animals like insects have remarkable capacities for perception and learning and memory and adaptive, flexible decision-making and communication with each other. Animals that we might have written off as simple, as mechanistic, are in fact incredibly complex, seemingly sensitive, seemingly intelligent. I think that has allowed people to have a little bit more empathy for some of these animals than they otherwise might.
How much of what we call animal intelligence is actually just animals doing the things that people happen to be good at? What kind of abilities are we overlooking when we think of animals and intelligence?
We do tend to look for markers of intelligence that we associate with human intelligence and that can sometimes lead us to overlook markers of specifically non-human intelligence. This can happen in so many different ways.
For example, for many years, the gold standard for self-awareness tests was a mirror self-recognition test. You would put a mark on the forehead of an animal and place them in front of a mirror and see if they notice the mark and if they try to remove the mark and that can signal a certain kind of self-awareness.
It took us a long time to appreciate that this might not be the best way to test self-awareness in many animals for a variety of reasons. Many animals are not primarily visual, so we might need to think about how to perform this kind of test with their sensory modalities. Also, many animals might not particularly care about whether they have a mark on their forehead, so we should probably not treat an attempt to remove that mark as a standard for self-awareness.
We hear that pigs are intelligent or that octopuses could solve puzzles and we think, “Oh wow, we should be treating these creatures better.” I wonder, is there a problem with that argument? Because what happens to the animals that just never impress us?
I think that learning more about animal intelligence and challenging our preconceived notions about animals is good, but I think it would be a mistake to treat a certain level of intelligence — and especially a certain level of human-like intelligence — as a necessary condition for moral consideration.
That might lead us to extend respect and kindness to elephants and chimpanzees and other relatively human-like animals while neglecting the other animals who are conscious and sentient, capable of feelings and emotions, and that have forms of agency and decision-making, even if it might not look like ours.
I think that bar should be lower and should at the very least include consciousness and sentience.
This is making me realize that I may not be clear on what it means to be sentient. How do we know if an animal’s sentient or not?
This is very difficult to know for sure, because sentience is the capacity for positive and negative experiences like pleasure, pain, happiness, and suffering. The only experiences that any of us can directly experience are our own.
With non-human animals, we can collect behavioral evidence, internal evidence, developmental evolutionary evidence. For example, behaviorally, we can ask, “Do they nurse their own wounds? Do they respond to analgesics and antidepressants the way that we do?” And then developmentally, evolutionarily, we can ask, “In their ancestral environments, did they face pressures that they could overcome if they developed the ability to experience pleasure, pain, happiness, and suffering?” None of this is proof, none of it establishes certainty, but when we find a lot of this evidence in an animal, that at least increases the probability.
In terms of ethics and policy, what matters is we should not wait for certainty that someone can suffer before taking basic steps to address welfare risks for them. If there is at least a realistic possibility that someone can suffer based on the evidence, then we should take reasonable proportionate steps to mitigate welfare risks for them when we make decisions that affect them.
I personally don’t think of plants as sentient, but one of the things I love about my monstera is whenever it’s moved around in my apartment, it turns itself towards the sun. Does it make sense to call them intelligent when they do things like that?
At least in a certain broad sense, I think that it does. Plants are remarkably sophisticated. Many plants have capacities for perception, for collecting information from the environment, for learning and memory, for retaining some information, for communication, sending signals to other nearby plants, and even for adaptive decision-making, for growing toward things that are good for them and away from things that are bad for them.
Now, this might not mean that plants are sentient, but whether or not it feels like anything to be a plant, they might still be agentic and intelligent in the sense of being able to process some information, being able to adapt to their environment in some ways. I think that can be worth acknowledging.
What would that change about our world and how it functions?
I think that if we seriously considered non-human sentience and welfare, then it would have transformative implications for how we live, but ones that could be very good for humanity as well.
Consider how we relate to food and consider how we relate to wildlife. On the food side, industrial animal agriculture is a leading driver of animal suffering, but then it is also a leading driver of public health and environmental risks for humans. It creates more antibiotic resistance, more disease outbreaks, more extreme weather events via climate change, more biodiversity loss via deforestation.
Similarly, we build an infrastructure primarily for humans, and that can lead to a lot of unnecessary conflict with wildlife. Wildlife can die because they fly into buildings or fly into cars or are trapped in light pollution or trapped in parks with no exit for them if there is a flood or a fire.
If we simply considered their interests when building our infrastructure, then we might be able to build an infrastructure that can be good for human and non-human residents at the same time. But it does require considering human and non-human interests together when making decisions that affect everybody.

With temperatures dropping, the holidays approaching, and relatives preparing to invade the sanctity of our homes, November is the perfect time to find a little peace and quiet in front of the TV.
Fortunately, this month’s lineup of must-watch shows offers plenty of excuses to escape, including a dramatization of one of the biggest scandals in cryptocurrency history, a return to the dystopian world of Blade Runner, and a dark comedy about desperate parents who turn to surveillance technology to find their missing daughter.
There’s also a return to Middle-earth, a deadly game of international espionage, and a mysterious archaeological discovery that sets off a globe-trotting conspiracy. Plus, we're revisiting two groundbreaking television series that helped shape our fascination with government secrets, surveillance, and conspiracy theories.
As always, we’re not just chasing the biggest names or the shows everyone is already talking about (as much as we do enjoy The Gilded Age). Instead, these picks reflect the kinds of stories WIRED covers every day, from technology and science to politics and culture, and the unexpected ways they often intersect.
Whether you’re in the mood for a mind-bending sci-fi thriller, a twisty international conspiracy, or a classic worth rediscovering, these are the TV shows worth making time for this month.
Black Doves
Ben Whishaw (Q in Daniel Craig’s Bond movies) is one of the finest actors working today, even if his name isn’t quite as recognizable as it should be. Fortunately, Black Doves gives him plenty of opportunities to remind us why.
The deliciously twisty British spy thriller stars Keira Knightley as Helen Webb, a seemingly ordinary wife and mother who just happens to be secretly passing government intelligence to a shadowy organization known as the Black Doves. Whishaw plays Sam, her longtime friend and a professional assassin who gets pulled back into her dangerous double life. Then there’s the always-brilliant Sarah Lancashire (Happy Valley) as Helen’s formidable handler, Mrs. Reed.
Season 2, which arrived November 5, raises the stakes considerably as Helen’s husband prepares to become Britain’s prime minister, putting her at the very heart of government. It’s a wickedly entertaining mix of political intrigue, espionage, dark humor, and double-crosses, with a stellar cast that makes even the most murderous characters hard to resist.
The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power
If you thought things were looking bleak in Middle-earth at the end of Season 2, just wait. Amazon's spectacularly ambitious—and wildly expensive—prequel to J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings returns for a third season, picking up five years after the fall of Eregion. Sauron (Charlie Vickers) has been busy building his armies and conquering much of Middle-earth, leaving the Elves, Dwarves, Men, and Wizards scrambling to stop him. Meanwhile, the Dark Lord is working on his most dangerous creation yet: the One Ring.
The new season promises plenty of political intrigue, epic battles, and the kind of jaw-dropping fantasy world-building that makes the series such a visual feast. Even if you know where Tolkien’s story ultimately leads, watching the pieces fall into place is half the fun. The first four episodes arrive November 11, with the remaining four rolling out over the following two weeks.
The Altruists
Remember when cryptocurrency was going to change the world? For a while, Sam Bankman-Fried seemed poised to make that happen. The young entrepreneur became a billionaire seemingly overnight as the founder of FTX, a cryptocurrency exchange that promised to revolutionize finance. Then it all came crashing down in spectacular fashion, exposing an $8 billion fraud that landed Bankman-Fried in prison for 25 years.
The Altruists dramatizes that astonishing rise and fall, with Anthony Boyle (Say Nothing) playing Bankman-Fried and Julia Garner (Ozark) portraying Caroline Ellison (no relation to Larry Ellison), his on-again, off-again girlfriend and the CEO of his trading firm, Alameda Research. Inspired by reporting from New York magazine, the eight-part limited series explores how two young idealists who embraced the philosophy of effective altruism—using wealth and resources to do the most good—became central figures in one of the biggest financial scandals in recent history. All eight episodes premiere November 19.
Dig
If Amy Poehler and Mike Schur taught us anything with Parks and Recreation, it’s that even the most mundane workplace can be a breeding ground for brilliant comedy. Their latest collaboration takes that idea to an archaeological dig in Greece.
Based on Kate Myers’ 2023 novel Excavations, the 10-episode comedy stars Poehler as Elise, an ambitious archaeologist who has spent years waiting for her boss (Hugh Laurie) to retire so she can take over the operation. When she and three fellow excavators (Geraldine Viswanathan, Antonia Thomas, and Fina Strazza) uncover a mysterious artifact that could rewrite history, they make the questionable decision to keep it secret. Naturally, things spiral out of control, drawing the women into an international conspiracy that threatens their careers—and possibly much more. With a cast that also includes What We Do in the Shadows’s Kayvan Novak (aka Nandor the Relentless), Dig delivers an entertaining mix of workplace comedy, historical mystery, and archaeological intrigue. All 10 episodes premiere November 23.
Blade Runner 2099
More than 40 years after Ridley Scott’s Blade Runner first introduced audiences to a dystopian Los Angeles, where synthetic humans are almost indistinguishable from the real thing, the franchise is still daring to ask science fiction’s most unsettling question. In this case: What makes us human?
Set 50 years after the events of Denis Villeneuve’s excellent Blade Runner 2049, this eight-part limited series stars Hunter Schafer (Euphoria) as Cora, a fugitive who assumes the identity of a Blade Runner, a special operative tasked with hunting down rogue Replicants. She’s forced to team up with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Replicant whose days are numbered, to track down another fugitive whose secret could unravel the very foundations of their society. With artificial intelligence advancing at a dizzying pace in the real world, the franchise’s questions about consciousness, identity, and the increasingly blurry line between humans and machines feel more relevant than ever. All eight episodes arrive November 25.
Where’s Wanda?
How far would you go to find your missing child? For Dedo (Axel Stein) and Carlotta Klatt (Heike Makatsch), the answer is: very far. And well beyond the boundaries of what’s legal. When their teenage daughter, Wanda (Lea Drinda), disappears without a trace, the desperate German couple takes matters into their own hands, enlisting their tech-savvy son to help them secretly install surveillance equipment throughout their seemingly sleepy suburban neighborhood. What they discover is that practically everyone has something to hide.
The delightfully dark German-language comedy blends a missing-person mystery with a surprisingly sharp examination of privacy, voyeurism, and just how easily technology can turn ordinary people into amateur spies. The eight-episode second season premiered October 21, with new episodes arriving weekly through December 9.
The X-Files
The truth is still out there. More than three decades after The X-Files premiered, Chris Carter's groundbreaking sci-fi series remains one of television’s most addictive explorations of government conspiracies, alien encounters, and things that go bump in the night (or creepily squeeze through air vents). It also made pop culture icons of David Duchovny and Gillian Anderson as FBI agents Fox Mulder, a true believer in the paranormal, and Dana Scully, a scientist and skeptic whose job was ostensibly to debunk his theories. Anderson’s character also helped to inspire a whole generation of women in STEM, a phenomenon known as “The Scully Effect.”
The pair’s chemistry, and seemingly endless will-they-or-won’t-they relationship, helped sustain the show through 11 seasons (including a two-season revival beginning in 2016), two movies, and countless monsters of the week. With Ryan Coogler’s (Sinners, Black Panther) reboot, starring Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel, recently receiving a series order at Hulu, now seems like the perfect time to revisit the original.
24
Twenty-five years ago this November, Kiefer Sutherland introduced the world to Jack Bauer, a counterterrorism agent who could save the country from almost certain destruction in a single day—but never seemed able to find five minutes to use the bathroom. Premiering just two months after 9/11, 24 became a defining television series of the post-9/11 era, with its real-time format, ticking digital clock, and seemingly endless cliff-hangers making it nearly impossible to watch just one episode.
Each season follows Bauer through a particularly hellish day as he races to thwart terrorist plots, uncover government conspiracies, and navigate an increasingly murky moral landscape. The Emmy-winning thriller also gave us one of television’s most recognizable phone ringtones (courtesy of the fictional Counter Terrorist Unit) and some truly bonkers subplots—including a memorable Season 2 encounter between Bauer’s daughter, Kim (Elisha Cuthbert), and a cougar. Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?
- Published
After a shock announcement 10 months ago that the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) would be held every four years, the governing body of football on the continent has reversed course.
The Confederation of African Football (Caf) will instead retain the tournament's traditional biennial staging, with its president Patrice Motsepe saying the U-turn was based on "advancing, protecting and promoting" the interests of the African game.
The first indication that the frequency of Afcon was being reconsidered came at Caf's strategy conference in Cape Verde earlier this month.
Questions are now being asked about the decision-making process and what this means for the future of African football.
Why was the planned change controversial?
Afcon has predominantly been held every two years since its first edition in 1957, barring two three-year gaps in the 1960s and one year between the 2012 and 2013 tournaments.
On the eve of the 2025 finals in Morocco, Motsepe announced all that would change from 2028.
The South African said the shift to a four-year cycle was, in part, to help the global calendar "be significantly more synchronised and harmonised".
In recent years Afcon has been staged midway through the European club season, leading to recurring disputes over the release of African players.
Fifa general secretary Mattias Grafstrom was sitting aside Motsepe when the plan was announced, and critics highlighted that the scheduling change favoured football's world governing body more than the African game.
"I think the general sentiment around the continent has been that the two-year cycle has served the continent very well," Football Association of Zambia (Faz) official Sydney Mungala told the BBC.
"The idea of pushing it to a four-year cycle was a bit of a surprise, maybe a concern, to the bulk of the African federations."
- Afcon to return to two-year cycle after Caf U-turn 
  - Published21 hours ago
- Afcon to be held every four years from 2028 
  - Published20 December 2025
What were the benefits of the switch?
Afcon has developed into Caf's biggest revenue generator, with a profit of $114m (£85m) forecast for Afcon 2025, up from $75m (£56m) for the previous finals in Ivory Coast.
In its stead, an annual Africa Nations League involving all 54 countries on the continent was proposed. Motsepe described the ambition as creating a "world-class competition every year".
The idea was to move beyond Caf's heavy reliance on Afcon and develop a more sustainable commercial model which could support football development.
Yet the last time an ambitious alternative competition took place in Africa, it failed to deliver on its financial promise and was quickly ditched.
The Africa Super League, announced by Caf in 2022 to revolutionise continental club competition, and with projected annual revenues of $200m (£149m), was discontinued after just one edition.
Motsepe later acknowledged that commercial deals fell short of expectations.
"We didn't proceed as quickly because the partners that were giving us money were not giving us the deals we thought we would be happy with," he said.
Why the U-turn on Afcon?
The decision to move to a four-year cycle was taken at a meeting of Caf's executive committee last December - without being tabled at a general assembly where all member nations are represented.
"These kinds of decisions should be put to the general assembly, they should be debated and discussed for months at a time," Algerian journalist Maher Mezahi told the BBC.
"Afcon is the locomotive by which Caf funds all of its other competitions."
Caf subsequently asked its 54 associations to express a preference between proceeding with the four-year format or retaining the original schedule, and the executive committee eventually voted to restore the status quo.
Motsepe said the decision was in the "best interest of African football" and would contribute to the development and growth of the sport.
He also admitted misgivings about the new Nations League, with concerns it would require "several years" before it could make "the substantial financial and football development contributions" to help the continental game be "self-supporting".
How does Fifa fit in?
Fifa president Gianni Infantino first publicly proposed holding Afcon every four years in February 2020, an idea Motsepe rejected after he was elected as Caf president 13 months later.
That has not stopped the South African cultivating a close relationship with his counterpart and Infantino's drive to expand the Fifa World Cup to 48 teams - and in the process increase African representation at the tournament - has won him backing across the continent.
Yet the Swiss' position has been under threat since his plan to sell stakes in Fifa's competitions was leaked in July.
Since then Infantino has been busy shoring up his power base ahead of his re-election bid, including at Caf's strategy meeting this month.
"He came to Cape Verde to generate support, And, by and large, Africa gave him that support," Mezahi said.
"But I think they did that in a quid pro quo - they gave him the support in return for some concessions.
"And I think the main concession was the return of the Africa Cup of Nations [to a two-year cycle].
"It shows that Africa is willing to assert its influence and look after its interests, even in the face of the global game's interest."
- Infantino says he is backed by 'vast majority' 
  - Published6 days ago
- Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president? 
  - Published6 August
Why is Afcon revenue so important?
Afcon is Caf's financial lifeline, accounting for a substantial share of the governing body's income.
Morocco 2025 was projected to generate $192m (£143m), representing 66% of Caf's total revenue from competitions across men's, women's and age-group football.
For many FAs, Afcon's importance extends far beyond the tournament because they cannot always rely on consistent government or corporate investment.
"We have 11 [Zambian] national teams and only two are partly sponsored by government," Faz official Mungala said.
"The rest have to be supported from the FA's coffers. We actually fund some of these programmes from the support that we get from Caf and Fifa."
What about upcoming Afcons?
The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to be held in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year.
Yet, on a visit to East Africa in September, Motsepe called for a "heightened sense of urgency" in order to make sure stadiums and supporting infrastructure are ready on time.
The next Afcon will be held just one year later in 2028 - a decision Caf made when planning for the switch to a four-year cycle and which it as has decided to stick with.
An announcement on where and exactly when the finals will be held is yet to be made.
Subsequent tournaments will be held in 2031 and 2033 to avoid clashes with the World Cup.
The proposed kick-off date for the Africa Nations League, meanwhile, is September 2029.
Motsepe's latest statement suggests the new competition will also be held every two years - rather than annually as he initially announced last December – but that begs the question of how space will be found for the fixtures to be played in an Afcon year from 2031 onwards.
While debate continues around the game's congested calendar, Caf's U-turn on scheduling has at least protected the tradition of Africa's biggest sporting showcase.
It also exposes, however, the challenge of finding a workable financial model which benefits African football as well as the demands of the global game.
