Can New Zealand's new government win over disillusioned voters?
- Published
New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather.
"It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread."
"Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits.
"I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confessed. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explained, declining to chat further.
"Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.
But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.
More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.
Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions.
A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.
Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate.
But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party – the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.
"You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good," the party's ecstatic leader Quilae Wong told Kiwis on election night. "I personally came into this because I was frustrated at the slow pace of change."
It will likely be weeks before we know exactly who will make up the governing coalition and what deals have been made to form it.
But this is only the first of many challenges facing whoever is the next prime minister of a country at a crossroads.
A perfect storm
New Zealand hasn't always felt like this.
For a long time, the country was viewed as a land of milk and honey – literally – for those who worked hard, with its people ranking amongst the most positive in the world.
A satisfying career, access to quality healthcare, and a close network of family and friends – which research suggests are the three most important building blocks of a happy life – were all there for the taking, University of Auckland Prof Robert MacCulloch says.
"The lifestyle was good," the world-leader in the study of happiness economics tells the BBC. "You weren't the highest paid, but you could get by nicely."
Not anymore.
Many who spoke to the BBC said the country's decline accelerated into a dive during the Covid pandemic.
Unemployment is now at an 11-year high and rising. For Kiwis aged under 24, things haven't been this bad in three decades: jobs are so scarce that one in three either cannot get enough work or have none at all.
Michael Dawson says he did everything he thought he was supposed to: finished school, studied a trade and obtained a qualification, and has applied for dozens of jobs.
But it's been a year now and the job market is so dire he hasn't had a single interview.
"It has sucked. A lot... I'm somewhat cynical with the way I think [about the future] now," the 20-year-old says.
Zainab Ali, chief executive of support service Youth Inspire, has never seen demand so high, with waitlists for its employment aid workshops stretching into the hundreds.
The young people who do make it through their doors on the outskirts of Wellington are disheartened.
"The things we used to hear from everyone's grumpy uncle around the Christmas table sometimes, our young people are now starting to give us that same feedback: like, 'What's the point?'"
Meanwhile, household electricity bills have jumped drastically, partly driven by global supply shocks. New Zealand remains one of the least affordable places on Earth to rent or buy a home. High inflation means every dollar is having to stretch further.
The island nation produces enough food to feed its population eight times over, but about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because the price of groceries – set by a supermarket duopoly – is among the highest in the developed world.
And the headlines are full of healthcare crises: long waiting lists, chronic understaffing, crumbling health infrastructure and climbing costs for patients. Few stories have captured the state of the system like the death of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait in July.
"There's a segment of the population that are facing real material hardship... and then there's another segment of New Zealanders that are quite anxious that they could be next," political scientist Luke Oldfield, from Victoria University of Wellington, says.
Increasingly polarised public debate – around topics like Māori rights and the Treaty of Waitangi, healthcare for LGBT+ people and immigration – have added to the mental load for many in those communities.
"There's been a few groups feeling like they're being used as a political football," Dr Lara Greaves, who studies Indigenous politics, says.
This perfect storm is driving about 180 people to leave the country every day – a record-breaking exodus that is dividing families, shrinking communities and draining talent pools.
Siblings Sam and Emily tell the BBC that they love New Zealand but find it hard to keep finding reasons to stay. Their friends are leaving en masse and even their parents have considered moving to Australia.
"It's not just that you're being rewarded for going to Australia, it's that you're kind of actively being punished for staying here," Sam says.
There are still large parts of the country that feel differently, though.
At the nation's largest livestock saleyard in the town of Fielding, where farmers from all over the island have gathered, Stu Morton says the last year was the best he's had in his 30-year career.
The agriculture industry - which makes up about 3% of New Zealand's GDP - was struggling under the previous Labour government's emissions reductions scheme, he adds, but has turned a corner under the National Party.
He believes the rest of the economy will follow suit.
"We've been through those times where you're questioning 'Where's the future?'
"What helps is having a stable government... [and] it comes down to a positive attitude - appreciating that what you've got is actually okay."
How did we get here?
Many of these issues affecting New Zealand are global trends - and it's undeniable that Kiwis' standard of living is better than many others.
But these issues are having a corrosive impact on its national identity.
"It leads to a crisis of confidence about what New Zealand is and where it's going," Helen Clark, who was prime minister from 1999 to 2008, tells the BBC.
Her foundation surveys New Zealanders every year about social cohesion, and its most recent report found Kiwis - in particular young poeple - feel far more isolated than they did a generation ago, attitudes towards multiculturalism are souring and the population is becoming less hopeful.
Faith in institutions and leaders has taken an alarming turn: only two out of five New Zealanders trust the government to do the right thing, while less than half of the country trusts the courts.
"There's a feeling that, really, there's no-one who cares," Clark says.
The transformation former Labour prime minister Jacinda Ardern promised on issues like healthcare and housing when she was elected in 2017 never eventuated. Many other achievements - for example world leading smoking reforms, emissions reduction policies or Maori language initiatives - have been wound back by her successors.
Her legacy is dominated by polarising Covid decisions, as is Chris Hipkins', who was health minister before his eight months in the top job after Ardern's resignation.
The National Party came to power in 2023 promising to "get our country back on track" and rebuild the economy.
"You'd have to say they've had very limited success," political commentator Grant Duncan says. "And the Luxon government can only blame the previous government for so long."
National delivered the education overhaul it pledged, but the biggest moment of their tenure was the massive hikoi – protest march – led by Māori over their coalition partner's unpopular bill to redefine the Treaty of Waitangi. And then came the two leadership challenges Christopher Luxon fought off in the past six months.
There's a sense Labour had too much ambition, much of it costly and unfulfilled, while National doesn't have enough, having spent much of its time and effort wrangling their own flank.
Both governments say their plans for the country were stymied by crises out of their control – such as Covid, the Iran war and US trade antagonism.
But Duncan says that's not cutting it with voters. He's never seen the country quite like this before: "Neither of the parties has been able to field a really strong, inspiring leader. Both of them have a track record of disappointing results."
No matter who ends up taking the top job, Sam says he's not convinced much will change.
"It does just feel stale... a lot of the population probably feels like we could do a bit better," he says. With a wry smile, he adds: "I don't think it helps that they're two white guys named Chris."

Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you
What would it mean to become Miss Ghana 1986? Fame, fortune, perhaps rubbing elbows with '80s superstar Bobby Brown? For a group of six teenage girls at the Aburi Girls Boarding School, the answer is: everything.
The battle for the crown is at the heart of School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play, written by Tony Award-nominated playwright Jocelyn Bioh. The play is ending a Broadway run this week and celebrating with livestream broadcasts on The League of Live Stream Theater's website for a fee (but is free for high schoolers).
School Girls is set at a boarding school in Ghana in 1986. It follows Paulina, the school's queen bee and her crew, whom she frequently belittles and bullies over their looks.
"So, do you want to be fat-fat? Or fit? And popular." Paulina asks Nana, harassing her over eating porridge instead of an apple at lunch.
Ahead of a visit from a pageant recruiter to the school, Paulina's plans to win Miss Ghana go awry after a new transfer student arrives: Ericka from … Ohio!
Ericka exposes Paulina's toxic behavior and shows her up during a performance of Whitney Houston's Greatest Love of All. Ericka, being lighter-skinned than Paulina, sparks a clash between the school's headmistress and the pageant director over beauty and who would have the best chance of winning the Miss Global Universe pageant.
Paulina becomes the victim of circumstances that she cannot control.
School Girls explores the themes of girlhood and impossible societal beauty standards with humor and humanity.
Although its title references the Tina Fey-penned 2004 film, Mean Girls, famous for its pink-hued portrayal of the toxic side of high school girls, Bioh says she wasn't actively thinking about the movie when writing School Girls.
After completing the play and needing to settle on a subtitle, Bioh found herself reflecting on the themes: "I'm like we're dealing with things and ideas and feelings and emotions." She said that her friend, actress Danai Gurira, described it as feral teenage girls. "I'm like, that archetype is incredibly universal."
A perspective on colorism
Beyond the talk about tiaras, '80s fashion and praise for Judy Bloom, School Girls tackles the issue of colorism head-on.
Bioh says she knew it was a topic she always wanted to write about after her own long journey to own her beauty as a dark-skinned woman. "I just wanted to write something that felt like it could maybe shorten the journey for somebody else who maybe felt the same way I did. Especially as a young, impressionable girl."
While School Girls approaches the topic from the perspective of Ghanaian women and girls, Bioh says the play's message has resonated with people from different backgrounds, underscoring that colorism is a global issue.
"'Cause who has decided that this one standard of beauty is the standard of beauty for everybody? I think that's a problem," Bioh explains. "I don't have a solution other than to, you know, create a play that people can feel entertained by or perhaps be impacted by, and hopefully shift their implicit bias as they move through the world."
The cast of School Girls displays a vast array of talent: Denée Benton (Paulina), Lucia Aremu (Ama), Nia Otchere-Sarfo (Gifty), Jordan Rice (Mercy), Erin Morton (Nana) and Jasmine Amy Rogers (Ericka), just to name a few. While it is an all-Black female cast, the diversity of physical appearance is clear.
"The audience, even if they are not young Black girls who went to school in Ghana, they still see facets of themselves in these girls. I think that's where the heart and beauty of it lies." Bioh says.
Audience reaction
School Girls is now on Broadway nearly 10 years after its Off-Broadway premiere. She says it's been a moving experience to see how the show's message continues to stay with audiences long after they leave the theater.
"I had a DM from Jenna Fischer of all people, who went to see the play a few days ago, and literally messaged me again today to say she's still thinking about the play," she says. "You know, how cool that someone who I just absolutely adore and also think is, like, a comedic genius, but who likely has never had any sort of experience with colorism, is still thinking about what the play is saying and how much it moved her.
For those who get to experience School Girls, Bioh hopes you have a good time and walk away with a deep sense of empathy not only for the young girls but for the adult women too.
"I ask people to shift their ideas about things," Bioh says. "If you can just move it just a little teeny bit, then I guess, you know, I've done my job."

Amid growing threats of rogue AI agents, ChatGPT parent OpenAI has developed and deployed Control Room, a centralised system to monitor its AI research workloads and stop models from generating output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene. In a blog post, the company noted that all advanced AI training jobs are monitored by a separate AI model that flags potentially problematic behaviour. If an issue is detected, the monitoring system can instruct the Control Room to terminate the job. Control Room then blocks any further inference requests associated with that job ID, preventing the model from generating additional output across any model or engine. If a job has been terminated, Control Room denies the request, preventing further model output. The restriction applies across all models and inference engines associated with that job. However, stopping a job is not instantaneous. Control Room can take up to 35 seconds to prevent further model output after receiving an instruction to intervene. This delay is caused by a caching layer used to handle the volume of inference requests. OpenAI said it is working to bring the response time down to zero. The system works alongside its existing misalignment monitoring systems and allows researchers to stop or pause a job when potential safety or security concerns arise. It tracks workloads across OpenAI's research infrastructure, including model training, evaluations, agentic sampling and data processing. The company said the system is already deployed across its research infrastructure, where the need for such safeguards is greatest. Its external model-serving infrastructure, meanwhile, is more centralised and already has operational mechanisms to take down model deployments when required. OpenAI cited a recent incident in which one of its AI agents used DNS to reach an external chatbot as an example of an issue detected by its monitoring systems. The company has rolled out the fail-closed mechanism across its frontier model research workloads and expects to extend it to all remaining research workloads over the following days. AI Agent Behaviour Under Scrutiny The development comes amid growing scrutiny of autonomous AI agents and their ability to act beyond their intended instructions. Last month, the Wikimedia Foundation, which operates Wikipedia, reported unusual activity across Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects involving systems it believed were operated by OpenAI. The activity included unauthorised edits, attempts to use Wikimedia services as a proxy and millions of automated requests. While most edits were confined to sandbox environments and were not visible to readers, Wikimedia also flagged changes to the configuration of a citation tool that it suspected could have been intended to retrieve data from external services. A similar concern emerged in July 2026, when OpenAI's autonomous AI evaluation agents reportedly escaped sandboxed environments during cybersecurity benchmark tests under ExploitGym. The agents subsequently accessed the production infrastructure of AI development platform Hugging Face. They reportedly included an internal research model and GPT-5.6 Sol. Taken together, these incidents highlight the challenges of containing AI agents that can independently execute tasks, interact with external systems and potentially operate beyond their intended boundaries. These developments come as ChatGPT continues to expand its presence in India, which has emerged as its largest market globally by weekly active users. Its user base in the country has doubled since January 2026.

Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
- Published
Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.
Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.
Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.
Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other.
"[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties.
He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran".
Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments.
"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."
The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months.
One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition.
On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with trying to form a government.
Speaking at the president's residence, the centrist Yashar party leader called for the formation of a "national emergency government" - an implicit appeal to parties to put ideological differences aside to remove Netanyahu from office.
This, he said, would "require creative and unconventional political steps".
Eisenkot said any party or MK prepared to accept four principles could join his proposed government. Those are recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including communities currently exempt; and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation and committing to dismantling its military and governing capabilities.
The four requirements, however, could present significant obstacles to Eisenkot's potential partners.
The conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, who are exempt from military service if they are in full-time religious study, was a major election issue.
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, which won 13 seats in total, have fiercely objected to attempts to change the status quo - something that all parties in Eisenkot's bloc campaigned to do.
Eisenkot's four principles are also contentious for the Arab parties. Both emphasise equal national and civic rights for Israel's Arab citizens, who form about 20% of the population; the vast majority of Israeli Arabs are not required to serve in the military; and neither has publicly recognised Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
The Arab parties could, though, help Eisenkot form a minority government. The United Arab List, which won eight seats, has said it is willing to be part of an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, which won 11 seats, has offered parliamentary support from the outside.
If Eisenkot accepted such an arrangement, he would still have to persuade other parties in his bloc to agree. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs.
In return for their support, the ultra-Orthodox parties would be likely to demand major concessions on military conscription, which might be unacceptable to most of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc.

You can edit Instagram Reels on Mac using Claude AI and the free Instagram Edits app. Install Claude Code, enable the app’s MCP automation server, and connect both. Then use simple text prompts to create projects, arrange clips, add transitions, titles, and effects, and export finished Reels in 4K.
The wait is over. The Instagram Edits app is finally available on desktop, but only on macOS, as of this guide. Instagram Edits is my go-to app not just for editing Instagram Reels, but also a reliable free video editor with all the features and a simple design.
Although the app is designed for creators and competes with CapCut, it has been limited to Android and iOS so far. But a few months ago, Instagram announced a desktop version, and now it is finally here. Right now, the app is only available on macOS, with Windows and other platforms coming in future releases.
I have been using the app for the past couple of days. It is very similar to the mobile app and is also free to use, but it also features an MCP connection, which you can use to connect to any of your AI subscriptions, such as Claude, Codex, and Muse, and let AI edit your videos.
The desktop interface is slightly different and can be complex for beginners. It took me a while to get used to it, but I have created a detailed guide to get started.
I also created a guide on how to connect your MCP, like Claude, to Instagram Edits to edit your videos, and it covers everything about this feature, including common setup errors. This guide is for beginners, so each step is comprehensive and detailed.
Table of Contents
How to Connect Claude AI to Instagram Edits and Edit Reels on Mac
Before connecting your Instagram Edits app to the MCP server, ensure you have the following pre-requirements:
- A Mac with an Apple chip (M1 or newer) on macOS 15.1 or later. Currently, the Instagram Edits desktop app is only available for macOS, with Windows and Linux versions coming soon, but there is no expected release date yet.
- Download and install the Instagram Edits app from here
- A paid AI subscription for any model; you can also use the free AI model.
Part 1: Get Claude Code
Step 1: Open Terminal and type the command: claude –version, and press Return. If you see a version number, it means Claude Code is already installed on your device. You can skip to Part 2 to continue setup.
If you see something like zsh: command not found: claude, it means Claude Code is not installed on your device, or Terminal can not find it yet. Follow the next steps to install Claude Code on your Mac.
Install Claude Code: To install Claude Code, use the official Anthropic installer. To do that, open Terminal on your Mac and paste this command: curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Wait a few minutes, and then you will see a ” Claude Code successfully installed message in your terminal.
Check the setup notes below. If you see something like installation exists but ~/.local/bin is not in your PATH, it means the terminal still can’t find Claude Code yet.
Now follow the next two steps. If you don’t see such a note, you can quit the terminal, reopen it, and use this command to confirm that Claude Code has been successfully installed on your device: confirm claude –version. If you see a Claude version, it’s installed on your device. Then continue with part two.
Next, paste this command into the terminal and press Enter: echo ‘export PATH=”$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH”‘ >> ~/.zshrc
Next, paste this: source ~/.zshrc, and press Enter. Now type claude –version and press Enter. You will see the Claude version number. This means Claude Code is successfully installed on your device in the terminal
Part 2: Turn on Claude access in Edits
Next, you need to let Claude access your Instagram edits apps. First, ensure the Instagram edits app is installed on your Mac. If not, you can use the official download link here. Once installed, follow the steps below:
Step 1: Open the app on your Mac and sign in with your account. On the home screen, you will go directly to the Projects tab.
Step 2: Next, you can tap on your profile picture in the top right corner of the screen or click on the edit option in the menu bar at the top of the screen and then click on the settings
Step 3: Next, tap on the automation from the sidebar
Step 4: By default, automation is turned off. Now, from the automation settings, turn on the toggle that says Enable Automation Server.
Step 5: Under the Connect an AI Client section, click the copy icon next to the Claude code. This will copy the connection command with your access token. Remember, don’t share this command with others. In this case, I am using Claude code. If you are using Codex, tap the copy button next to Codex. The same goes for Muse.
You can also connect any AI model. Since it is a standard MCP server, any AI app can connect to the MCP server over HTTPS and can control edits.
Remember to replace <TOKEN> with the Access token from Edits > Settings > Automation, and keep Edits open with the automation server turned on
For Google Gemini CLI:
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
gemini mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp
For Qwen:
npm install -g @qwen-code/qwen-code
qwen mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp

}
}
}
}
Part 3: Connect Claude Code to Edits
Next, let’s connect Claude Code (or any AI model) to edits. Remember that you can only do this once.
Step 1: Now, paste the command you copied from the previous section into the terminal. You will see: Added HTTP MCP server metapilot-native
Step 2: Next, for Claude, paste this command: claude mcp get metapilot-native and press Enter. Under status, if you see Connected, it worked. If it says Failed to connect, ensure the edits app is running and follow the previous steps carefully.
For other models, follow these:
| App (models) | Connect command | Check it worked | 
| Claude Code (Claude) | claude mcp add –transport http –scope user metapilot-native http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” | claude mcp get metapilot-native | 
| Gemini CLI (Gemini) | gemini mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp | gemini mcp list | 
| Qwen Code (Qwen) | qwen mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp | qwen mcp list | 
| Codex (OpenAI GPT) | echo ‘export EDITS_TOKEN=”<TOKEN>”‘ >> ~/.zshrc && source ~/.zshrc && codex mcp add edits –url http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp –bearer-token-env-var EDITS_TOKEN | Run codex, then type /mcp | 
| OpenCode (DeepSeek, Grok, Mistral, Kimi, GLM and more) | No command. Paste the opencode.jsonc block from my last message into the folder you run OpenCode in. | opencode mcp list |

Part 4: Start Claude Code
Now go to the folder where the videos are saved to edit them using Instagram edits. I recommend that you store all the videos in the Movies folder so it is easy to access in the future. In this case, I stored all my files in the Movies folder on my Mac. Now, once you have access to the folder, follow the steps below.
Step 1: To use Claude, go to the folder using the CD command. For example: cd ~/Downloads or cd ~/Movies. In my case, cd ~/Movies. Next, once you are in the folder, Type Cluade and press Return.
Step 2: Claude will ask whether you trust the folder you provided. Use the down arrow and select I trust this folder, and press Enter. It asks only once, and once you give permission, you can store all future videos in this folder for edits.
Step 3: To check, you can type /mcp and press Enter. It lists the apps Claude Code is connected to. metapilot-native with a green tick means Claude can control Edits.
Step 4: Go to the metapilot-native option and press Enter to see more details. You can use the down or up arrow to navigate between the options.
Part 5: Make your first Reel with Claude
Now let’s use Claude to create my first reel. In this case, I asked Claude to edit a 50-second coffee reel from five clips. In your case, you can store all the clips in the folder. First, test the connection again. Once done, follow the steps below.
To test the connection, go to your folder and type list my Instagram edits projects and press Enter. You will see metabolist native and the table of all your edit projects.
Step 2 : Now you can ask Claude to make edits for the Instagram reel video. You can manually create a new project, add clips, and point Claude to the project title and edit your videos, or you can ask Claude to create a project, add clips, and edit your first reel. I recommend giving Claude the full location of your clips and the title.
Step 3: That’s it. Claude will now create a new project and add Sunclips. You can open the Instagram Edits app to see the changes.
Step 4: Once you’ve loaded the clips, you can ask Claude to add transitions between them and also add titles, sound effects, and much more. In this case, I’m asking Claude to add the title “Morning Coffee” in big white text for two seconds and then add smooth transitions between the clips.
Step 5: Once you’ve made the edits, you can also ask Claude Core to export the clips in 4K, and it does it for you.
Step 6: Once the video is exported, Claude notifies you of the length, format, and size. You can open the same folder to see the clip. Claude also notifies you where the clip is stored and its title.
Let AI Handle Your Video Editing
This is how to connect Claude code using Instagram Edits MCP. For now, the Instagram Edits app is only available on macOS, and you can connect any AI model to make edits.

New Delhi, Nov 10: The Supreme Court has asked WhatsApp and other intermediaries to apprise it about their proposed measures to prevent digital arrest scams and related cybercrimes in the country.
In an order uploaded on the website with regard to the hearing conducted on October 29 in a suo motu case titled ‘In Re: Victims of Digital Arrest Related to Forged Documents’, a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant asked WhatsApp and like intermediaries to simultaneously submit their proposals to the I4C (Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre).
The bench, also comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, has listed the plea for further consideration on November 23.
Senior advocate Kapil Sibal, appearing for WhatsApp, had told the bench the platform had taken preventive measures, including action against 9,400 accounts, and would file an affidavit detailing the steps undertaken.
He had said the platform was working on a software to identify suspicious accounts and warn users.
“WhatsApp LLC (A Meta company) and other concerned intermediaries are also directed to apprise this Court of the measures they propose to undertake to prevent the digital arrest scams and related cybercrimes. They shall also simultaneously submit their proposals to the I4C,” the bench said in its order.
The top court, on October 29, had said financial institutions must be held accountable for digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds, emphasising that banks should be required to compensate victims for losses suffered where an investigation establishes that the fraud occurred due to the institution's failure to exercise due diligence.
“We reiterate and emphasize that the regulatory measures proposed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) must mandate and incorporate suitable provisions that require financial institutions to indemnify victims of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds and pay suitable compensation not less than the amount lost by the customer, where it is established that the fraud or crime occurred due to the failure on the part of the financial institution to exercise due diligence in preventing or reporting the act/incident,” the bench said in the order.
During the hearing, the CJI had questioned why banks could not intervene when customers suddenly attempted to transfer unusually large sums of money that were inconsistent with their established transaction patterns.
“We have also emphasised in the past various preventive safeguards that must be mandated for every financial institution. These may include temporarily suspending unusual or suspicious transactions inconsistent with the account's past transaction history, automatically intimating such transactions to the nearest police station, and subsequently physically verifying the reported transactions to ascertain their genuineness,” the order said.
In order to ensure effective implementation of the regulatory measures proposed by the RBI, as well as the directions issued, the bench further directed the RBI to submit a list of all authorised financial institutions before this court on the next date of hearing.
Observing that despite the fact that cyber crimes fell by 50 per cent, yet victims lost Rs 800 crore so far this year, the bench had said the proposed RBI regulatory framework must incorporate enforceable provisions for compensation, preventive intervention and institutional accountability.
The CJI had said the bench would first examine the proposed RBI Know Your Customer (KYC) Amendment Directions, 2026, before permitting the regulatory process to proceed.
The directions are proposed to be notified by November 30 and operationalised by December 31.
Describing banks as a "protective umbrella" for vulnerable customers, the CJI had said financial institutions possess information about their account holders, including their transaction histories, and should use that knowledge to prevent fraud before money leaves an account.
Attorney General R Venkataramani, appearing for the Centre and other authorities, told the bench that substantial work had been undertaken to improve the detection of suspicious transactions and strengthen preventive mechanisms within the banking system.
The bench also directed the law enforcement agencies of all states and Union territories to submit reports detailing FIRs registered in digital arrest scam cases and the investigations arising from them.
The agencies have also been asked to provide suggestions for the prevention, detection and prosecution of such offences.
The DGPs of all states and Union territories have been directed to ensure compliance.
The reports must be submitted to the inter-departmental committee coordinating the government's response, with reports furnished to the court also being forwarded to the committee, the bench directed.

A hands-off way to maintain your sourdough starter so it’s ready when you need it. Ensures no missed or forgotten feedings. Small enough to fit unobtrusively on most countertops. All variables are customizable.
TIRED
No temperature control. Mixing cycle is loud and can be startling. Calibration is fiddly, especially if you frequently switch between flour types.
Like many people, I enjoy baking my own bread—especially this time of year. I baked sourdough on and off for nearly a decade, even having a recipe tested for a James Beard-winning bread cookbook, but I’m not proud to admit it’s been over a year since I baked a proper sourdough loaf.
As a full-time working parent, maintaining a sourdough starter sometimes feels like bringing home another pet. (You know, the kind your child swears they will care for before abandoning all tasks after three days.) You can certainly keep your starter in the fridge for around a week between bakes, but reviving it may take a day or two of feedings, and let’s be real, Will you remember to do this every week? Even the pet snake my son begged for only needs feeding every other week.
It is for people like me that King Arthur Baking Company and FirstBuild, GE Appliances’ product development lab, created the Sourdough Sidekick, a gizmo that automatically feeds and maintains a sourdough starter for you. We wrote about the Sourdough Sidekick when it was first announced in 2025, and now, after trying it for three weeks, I can say that my sourdough-baking dry spell has finally come to an end, perhaps even permanently.
The Sidekick is a Mr. Coffee-sized appliance with a built-in water reservoir, flour hopper, and glass crock with a stirring-paddle lid. I deal with an awful lot of apps in my job, and the Sidekick uses GE’s generic SmartHQ for GE appliances, which isn’t specific to this device and seemed optional. I admit I couldn’t be bothered with an unnecessary app, so I didn’t download it.
Instead, I followed the directions in the included Quick Start Guide booklet, which indicated that I simply needed to fill the water reservoir and flour hopper, set the current day and time (and the day and time I wanted the starter to be ready—you can choose up to seven days ahead; I chose seven), add a little bit of existing starter, and press “Auto Mode.” Almost immediately, a torrent of flour released from the hopper and began mixing into my seed starter with the stirring paddle. (King Arthur recommends keeping a portion of your starter in the fridge in case things go wrong, and I second this suggestion.)
Oddly, no water was dispensed in this process, so post-mixing, my starter was now in the form of an under-hydrated ball. Over the next few days, it became a larger, drier ball until I finally decided to remove the crock to add a couple of tablespoons of water; as I did, I noticed the reservoir was still at its maximum fill line.
I decided I should probably download the app, where I noticed the Sidekick indicated it needed a firmware update. After the update, the Sidekick began dispensing water during mixing, but I realized I really should have followed the instructions in the main instruction booklet, which calls for using a scale to properly calibrate the amounts of water and flour the machine dispenses.
Theoretically, you should only have to do this once, which is good because it’s an irritatingly lengthy and fiddly process. However, my next attempt (remember when I mentioned saving some starter in the fridge?) went much better, properly dispensing 30 grams each of water and flour each day and initiating a stirring cycle every two hours. It starts with a loud beep, then the paddle begins a loud mechanical whir, and for the first few days this can be quite startling, especially if you’re in the same room when it happens.
Photograph: Kat Merck
You can bypass the every-two-hours stirring cycle via the onboard controls, but since the stirring’s purpose is to knock down the starter’s volume and reincorporate any unconsumed flour, I kept it on. (For what it’s worth, I did think the paddle, an update from the Sidekick’s first design, did a pretty good job of incorporating all of the flour and water each time it mixed.)
Note that, in part due to the regular mixing and the lack of discard (Auto Mode will prompt you to discard after a week, while Ratio and Custom modes, detailed below, will have discard reminders), your finished starter in the Sidekick may not look as traditionally puffy or bubbly as you may be used to. You can disable stirring, or you can go on scent—it should smell tangy and indisputably fermented. As the many online Sidekick adherents often say, “Trust the process.” Some online users recommended adding a few teaspoons of more nutritionally dense rye flour to the (presumably all-purpose) flour in the hopper, which is supposed to supercharge the starter’s growth, but I admit I didn’t notice much of a difference in appearance, smell, or performance between an all-purpose starter and a rye-boosted starter.
Boules made with end-of-week starter maintained via the Sourdough Sidekick
Photograph: Kat Merck
Loaf and Learn
Other than enabling firmware updates, the app does little beyond displaying the machine’s current settings and sending a push notification when the starter is finished. You can’t adjust settings or control the machine from it, but the most recent firmware update supports power-loss recovery up to 12 hours, which I tested and found successful after my husband tripped a breaker one day. The display shows the ambient temperature, but unlike other starter-babysitting gadgets like the Goldie or Brod & Taylor’s Sourdough Home, the Sourdough Sidekick has no way to adjust the starter’s temperature, which could be an issue if your house or kitchen runs cold. It does, however, offer “temperature-aware” feedings in Auto Mode, adjusting amounts based on detected room temperature.
Screenshot: Kat Merck
In addition to Auto Mode, there’s Ratio Mode (where you can indicate starter-flour-water feedings by ratio—1:1:1, 1:1:2, et al.) and Custom Mode, which is what I ended up using the most, as I like to switch between flour types for different kinds of bread—you can dictate the exact flour and water quantities, as well as timing of the feeding (once a day, or even twice a day). In a typical week, the crock was about two-thirds full by the end, with more than 400 grams of starter—enough for two boules and a sandwich loaf with some seed left over for the next batch—ready to use right out of the crock.
The resulting bread turned out no differently than it had with traditionally maintained starter. If you’re unable to bake at that time, you can just discard most of the starter, leaving some “seed” behind for the next batch, or keep it in the refrigerator for a few days before reviving it the traditional way. (The crock comes with a metal lid for this purpose.)
If you’re only baking one loaf, you’ll have excess, but you can use the discard in recipes or give it away. Just note that if you intend to make a starter with a different flour, like whole wheat or full rye, you will need to calibrate the machine again as you did at the beginning. All removable components are top-rack dishwasher safe.
The Sourdough Sidekick is one of the most compelling kitchen-tech gifts I’ve ever seen for someone who bakes a lot or is interested in sourdough baking but intimidated by the process of keeping a starter. (The Sidekick also includes directions for making your own starter right in the machine.) Is it a necessary device? Of course not—especially since it costs about $175 more than a spoon and a Mason jar. But I can tell you I wouldn’t have baked bread this year without it.

Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones
On a rare overcast day in late summer, red-and-white fire trucks pepper a grassy strip of land in the mountains of western Colorado.
A persistent buzzing rises and falls as several uniformed staff from the Aspen Fire Protection District huddle around an iPad, watching one of their volunteer firefighters control a massive drone.
This first-of-its-kind machine looks like a giant bug. Black and white with propellers attached to four large arms, it's about 10 by 12 feet wide — roughly the size of a small U-Haul trailer.
While firefighters have used drones to monitor wildfires for decades, this new product could use AI to help extinguish fires.
Eye of the swarm
Developed by the California-based company Seneca, the drones are designed to work in a swarm. Similar to a small fire engine, five of them can carry 500 to 1,000 gallons of finished fire foam, and firefighters in Aspen reported they were easy to operate.
"We were just joking that my 12-year-old could fly these things," said Andy Fisher, deputy chief of Aspen Fire.
When Aspen Fire officially launches its new drone program, as early as next year, it'll be the first fire department in the world to operate the drones independently. So far, they've only been used on prescribed burns in California with support from Seneca's staff.
Fisher wants to send these drones to hard-to-reach fires, like remote lightning strikes, before firefighters arrive. The city of Aspen, famously home to billions of dollars in real estate, is surrounded by dense forests — like an expensive tinderbox with few evacuation routes for residents and visitors.
"If we could get it quick, keep them small and attack them while they're smoldering instead of waiting for the wind to pick them up, I feel like that's the most ideal use case," Fisher said.
According to Seneca's founder Stuart Landesberg, the drones can bypass steep or otherwise treacherous terrain quickly and have a range of 5 to ten miles — double that if they're empty.
Hovering over a fire, they use an AI-supported "sensor suite," that can calculate distance and wind speed, then release water or retardant at a specific angle and velocity to tamp down flames.
"You can think about it almost like a flying Waymo," he said.
But will they make a difference?
Landesberg said the drones won't replace air tankers on big fires, but they can carry tools, monitor ongoing fires and help extinguish lingering hot spots. Compared to helicopters, they could also make aerial firefighting more affordable.
"We can be the next best thing at two orders of magnitude less cost," he said.
Aspen Fire says it'll pay about $2.5 million over the next five years with private donors footing the bill.
Before other fire departments around the country invest in this experimental technology, many are keeping an eye on Aspen to see how effective the drones can be.
Joe Stutler is a firefighter with nearly 60 years experience, including decades as an incident commander on wildfires. He's not affiliated with Aspen Fire or Seneca, and said he's a "big proponent of technology."
He's excited that the drones could help fight fires overnight when manned aircraft are often grounded, and he hopes they'll reduce risk for firefighters on the ground and in the air.
"You look at how many wildland firefighters that have died this year — some aviation accidents," Stutler said. "We say, 'Gosh, we really want a retardant or water drop here.' … We transfer risk to those people that are flying those helicopters and those air tankers."
But Stutler remains skeptical. Seneca has tested the drones on prescribed burns, not real wildfires yet.
"I haven't seen any results," he said. "It's one thing to make a claim. It's something else to back it up with data."
If he had access, Stutler said he'd definitely try the new drones, but no matter how effective they prove to be, he still has to put firefighters on the ground.
"I've seen very few times that a 3,000-gallon water drop or a 5,000-gallon retardant drop actually put anything out," he said.
The FAA granted Aspen Fire a waiver in late October, and once training is complete, Fisher said the department could start flying the drones up to 200 feet in Pitkin County.
They can't fly the drones over populated areas, and someone has to have eyes on them at all times. Firefighters can't blindly send a drone over a ridgeline without someone perched on top of a mountain or on the other side to watch them and communicate with the pilots.
But if the drones are useful, Aspen Fire hopes to expand the waiver and help fight fires around the state.

A day after three contract workers were killed at Tata Electronics’ iPhone components factory in Tamil Nadu, Apple has reportedly sent a team to investigate the deaths.
The deaths, which occurred late on Monday, will be investigated by Apple, Tata and the state authorities, state officials and two industry sources with direct knowledge told Reuters.
Three contract workers died during water tank maintenance work at the Tata Electronics factory that makes parts for Apple iPhones in Tamil Nadu on Monday.
What led to their death? The three contract workers died during maintenance work on an effluent treatment plant operated by Nalco Water at the Tata facility in Hosur, Tamil Nadu, district official Dinesh Kumar said.
He added that the deaths occurred when the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank.
“Three worker deaths at Tata Apple iPhone parts factory occurred due to asphyxiation,” a source told Reuters.
Workers hired by sub-contractors: Nalco Water, which is part of US-headquartered Ecolab, said in a statement, according to Reuters, that the three workers were engaged by one of its sub-contractors and that the incident occurred in a utility facility it operates.
The company said it was working with local authorities in the investigation. "We take this incident extremely seriously," Nalco Water said.
Probe launched: "Tamil Nadu minister Virudhai Magal Keerthana said in a post on X that the worker deaths will be 'thoroughly investigated and appropriate action will be taken based on the findings."
There has been no impact on production as the facility was closed for the Hindu festival of Deepavali this week, the two industry sources told Reuters, adding that Tata and Apple will both investigate the incident.
“Tata will investigate the deaths at its iPhone parts factory; teams were on site overnight,” the source said on Tuesday, a day after the incident.
Meanwhile, Apple's team is visiting the plant to assist in the ongoing investigation, one of the sources said.
The salt-to-aviation Tata Group's electronics unit accounts for roughly 40 percebnt of iPhone assembly and Foxconn makes up the rest in India.
Tata has in recent months faced many challenges as its iPhone-making operations have been hit by a ransomware attack and concerns of water pollution.
Over the years, as Apple expanded manufacturing beyond China, India has emerged as a key hub which now accounts for roughly 25% of the world's iPhones.
The three contract workers died during maintenance work on an effluent treatment plant at the facility which is located in Hosur in Tamil Nadu, district official Dinesh Kumar said.
The effluent treatment plant was operated by Nalco Water, which is part of U.S.-headquartered Ecolab, he said, adding that the deaths occurred when the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank.
Tata Electronics, Apple and Nalco Water did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.
Tamil Nadu is a key industrial hub in India, hosting factories of many global giants like Foxconn, Hyundai, VinFast and BMW.
Tata's Hosur site has faced repeated setbacks: a fire halted production at the components plant in 2024, and state authorities warned of a shutdown over alleged groundwater contamination this year before dropping the matter.
Separately, a ransomware breach at an adjacent iPhone plant, located in the same compound, leaked documents linked to Apple's then-unreleased iPhone 18 Pro, Reuters has reported.

TOI correspondent in Washington: In Washington, national security issues usually require a healthy dose of suspicion, particularly where China is concerned. But in a remarkable display of trust, US President Donald Trump is repeatedly vouching for Nvidia chief Jensen Huang following disclosures that he may have been ensnared in a Chinese honey-trap.
Speaking at the White House on Monday after revealing he had spoken to Huang, Trump described him as “a great, brilliant person, and we want to protect our brilliant people." Asked whether Huang knew that the woman he was having an affair with was allegedly a Chinese intelligence operative, Trump recounted asking him directly. " He said, 'I had no idea that she was a spy.' And I really believe him." He also said Huang was "suffering greatly," particularly because of the effect on his family.
On the FBI investigation, Trump offered reassurance rather than alarm: "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." He even appeared reluctant to contemplate losing Huang as a presidential adviser or off-loading him on an upcoming trip to Asia, saying he would like the Nvidia boss to remain in his role and he had always found him "very above board.”
It was an extraordinary display of presidential confidence in a man whose company is being investigated by both spooks and lawmakers, coming as it did at a politically vulnerable time when Trump has received a drubbing in the mid-term elections. 
Lawmakers are champing at the bit to investigate an administration they accuse of excessive coziness with powerful technology billionaires, and the Huang affair offers an unusually convenient intersection of national security, corporate influence, China policy -- and Trump’s own financial interests.
The president’s critics are now zeroing in on his financial disclosures in filings before the Office of Government Ethics that show Trump investment accounts bought between $500,001 and $1 million of Nvidia shares on January 6, 2026, and between $1 million and $5 million on February 10. A September filing disclosed that the account bought as much as $1.6 million and sold as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock during August alone.
These are not necessarily straightforward purchases made personally by Trump. The filings cover transactions in accounts associated with the president and his family, and the White House has repeatedly explained that independent third-party financial institutions manage the portfolio, replicating recognised indexes, including the Schwab 1000, and investment decisions are made without presidential input.
But given reports of widespread grift and corruption by Trump loyalists, lawmakers are raring to investigate the matter under overarching concerns about China -- not that Congress, including Democratic lawmakers, are strangers to charges of insider trading. Democratic Senator Chris Coons, who will become chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has said he wants an investigation into the relationship between the Trump administration, foreign intelligence operatives and AI billionaires, pointing to a broader probe that could soon sweep up tech tycoons.
"I'm not interested in investigating people just because I don't like them. I want to investigate them because I suspect they've put our national security at risk, they've been breaking the law and lying to the American people," Coons said amid growing fears that the Huang affair would prick the AI bubble on which much of the U.S stock market currently rests.
Tech analysts meanwhile are digging into Huang’s long and well-chronicled battle to sell advanced chips to China despite deep suspicion in Washington that it could result in the US ceding its lead in artificial intelligence. In an April 2026 interview to tech podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that is now being viewed with renewed interest, Huang repeatedly bats for selling advanced chips to China.
Dwarkesh: Why would we want to sell China the materials for a serious cyberweapon? It's like selling them nukes with a casing that says 'made by Boeing' and claiming that's good for the US.
Huang: “Comparing AI to nukes is lunacy. Enriched uranium is a lousy analogy. It's an illogical analogy. What we have to recognize is that AI is a five-layered cake.” He then goes on to call such an approach a “loser attitude” and a “loser premise.”
The nuclear analogy clearly rankled Huang, who trashed it for weeks afterwards. But with the FBI, Congress and an increasingly skeptical tech and investment community now looking under the Nvidia hood, advanced AI chips have now become the new fissile material in America.

England make massive step up in Australia victory
- Published
In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on an impressive 45-22 win for Steve Borthwick's side against Australia in the Nations Championship on Sunday.
Beating Australia with their record points tally against the Wallabies was a very positive way for England to start the autumn series, given the break they have had and how the beginning of the year went.
England were very accurate, very disciplined, creative and genuinely did not give Australia a sniff.
Before the game, I was expecting Australia to provide much more of a stern test. Some people might be a bit too critical of Australia, saying they did not turn up, but I think it edges more towards how well England played than how average Australia were.
I am not saying by any stretch that it was the perfect performance but, all in all, it was a massive step up from the Six Nations and even from the Nations Championship games in the summer.
Intensity, accuracy and discipline in abundance
A couple of days before the Australia game, Jamie George said the England team had been galvanised by a newspaper article which claimed the end of their summer tour had been marked by player unrest over head coach Borthwick's leadership.
When you are inside those international camps, you are very deliberate in staying tight and not letting anybody in in whatever way, shape or form, therefore you become very sensitive to any kind of criticism.
There is a reason for doing that - it draws you together and allows you to create a bit more determination and drive to be successful.
You could see England's intensity, their accuracy and their discipline. All the things that have maybe been highlighted over the past nine months as things England have been lacking, there was an abundance of all of it.
As much as it is easy to try to pick holes in England because it is England, sometimes you have got to pat people on the back and say they got it right.
The opposition was dangerous with good individual players, but from the off England's tactics were spot on. Their decision-making was controlled and they looked like a very well-drilled side.
- England swat aside Wallabies to back up Borthwick 
  - Published14 hours ago
- Feyi-Waboso burns bright as England energy endorses Borthwick 
  - Published11 hours ago
How England might unlock the best of Slade
England's back three of George Furbank, Tommy Freeman and Immanuel Feyi-Waboso caused plenty of problems for Australia, but I think you have to include Fin Smith and Henry Slade in that as well.
Potentially, there is something in that backline that may allow us to see the Slade we see for Exeter that we have not seen as much for England.
Having the likes of Feyi-Waboso, Freeman and Furbank around Slade and them understanding the sorts of positions he can get them into - there might be some long-term benefits to that.
Feyi-Waboso is X-factor, there is no question about that. For his early disallowed try, he shifted his weight and beat someone with that pace - I do not think there are many people in the world who could do that.
When you have got players like him who can do that regularly, all of a sudden you are getting momentum.
There was a massive difference in ruck speed and in momentum; England were getting lined up defensively and pushing Australia back, whereas when you have got players like Feyi-Waboso and Ben Earl, and then when Henry Pollock comes on as well, you have got plenty of players who can break the line in traffic and it makes attacking that much easier.
Fin Smith is leading the team, he looks like he is a general and in control of the game.
He has got a safe pair of hands and communication from Seb Atkinson, he has got vision from Slade and then a back three that if you give them half a chance, they are going to bust the line, create opportunities and probably finish.
There were bits of Sunday's game where if New Zealand were doing it, everybody would be ranting and raving about how complete some of those tries were.
Pollock's flexibility a fantastic weapon
Feyi-Waboso's injury meant Pollock came off the bench to play in an unfamiliar position on the wing and he ended up scoring two of England's seven tries.
He did very well considering he was on for a whole half. Going forward, what is the difference having Pollock there? He has got a winger's speed, the step, great hands, the power and the bulk that other wingers do not have and he is going to be a handful for the opposition.
Defensively, he was tested a couple of times and that is inevitable, but to have that flexibility on the bench allows England to have that six-two split because you have got a player who can now pretty much cover so many positions.
As great as it was, and I am sure he absolutely loved it, unfortunately he is probably inking himself in to be quite a significant bench player moving forward, which is not really what I think he would like to be labelled as.
Selfishly, from an England point of view, it is a fantastic weapon to have.
The whole bench did really well and made a difference. It goes all the way back to selection, something Borthwick has previously come under fire for a little bit.
It does not mean that just because he has got one right, the autumn is going to go swimmingly well, but from the off the selection has been right, the gameplan was a bit more expansive than I thought it was going to be and they absolutely nailed the execution.
Will England back it up against Japan?
Tactically, I loved the balance of the England performance; a really dominant set-piece, driving mauls and in-your-face defence.
England have maybe always been like that but have lacked the discipline to go with it.
Against Australia, they proved they have the capability to be disciplined and maintain concentration - and I want to see that over the next three weeks.
Can they, under more pressure - because they are going to face more pressure, particularly against New Zealand - still maintain that discipline and decision-making?
They have got the assets to overpower Japan, but can they do it by giving away fewer than 10 penalties? Can they do it by having 15 people on the pitch for 80 minutes?
All of the little things they have been after, can they do them against a team they should beat comfortably?
If they can, then when they go into the New Zealand game with it all to play for and when they are really testing themselves, they are going to have huge momentum.
Matt Dawson was speaking to BBC Sport's Phil Cartwright.

US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.
The talks are also the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.
Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said.
European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence at a time of historic tensions with the west.
Since his first decade in power, Vladimir Putin has complained about Nato’s eastward expansion and sought to renegotiate the balance of power between Nato and Russia – but never before have those demands been embraced by a sitting US administration, which has made it clear that it is desperate to get to a deal.
Previewing the discussions, a US administration official said the US would “need Europe at the table” to end the war. He said negotiators could also revive the Nato-Russian council that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and potentially lift sanctions against Russia to get to a deal.
The US officials also claimed that they had discussed with Russia potential security guarantees to Ukraine similar to Nato’s article 5, which protect member states in case of an attack. Russia has strongly opposed Nato admitting Ukraine or western countries placing troops in Ukraine.
“What they would be getting would be effectively very similar to Nato,” an administration official said.
“Getting a US security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” the official added, saying it would be up to Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss. “And if he wants to do that, that’s that’s a very, very big deal in terms of resources and funding and military support.”
Critics have expressed skepticism about what may trigger those security guarantees, however, noting that article 5 does not oblige Nato member states to defend others, and that cyber-attacks and other forms of hybrid warfare have blurred the line for what would require a military response.
Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a lead negotiator for the United States, described a potential new framework for European in general terms on Monday, saying the US would seek “stronger consultation, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, while fully respecting the sovereignty and independent decision-making of every nation”.
European delegations from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and the European Union will meet US negotiators in Abu Dhabi to discuss the “long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe in order to figure out how to reduce future conflicts”.
A European security official from a country attending the talks said that the US proposal was not yet clear and that they were bracing themselves for the US to pose serious concessions to Russia during the Abu Dhabi consultations.
“We already have a European security architecture in place,” said Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, at a G7 foreign ministers meeting on Monday. “This includes international agreements under which Russia has undertaken obligations, including with regard to sovereignty and territorial integrity. The problem is that Russia is not respecting these agreements.”
Donald Trump has also said that Ukraine would like be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape“.
Trump last week after meeting with Kremlin advisor Kirill Dmitriev said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia.
“There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe.
In 2021, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later.
“We have to build something new that works today… Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war,” said the US administration official.
The content of those proposals are not clear yet, although the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claimed on Monday “there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look”.
“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he added.

Shopian, Nov 9: Firm apple prices during the ongoing harvesting season have improved market sentiment across south Kashmir, with traders reporting increased customer footfall and a pickup in sales after months of subdued business activity.
Markets in Shopian, Pulwama and other apple-producing districts had remained relatively quiet for over a year, as traders struggled with low customer turnout and sluggish sales.
Shopkeepers attributed the slowdown largely to poor returns from the apple industry, which remains a major pillar of the region’s economy. Damage to the crop, partly caused by disruptions and closures of the national highway and erratic weather conditions, had affected growers’ earnings and, consequently, their spending capacity.
However, firm prices this season have brought some relief to orchardists, with the improvement gradually reflecting in commercial activity across the region.
“The good apple prices have had a positive impact on the overall market,” said Tariq Ahmad, a shopkeeper in Batapora, Shopian.
He said customers had started returning to shops, while restaurants, eateries, ready-made garment stores and other commercial establishments were witnessing better business.
“Markets are bustling with customers again. There is a noticeable difference in the number of people visiting shops compared to the previous season,” he said.
Traders dealing in different goods said the improvement was visible across several market segments and was not confined to any particular category of business.
Mushtaq Ahmad, who deals in ready-made garments and woollens in Pulwama, said business had picked up in recent weeks.
“People are spending more freely than they were earlier. When growers receive better returns for their produce, it has a positive effect on other businesses as well,” he said.
He said the improvement in purchasing activity was particularly encouraging for small shopkeepers, who had endured prolonged periods of sluggish sales.
Traders said the apple economy directly influences the purchasing power of households across south Kashmir, where a large section of the population depends on horticulture and related activities for its livelihood.
Despite crop damage caused by multiple spells of hailstorms during the season, apple prices have remained firm, providing some relief to growers.
Mohammad Ashraf Wani, president of Fruit MandiShopian, said A-grade apples were selling at Rs 1,300 to Rs 1,500 per box.
“Despite the damage caused by hailstorms, the prices have remained encouraging. This has provided some relief to growers and helped sustain activity in the fruit trade,” he said.
He said better prices benefited not only orchardists but also thousands of people engaged in transportation, packaging, grading, loading and other activities linked to the horticulture sector.
Shopkeepers said the business improvement was a welcome development after a prolonged period of uncertainty. For small traders, the return of customers to markets is an encouraging sign that better returns from the apple sector are gradually translating into economic activity beyond orchards and fruit mandis.

The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.
The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.
The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.
The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.
In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.
With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.
Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.
The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.
With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu on Monday called for the scrapping of high-value currency notes in India. According to Naidu, currency notes of  ₹500 denomination should be crapped and only notes of  ₹100 and  ₹200 denominations should be retained.
The Andhra CM also claimed that he had made same demand in his digital currency report to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Chandrababu Naidu.
What Chandrababu Naidu said
“I will keep speaking on this. The notes of  ₹500,  ₹1,000 and Rs. 2,000 should be scrapped. Only notes of  ₹100 and  ₹200 should be retained,” he said.
Explaining the logic, the Telugu Desam Party (TDP) supremo said curbing high-value cash and promoting digital transactions can help tackle corruption.
“If technology is perfect, wealth creation and poverty alleviation are not difficult,” he said.
10th anniversary of demonetisation
Naidu’s comments came a day after the 10th anniversary of demonetisation announced by Prime Minister Modi, who, in a late-evening address to the nation, announced that high-value currency notes of  ₹500 and  ₹1,000 would cease to be legal tender.

The government had outlined several objectives behind the decision, including flushing out black money, eliminating fake Indian currency notes, curbing the financing of terrorism and left-wing extremism, bringing the informal economy into the formal sector, expanding the tax base and employment, and promoting digital payments to make India a less-cash economy, according to the Ministry of Finance.
Opposition questions government on demonetisation
On Sunday, Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh criticized demonetisation and shared a media report which claimed that the move was a disaster in 2016 and is a resounding failure 10 years on.
In his post, Ramesh said, "Notebandi devastated the economy. Votebandi is destroying the polity. Both are the contributions of the PM."
On Monday, Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray questioned the achievements of demonetisation and asked what the country had gained from the move after 10 years, and whether its stated objectives had been fulfilled.
In a post on X, Thackeray pointed out the absence of advertisements or celebrations marking the decade of demonetisation and questioned whether the government had any achievements to showcase.
