Connectivity includes USB-C, 3.5-mm aux, optical, or HDMI, and it supports Bluetooth 5.0.
Edifier QR65 for $314: Delivering classy looks with supercool lighting effects and a seriously big, powerful sound, these speakers are excellent for music, movies, or games. They also come with two angled stands to point them at your ears. They have USB, RCA, and Bluetooth 5.3 connectivity and USB ports for charging your gadgets. Controls are decent, with a physical button on the right speaker for power and cycling through modes. The problem is that they are huge and won’t fit on most desktops, including mine.
Creative Stage V2 for $150: This affordable soundbar offers excellent connectivity with HDMI ARC, optical, USB, 3.5-mm aux, and Bluetooth 5.0. But it’s not especially powerful, can sound muddy and flat, and has a short cable (no good for sit-stand desks). The subwoofer lends some decent bass, there’s a remote control, and I like the Clear Dialog option to sharpen voices, but you can do better.
House of Marley Get Together Duo for $170: Sporting an attractive and eco-friendly blend of bamboo and fabric, the Get Together Duo from House of Marley is affordable. They connect via Bluetooth 5.0, RCA, or 3.5-mm aux. There’s no subwoofer, the midrange is dominant, and they are lacking something at the high end. The battery-powered right speaker can also double as a portable speaker, and you can use these as bookshelf speakers, but as computer speakers, they are just OK.
SteelSeries Arena 3 for $150: Sporting a nice pear-shaped design with tiltable speakers and subtle branding, the entry-level Arena 3 from SteelSeries can get loud. But they lack bass, lose detail in the highs, and sound a bit fuzzy for music. Even for SteelSeries fans, there isn’t much reason to choose these over some of our picks above. They don’t have lighting, USB, or any other extras.
Logitech Z906 5.1 Surround Sound Speaker System for $450: This 5.1 system is THX-certified and comes with a huge subwoofer, five speakers, and a central control unit. The design feels dated, maybe even a bit ugly, and you need to run cables around your room. The surround sound effect is solid, and you can even convert stereo with the 3D mode, but overall, it’s a bass-heavy system.
Are Computer Speakers Worth It?
Budget is a deciding factor for most folks, but even cheap desktop speakers offer far better sound than your monitor. Headphones are a great alternative, but not everyone wants to wear headphones all the time. You can spend as much as you like on audio gear, but I have focused on reasonably affordable desktop systems here, starting from as low as $35 and not exceeding $700.
What Should I Look for in Computer Speakers?
It depends. There’s plenty to weigh when shopping for a set of computer speakers, so it’s vital to start by deciding what’s most important to you. For example, I work and play on the same desktop PC, so I need speakers that perform well for video calls, long gaming sessions, listening to music, and watching movies. I also have a standing desk, and my monitor setup doesn’t leave much room, so I prefer compact all-rounders with long cables.
Sound quality: The top consideration for most folks, you want the best sound quality you can afford. A good set of speakers will offer a balance of clear vocals, rich treble, and rumbling bass. If you crave bass you feel in the pit of your stomach, a subwoofer is essential, though it might not be a good idea for folks who have downstairs neighbors. For accurate positional sound, you might want to look at a surround sound system with multiple speakers.
Design: Consider the finish. Your speakers will be on show, so you’ll want to pick something that fits your decor.
Brand: Gamers with devices from an existing brand might lean toward the same brand of speakers because they can be configured in the same software. This is particularly important with speakers that have built-in lights, so you can sync up your entire setup.
Extras: Some people will consider these superfluous, but if you want a remote control for kicking back or RGB lighting to bring a splash of color to your desk, these are extra perks on higher-end speakers. Snag speakers with a decent range of connectivity, and you can always repurpose them later. Most speakers come with all the cables you need, but it’s worth checking before you buy. I have listed what you will find in the box with all the computer speakers I recommend.
Where Should I Position My Desktop Speakers?
You ideally want the speakers to be angled slightly up (around 15 degrees) and pointed at your ears. Since you know the exact spot you’ll be in when listening, you can tweak the position of your speakers for the best results. Don’t just chuck them on the desk and leave it at that. Try moving and angling them until you find that sweet spot.
Do I Need Speaker Stands?
Speaker stands can maximize sound quality by helping to reduce vibrations from your desktop that can muddy the sound. Angled speaker stands are also a good way to direct the sound toward your ears. Some manufacturers, such as Edifier and Onkyo, include stands; IK Multimedia and Razer include adjustable bases or fold-out feet; Audioengine sells stands separately. You will also find a wide choice of third-party stands online.
What Size Speakers Should I Get?
If space is limited, a compact set of speakers will work best. The trade-off is power and volume, as small speakers generally don’t produce as big or high-quality a sound as large speakers. If you opt for a subwoofer, you will want a suitable space under your desk. For surround sound systems, you must run cables and find suitable spots for speakers behind you. If you have a wide monitor on a mount, a compact soundbar beneath it could be the best fit. Check the dimensions carefully and measure the space on your desk before you buy.
What’s the Best Way to Connect My Speakers to My Computer?
Speakers can come with a multitude of ports and connectivity options. USB connections usually sound best because they output the digital signal for the digital-to-analog converter (DAC) in the speakers, which is likely to be better unless you have a good sound card. But the best way to be sure is to try both and see which sounds better. If you want to be able to connect a phone or laptop wirelessly, then Bluetooth is paramount. Most speakers have a 3.5-mm aux input, and some have an output for headphones. Just make sure your preferred speakers support the connectivity you want. You should also make sure that you have the necessary free ports on your PC or laptop, though you can always add more with a USB hub.
How I Test Computer Speakers
Every set of speakers in this guide was tested for at least a week, sometimes longer. I don’t use headphones, so they were all used for video calls throughout my work day, listening to music and podcasts, and for movies and games in the evening. While I played several games, watched many movies or shows, and listened to lots of music and podcasts, I ran through a specific list of test content with every speaker system to make it easier to compare them.
My test content included the game Halo Infinite, the movie Dune, and a music playlist including “Hip-Hop” (Dead Prez), “The National Anthem” (Radiohead), “All Along the Watchtower” (Jimi Hendrix), “Hey” (Pixies), “Sabotage” (Beastie Boys), “A Day in the Life” (the Beatles), “Nothing Compares 2 U” (Sinéad O'Connor), and “Only God Knows” (Young Fathers).

A few hours of exposure to firecracker smoke can be enough to trigger coughing, wheezing or breathlessness, particularly in people living with asthma or other respiratory conditions. The effects, however, are not limited to those with an existing diagnosis. High concentrations of particulate matter and gases can irritate the airways in anyone.
The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a numerical measure that converts the levels of different air pollutants into a single figure to indicate how polluted the air is and the likely health effects. India’s Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) calculates it using eight pollutants, including PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide.

Bihar govt bans firecrackers near ghats, private boat operations during Chhath Puja
The Bihar Disaster Management Department has directed all districts to enforce strict safety measures during Chhath Puja from November 13 to 16.
The Bihar Disaster Management Department has directed all districts to enforce strict safety measures during Chhath Puja (November 13-16), including a ban on firecrackers near ghats and private boat operations, officials said.
According to a statement issued by the department on Monday, district magistrates have been asked to identify and barricade dangerous ghats, and deploy adequate security personnel and volunteers.
It has also directed that trained divers, swimmers, motorboats and life-saving equipment be stationed at river ghats. Medical teams, ambulances and Quick Medical Response Teams (QMRTs) must remain on standby, the statement said.
The directives also call for adequate lighting at ghats and approach roads, round-the-clock functioning of district control rooms and continuous public announcements through loudspeakers. All electrical installations must be inspected in advance to prevent electrocution, it said.
To prevent panic and stampedes, district magistrates have been asked to prepare disaster management and communication plans, hold coordination meetings with Chhath committees and ensure strict monitoring throughout the festival.
The four-day festival will begin on November 13 with the 'Nahai Khai' ritual and conclude on November 16.
Observed on the sixth day of the Hindu month of Kartik, six days after Diwali, Chhath Puja is dedicated to the Sun God and Chhathi Maiya. Devotees offer prayers seeking blessings for the well-being and prosperity of their families.

A 45-year-old garment factory worker from Bengaluru Rural diagnosed with stage IV-A cancer of the mouth faces an arduous course of treatment: chemotherapy to shrink the tumour, extensive surgery involving reconstruction, followed by radiation and chemotherapy. The cost of medicines and supportive drugs of around ₹93,000 alone, besides treatment costs, are staggering for her family with a modest monthly income of ₹28,000. With funds running out, she is facing the risk of discontinuing the final stages of treatment.
Likewise, a 56-year-old shopkeeper from Mysuru district, diagnosed with recurrent, inoperable hypopharyngeal cancer involving the oesophagus, has a different but equally difficult challenge. After three cycles of chemotherapy, the disease has shown partial response. Immunotherapy could offer another treatment option, but its cost remains prohibitive. Spending another ₹2.4 lakh to ₹8 lakh over the next 2 to 3 months for bi-weekly immunotherapy is virtually impossible on a ₹45,000/month income.

Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting.
The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real.
Attackers conducting “mature intrusions”
Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions” into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI.
Greynoise said that GT10 is also installing the Python3 release on machines that don’t already have it because the package is required to run the hacker’s backdoor, which is tracked under the name TAC Agent. TAC Agent supports a wide range of functions, including shell commands, system reconnaissance, and persistence. OpenSSH has released a fix that prevents attacks from working.

For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with the development of newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence.
At last week’s UP.Summit conference in Florida, the vice president of launch at SpaceX, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company’s changing focus, how it is embracing AI, and why the Falcon 9 rocket—which has dominated global launch for a decade and remains the world’s preeminent launch vehicle—is firmly on the road to retirement.
“In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point,” Dontchev said. “We’re building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars.”
Using AI at SpaceX
Earlier this year, SpaceX acquired one of founder Elon Musk’s other companies, xAI. SpaceX engineers were already using xAI’s tools, Dontchev said, but in recent months, employees have really started to figure out how artificial intelligence can speed up their work.
“What’s happened at SpaceX is we’ve really gone through a huge acceleration of adoption,” Dontchev said. “Even just a year ago, we weren’t adopting it that quickly, but really starting this year, we started to adopt it extremely rapidly. And the acceleration we have seen in our ability to do engineering is unlike anything I’ve ever seen at the company in my 16 years.”
Tasks that would take SpaceX employees hours to days now take seconds to minutes, he said. And it’s not just the engineers. Dontchev said the work of identifying foreign object debris, or FOD, in aerospace parts has been largely automated using the AI assistant Grok. This debris can cause catastrophic damage to engines and other spacecraft components.

Jammu, Nov 10: Major General Mukesh Sharma, who on Tuesday took over as the Additional Director General of the National Cadet Corps (NCC) Directorate for the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, outlined a vision to expand the organisation's outreach, empower youth and modernise its training programmes.
Under the theme "Envision and Evolve: Empowering Youth, Strengthening NCC, Building the Nation", Sharma said he would focus on expanding NCC's presence in schools and colleges, particularly in remote, rural and border areas; empowering young cadets, especially girls; and making training more contemporary and relevant.
Emphasising the NCC's guiding principles of "Unity and Discipline", he said the organisation aimed to develop confident, disciplined and responsible young citizens equipped with leadership qualities and a spirit of service.
Highlighting the achievements of 20 girl cadets who successfully crossed the 5,578-metre-high Parang La Pass during the Aparajita Expedition, Sharma described it as a shining example of their courage, determination and leadership.
"Efforts would be made to create more such opportunities for girl cadets and ensure that geographical challenges did not restrict young people from joining the NCC," he told reporters after taking over as the new chief of NCC in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh region.
Stressing the need to modernise the organisation, he said training would be made more engaging and relevant to changing times, while teamwork and partnerships with educational institutions, civil administration and other stakeholders would be strengthened.
Sharma urged the young cadets to dream big, embrace challenges, become physically fit, keep off drugs and continuously develop their skills.
"NCC is not merely about uniforms, drills and parades; it is about building character, leadership and responsible citizens," he said.
He also appreciated the contribution of NCC officers and staff at the grassroots level in shaping young cadets into disciplined and responsible citizens, and sought continued support from the Jammu and Kashmir government, Ladakh administration, educational institutions, parents and media.
Describing media as an important partner in highlighting the achievements and contributions of cadets, he said the aim was to reach more youths, create greater opportunities and build a stronger NCC for a stronger nation.

Could US Marines sustain a war with China? Officers warn of Pacific weaknesses
Japan and the Philippines impose restrictions on US operations, raising questions about wartime strikes launched from allied territory

US Marines deployed across the western Pacific could struggle to sustain their forces, move missile batteries and secure permission to launch operations from allied territory in a conflict with China, according to assessments by Marine Corps officers and independent analysts.
Writing separately in the November issue of the US Naval Institute’s Proceedings journal, retired lieutenant general Stephen Sklenka and serving Lieutenant Colonel Merritt Mitchell identified vulnerabilities in the logistical and political arrangements supporting dispersed marine operations along the first island chain that stretches from Japan through Taiwan and the Philippines towards Borneo.
Sklenka warned that in a conflict Chinese attacks on American bases and supply routes could isolate forward-deployed marines, while Mitchell questioned whether dispersed units could relocate quickly enough to evade Chinese strikes or secure permission to operate from allied territory.
The latter political challenge was underscored on November 6 when Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr reaffirmed that, under the Philippine constitution, United States forces could not launch offensive operations from Philippine territory in the event of hostilities involving Beijing and Taipei. The restriction also covered facilities under the allies’ Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement.

Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

New-age tech stocks extended their rally this week, with 54 of the 69 companies under Inc42’s coverage posting gains ranging from 0.4% to 23.3%. CarTrade led the gainers, rebounding 23.3% after last week’s steep decline to close at ₹2,699.30. Awfis followed with a 20.4% rise to ₹281.65, while ixigo climbed 19.1%. Recently listed Tonbo Imaging and Zetwerk touched fresh highs during the week. Lenskart, Ather Energy, Eternal, and Nykaa were also among the stocks that hit 52-week highs. The gains lifted the combined market capitalisation of the 69 companies to $169.3 Bn from $160.9 Bn last week, an increase of 5.2%. Among the losers, RateGain fell the highest by 9.19% to close the week at ₹725.90. Here are some key developments from listed new-age tech companies during the week: Kissht’s AUM Crosses ₹10,000 Cr: Kissht’s assets under management (AUM) crossed ₹10,000 Cr, driven by growth in personal loans and its expansion into loans against property. The company attributed the growth to its AI-led underwriting and digital collections infrastructure, adding that its recent ₹832.2 Cr preferential issue strengthened its capital base. MobiKwik Secures NBFC Licence: MobiKwik received an RBI licence to operate as an NBFC, following in-principle approval in April 2026. It plans to begin operations within three to six months and disburse ₹5,000 Cr in consumer and MSME loans over three to four years through an asset-light co-lending model. Pine Labs Partners With Stripe: Pine Labs partnered with Stripe to offer Singapore retailers a unified platform for online and in-store payments, combining Stripe’s online infrastructure with Pine Labs’ terminals and merchant tools. The companies plan to expand the offering to other Southeast Asian markets in 2027. Pine Labs served 11.6 Lakh merchants across more than 22 markets at the end of Q2 FY27. Here’s a look at the performance of the broader markets this week. Benchmarks Jump Over 8% Indian equities recorded a sharp weekly recovery, with the Nifty 50 gaining 8.6%, or 1,977 points, to close at 25,030.35. The Sensex rose 8.8%, or 6,568 points, to 81,028.02. Both benchmarks advanced in all five sessions, with the Nifty ending at its weekly high. The broader market’s gains were smaller, with the Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 100 rising 5.8% and 2.8%, respectively. Renewed foreign investor buying, strong Q2 FY27 earnings, easing geopolitical concerns, and lower crude oil prices supported sentiment. Lower bond yields and a softer dollar also helped. Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) bought a net ₹45,960 Cr of equities across the five sessions, marking their second consecutive week of buying after a 10-week selling streak. The inflows exceeded the ₹45,162 Cr they sold during October. Domestic institutional investors (DIIs) sold a net ₹24,197 Cr, ending an 11-week buying streak. Together, the two investor groups remained net buyers of approximately ₹21,763 Cr. Geojit Investments’ head of research Vinod Nair attributed the improved sentiment to strong Q2 earnings, healthy October auto sales, and firm GST collections, alongside easing concerns around the Iran conflict and tariffs following the US midterm election verdict. He also pointed to foreign investors rotating out of crowded AI trades. The Indian market’s rally coincided with a selloff in global AI and semiconductor stocks. Private banks led the gains following renewed foreign investor interest in a segment previously weighed down by concerns over net interest margins. Automobile and consumption stocks benefited from festive demand, while IT and PSU banks recorded relatively modest gains. The sustainability of foreign inflows, crude oil prices, and developments in West Asia will remain key market triggers. Remaining Q2 results, US inflation and jobs data, and India’s inflation print will also influence trading. Nair cautioned that intermittent profit booking could follow the sharp gains, although the near-term outlook remains constructive. He favours large-cap companies with earnings visibility and a buy-on-dips approach. Meanwhile, the stock market will open for a special Muhurat trading session tomorrow, from 14:20 IST to 15:30 IST, on the occasion of Diwali. Now, let’s take a detailed look at the performance of Awifs and RateGain this week. Awfis Rallies After Q2 Results Awfis shares gained 20.4% this week to close at ₹281.65, following a near-doubling of its consolidated net profit in Q2 FY27. Net profit rose 92.8% to ₹30.8 Cr from ₹16 Cr a year ago and increased 28.5% from ₹24 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue grew 19.6% YoY and 3.2% QoQ to ₹438.7 Cr. Awfis reported normalised revenue of ₹451 Cr, including an adjustment of around ₹13 Cr for actual rent received under finance lease arrangements. On this basis, coworking and allied services contributed approximately ₹376 Cr, while construction and fit-out projects under its Transform vertical generated ₹75 Cr. Awfis added six centres during the quarter, taking its network to 254 centres with approximately 1.74 Lakh seats across 18 cities. Portfolio occupancy stood at 76.2%, rising to 84.1% at centres operational for more than 12 months. Its premium portfolio comprised 29 Gold and 10 Elite centres. The company said incremental premium seats were being signed at prices around 35% higher than its flagship offerings. Awfis plans to prioritise occupancy, client renewals, and capital-efficient expansion, while adding premium workspaces in Pune, Bengaluru, Mumbai, and Delhi NCR. RateGain Falls Despite Growth RateGain shares declined 9.2% this week to close at ₹725.90, despite reporting a 46.5% YoY increase in consolidated net profit to ₹74.7 Cr in Q2 FY27. The company’s stock plunged by over 11% on Friday, the next trading session after its quarterly disclosures. Operating revenue surged 152.6% YoY to ₹745.4 Cr, largely reflecting the consolidation of travel marketing platform Sojern, acquired for $250 Mn in November 2025. Sequentially, however, revenue fell 5% from ₹785 Cr, while net profit declined 21.3% from ₹94.9 Cr. Excluding expenses related to deferred deal consideration for Sojern, adjusted net profit rose 78% YoY to ₹90.8 Cr. Adjusted EBITDA more than tripled to ₹169.1 Cr. The acquisition has reshaped RateGain’s business mix. Marketing technology accounted for 80.2% of revenue, followed by data-as-a-service at 13.2% and distribution at 6.6%. Its customer base stood at 14,538 at September-end, around 4.5 times the 3,224 customers reported at the end of FY25. Customers include hotel chains, online travel agencies, airlines, car rental companies, and destination marketing organisations. RateGain’s UK subsidiary repaid another $46.3 Mn of acquisition-related debt during the quarter. Cumulative repayments reached $93.8 Mn, or 75% of the original $125 Mn facility from HSBC and Citibank, leaving outstanding debt of $31.3 Mn. The company reported a sales pipeline of ₹660 Cr and new contract wins worth ₹277.7 Cr. Chairman and MD Bhanu Chopra said its second-half priorities included expanding the combined RateGain-Sojern offering and increasing customer adoption of its AI products.

MobiKwik’s wholly owned subsidiary, MobiKwik Financial Services Pvt Ltd (MFSPL), has received a Certificate of Registration (CoR) from the RBI to operate as a non-banking financial company (NBFC). The certificate was issued on November 5, following the RBI’s in-principle approval in April 2026. The dedicated NBFC was officially incorporated on March 13, 2025. With the regulatory clearance in place, MFSPL intends to commence operations over the next three to six months. It intends to operate on an asset-light co-lending model, partnering with banks and other NBFCs. In a statement, the company said that it plans to complement its existing lending service provider (LSP) business with the ability to originate credit directly through its NBFC. "This will provide greater flexibility in product development, faster go-to-market execution and opportunities to improve lending economics, while allowing the group to continue leveraging its partnerships with established lenders," the company said. MobiKwik aims to disburse loans worth ₹5,000 Cr over the next three to four years, covering secured and unsecured credit for consumers and MSMEs. Cofounder and CFO Upasana Taku said that the NBFC extension would allow MobiKwik to build on its existing lender partnerships and technology infrastructure while participating more actively in the lending value chain. The company plans to focus on responsible lending, prudent underwriting and sustainable growth. During its Q2 earnings call, the CFO noted that MobiKwik could initially route around 10% of its digital lending disbursals through the NBFC. If the company disburses ₹6,000 Cr through its digital lending business next year, it would aim to route ₹600 Cr through MFSPL. Under a proposed 10:90 co-lending arrangement, MobiKwik would contribute 10% of the loan amount, while its lending partner would fund the remaining 90%. This would require around ₹60 Cr in capital from MobiKwik to support ₹600 Cr in disbursals, allowing it to limit its on-book exposure while leveraging its existing underwriting and collections capabilities. The NBFC launch comes amid an uptick for MobiKwik’s business. MobiKwik reported a consolidated net profit of ₹11.8 Cr in Q2 FY27 against a net loss of ₹28.6 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Operating revenue increased 9.4% YoY to ₹295.7 Cr from ₹270.2 Cr. The company said it recorded its highest-ever quarterly net profit, marking its fourth consecutive profitable quarter. During the quarter, MobiKwik’s financial services business segment, which includes its ZIP EMI credit offering, increased 41.8% YoY to ₹86.9 Cr. Loan disbursals through its lending partners rose 34.1% YoY to ₹1,082.6 Cr, up 46.9% sequentially from ₹736.7 Cr. The sequential recovery followed a temporary dip linked to technology infrastructure migration during the transfer of its lending business. MobiKwik increased its major lending partners to 11 from six a year earlier. It classifies partners with quarterly disbursals exceeding ₹5 Cr as major lenders. Of the total disbursals, 21% came through its distribution model, while the remaining 79% were under its first-loss default guarantee (FLDG) model, under which it shares credit risk with lending partners. Lending-related expenses, including operational and financial guarantee costs, declined 16.4% YoY to ₹29.8 Cr. The company attributed the reduction to improved credit quality and better commercial terms with lending partners. MobiKwik expects lending disbursals to maintain strong double-digit growth as newer partnerships mature and it introduces additional product categories, although management cautioned that the growth rate may moderate. Shares of MobiKwik ended today's trading session 2.3% higher at ₹224.75 apiece on the BSE.

These matters figured at an India-EU strategic partnership review meeting held in New Delhi, weeks ahead of an expected visit by Prime Minister Narendra Modi to Brussels in mid-December for the signing of the FTA. The two sides concluded negotiations for the trade deal in January.

India and the EU reviewed engagements aimed at boosting trade and investment cooperation, including the “timely signing and implementation of the India-EU Free Trade Agreement”, and to conclude the investment protection agreement and the agreement on geographical indications, both sides said in a joint statement.
The discussions also covered strengthening supply chains and economic security, including strategic engagements in the Trade and Technology Council (TTC) and Blue Valleys initiative.
The meeting, co-chaired by Sibi George, secretary (West) in the external affairs ministry, and Matti Maasikas, deputy secretary general for geoeconomics and inter-institutional issues of the European External Action Service, also discussed cooperation in critical and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), quantum technologies, digital public infrastructure (DPI), advanced semiconductors, clean tech and biotechnology, as well as engagements to advance a conducive digital environment and promote DPI.
ALSO READ: India, EU conclude negotiations for association with Horizon Europe research programme
The two sides expressed satisfaction at deepening research collaboration, including India’s potential association with Horizon Europe, the EU’s €93.5-billion flagship research and innovation programme. The conclusion of negotiations for India's association with the programme was announced by both sides last week.
The two sides emphasised the importance of strengthening connectivity partnership, including Global Gateway, India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) and trilateral projects in clean energy, climate resilience, green mobility and digitalisation. They agreed to enhance coordination and cooperation towards shaping effective global governance, the statement said.
The meeting discussed ways to enhance people-to-people contacts, including in talent mobility, education and skills development, and reviewed updates on the European Legal Gateway Office. They also looked forward to the next edition of the India-EU human rights dialogue.
“As trusted, predictable and like-minded partners, they reaffirmed their commitment to deepen the India-EU Strategic Partnership, and to deliver mutually beneficial, concrete and transformative outcomes,” the statement said, adding that the meeting also reviewed preparations for future meetings at the leaders’ level.
Both sides welcomed the “very positive momentum” in India-EU relations, and reviewed the implementation of the joint comprehensive strategic agenda adopted at the India-EU Summit in New Delhi in January. They further renewed their commitments to advance the clean transition, and to pursue cooperation to include Indian ship recycling yards that comply with the EU Regulation on Ship Recycling in the bloc’s list of ship recycling facilities.

What if improving the health of a village meant doing more than building a hospital, treating patients and performing surgeries? In Aragonda, a village in Andhra Pradesh’s Chittoor district, an initiative that began with a 50-bed rural hospital has evolved into a community development model that links healthcare with education, nutrition, sanitation and preventive health.
Through its Total Health programme, Apollo Foundation is attempting to address the wider social determinants of health, with interventions spanning different stages of people’s lives, from maternal and child healthcare to youth development, women’s economic independence and elderly care.
The programme’s interventions include 1,200 antenatal and postnatal check-ups for new mothers, training in hygiene practices across 2,600 schools and industry-related and sports skills for more than 545 young people. It has also conducted over two lakh yoga sessions, alongside free screening and care for non-communicable diseases (NCDs), while more than 10.8 lakh meals have been served to elderly people through its geriatric nutrition centres.
Prathap C. Reddy, founder chairman of Apollo Hospitals Group, said the initiative reflected his belief that quality and affordable healthcare should reach every Indian, irrespective of where they lived. While the hospital initially brought modern medicine to his village, the larger vision was to create conditions in which people could lead healthier lives, he said. “Medicine can save lives, but to change the health of a generation, we must also change the conditions in which life is lived,” he added.
Specialised orthopaedic care in a rural setting
Alongside preventive and community healthcare, Apollo Hospitals Aragonda has also expanded its specialised surgical services, completing 1,000 total knee replacement (TKR) procedures. Established as a 50-bed hospital in 2000, it has served more than 1.67 lakh patients and performed over 12,000 surgeries in 26 years.
The knee replacement programme has grown from 100 procedures in 2019 to 500 in 2022 and 1,000 in 2026. “The 1,000 procedures have been completed without a single reported infection,” said Sangita Reddy, joint managing director of Apollo Hospitals.
From a rural hospital to a community health model
Telemedicine was another early intervention. With a network of three telephone lines, Apollo connected specialists in cities with patients in rural areas, allowing doctors to examine CT scans and ultrasound images remotely. The initiative enabled specialists to guide local doctors in treating patients who otherwise would have had to travel to distant hospitals. She recalled that former President of US, Bill Clinton, witnessed a telemedicine demonstration from Aragonda during his visit to Hyderabad.
A healthcare model looking beyond the hospital
Preetha Reddy, executive vice-chairperson of Apollo Hospitals Enterprise Limited said the organisation remained committed to narrowing the divide between rural and urban healthcare. “The ability to perform specialised procedures such as knee replacements in a village demonstrates the potential for such models to be replicated in other parts of the world,” she added.

Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared for pollution?
- Published
There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.
"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.
She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.
Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.
Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.
The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?
This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.
Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.
Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.
This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.
For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.
Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.
The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.
Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.
These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.
Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.
Experts say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.
"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.
Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.
"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."
Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.
"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."
Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.
This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.
In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.
During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".
On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.
The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.
Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".
Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.
A 2025 report, external by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.
For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.
Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.
While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.
Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.
Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.
The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others, they are not planning to move out of Delhi.
"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.
"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

SpaceX announced a new version of its all-in-one satellite internet terminal that integrates a dish, Wi-Fi router, and now a battery into a single device about the size of a laptop. According to some users on X who shared screenshots of invitations to order Starlink Mini 2, the dish is priced at $999, which includes a full year of Roam Unlimited service that SpaceX values at $2,100.
Starlink Mini 2 adds a swappable battery
The all-in-one satellite dish can now operate for over four hours without an external power source.
The Starlink Mini 2 will run for up to 4.5 hours on a full charge, SpaceX claims, but that can be expanded by hot-swapping in additional batteries that will be sold separately, or by connecting the dish to a 60W power source over USB-C.
Despite the addition of an integrated battery, the Starlink Mini 2 dish is thinner than the original Mini. SpaceX has managed to slim it down to 23.1mm thick, while the previous version of the Mini was 38.5mm. The Starlink Mini 2 is slightly heavier at around 3.5 pounds as a result of the added battery weight, but carries forward an IP67 dust- and waterproof rating so it’s still safe to use outdoors.
Preorders are now open “by invitation for select US customers,” according to the Starlink website, but “coming soon” to more customers and countries.

The Delhi High Court, on Friday, disposed off the contempt petition filed by players Somdev Devvarman and Purav Raja against the All India Tennis Association’s (AITA) interim office-bearers after the body gave an undertaking that all information sought by administrator Justice (retd.) Gita Mittal has been provided, and that it would continue to do so until the end of the administrator’s tenure (November 27).
To Justice Mittal’s request to implead the AITA Trust and the Delhi Lawn Tennis Association (DLTA) for corruption, the Court is learnt to have said that the allegations could be probed by the new AITA body that will take charge after elections, and the Court could re-engage Justice Mittal if required.
The administrator, in a report dated September 14, had submitted to the Court that looking into the matters of the AITA Trust was a necessary step under her Court-mandated “obligation to supervise the financial affairs of AITA” because the AITA had “assigned and abdicated all its functions, properties and income to the AITA Trust”.
Polls under the amended AITA Constitution are scheduled to be held on November 27, with the filing of nominations for the Executive Committee and Athletes Committee elections beginning on November 14.
The High Court is scheduled to hear the matter again on January 22, 2027, and all actions pertaining to amending the Constitution in line with the National Sports Governance Act and elections will be subject to the final outcome of the case.

Meta Platforms said on Monday it would expand its AI age-estimation technology globally to move millions more teens on Instagram into Teen Account protections, even if they have given birth dates showing they are adults, as the company faces lawsuits alleging its platforms harm young users.
Teen Accounts, available on Instagram, Facebook and Messenger, include built-in protections that automatically limit who can contact teens, the content they see and their time on the apps.
Parents in the US will begin receiving Instagram notifications this month explaining how teens are placed in age-appropriate protections, Meta said.
In Australia, Meta has begun using Apple’s age-range signal as an additional method to help determine users’ ages.
Meta said it is continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook and will begin launching similar technology globally on Threads later this year.
Meta faces multiple lawsuits over allegations that its platforms harm teens.
In August, Meta struck settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every US state and territory to resolve lawsuits brought by attorneys general over the platforms’ harm to teens.
Under the settlements, Meta agreed to improve how it identifies teens and children under 13.
Meta settled with a teen plaintiff last month in a Los Angeles trial testing claims that Instagram and Facebook were designed to be addictive, causing mental health problems and an eating disorder.

I return to my room as my mother-in-law leaves for her office in the building adjacent to our home. I am about to start my bath when I hear a series of explosions, as of firecrackers, but different. I freeze. Someone comes pounding frantically on my bathroom door. It is Ongmu, the children’s nanny, crying hysterically. I fling open the door, my heart thumping. She is gesticulating wildly, speechlessly, towards the garden.
I run along the path leading to Akbar Road. I see the white Ambassador car slowly moving towards the same path. I hesitate. I stop, heart in my mouth. Dread, panic, fear. I feel suffocated. I can’t breathe. I am about to collapse. No, no, I can’t. I have to walk to the car. I see her being carried into it. I understand; I scream.
I’m in the car now, crouching on the floor, facing her … Blood – blood on her sari, blood on her chest. Her large eyes are wide open; her face wears a surprised expression. She doesn’t move. I attempt to speak to her, to call out, “Mummy, Mummy”, but no word comes out. I try again; she doesn’t reply.
Her aides are in the front of the car, screaming. Heavy, slow traffic, the car barely moves, it has no siren. One red light, then another. Then the hospital. The gate isn’t opening. Chaos. We are stopped; someone looks through the window in a questioning attitude. They let us in.
We reach the emergency department, teeming with people. We are stopped again, not allowed in, we have to wait for our turn. Someone calls out to the driver, signals him to move forward. They identify us; she is placed on a trolley. We are led somewhere – an operation theatre? They ask me to follow. I’m taken to a room nearby. No, no, I want to stay by her, I insist. I want to know. I have to see. They don’t reply; they are immersed in their emergency procedures.
I feel confused, lost … I don’t recognise anyone there. I’m shivering under my dressing gown. I feel scared, my mind is racing. Where is Rajiv? I try to remember. I can’t, I can’t. The children, yes, they’re in school; they must be brought home. Oh God, no, no. Let them be safe, let Rajiv be safe … Whom do I tell, whom do I speak to? I sense someone in the room. I don’t know who it is. I try to speak, to put some words together; nothing comes out. “There’s blood all over her clothes,” someone says. Some clothes are brought in for me. I am helped into them in a nearby closet.
Hours go by, agonising hours. More people come in and crowd around. I signal a question to the doctor; he shakes his head. I understand, yes, I understand. I break into sobs, uncontrollably. Someone tries to calm me. I feel numb, cold.
At two in the afternoon of 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was declared dead. I was driven home to collect some clothes for her body to be changed into. On the way, a group of men tried to stop our car, banging on its windows. They were angry, shouting something I couldn’t understand.
At home, the children, Rahul and Priyanka, rushed to my arms in tears. When they had been abruptly picked up from school by black-uniformed commandos, they sensed a catastrophe. Once home, they saw some of the staff sobbing. They asked question after question. “Where’s Mama?” “Why have we been brought home?” “Where’s Papa?” “What’s happened?” “Where’s Dadi?” “You aren’t telling us the truth!” My friends Nina and Sterre had been with them, trying to calm them down, not knowing what to say to them. I wanted to sit with them and hug them, to break the news to them gently, but I was unable to – I had to go back; Rajiv was coming to the hospital.
Rajiv had been in West Bengal at a political rally when his cavalcade was stopped by a police patrol. He was told there was a message from Delhi to say he should rush back – a serious accident had taken place. He was driven to the helipad, from where he flew to Calcutta and then to Delhi. He’d heard on a BBC bulletin that Mrs Gandhi was wounded and in a grave condition. Nobody told him directly that his mother was no more, but he understood.
He landed at 3.30pm and was driven straight to the hospital. He walked in with other people, and I remember longing to be left alone with him for a moment at least. We held each other, and as he spoke to me, it sunk in that he was saying something I didn’t want to hear. “I have been asked … They want me to be sworn in as prime minister.”
I felt as if a knife had been plunged right into my heart. I felt a pounding in my chest, a rage welling up deep inside me. I was about to explode. I attempted to hold it in. “You have been asked to? How dare they ask? How dare they? Who are they? Why you, why does it have to be you? Why did you allow them to ask you? No, it cannot be; this time it’s not going to be!” Seized by utter pain and anguish, soaked in perspiration, I felt like throwing up. I wanted to scream, to ask for help. “Someone please help me put an end to this.”
I burst out crying, pleading, begging him with folded hands, “No, no, you can’t think of it. You have to stop them, you must refuse, you must say no – for the children’s sake, for yourself. You can’t do this to us. They will kill you; they will kill you, too!” I cried out. He replied, “They will kill me anyway.”
We brought my mother-in-law home. The dining room had been emptied out, and we laid her body down on the floor, her feet pointing south as Hindu custom decrees. The same evening at around 6.30pm, Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister of India. I was too broken to even register what was happening around me. His mother lay there, her body pierced with more than 30 bullet holes. I knew, I knew it then in my heart: Rajiv’s path would lead to the same end.

Three social media content creators from West Bengal — Akash Sarkar, Surajit Shee and Srimoyee Chakraborty — were recently arrested after making posts which questioned the ruling BJP government and its policies.
While Sarkar was granted bail on October 29 after spending three days in police custody, Chatterjee was released from detention on a personal bond on October 26. Shee was first sent to judicial custody and held at Medinipur Central Jail. At present, he is in police custody till November 6.
An FIR was lodged against Shee under Sections 152, 197 and 353 of the BNS, pertaining to acts endangering integrity of India, assertions threatening national integration, and statements amounting to public mischief, respectively.
In the FIR registered against Sarkar, the police invoked Sections 356(1), 353(1)(2) and 299(1) of the BNS, pertaining to criminal defamation, spreading false information/hate speech, and intentionally outraging religious feelings, respectively.
Surajit Shee: Posts on Durga Puja Stampede
Surajit Shee, hailing from Dantan village of West Midnapore district, runs a Facebook page called ‘Core Bangla-Janakantha’, which has over 2,52,000 followers. Shee shares posts on a range of social, political and scientific issues. The two last posts on his page were made on October 19. In one, he is seen appreciating the BJP government for banning DJs and loudspeakers during processions in the state, and in the other post, he talks about allegations that followed the Chorbagan stampede which killed 19 people in Kolkata at a Durga Puja.
Another post by Shee from October 18 caried a video that has been restricted in India. The caption reads, translated from Bengali, “What is the actual truth behind the Chorebagan incident? Which version is correct? The official government figures or the claims made by the public? The government itself is abusing the law. Those in power are misusing their authority to silence the voices of ordinary citizens.”
Shee is a member of ‘Bharatiya Biggyan o Juktibadi Samity’ — an organization which aims to promote scientific temperament in the society.
Alt News spoke with Dipak Roy, a key member of the outfit. Roy mentioned that beside discussing political issues, Shee was vocal about various scientific and social issues.
“Surajit had been telling us that for almost a year that a section of local BJP-RSS workers had been harassing him over his social media content. The intensity of the harassment increased after May 4 (as BJP came to power in the state). On either October 17 or 18, Shee told me that his house had been attacked by the same group, who claimed that he was posting anti-national content. I suggested that he take shelter elsewhere. He then went to a friend’s house in Contai. The police arrested him from there on October 24,” alleged Roy.
Although Shee was detained by police on October 24, he was shown as arrested on October 25, Sunday, from his residence in Dantan, instead of Contai.
According to Roy, the group that attacked Shee’s house claimed that a complaint had been lodged against him at Dantan police station over his alleged ‘anti-national’ activities. Roy told Alt News that when Shee’s father and father-in-law went to the police station to enquire about the alleged complaints, the police could not produce any complaint lodged against him. Police allegedly told them that the chief minister had ordered Shee’s arrest and that it “would be better if he surrendered” or else they would “make an example out of him”.
During the arrest, Roy alleged that only three to four police personnel were present while nearly 20 RSS-BJP workers rounded him up. “Around 15-20 RSS-BJP workers surrounded the house of his friend in Contai. These people assaulted him before handing him over to the police, who then took him away in a car,” alleged Roy. “We thought Contai police had arrested him and arranged for a lawyer to represent him at the Contai sub-divisional court. However, later we realised that Shee had been arrested by Dantan police and was produced before the Dantan court.”
Roy further alleged that Shee’s family could access the legal documents related to the case two days after his arrest. Police have also allegedly seized Shee’s mobile phone, but no seizure list has been provided to his family.
Alt News’ attempts to contact both Dantan and Contain police were unsuccessful till publication time.
Alt News spoke to Tapan Jana, Shee’s maternal uncle, who said, “Surajit was produced in Dantan court on November 2, and police sought seven days of custody. However, the judge allowed only four days.”
“After he was remanded to police custody, an officer from Dantan police station verbally abused us when we went to meet him. The officer said that Surajit had insulted Sanatan Dharma, the state and central governments, and was inciting the public through his Facebook posts. He told us to make sure that Surajit reveals during questioning who had instructed him to make those posts,” Jana said.
“The officer further said that unless Shee confessed, he would make it difficult for him to get bail,” Jana added.
Akash Sarkar: Posts on Stampede and Suvendu Adhikari
Akash Sarkar (30) was arrested from his home in Nagerbazar on October 25, produced before the Barrackpore court on October 26, which ordered three days of police custody. He was released on bail on October 29.
Sarkar told Alt News that during interrogation, police pointed to three aspects of his posts which they claimed led to his arrest — his reference to Suvendu Adhikari’s ‘bhaipo’ (nephew) in connection with the Chorbagan stampede, his comments about the government’s handling of the situation following the stampede, and his use of the term ‘teen bati’ (three bowls) to refer to Adhikari.
Sarkar said, “In one of my Facebook posts, I had mentioned that Suvendu’s nephew was the chief patron of Chorbagan Sarbojonin, the puja where 19 people were trampled, and that he should take responsibility for the tragedy. I had also flagged the manner in which the Durga idol, with its hands tied, was taken away by the police for immersion.”
“I had written in my Facebook post that, according to the BJP, previous governments in West Bengal were not Sanatani. But even those governments did not treat the goddess in the way the Sanatani government treated her. The police flagged my post as religiously inflammatory and kept me in custody for three days,” added Sarkar.
According to Sarkar, in another post, he had addressed chief minister as ‘teen bati’ — a political jab aimed at Adhikari.
“The ‘teen bati’ jab was popularised by Ali Aftab Chand, a lawyer at the Calcutta high court who identifies himself as a ‘Rashtravadi Muslim’. He was not arrested. Is it because he is close to the BJP?” asked Sarkar.
According to the FIR, a person named Soumen Das had lodged a complaint against Sarkar, alleging that Sarkar “has been using his Facebook profile to publish false, defamatory, religiously inflammatory and provocative posts concerning the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Sri Narendra Modi and Hon’ble Chief Minister of India, Sri Suvendu Adhikari.”
“While I was in the lock-up, I heard from a few police personnel that our local MLA, Tarunjyoti Tiwari, had visited the police station and taken a personal interest in my case. Police hinted that although the charges against me were flimsy, orders from higher-ups were forcing them to keep me in custody,” he alleged, adding that the police was yet to return his phone.
Srimoyee Chakroborty: Posts Critical of State Government
Chakraborty had posted an update on her Facebook profile on October 26, mentioning that she had been held at the Bidhannagar East police station. She was later released the same day on a bond of Rs 2,000.
On October 26, she announced on Facebook that she was detained, while vowing to continue her fight. Her posts on Facebook reflect a similar pattern of posts critical of the BJP-led state and central government and its policies. However, it is not clear which particular post led to the administrative action.
A scroll through her Facebook timeline shows her vocal support for the Left.
Similar to Shee and Sarkar, Chakraborty had also made a series of posts critical of the government’s management of the Chorbagan stampede and the immersion process. On October 21, she shared the chief minister’s video where he announced that only people who follow Sanatana Dharma would participate in the Durga idol immersion process. In the caption, she referred to Adhikari as ‘teen bati’.

Anthony Andrews improved his stature as a coach in women’s football after leading East Bengal to a historic knockout qualification in the AFC Women’s Champions League, making it the first Indian club to reach this stage in the tournament’s history.
After opening the group stage with a 2-1 win over Ho Chi Minh City of Vietnam, the double Indian Women’s League (IWL) defending champion suffered defeats to South Korea’s Hwacheon KSPO WFC and North Korea’s 4.25 SC. However, its goal difference was enough to take the Kolkata club through as one of two best third-placed teams.
After sealing the last-eight berth, Andrews was promptly propped up by his players on their shoulders as the bunch soaked in the atmosphere created by the scant fan-base presence at the Kishore Bharati Krirangan in Kolkata. But, the 30-year-old almost didn’t stay on to experience this red-letter moment.
Earlier this year, Andrews had received an offer to join an Indian Super League team as its first team assistant coach. The talks were initiated back in January and went deep till around June-July. The interested ISL team is one of the five sides in the ongoing season which have been part of the league since its start back in 2014. However at the eleventh hour, he decided to not leave East Bengal.
“Whoever spoke with me from the ISL club was very professional. They were very clear with my plan and never said no to me for anything. I really wanted to go there, but one thing which was holding me back was the East Bengal team we have built with a lot of hope and trust and the players who have been with me since I joined. My team also said, ‘Let’s finish this, what you have left’. We also had a goal that we have to be in the top eight in AFC,” Andrews told Sportstar on Monday.
The talks for this new role were happening in the backdrop of uncertainty around ISL, with no start date for the new season in sight. Stability, that was present at his current role with the IWL champion, was missing from the ISL job, at that point in time. That was another reason for Andrews and his team to not go ahead with the move.
“One last time, I had a focussed conversation with Anthony to weigh the pros and cons of this move before going forward with it. Here [at East Bengal], he has full control of the team; he can go around making decisions which are beneficial for him. At the end, I told him staying is the better option because he has already built something which nobody has done before. There is something left in AFC for him to prove. He has proved everything in India now,” Mizpha Richards, a member of the talent agency associated with Andrews, recalled.

“His profile in women’s football has moved to bigger heights where there have been enquiries for him from foreign clubs also. With them, it was all initial level of talks and there was the element of skepticism attached to moving to a new country. So we dropped that plan and the ISL offer seemed to be a better option, but eventually we discussed and thought there is some job left to do here,” Richards added.
Come November 13, East Bengal will begin its title defence against Andrews’ former side, Gokulam Kerala FC, with which he won back-to-back titles as well. This time, he would hope to better his best yet: go for a three peat.
But Andrews quite frankly revealed that a combination of his desire to coach in men’s football — the reason behind his venturing into coaching — and the many obstacles dotting the path in women’s football have made him look out in recent times.
“There are a lot of things which you have to take care of. And I’m not saying that I have to run with the responsibility, but I think whoever is involved in the game has to be a little serious about the development of the women’s game. It’s not a one-person job. So if that happens, I’ll maybe stick to women’s football. But yeah, I have another year with East Bengal. We see how things work in the future,” Andrews concluded.
