Past talks involving Russia and Ukraine have yielded little progress toward peace
Negotiators from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington are scheduled to meet in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and Wednesday for talks aimed at trying to end Russia's 4 1/2-year-old full-scale invasion of Ukraine
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in the latest bid to end the war.
Key developments from past sessions since Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022:
Feb. 28, 2022: Ukrainian and Russian delegations meet in neighboring Belarus for the first time after the invasion. Talks continue for two weeks, deciding only on humanitarian corridors for evacuating civilians.
March 10, 2022: Russian and Ukrainian Foreign Ministers Sergey Lavrov and Dmytro Kuleba meet in Antalya, Turkey.
March 21, 2022: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy calls for direct talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, an idea rebuffed by Lavrov.
March 28-30, 2022: Delegations meet in Istanbul to work on a draft peace agreement. Moscow says it's willing to “fundamentally cut back” military activity near Kyiv and the northern city of Chernihiv; Ukraine says it's open to discussing neutral status for Ukraine if its security is backed by other nations.
April 7, 2022: Lavrov rejects a Ukrainian proposal as “unacceptable," saying Kyiv has walked back on an agreement to exempt the Crimean Peninsula from wider Ukrainian security guarantees. Russia illegally annexed Crimea in 2014.
April 26, 2022: U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres visits Russia to discuss ending the war.
May 13, 2022: U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin calls his Russian counterpart, their first contact since war began.
July 22, 2022: Russia and Ukraine, with mediation by Turkey and the U.N., agree to unblock grain supplies stuck in Ukraine’s Black Sea ports. Russia withdraws from the deal a year later.
Sept. 30, 2022: Russia illegally annexes the Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, even though it doesn’t fully control any of them. Ukraine responds by applying to join NATO and by enacting a decree that declares negotiations with Putin “impossible.”
Nov. 15, 2022: Zelenskyy unveils a 10-point peace plan at the G20 summit in Indonesia.
June 16-17, 2023: African leaders travel to Kyiv and St. Petersburg on a peace mission, without success.
June 25, 2023: Officials from 15 countries, including the U.S., India, Brazil, South Africa, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and several representatives from the European Union, meet in Copenhagen, Denmark, to discuss Zelenskyy’s peace plan.
Aug. 5-6, 2023: Two days of discussions on the war begin in Saudi Arabia with delegates from 40 countries, including China, India, South Africa and Brazil, but not Russia. No joint statements are issued.
Oct. 28-29, 2023: Delegates from 65 countries meet in Malta to continue talks on Zelenskyy’s peace plan. Russia, which dismissed the talks, was not invited. China, though invited, did not participate.
June 15-16, 2024: Representatives of 92 nations meet in Nidwalden, Switzerland, to discuss Ukraine’s peace plan, but a consensus remains elusive. The summit’s final statement is backed by most — but not all — participants.
Dec. 7, 2024: U.S. President-elect Donald Trump travels to Paris and meets Zelenskyy and other European leaders.
Feb. 12, 2025: Trump and Putin speak directly via telephone and agree to begin negotiations on ending the war. The conversation ends a three-year U.S.-led effort to isolate Putin.
Feb. 18, 2025: Russian and U.S. officials, including Lavrov and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meet in Saudi Arabia and agree to work toward ending the war, as well as restoring bilateral ties. Ukrainian officials are not invited.
Feb. 28, 2025: Zelenskyy holds a contentious meeting with Trump, Rubio and Vice President JD Vance in the White House. A proposed minerals deal between the countries is left unsigned.
March 11, 2025: U.S. and Ukrainian officials meet in Saudi Arabia, with Americans proposing a plan for a 30-day ceasefire. Kyiv agrees to the proposed truce.
March 13, 2025: Putin effectively rejects the ceasefire plan, stating certain issues still must be resolved. He also meets with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Moscow. Witkoff travels to Russia twice more in April to meet Putin.
March 23-24, 2025: The U.S. holds separate talks with each side in Saudi Arabia. The White House says they agreed to a Black Sea truce.
May 16, 2025: Russia and Ukraine meet directly in Istanbul, under Turkish mediation, for the first time in three years and agree to swap 1,000 prisoners from each side. Ukraine's delegation was led by Defense Minister Rustem Umerov, while Russia's was headed by Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky.
June 2 and July 23, 2025: Two more rounds of talks between Russia and Ukraine in Istanbul produce an exchange of draft memorandums.
Aug. 15, 2025: Trump and Putin meet in Anchorage, Alaska. The summit produces no concrete peace agreement, ceasefire deal, or specific resolution on the war in Ukraine. International observers widely view it as a symbolic boost for Moscow.
Aug. 18, 2025: Trump hosts Zelenskyy and European leaders at the White House. Discussions center on establishing robust security guarantees for Ukraine.
November 2025: A 28-point U.S.-Russian peace plan emerges, and critics say it favors Moscow. On Nov. 23, it's cut to 19 points during discussions involving Washington, Kyiv and Ukraine’s European allies in Geneva.
Dec. 2, 2025: Putin, his adviser Yuri Ushakov and Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev meet Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner in Moscow. Ushakov describes the meeting as constructive but says much work remains.
Dec. 4-6, 2025: Witkoff and Kushner meet a Ukrainian delegation headed by Umerov and Chief of General Staff Gen. Andriy Hnatov in Miami.
Dec. 14-15, 2025: Ukrainian officials, including Zelenskyy, travel to Berlin for talks with Witkoff and Kushner. U.S. officials say Washington agrees to provide Kyiv with unspecified security guarantees.
Dec. 20-21, 2025: Dmitriev holds talks with Witkoff and Kushner in Miami. The Americans meet separately with a Ukrainian delegation.
Dec. 28, 2025: Zelenskyy meets in Florida with Trump, who calls Putin beforehand.
Jan. 6-7, 2026: Zelenskyy and other Ukrainians attend a summit of the “Coalition of the Willing” in Paris and hold talks with Witkoff and Kushner. Kyiv’s allies tout major progress for defending Ukraine if a peace deal is struck, saying they were ready to provide international guarantees to deter Russia from attacking again.
Jan. 17, 2026: A Ukrainian delegation arrives in the U.S. for talks.
Jan. 20-22, 2026: Witkoff and Kushner meet separately in Davos, Switzerland, with Ukrainian and Russian delegations. Zelenskyy then meets Trump for what the U.S. leader calls “very good” talks. Zelenskyy calls them “productive and meaningful.”
Jan. 23-24, 2026: Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. delegates meet in Abu Dhabi in the first known instance of Trump administration officials sitting down with both countries to try to halt the war.
Feb. 4-5, 2026: A second round of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi leads to swapping 157 prisoners from each side.
Feb. 17-18, 2026: The third round of trilateral negotiations in Geneva, Switzerland, ends without a breakthrough.
Feb. 28, 2026: The U.S. and Israel begin a war with Iran, leading the Trump administration to wind down talks with Russian and Ukrainian officials.
May 7, 2026: Umerov meets in Miami with U.S. officials, as negotiations remain stalled.
Sept. 5-6, 2026: Witkoff and Kushner meet Putin in Moscow on Sept. 5, and in Kyiv with Zelenskyy the next day.
Oct. 21, 2026: Ushakov says Putin agrees “in principle” with Witkoff to resume talks after Nov. 10.
Oct. 27-Nov. 1, 2026: After intervention by U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, a localized ceasefire is reached for the region around the Russia-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine to allow the evacuation of some of its residents and the delivery of food and other supplies.

It was not possible to find evidence of Kirk publicly saying Texas would never turn blue in his lifetime, though it may have been something he said in private.
In November, a rumor circulated that Charlie Kirk, the deceased co-founder of conservative nonprofit network Turning Point USA, once said Texas would "never turn blue" within his lifetime.
People posted examples of the claim across social media, with one Facebook user writing (archived):
"Texas will never turn blue in my lifetime." - Charlie Kirk
Well, I'll be damned! He was right. He's looking up right now and shaking his head in shame.
The rumor spread following the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, which saw the Democratic Party flip Texas blue after James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won their races for a Senate seat and the governor's office, respectively.
Kirk was fatally shot in September 2025. Snopes has covered numerous claims about his assassination.
In short, there is no evidence Kirk ever publicly said Texas would never turn blue in his lifetime. Therefore, the posts above incorrectly attributed the in-question quote to him.
Most of the posts featuring the rumor include no evidence supporting the claim, such as an old social media post or podcast episode showing Kirk making the statement. There has been such proof when Snopes has looked into quotes that were correctly attributed to him.
Searching for the alleged quote on Bing, Google, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo yielded no credible results, only more internet users spreading the claim. Likewise, searches of Kirk's official X and Facebook profiles returned no such proof of him saying it. If he had publicly said the comment, the results would have likely provided evidence of him doing so.
Similarly, videos or audio likely would have resurfaced and credible media outlets would have reported on the remark considering the Democrats' sweeping victory in the 2026 midterms. That was not the case.
Rather, it appears users fabricated the quote, which led to several posts that seemingly intended to be satirical — like one attributing the statement to "Charlie Kirkstradamus," a reference to French astrologer Nostradamus who is known for his prophecies (Snopes has also debunked numerous prophecies incorrectly attributed to Nostradamus). Others simply repeated the claim as though it is authentic.
Several posts include a screenshot or reference of something Kirk did post to X on Nov. 3, 2020, the date of that year's presidential election. That post reads, "Texas is not going blue. Don't listen to the activist media."
Some people who shared that authentic message alongside the in-question false quote seemingly misrepresented the legitimate quote's context to suggest Kirk had said Texas would "never turn blue" in his lifetime.
A majority of Texans did vote for Trump during the 2020 presidential election.
In January 2026, the state's Hood County announced its intention to rename one of its roads, "Charlie Kirk Memorial Parkway."

New York will independently test AI models
The state’s research center will check AI companies’ work instead of taking their word.
As the federal government essentially leaves us all at the mercy of the AI industry, New York is taking matters into its own hands. On Tuesday, Governor Kathy Hochul launched the nation's first state-run AI testing program. Instead of trusting AI companies to police themselves, New York's system will task independent researchers with checking their work. "The stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word," Hochul stated in a press release.
The work will be handled by the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University. More than 80 New York scientists will contribute. They'll use computing power from Empire AI, the state's $500 million public-private AI partnership.
Hochul's office said the center will test advanced AI systems, study their risks and provide evidence to inform public officials' decisions. It will also look at how AI can be used responsibly in areas like medicine and scientific discovery.
One potential hole in the program is that it can only study what AI companies disclose publicly. New York's RAISE Act, signed by Hochul last year, requires large AI developers to register with the state by January 1, 2027. Starting then, companies will have to publish safety frameworks and transparency reports and report critical safety incidents within 72 hours. The RAISE Act won't plug the hole on unreleased models, but it will at least force companies to disclose more.

AvenuesAI (formerly Infibeam Avenues) reported a 6% growth in its net profit to ₹71.7 Cr in the quarter ended September (Q2 FY27) from ₹67.7 Cr a year earlier. On a sequential basis, net profit declined 15.4% from ₹84.8 Cr. Meanwhile, its operating revenue grew 46.5% YoY and 7.4% QoQ to ₹287.9 Cr during the quarter under review. Including other income of ₹2.8 Cr, total income during the quarter stood at ₹290.7 Cr. The fintech company’s operating EBITDA, excluding other income, grew just 3% YoY to ₹9.9 Cr. This came as its total expenses rose 49.4% YoY and 7.7% QoQ to ₹282.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, outpacing the growth in operating revenue. At the same time, its consolidated net revenue, after accounting for payment processing and other costs, declined 1% YoY to ₹151.3 Cr in Q2 FY27. AvenuesAI attributed the decline to its ‘competitive pricing strategy’ amid efforts to deepen merchant relationships and increase transaction volumes. As a result, its net take rate moderated 4% to 5.06 bps despite a 19% sequential increase in its total payments volume to ₹1.77 Lakh Cr. The company generated ₹282.2 Cr in revenue from its payment business, which includes its CCAvenue payment gateway, payment infrastructure services to banks (CPGS), and credit and lending-related services, accounting for nearly 98% of its operating revenue during the quarter. The remaining ₹5.7 Cr was derived from its ecommerce platform business, Rediff. AvenuesAI Looks To Unlock Value Across Subsidiaries Alongside its financial performance, AvenuesAI outlined its plans to expand its AI capabilities, with advanced technology development and AI software-related work remaining among the key objectives of its rights issue. In June last year, the company had raised ₹700 Cr via a rights issue, primarily for the repayment of outstanding loans, expansion of its IPO-bound digital content and ecommerce marketplace Rediff and further investments in its AI arm, Nueromind, for which it had earmarked ₹294 Cr. Almost 42.7%, or ₹297.2 Cr, of the net proceeds remained unutilised at the end of the September quarter. AvenuesAI has now announced that it will directly utilise the funds for AI development and software-related activities instead of routing the investment through Nueromind. It clarified that the change was limited to the mode of implementation, with no alteration to the end use of the proceeds. In the June quarter, AvenuesAI announced plans to amalgamate Nueromind with itself, subject to NCLT approval. It is also developing its Transaction Intelligence Score (TISco), an AI-led initiative that will use permitted transaction and merchant-behaviour signals for risk assessment, fraud prevention, merchant intelligence and financial services workflows. The company aims to use its transaction infrastructure to build an intelligence layer that can support merchant and enterprise services. On the investment front, AvenuesAI said it made investments in two financial services companies during the September quarter. It acquired a stake of up to 7% in Online PSB Loans Limited for a consideration of up to ₹65 Cr. It also invested up to ₹34.5 Cr to acquire a stake of up to 1.38% in Ratnaafin Capital Private Limited. The company also reiterated its plans to expand CCAvenue's international payments business, particularly in the US, by leveraging its payment technology, enterprise relationships and regulated infrastructure. Meanwhile, its ecommerce arm, Rediff, is on its way to the bourses for a separate listing. After filing for an IPO confidentially earlier this year, the markets regulator SEBI approved the draft papers in August. However, the Q2 disclosure did not provide an update on Rediff's proposed IPO. As per sources, Rediff would look to raise in between ₹600-800 Cr via the IPO AvenuesAI outlined that unlocking value from Rediff is one of its three strategic priorities for FY27. It plans to integrate Rediff's consumer and enterprise digital ecosystem with its payments and AI capabilities. This includes RediffOne, which offers digital commerce and communication services, and RediffPay, which is intended to expand consumer payment engagement. AvenuesAI has maintained its FY27 consolidated revenue guidance of ₹1,100-1,300 Cr. The company said its focus for the remainder of FY27 will remain on expanding merchant relationships, improving operating discipline and creating additional monetisation opportunities through Rediff, enterprise technology and applied AI. It is also monitoring potential changes to the merchant discount rate (MDR) policy for eligible UPI transactions, with any introduction, timing or scope remaining subject to government and regulatory decisions. Shares of AvenueAI ended today’s trading session 3.72% lower at ₹129.25.

Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
- Published
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.
In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

India has reaffirmed its commitment to climate multilateralism and the principles of Equity and Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC), calling for a fair, equitable and ambitious outcome at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), being held in Antalya, Türkiye.
Delivering India's Opening Statement at the COP31, Secretary, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Government of India, Narendra Bhooshan expressed gratitude to Türkiye and Australia for their leadership of COP31.
He commended all Parties and negotiating groups for their efforts towards strengthening climate multilateralism and stated that India aligns itself with the statements made by G77 and China, LMDC, and BASIC, as per a statement, issued by the PIB.
Emphasising the importance of multilateralism, India underlined that the UNFCCC and its Paris Agreement remain the most inclusive platforms where every country has a voice.
India reaffirmed its faith in this process, rooted in equity and the principle of CBDR-RC. Welcoming the Presidency's vision of a ‘COP of Implementation’, guided by Dialogue, Consensus and Action, India noted that dialogue builds trust, consensus ensures collective ownership of outcomes, and action translates commitments into progress on the ground.
Highlighting the growing challenges posed by the prospect of crossing 1.5°C warming, India stressed that equity has become particularly urgent to ensure that no one is left behind in the collective effort to address climate change. India reiterated its commitment to contributing its fair share to global climate action while pursuing the development and well-being of its people. It also underscored that just transition and meeting adaptation needs remain significant challenges, particularly for the Global South, where these are closely intertwined with the challenge of development itself.
On climate finance, India emphasised that public finance from developed countries remains central to catalysing climate action in developing countries and strengthening adaptation finance flows to address their vulnerabilities.
It underscored the fundamental importance of Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, which establishes the obligation of developed countries to provide financial resources to developing countries. Reaffirming its constructive engagement at COP31, India stated that it would work with all Parties towards achieving a fair, equitable and ambitious outcome.

Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

Pochettino, Howe, Emery... or Carrick? Man Utd's managerial options
- Published
With one victory in their first 10 Premier League matches, Manchester United have made their worst start to a top-flight campaign since the 1986-87 season.
They are 18th in the table, one point above bottom club Crystal Palace.
United directors will meet in Monaco on Wednesday to discuss Michael Carrick's future as his 10-month spell as head coach comes under major scrutiny.
If the 45-year-old former player departs, it would mean an eighth permanent boss for the Red Devils since Sir Alex Ferguson retired 13 years ago.
That would be as many managerial changes as they have made across the previous 68 years dating back to Sir Matt Busby's appointment in 1945.
BBC Sport takes a look at the leading candidates who could replace Carrick.
Mauricio Pochettino
Major trophies won: 1 Ligue 1, 1 French Cup
Premier League record: P294, W150; Win percentage: 51; Points per game ratio (PPG): 1.77
Did you know: Pochettino averaged 1.89 points per game during his spell at Tottenham, the best ratio of any Spurs manager to have taken charge of 25 or more Premier League games.
United's long-standing interest in the Argentine, 54, dates back a decade.
At Spurs, he moulded their best team in a generation, but ultimately came up short of winning a trophy, losing both the Champions League and League Cup finals, and posted second and third-placed finishes. Silverware did come at Paris St-Germain with a league title, but a spell at Chelsea proved tougher with a League Cup final defeat by Liverpool in 2024.
Having led the USA to the last 16 of the World Cup on home soil he signed a new contract taking him up to the 2030 tournament. Pochettino has an exciting group of young players to work with for the national team - led by Manchester City-bound 17-year-old Cavan Sullivan - but he has always made it clear he has unfinished business in the Premier League.
A reported buyout clause in Pochettino's contract is worth $10million (£7.44m), while it is also understood to contain clauses that would allow him to leave for specific high-profile jobs.

Julian Nagelsmann
Major trophies won: 1 Bundesliga
Premier League record: N/A
Did you know: Only Hansi Flick (88.9%) has a better win percentage by a Bayern Munich manager in the Champions League than Nagelsmann's 83.3%.
Nagelsmann first impressed with his work at Hoffenheim, where he became the youngest head coach in Bundesliga history aged 28, leading them from relegation struggles to the Champions League.
He followed that by taking RB Leipzig to a Champions League semi-final in 2020 and Bayern Munich understandably came calling.
But despite winning the Bundesliga title in his first season he reportedly fell out with key players and did not survive a full second season.
In 2023, Nagelsmann took charge of a Germany side in transition, and they were narrowly beaten in the quarter-finals of Euro 2024 by eventual winners Spain, but stepped down in the summer after Die Mannschaft were humbled by Paraguay in the World Cup last 32.
Still only 39, his reputation may have taken a bit of a hit, but the German is still regarded as one of Europe's best coaches. Manchester United's director of recruitment Christopher Vivell also knows him well, having worked together at RB Leipzig.
Eddie Howe
Major trophies won: 1 League Cup
Premier League record: P369 W140; Win percentage: 37.9; PPG: 1.36
Did you know: Eddie Howe (five) is one of only three managers with five or more wins against Mikel Arteta in all competitions, along with Pep Guardiola (11) and Jurgen Klopp (six).
His body of work in English football needs little introduction having led Bournemouth to the top flight for the first time in their history, before he confirmed his place in Newcastle folklore with their first major domestic trophy since lifting the FA Cup in 1955.
The League Cup final triumph over Liverpool was one of the greatest days in the club's history, while he also secured two top-five finishes to take the club back into the Champions League for the first time in 20 years.
Howe, 48, left in the summer after an underwhelming 12th-placed finish last term and Newcastle would only be due a a relatively small amount of compensation should he be tempted by the Old Trafford job.
Antonio Conte
Major trophies won: 5 Serie A, 1 Premier League, 1 FA Cup
Premier League record: P132, W83; Win percentage: 62.9; PPG: 2.03
Did you know: Chelsea won 30 of their 38 Premier League matches as they claimed the title in Antonio Conte's first season in charge in 2016-17.
A serial winner, Conte's managerial credentials are not in doubt.
He left Napoli of his own accord this summer just 12 months after delivering only the fourth top-flight title in their history.
That added to Serie A triumphs at Juventus (three) and Inter Milan, and spells at Chelsea and Tottenham.
Conte, 57, would appear to be a no-brainer of a choice to take over at United, but could the Italian's fiery nature and history of falling out with clubs count against him?
His last stint in English football ended under a cloud of controversy as he left Tottenham in 2023 following criticism of the players and the club's culture.
While he had success at Chelsea, Conte also reportedly clashed with both players and the board.
Unai Emery
Major trophies won: 5 Europa League, 1 Ligue 1, 2 French Cups, 2 French League Cups
Premier League record: P200, W101; Win percentage: 50.5; PPG: 1.75
Did you know: Unai Emery has the best Premier League win percentage (51%) and points per game ratio (1.75) of any permanent Aston Villa boss.
Vastly experienced, the Spaniard's stock is at an all-time high courtesy of the superb job he has done since taking over at Villa in October 2022.
Having taken the club into the European Cup/Champions League for the first time for 41 years, the 55-year-old then ended their 30-year wait for silverware with success in last season's Europa League.
Despite having lost the spine of his team over the summer, Emery's new-look side are finding their feet again and the chances of him leaving for United look even slimmer with recent news he is expected to sign a new contract.
Michael Carrick
Major trophies won: N/A
Premier League record: P29, W14; Win percentage: 48.3; PPG: 1.76
Did you know: After his initial appointment as United's interim boss in January, Michael Carrick had the most wins (12) and points (39) of any Premier League manager during the rest of the 2025-26 season.
Still clinging on to his job in the Old Trafford hot seat, could United's hierarchy actually decide to keep faith with Carrick?
After such a brilliant start and end to the season following his arrival in January, the wheels have come off spectacularly this term with only three wins from 15 matches in all competitions.
His team have at least shown fight with comebacks in recent games to beat Roma and salvage a point in a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, but their overall stats are damning and the outlook doesn't look good for the 45-year-old, who won five Premier League titles and the Champions League as a United player.
The club are in the relegation zone and 18th is their lowest position after 10 games of a season for 40 years. It is also only the second time they have gone eight Premier League games without a victory.

Srinagar, Nov 10: A court in Jammu and Kashmir has acquitted two youths who were undergoing trial under anti-terror charges in Baramulla district, noting that the evidence against the accused was unreliable.
Special Judge (UAPA/NIA cases) Baramulla, Feroz Ahmad Khan, acquitted Huzaif Firdous Bhat and Aijaz Ahmad after finding contradictions in the prosecution case.
The two youths were arrested in September 2020 during a joint naka checking by police and the Army at Kanispora in Baramulla district.
Police registered a case against the two youths under Sections 18, 23 and 39 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) and Section 7/25 of the Arms Act, claiming to have recovered two hand grenades, 100 rounds of ammunition and posters of the terror outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba.
"On an overall assessment, the court finds that the prosecution evidence suffers from such material inconsistencies and infirmities that it would be unsafe to base a conviction upon it," the court said in its 71-page order.
The court held that the prosecution has not established "through cogent and dependable evidence" that the arms and ammunition produced in the court were recovered from the "conscious possession" of the accused in the manner alleged.
"Once the alleged recovery itself becomes doubtful, the foundation for the offences under Sections 18 and 23 of UAPA and Section 7/25 of the Arms Act is substantially weakened," the court said.
The court also noted that there was no independent witness to the recovery of the arms and ammunition, and glaring contradictions were found during the deposition and cross-examination of police witnesses.

Congress to host second Bharat Summit in Hyderabad from Nov 12 to 14; 70 countries to attend
This year’s edition will also be held in Hyderabad, with international deliberations at HICC and Telangana-focused sessions at the HITEX venue
The Congress on Tuesday announced the second edition of the Bharat Summit, an international gathering of “progressive” political leaders, policymakers and thinkers, bringing together more than 1,000 delegates from 70 countries in Hyderabad from November 12 to 14.
The three-day summit, hosted by the Congress-led Telangana government, will focus on global political and economic developments, democratic values, and cooperation between countries of the Global South and Global North. The event will also mark the 137th birth anniversary of Jawaharlal Nehru on November 14.
“The Bharat Summit is providing a platform for progressive parties across the world to come together, share their experiences and collectively formulate strategies to bring politics back to serving the people, rather than serving politicians,” said Samrudhha Bharat Foundation trustee, Gurdeep Sappal.
“We hope and expect that the event will reflect Shri Rahul Gandhi’s vision for India and the world of tomorrow, the emergence of a new global order, and how the country should navigate it,” senior Congress leader Salman Khurshid added.
Khurshid said the summit would feature 12 international sessions and eight sessions focused on Telangana. The international programme will include discussions on recent electoral developments involving “liberal parties” in Brazil, Hungary, Serbia and the United States, making renewed engagement between the Global South and Global North particularly important, he said.
“What we are undertaking—reinventing, reinvigorating and reviving contact and dialogue between the Global South and the Global North—is extremely important,” he said.
Congress leader Sridhar Babu said the international programme would feature four thematic tracks covering geo-economic issues in the context of Hyderabad as a technology-driven and industry-led state; political renewal, including youth participation and gender justice; geopolitical developments, South-South cooperation and reforms in multilateral institutions; and societal challenges such as climate change, the role of media and information integrity.
“We are also hosting eight Telangana Rising sessions covering themes such as Future City and Organisation, economic justice, social justice and welfare policies,” Babu said, adding that the sessions would align with Telangana’s ambition to become a USD 3 trillion economy by 2047.
Sappal said the summit also aimed to enable “progressive parties” to develop a collective response “politics driven by hatred and division”. He added that international political parties were interested in understanding the Congress’s approach under the leadership of Rahul Gandhi, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, to counter such politics.
The inaugural Bharat Summit was held on April 25 and 26, 2025, at the Hyderabad International Convention Centre (HICC). This year’s edition will also be held in Hyderabad, with international deliberations at HICC and Telangana-focused sessions at the HITEX venue.
Congress leader Mahesh Kumar Goud said Rahul Gandhi was expected to attend the summit and that the party will also invite other senior leaders. He added that the Bharat Summit will be organised annually and will also help build participation for the state’s Invest Telangana Global Summit, scheduled for December 7 to 9.

Anjali Sardana and Pronto entered India’s domestic services market in 2025 to solve a familiar urban problem: finding reliable house help on demand. The result was a quick commerce-style home services platform, combining technology-led recruitment, standardised training and a hyperlocal network of professionals. Pronto, which competes with Snabbit and Urban Company, says it has served more than half a million households across 11 cities. But the real story of Pronto is being developed far away from the homes and houses that its professionals visit. This is being built in Silicon Valley. Footage recorded by professionals working in thousands of homes every day is helping shape the next generation of robots. The first signs of this ambition emerged in May 2026, when Pronto was reported to be exploring ways to generate physical AI training data using footage captured during household chores. And since then Sardana and Pronto’s ambitions have solidified. In July, Pronto formalised the experiment through Verified, an opt-in premium service in which housekeepers and cleaners wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras during visits. In October 2026, Sardana set up Provision Labs, a physical AI venture based in San Francisco, which will collect data to train and test AI systems designed to perform real-world tasks using robots and other machines. It will work with developers building physical AI models. A few days later, Provision Labs announced that it is acquiring Mumbai-based Basilisk Industries, a 2023-founded company focused on perception technologies, which help machines interpret their surroundings. Basilisk founder Shourya Watwani will lead Provision’s hardware efforts and work on its in-house post-processing models. Watwani and his team are said to have developed a 3D hand-tracking model and built the first version of a lightweight tactile glove to capture touch-related data. Given this timeline, the fact that Pronto doubled-down on its experiment after the May 2026 introduction does not seem surprising at all. The relationship between Pronto’s household data collection and Provision Labs’ operations, however, remains unclear. Inc42 asked Pronto how the two businesses work together, if at all, but the company declined to comment. The unanswered question is significant: could a network originally built to deliver household services become an acquisition channel for the data needed to train global robotics systems? Why Record Workers? The first reports around Pronto’s collection of worker data triggered a backlash over surveillance and privacy of house help professionals. To assuage some of the critics, Pronto said that customers are informed about the terms several times before recording begins, while personally identifiable information is automatically blurred or removed on the device. “The raw footage is deleted immediately after the work is done, and no one ever accesses it. For 48 hours, an anonymised, end-to-end encrypted recording is available only to the customer, who can watch it in the app to check the work. After that, we use the anonymised footage for AI training, as our terms set out,” the company told Inc42. Pronto said more than half of the professionals participating in Verified already earn over ₹40,000 a month. The company claims workers feel safer knowing there is a record of their work, but no independent studies have been conducted to validate these claims. What’s the point of all this? Unlike chatbots, which can learn from the enormous repositories of text and images available online, physical AI systems need to understand how the real world works. A robot must learn how to pick up objects, fold clothes, navigate a room, and respond when something does not go as expected. This requires large volumes of real-world, multimodal data capturing movement, spatial information and interactions with objects. Such data is considerably harder and more expensive to collect than internet-sourced text and images. ANI quoted a Goldman Sachs report estimating that general-purpose robots could require around 10 Mn hours of high-quality physical interaction data to reach production-level capabilities. The Missing Data Layer One can see the physical AI stack through four layers. The data layer captures real-world interactions, while the model layer uses this information to train vision-language-action models that translate what a robot sees into actions. The simulation layer through platforms such as NVIDIA’s Isaac Sim allow these models to be tested in virtual environments before deployment. Finally, the edge layer runs them on physical robots, with real-world feedback informing and enhancing the training process. Global technology companies such as NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, Amazon, OpenAI and Anthropic are building capabilities across the model and simulation layers of physical AI. India has some representation at the robotics and deployment end, with companies such as Addverb, CynLr and Perceptyne developing robotic systems and automation technologies. But it is the data layer that is seeing a growing crop of Indian startups, alongside global data companies building collection operations that rely heavily on India’s workforce and physical environments. Humyn Labs, EgoData, Egolab.ai, Neocambrian AI, Human Archive, and Objectways have deployed people on the ground to collect footage across household chores, but several are also working with manufacturing units and other industrial environments. Head-mounted or body-mounted cameras and sensor-equipped gloves or even full body suits have become commonplace as the next phase of robotics takes shape. For India, the opportunity has echoes of its earlier role in the AI supply chain. Over the past decade, India has become a hub for data annotation, with workers labelling images, text and audio used to train AI models. Physical AI takes that outsourcing model a step further. Indian workers’ movements, workplaces and interactions with objects are becoming the training material. Abhinav Kukreja, founder of Neocambrian AI, sees India’s large and diverse physical environments as an advantage over markets such as the US, where access to comparable real-world data is more limited. He believes the next phase of robotics will see an explosion of different embodiments and form factors. For India to participate meaningfully in this transition, it needs to control an important part of the underlying ecosystem. “I strongly felt that this layer would not be compute, architecture or algorithms, but the data layer,” he said. Y Combinator-backed Human Archive is pursuing a similar opportunity, with a model that involves home service workers, cooks, cleaners and domestic help wearing cameras inside homes and private properties. Cofounder Rushil Agarwal told Inc42 earlier that the Indian market’s appeal lies in the diversity of industries accessible within the geographical boundary and the large labour pool. This is difficult to replicate in the US. Notably, Human Archive was evaluated by Snabbit too as it looked to launch a Pronto-like data collection pilot. However, the home services company eventually dropped the proposal. Human Archive raised $8.2 Mn in a seed round led by Wing Venture Capital and NVP Capital. Pronto’s $45 Mn Series B also saw participation from Lachy Groom, cofounder of robotics model startup Physical Intelligence; Groom has also backed Provision Labs. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs, led by former Nazara CEO Manish Agarwal, has committed $20 Mn towards expanding its data collection network. The supply side, meanwhile, is becoming more competitive. Data collection rates fell 30% between January and June this year, an industry executive told Inc42 earlier. More suppliers have since entered the market and synthetic data generation has improved rapidly. But in the long run, the demand for human-captured footage could shrink as physical AI models mature. The larger question is who captures the value and what happens to the workers. We’ll come to the latter soon, but the current situation does not give us any clarity on what this segment might look like in a few months. While Pronto says more than half of its Verified professionals earn over ₹40,000 a month, Human Archive has cited compensation in the range of $1-10 per hour for its data collection work. These disparate compensation structures highlight the lack of clarity on the economic model. One cannot draw parallels between the kind of data captured either till the industry further matures. At this point, companies are throwing a lot more money than they are willing to to attract workers who will readily collect data that can in a few years replace them. Indian manufacturers and industrial units may recruit workers, deploy cameras and collect footage, while the resulting models and intellectual property are developed and owned elsewhere. This value drain could have serious consequences on the Indian economy and the jobs landscape. For data suppliers, the challenge will be moving beyond one-off collection contracts to building differentiated datasets that command lasting value. As more and more companies come into the picture, the collection of egocentric data and first-person footage is about to become highly commodified and consumerised. The Elephant In The Room: What About The Workers? Like we mentioned, the business opportunity comes with a difficult labour question. The blunt reading of the matter is that Indian workers are training the robots that could eventually replace them. Videos circulating on social media have raised concerns about whether workers even understand why they are wearing cameras. Some workers have reported discomfort from prolonged use, which may stretch to 5-10 hours a workday, while others believe the devices are intended to monitor their productivity. Every company maintains that workers are informed about what is being captured and why. However, when collection happens through partner businesses, the responsibility for communicating this information shifts to those partners. An openDemocracy investigation, meanwhile, found that workers at two Delhi factories were asked to wear cameras supplied by Egolab.ai without being told their purpose. Such incidents raise questions about informed consent, compensation, the privacy of other people captured in recordings and ownership of the resulting data. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose implementation is scheduled for May 2027, adds another layer of regulatory uncertainty. Speculation is that the government may regulate these services, but to what extent can it stop individuals from participating is unclear. For Sardana and Pronto, the opportunity is significantly larger than just a quick home services platform. The data from the broad range of everyday human activity by Pronto workers can fuel Provision Labs and Basilisk’s next big plays and turn them into even bigger companies than Pronto. Whether Pronto and Provision Labs will eventually work together has not been answered. But the value of Pronto’s network may very soon be the footage of what its professionals do, rather than the quality of the service itself.

Confidence among mortgaged households has crashed to its lowest level in more than three decades amid a growing sense of “helplessness” about the economy, even as a dramatic shift in financial markets suggests there is now a strong chance of a Reserve Bank rate cut by this time next year.
The latest Westpac survey showed its consumer sentiment index sinking again in November to reach a four-year low, amid deepening pessimism about the near-term prospects for the economy.
As Labor comes under increasing pressure over persistent cost-of-living pressures, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, played down tensions with the treasurer, Jim Chalmers.
A day after the frontbencher Murray Watt called for colleagues to stop undermining Chalmers, Albanese said: “The treasurer is doing a great job”.
The PM said he was working closely with Chalmers in the lead-up to next month’s mid-year budget update, which will include cuts to government spending as pressure mounts to contain inflation.
“This is a treasurer who’s produced a couple of budget surpluses, lower deficits, [who is] producing economic reform,” Albanese said.
Matthew Hassan, Westpac’s head of economic forecasting, said the mood among households was last this bad in 2022, when inflation was running close to 8% and after the RBA had lifted borrowing costs by 4 percentage points over the previous year.
“Prior to that, readings this weak had only ever been seen in the economy’s darkest moments: at the onset of the Covid pandemic; the height of the GFC; and during the recessions in the early 1990s and early 1980s,” Hassan said.
Hassan said while the economic backdrop was not as extreme now as it was during the pandemic and its immediate aftermath, there were “shades of Covid in the responses” from households.
Confidence in the economic outlook over the coming year reached its weakest since August 2020, the survey showed, matching a low point last recorded during the pandemic.
“The comparison with August 2020 is quite useful as that was when Melbourne went into its second lockdown and just before the government massively scaled up income support,” Hassan said.
“There was a sense of helplessness at that stage; there was nothing we could do to avoid the pandemic, and there was nothing the government could do [to avoid the pandemic]. Obviously when the jobkeeper measures were put in place that comforted a lot of people.
“There is a similar feeling of helplessness now. You can argue a substantial portion of what is happening is out of our control, such as rising fuel prices, and there’s only so much the authorities can do to cushion Australians from that impact.”
Indebted households were gloomier still, the survey showed, with pessimism among this group at its worst in records stretching back to 1994.
The latest survey comes a week after Michele Bullock, the RBA governor, warned that the year ahead would “feel like it’s a recession” thanks to persistent cost-of-living pressures alongside weak economic growth.
After five rate increases this year, nearly three in four respondents said they expected another rate hike over the coming 12 months.
Even as the mood in the community darkens, financial markets have begun factoring in the chance of lower interest rates from the middle of next year.
The implied probability of an RBA rate cut was more than 50% by August next year, according to ANZ data, and a decrease to 4.6% was fully priced in by December 2027.
Investors have been rethinking their forecasts for central bank moves alongside a rapid retreat in the global oil price.
After testing a post-Iran war high of nearly US$118 a barrel at the end of October, the global benchmark, Brent crude, has plunged by 20% to below US$94.
“Our base case is that rates do start to come down from August next year, and we don’t see any further hikes,” Hassan said.
– Additional reporting by Tom McIlroy

At St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, Keralam, faith and fitness go hand in hand. An open gym on the church premises is drawing parishioners of all ages to stretch, sweat and stay fit. The unusual initiative is adding a healthy new dimension to church life.
Set up in a corner of the church campus, the facility has quickly become a meeting point for fitness enthusiasts. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass. The altar boys, numbering around 60, are among its regular users. Parents also bring their young children, while senior citizens use the basic equipment to stay active.
Roots in fitness routine of vicar
The initiative has its roots in the personal fitness routine of the church’s vicar, Fr. Frederick Eluvathingal, 69. A footballer and basketball player during his student days, he has never allowed age or a demanding schedule to come in the way of exercise.
“I have been working out for the past 51 years, ever since my days at the Papal Seminary in Pune,” he says. His fitness routine continued during his higher studies in Rome and Jerusalem and his church assignments in Australia.
When he arrived at Kuriachira more than a year ago, he began looking for a suitable space to continue his regular exercises, including push-ups and pull-ups. Parallel bars were installed first, followed by a basketball hoop. The idea gradually grew into a community gym.
“I wanted to create a space where people could develop the habit of working out. We generally do not have a strong workout culture. If people can fit in some basic exercise when they come to church, they may gradually make fitness part of their lives,” he says.
The need is particularly pressing at a time when lifestyle diseases and obesity are on the rise. The initiative also seeks to draw more youngsters into church activities and channel their energy into constructive pursuits.
The parish welcomed the proposal, and a space around a well on the church premises was chosen for the facility. The limited space available in Kuriachira meant that the gym had to be modest, but the response has been encouraging.
“Within a week of starting the gym, quite a few people began coming here. If the demand grows, we will have to think about expanding the facility,” says P.R. Wilson, one of the church trustees.
For regular user John Vazhappilly, a real estate broker who lives nearby, the gym has come as a timely help. “I have been coming here every evening for the past week. After an accident and surgery, the muscles in my leg became weak. I want to strengthen them. This is a comfortable place to exercise, with fresh air and an open campus,” he says.
‘A form of spiritual service’
The church sees the initiative as more than a fitness facility. “We want to groom a healthy generation. Many people suffer from lifestyle diseases, while youngsters often turn to private fitness centres. We felt that providing basic facilities here would benefit the community. Spirituality is also about nurturing a healthy mind and body. We consider this a form of spiritual service,” says assistant vicar Fr. Jees Akkara.
For Fr. Eluvathingal, there is another purpose. “Youngsters rarely come to church or participate in its activities these days. This is also an opportunity to bring more of them into the church community,” he says.

Delhi pollution monitors went dark as AQI surged on Diwali
DPCC data showed a peak of 3,744 and a worst-hour average of 1,480, suggesting the official AQI understated the pollution.
PM2.5 readings, which capture levels of smoke, at many of Delhi’s air monitoring stations went blank on Diwali night as they climbed towards 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre, pulling down the capital’s official air quality index (AQI) for the day after, HT’s analysis of records kept by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) shows.
The missing hours, filled partially by on Monday evening by the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), one of the three agencies that run the stations, show the smoke reaching a peak level of 3,744 µg/m³, more than 60 times the national 24-hour standard of 60.
CPCB did not explain the outage. A Delhi government official, who asked not to be named, acknowledged a glitch but gave no details: “The air quality monitors are giving hourly data. There were some technical glitches but all our 43 stations are giving data.”
Deep Dive
While the PM2.5 data was missing, the stations were still working. All through the night they kept sending readings for gases such as nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide and ozone. For the 1am hour on November 9, 38 of the 39 long-standing Delhi stations HT examined sent a nitrogen dioxide reading while 13 sent one for PM2.5. The PM2.5 readings mostly stopped just as they neared 1,000 µg/m³, and no reading in CPCB’s records for the night went past that figure.
DPCC’s release on Monday evening showed how high the missing readings had gone. Every one of the 125 station-hours missing from CPCB’s records at DPCC’s stations was above 1,000 on DPCC’s site. A station hour is one station’s reading for one hour. The readings dropped out somewhere between the stations and CPCB’s records, and the pattern points to a cut-off at about 1,000 µg/m³. Why it exists, and whether it is new, was not clear.
Also Read | AQI of 387 in India would be nearly 1,500 in US and 10 in UK. Why the range is so wide
The data gaps pulled the official figure down. Delhi’s AQI, the average of its stations’ scores over the past 24 hours, came in at 344 in CPCB’s 4pm bulletin on Monday, the day’s official reading, with the night’s worst hours missing from the stations’ averages. AQI is a composite number, capped at 500 for the official figure, that factors in readings of individual pollutants such as PM2.5.
In CPCB’s 4pm bulletins since 2015, Delhi’s air has been worse the day after Diwali than in the day before it every year. This year’s initially published figures broke that run: 344 the day after, against 369 on Diwali eve.
The late evening revision by DPCC changed how air pollution this Diwali will be recorded. Counting the readings DPCC released, HT’s estimates show, the AQI in the bulletin would have read about 360. The 9am figure, 370 as published, would have been about 384. Both estimates leave the blanks at stations run by CPCB and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM) as they are, so both are a floor.
PM2.5 is fine dust, particles 2.5 micrometres across or smaller, and micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³) is the unit for measuring how much of it is in the air. PM2.5 originates from burning, such as of firecrackers or paddy stubble.
The highest reading in CPCB’s records for the night was exactly 1,000.0, at Sirifort for the 15 minutes from 4.45am and at ITO for the 15 minutes from 6.15am. Last Diwali, 29 of the 39 stations recorded at least one hour averaging above 1,000, the highest 2,224 at NSIT Dwarka, according to OpenAQ’s copy of CPCB’s live feed.
Also Read | The Air We Breathe
At the worst of the night, the 1am hour, PM2.5 across the 22 stations with a full night of readings averaged 1,480 µg/m³, HT’s analysis of DPCC’s released readings shows. In CPCB’s records, where only eight of the 39 stations had a full night of readings, that hour had averaged 547.
Both figures are worked out as HT measured last Diwali: an average over the stations with a PM2.5 reading for every hour from 10pm to 6am, so that each hour is compared on one set of stations.
The released readings also show where the night was worst. Mundka recorded 3,744 µg/m³ at 2am, JNU 3,023 at 4am and NSUT’s West Campus 3,008 at 5am; Mandir Marg, Nehru Nagar and Wazirpur all went past 2,700.
Eleven of DPCC’s 30 stations went past 2,000. Where both sources had a reading, the figures matched in every hour.
Last Diwali, the worst hour of the night averaged 1,137 µg/m³ of PM2.5 across the 27 stations with a reading for every hour. This Diwali, once DPCC’s readings are counted, it averaged 1,480 across 22 stations. The two sets of stations differ, so HT also compared like with like.
Thirteen stations have a full set of readings for both nights. On those 13, this year’s worst hour averaged 1,173, against 1,017 last Diwali, about 15% higher.
The Supreme Court allowed firecrackers on Diwali only from 6am to 7am and from 8pm to 10pm, but they were burst across the city well beyond that window. PM2.5 rose steeply through the last hours of the window and stopped soon after. At North Campus, an IITM station, the 15-minute reading climbed from 291 µg/m³ at 8pm to 999 at 10pm, and the next readings were blank. Moreover, farm fire smoke and calm winds held pollution at a high level even before the city went into the festival. Diwali eve was the most polluted in a decade, HT reported on Sunday.
For this year’s Diwali analysis, HT considered the 39 stations that were also live last Diwali. Since then, 20 more have been added, including 13 in October, many of them on the outer edge of the city ,that have dragged down the city’s overall AQI, HT reported on November 6.
Across all 59 Delhi stations, 43 had a gap in PM2.5 between 10pm and 6am. Of those, 23 sent a last reading of 800 µg/m³ or more before it, and 14 of 900 or more. Stations run by all three operators went blank: CPCB, IITM and DPCC.
Between 10pm and 6am, 148, or 42%, of the 351 station-hours across the 39 long-standing stations were blank . The rate of failure was about six times the season’s baseline: on CPCB’s hourly data feed, which HT has stored since October 3, these stations had a blank in only 7% of their PM2.5 station-hours between 10pm and 6am, up to Diwali eve. .
HT had flagged a similar problem of unreliable data last year, when stations went dark. But even then, 27 of the 39 reported PM2.5 every hour from 10pm to 6am; this year, only eight did until DPCC updated the data. The DPCC update came late in the evening, meaning the 4pm bulletin -- the official record for the day -- for day the day after Diwali 2026 would not account for these emissions -- or the others from CPCB and IITM sources that remained blank.

Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) who examined CPCB’s data, said many of the readings went missing as PM2.5 approached what he described as the instruments’ upper measurement limit of 1,000 µg/m³. “These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels,” he said, adding that 1,000 µg/m³ should be taken as a lower bound.
“This requires attention and transparency as one cannot completely blank out data when readings are expected to be alarming,” said Sunil Dahiya, founder and lead analyst at Envirocatalysts.
Political parties attacked the Delhi government over the readings on Monday. Aam Aadmi Party leader Saurabh Bharadwaj accused it of “AQI data fraud” in a video posted on X, alleging that the 20 new monitoring stations had been put in open, green areas and that water was being sprinkled around stations in heavily polluted localities to lower their readings.
Responses from CPCB, DPCC, IITM, the Delhi government and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) were awaited at the time of going to print.

After the Democratic Party's sweeping victory in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, a rumor spread that Time magazine had published a cover with a black-and-white photograph of Republican U.S. President Donald Trump with a sticker on his mouth that read "I Voted" and included the illustration of a U.S. flag.
The supposed magazine cover spread across social media, including on Facebook and Reddit. One X post read "TIME Magazine unveils new cover" (archived):
Several Snopes readers searched the website and emailed us seeking to confirm the claim was true.
The image is real; Time published it as the cover of its Nov. 23 issue.
The magazine's Instagram account shared the cover on Nov. 4, the day of the midterm elections (archived):
The caption read, in part (emphasis ours):
If Democrats had spent much of President Donald Trump's second term searching for a way to break his grip on Washington, voters had now handed them one. The midterms generated a blue wave that swept Republicans out of power in the House and the Senate, reversing the party's fortunes just two years after Trump's return to the White House. The results amounted to a decisive rebuke of a President whose handling of the economy, rising prices, and the war with Iran had fueled widespread discontent, and who spent the closing days of the campaign musing about candidates' anatomy and dismissing Americans' concerns over their bottom line.
Time also shared the image on its X account (archived) and its website, in a cover story analyzing the outcome of the elections (archived) and outlining the path ahead for Democrats.
The image appeared to suggest that voters in the U.S. had handed a definitive loss to Trump and his camp after two years of brash rhetoric and policies that resulted in the opposite of what his supporters believed he and his allies had promised, including an end to wars and more affordable cost of living.
According to Time, Trump has appeared on the cover of the magazine more times than anyone else.
For further reading, Snopes has verified other covers of Time, including a cover it titled "The Transgender Tipping Point" in 2014.

Cricket Scotland said it will not schedule matches against Afghanistan outside International Cricket Council (ICC) events, citing concerns over the treatment of women and girls under the Taliban government and broader human rights issues.
“Cricket Scotland will not proactively schedule bilateral series or participate in tri-series involving Afghanistan Men unless there is a material change in the circumstances surrounding Afghanistan women’s cricket and wider human rights considerations,” Cricket Scotland said on Monday.
Women’s sport has effectively disappeared in Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, while access to education and employment opportunities for women has been severely curtailed.
The Taliban says it respects women’s rights in accordance with its interpretation of Islamic law and local customs and that internal matters should be addressed locally.
Scotland’s move aligns with decisions by Cricket Australia and the England and Wales Cricket Board to suspend bilateral ties with Afghanistan, which the ICC made a Full Member in 2017.
“This policy will be kept under review annually or following any significant ICC decision or material change in circumstances,” the statement added.

Scotland has not faced Afghanistan in a full international match since the 2021 T20 World Cup, but the governing body said the ACB requested training facilities in July ahead of its men’s series against Ireland.
The ACB had made another request for training facilities in Scotland in September regarding the T20 Afghanistan Premier League, it added.
Cricket Scotland also said it would continue to consider its contractual obligations to players and would issue no-objection certificates (NOCs) if the ICC gives the Afghan league official approval.
“If an NOC is issued, participation by that player/s must not be interpreted as an endorsement by Cricket Scotland of the current Afghan regime or its policies,” the statement said.

Psoriasis is an autoimmune condition that causes thick, scaly patches on the skin. However, it often remains unidentified and undiagnosed because it does not look the same on all parts of the body: it could be mistaken, for instance, for dandruff on the scalp, persistent eczema on the palms, or a fungal infection. You can’t always judge psoriasis by looking only at visible parts of the skin.
Why does this happen? Our skin isn’t the same everywhere. The thickness of the skin can vary considerably depending on the diversity of the environmental conditions that it is exposed to and the kind of treatment given to it. These factors can contribute to how psoriasis appears and feels.

If a good night’s sleep has become your holy grail, who are the knights in shining armour you will employ to reach that chalice? Most people seem to be deploying melatonin and magnesium supplements, over the counter, but the question that remains is: are they effective, and if so, at what combinations or levels?
The consensus among most sleep specialists, is that both melatonin and magnesium (glycinate) can have an ameliorative impact – in the short term. Both these supplements, however, work differently – while melatonin is a key body clock signal, magnesium helps relax the body. When and how you take both supplements makes a great deal of difference to your hours of sleep and sleep quality as well.

Nasdaq-listed traveltech major MakeMyTrip has expanded into the carpooling segment via the acquisition of a majority stake in Bengaluru-based Quick Ride for an undisclosed amount. In a statement, MakeMyTrip said that the acquisition will allow it “to establish a presence in the ride pooling segment, which is complementary to the group’s existing ground transportation portfolio.” As part of the transaction, Quick Ride’s brand and ride-pooling business have been transferred to a newly formed entity, Co Ride Mobility Private Limited, in which MakeMyTrip has acquired a majority stake. Quick Ride’s promoters will continue to lead the business. However, Quick Ride’s erstwhile electric vehicle (EV) taxi business will remain with its predecessor entity, iDisha Info Labs Pvt Ltd. Founded in 2014 by KNM Rao, Quick Ride offers a ride-sharing application that connects passengers to riders. It connects the commuters travelling in the same direction. It also offers an enterprise solution for shared mobility and counts IT companies such as Wipro, TCS, Infosys, IBM and Cognizant, among others as its clients. Its services are available in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune, Kochi, Delhi NCR, Mumbai, and Kolkata. The startup has raised over $14 Mn from investors like Sequoia, Prosus and Venture Highway. Sequoia exited the startup in 2021. MakeMyTrip's Acquisition-Led Expansion The Quick Ride acquisition is part of MakeMyTrip's broader strategy to expand its presence across adjacent travel and mobility segments through strategic investments and acquisitions. Commenting on the acquisition, MakeMyTrip group CEO Rajesh Magow said that the investment would help the company establish a presence in daily intra-city commutes while strengthening its intercity travel offerings. “As part of our expansion strategy, we have pursued selective strategic partnerships, investments and acquisitions that complement and strengthen our existing business and expand the breadth and depth of our offerings. Ride pooling gives us a presence in high-frequency daily commutes within cities, as well as intercity travel,” he added. The company plans to leverage its experience in building redBus across India and overseas markets to scale Quick Ride's ride-pooling business. In the past few years, MakeMyTrip has acquired Savaari to strengthen its car rental services, Happay in corporate travel and expense management, and Flamingo Transworld in regional group holiday packages. It has also made a strategic minority investment in visa processing platform Atlys. The development comes as MakeMyTrip looks to deepen its presence across the travel value chain, moving beyond conventional travel bookings towards a broader set of transportation and ancillary services. On the financial front, the travel tech major’s consolidated net profit for the three months ended June 30, 2026 (Q1 FY27) plunged 65% to $9.1 Mn from $25.8 Mn in the year-ago period. MakeMyTrip’s revenue grew 6% YoY to $285.6 Mn.

Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany has returned to the club’s training ground for the first time since he collapsed during practice last month. Bayern also revealed he suffered a shoulder injury.
The 40-year-old Kompany had medical treatment scheduled at the Säbener Strasse complex as he took another step toward his planned return after the international break.
“Vincent Kompany is on the road to recovery and has been back at the training ground at Säbener Strasse since the start of the week,” the club said on Tuesday. “The FC Bayern head coach is also completing rehab on his injured shoulder there. Kompany was under medical care recently, with assistant coach Aaron Danks filling in.”
Bayern had no team training on Tuesday with most of the players away. The team’s next game is at home to Cologne in the Bundesliga on Nov. 20.
Bayern powerbroker Uli Hoeness said on Sunday that Kompany would return in time for that match.
Kompany collapsed while observing a training session on Oct. 23 and was hospitalized for meningeal irritation, an inflammation of the tissue around the brain or spinal cord. He had been dealing with a viral infection and hip injury.
Danks took charge of the team while Kompany was away and oversaw wins against Freiburg, Magdeburg, Atlético Madrid and Mainz with the only blot a 2-2 draw with Borussia Dortmund in der Klassiker on October 31.

After protests in Arunachal Pradesh against the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) turned violent on October 23, the state has unleashed a massive crackdown on the movement. The response has included the use of force by armed forces and law enforcement agencies, internet shutdowns, a paid PR campaign, censorship of social media content, and action against journalists and lawyers.
A 12-hour Arunachal bandh was called by local bodies and youth groups, including the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum (SIFF), Adi Baane Kebang United and the Adi Galo Welfare Society, on October 23. The bandh was followed by large-scale arson in Pasighat, East Siang district, targeting an office of the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC), a police station, and the homes of two MLAs and the BJP’s state president.
The proposed SUMP, with an estimated capacity of 11,200 megawatts, is planned on the Siang River across the Upper Siang and Siang districts. First proposed in 2008-09 by the UPA government, it was initially conceived as two smaller projects, with memorandums of understanding signed in 2013. On September 26, 2017, following a meeting between chief minister Pema Khandu, state delegates and NITI Aayog, the plan was changed to a single 250-metre-high dam, which would be the country’s largest in terms of installed capacity. However, stiff local resistance forced survey teams to withdraw, bringing the project to a temporary standstill.
The BJP-led governments at the Centre and in Arunachal Pradesh revived the project in 2020, following reports of China’s plan to build a dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo River, known as the Siang in India. In April 2022, the Centre directed the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC) to conduct a pre-feasibility survey to assess the project’s technical, economic, social and environmental viability. The exercise involves geological investigations, including drilling, and identifying villages that may require relocation.
Chief minister Pema Khandu and other state representatives have maintained that the survey does not amount to a decision to build the dam. NHPC has said that preliminary topographical, geological and geophysical work is complete, but core drilling to assess rock characteristics remains on hold because of local opposition.
However, the manner in which the survey was pursued has fuelled distrust. In May 2025, Central Armed Police Forces were deployed at several locations. Police maintained that the deployment was necessary to maintain law and order and that the required clearance had been obtained months earlier.
In September 2026, the state Cabinet approved an empowered committee to oversee the survey, alongside a significant deployment of central forces. Villagers, however, fear that the survey is a precursor to the dam’s construction and have accused the government of using security forces to suppress their opposition.
Questions over consent have further deepened the mistrust. Activist and politician Tadak Nalo alleged that many consent forms cited by the government were false, with endorsements largely coming from villagers whose lives would not be directly affected by the project.
Several indigenous communities, including the Adi, Galo, Nyishi, Apatani and Idu Mishmi, inhabit the Siang valley and depend heavily on the river, not only for their agricultural practices but also for their cultural identities and religious beliefs. They call the river Ane Siang, or Mother Siang. According to independent fact-finding reports, the SUMP would completely submerge nearly 27 villages across the Upper Siang and Siang districts and displace an estimated 1.5 lakh people, almost 11% of Arunachal Pradesh’s population.
With their homes, livelihoods and cultural heritage at stake, people in the Siang valley have only intensified their resistance over the past two weeks. The BJP government’s response, however, has been one of force and intimidation rather than dialogue. It bears resemblance to the way dissent has been dealt with elsewhere under BJP rule — in Delhi, for example, against ongoing protests demanding accountability from chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Use of Force, Detentions and Internet Shutdown
One of the issues against which the October 23 bandh was called was the detention of anti-SUMP protesters since October 9. According to reports, The state government invoked the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (APUAPA) and detained at least 10 protesters. Four of them — Adum Tayom, Omak Paron, Okut Paloh and Oson Paron, picked up from Pasighat — were reportedly held under APUAPA. Among those detained was the president of the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum (SIFF) Youth Wing, a vocal opponent of the mega project.
The crackdown intensified after the October 23 violence. A further 69 people were arrested and four detained in connection with the violence. A total of 55 cases were reportedly filed: 26 criminal cases in Upper Siang, 21 in Siang and six in East Siang district. Arrests and detentions were also carried out under the APUAPA. Those arrested reportedly face charges relating to rioting, the torching of vehicles and the vandalism of office buildings and residential houses.
The state has also significantly increased its security deployment in the region. At least 30 companies of Central Armed Police Forces and three companies of Assam Police have been deployed, in addition to Arunachal Pradesh Police personnel. The Centre also flew in two additional companies of the Rapid Action Force (RAF).
There were also reports of police using tear gas and batons against protesters on October 23. Five women were reportedly taken to hospital after experiencing breathing difficulties. The police, meanwhile, maintained that some protesters had allegedly attempted to breach barricades and attack security personnel.
The crackdown has not been confined to Arunachal Pradesh. On October 31, a solidarity protest against the SUMP outside Arunachal Bhavan in New Delhi, organised by Youth for Change (YFC) Arunachal and Himkhand, also ended in the detention and alleged manhandling of protesters by the Delhi Police.
