The protesters alleged that the Delhi Police used brute force and even subjected some of them to sexual assault during the detention. A member of Himkhand alleged that they were pinched in their private parts and their shirts were lifted. Around 40 protesters were detained during the protest in Delhi, including female protesters who reportedly were detained after 9 pm.
All of the detainees were later released after the intervention of senior Congress leaders.
As of November 2, internet services were suspended in Upper Siang as the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum (SIFF) and the SUMP Affected Area Youth Association (SAAYA), with the support of various student unions and community-based organisations, enforced a 36-hour bandh in parts of the Siang and all Upper Siang districts from 5 am. Protesters demanded the release of the detainees under APUAPA.
Censorship of Social Media Content
The crackdown on the anti-SUMP movement has also extended to the online space, with social media accounts of activists, journalists and news outlets being restricted or taken down. The censorship is part of a wider pattern in India, where government orders and platform restrictions have increasingly curtailed the circulation of content critical of those in power.
Tadak Nalo, founder and president of the political party Arunachal Frontier Tribal Front (AFTF), released a video statement after his Facebook account was restricted. Describing the situation in Arunachal Pradesh as “emergency-like”, he said fundamental rights, including the right to freedom of speech and expression, were being suppressed.
“My Facebook page, ‘Tadak Nalo for Revolution’, has been misused under the Information Technology Act and restricted completely within India today. If you want to view my page, you will have to go outside India. That is how they have set it up,” he said in the video.
Nalo alleged that his commentary on the SUMP was among the reasons behind the restriction. “A project this big is being built in our Arunachal, and it will cause displacement and render the indigenous inhabitants here landless. I had made some commentary on this and written some posts,” he said.
Several journalists and news pages have also reported having their Facebook pages disabled. Shaan Jijong, managing director of Upper Siang News 24*7, released a video statement saying that the outlet’s official Facebook page had been disabled. He also named two others, Ebo Mili and Katon Moyong, whose Facebook pages had allegedly been taken down.
“We are journalists, and we have been covering the SUMP from the ground also. But our news channel was disabled. Is this okay? We are journalists; we are the fourth pillar of democracy,” Jijong said.
The #Facebookpage of Upper Siang 24X7, a social media-based news channel, has been #blocked by the Government of India. The channel extensively reports on people’s resistance to the government’s proposal for the #SiangUpperMultipurposeProject, a 10,000 MW-plus #hydropower project on the #SiangRiver. Shan Jijong, the reporter behind the popular news platform, says he will continue to report on the issue. Several other Facebook accounts critical of the government’s action have also been withheld.
— The Arunachal Times (@arunachaltimes_) October 5, 2026
Katon Moyong, popularly known as Aborman Anbo, also found his Facebook page had “disappeared”, Northeast Today reported. He created a new account and published a post declaring that the censorship would not silence his opposition to the SUMP and that he had not lost his voice. However, we could not locate the new account on Facebook either, suggesting that it may have been taken down as well.
Two news reports published by Arunbhoomi News were also made unavailable for viewing in India. The outlet’s editor-in-chief, Takam Sonia, released a video statement condemning the move.
Human rights lawyer and activist Ebo Mili, whose Facebook account was also restricted, reportedly described the action as “deliberate and linked to his use of social media to raise public awareness about the project”.
The Facebook page Save Aborland and the general secretary and spokesperson of Adi Baane Kebang United, Datik Ratan, have also faced restrictions.
The Arunachal Press Club (APC) and the Arunachal Pradesh Union of Working Journalists (APUWJ) have condemned the restrictions on news reports and videos relating to the SUMP on social media platforms in India, and demanded transparency and their immediate restoration.
Targeting Arunachal Times Deputy Editor and Lawyer Defending Activists
Arunachal Pradesh Police have also moved against a journalist covering the anti-SUMP movement, seeking a search warrant against Tongam Rina, deputy editor of The Arunachal Times, in connection with the violence in Pasighat on October 23.
Police have also sought a search warrant against her lawyer, Sunny Tayeng, along with youth leader Otul Jerang, who has been arrested, and activist Tajong Talom, who was previously detained and allegedly harassed.
Rina took to X to assert that the police action would not deter her from her journalism or activism. “…I have seen enough intimidation in my life, so this isn’t something that will stop me from writing or my activism. More power to the people of Siang Valley and Arunachal. We owe it to Siang and her people…” she wrote.
She also criticised the move against Tayeng, pointing out that the lawyer was representing several activists, including Ebo Mili, Tajong Talom and Otul Jerang. Rina said she wanted Tayeng to be able to “focus on her practice rather than be burdened by extra work”.
The application for the search warrant, as reported by The Wire, describes Rina and the three other individuals as “accused persons”. It states that searches were “necessary to establish the individual roles of the accused, ascertain their alleged involvement in the offences and collect relevant material evidence”. However, the application does not specify how Rina or the other three individuals were linked to the violence.
The application states: “It is reasonably suspected on the basis of the facts and material collected during the investigation that certain articles and material connected with the commission of the alleged offences including clothing worn during the incident, mobile phones and digital devices containing relevant photographs or video recordings and other case-related articles may be found at the residences or premises…”
The Press Club of India also issued a statement expressing solidarity with Rina and condemning the Arunachal Pradesh Police’s move.
Paid PR Campaign
Actress Taba Reema, who has been vocal against SUMP, has posted a video alleging that PR firms were reaching out to content creators to speak about the construction of the dam in a positive light. “A few months ago, I also got an email from PR teams and agencies… they said they would pay this much for one reel and a list of pointers of advantages of building a dam. And now every reel or content like this I see… same to same…”
According to Reema, they tried to reach out to a lot of content creators from Arunachal, but they all declined. “And not that Arunachali creators have refused; they are using outsiders for this kind of content….”

According to an Indian Express report, Mumbai-based Concept Public Relations was awarded a one-year contract in July 2025, which was subsequently extended until November 2026, to build opinion in favour of the project, at a total cost of Rs 10.91 crore.
Asked about the agency’s appointment, an NHPC official told the newspaper that it had been hired to put forward “their side” and help supporters within the community speak out, despite “the pressure from violent elements”.
Alt News located several X posts which appear to be part of a concerted effort to delegitimise the protests by portraying protesters as Chinese stooges and calling for them to be “dealt with an iron fist”. While these posts do not, by themselves, establish any link with the PR campaign, they illustrate how opposition to the project was being framed in online discourse.
A short video on Instagram by user @creaatingchaaos has her saying, “You people in Arunachal, have you gone mad? China is making a dam of 60000 megawatts; India also has to do it…” In another video, she can be seen dancing while the text reads, “Arunachal does not have a problem with the dam; the convertereds do”. Several other reels show her making fun of anti-dam protesters, including their accent.

No executive has pulled the strings in the artificial intelligence era quite like Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang. He parlayed the boom into incredible wealth, became a close confidant of President Donald Trump, and emerged as a prominent voice in US-China relations. That now all stands in the balance.
Over the last few days, Huang’s status as an AI titan has come under scrutiny amid an admission that he had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence services concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia’s board of directors said that the company would launch an investigation into the incident. Huang, the company said, “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.” Huang earned $36 million last year, owned about 3.5 percent of Nvidia as of March, according to a corporate filing—which also noted that Huang is an at-will employee who can be let go anytime without severance.
How exactly the investigation shakes out, and what it means for Huang’s future at the company, remains to be seen. But the incident at least puts his position at risk, and raises questions about how the industry will respond.
“He’s the person who decides who gets the chips and who doesn't,” says David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School who tracks the chip industry.
Nvidia, which Huang cofounded in 1993, controls 90 percent of the market for chips used in training frontier AI models. With those chips in short supply, Huang has the power to determine which areas of AI get a boost next. Nvidia has also bankrolled much of the AI buildout, investing billions in the very companies buying its chips, such as OpenAI and Anthropic. When Elon Musk wants to build a new data center, Yoffie says, he can put in a call to Huang.
Internally, Huang closely manages even small details at Nvidia, responds to emails from any one of its roughly 60,000 staffers, and raises his voice to get points across, according to current and former employees. He’s a regular on cable TV and at tech conferences, where he’s been trying to deflate concerns about an AI market bubble and boost the positioning of his company.
But Nvidia has no other executive anywhere close to Huang’s prominence, and no apparent potential successor. “We have no idea who would replace him,” Yoffie says. “You put someone new into that position, if you're a customer, who knows what that's going to mean.”
Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, says that Huang has played such an important role—and become so close to the president—that he has become load-bearing for the entire US AI industry.
“On the one hand, Huang is irreplaceable. He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution,” Fedasiuk says. But he says that the company, which is indispensable to the AI industry, has to come first.
“He has to be replaceable as the CEO of the world's largest company, at $4 trillion in capex.”
Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday, even as broader stock market indices rose.
The board’s investigation will most likely focus on whether Huang violated any company policies, Yoffie says. But the FBI could also investigate whether laws were broken, and Congress may decide to look into whether Huang’s affair influenced the US government’s policy on selling chips to China.
Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The scandal also raises serious questions about whether China may have gained sensitive information about US AI companies and the government’s strategy on China, Fedasiuk says.
Huang’s affair appears especially damning given how outspoken he has been in recent years against calls for more aggressive technology export controls on China. His credibility on the topic could be permanently in doubt.
Both the first Trump administration and the Biden administration imposed export controls designed to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips, as well as technology required to mint advanced semiconductors. In his second term, however, Trump loosened these controls, giving China access to older generations of Nvidia chips; it was better to make China reliant on US technology, the argument went.
Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, says the Huang scandal is likely to accelerate efforts to crack down on chip exports.
“There was going to be more of an impetus to control what chips are getting sent to China anyway,” he says. “I expect there to be more scrutiny on what's going on, what's getting sent to China. I think there's also going to be more scrutiny from the Commerce Department.”

Amid rising concerns over the spread of Ebola to neighbouring countries, the Department of Health, Medical and Family Welfare, A.P., has stepped up surveillance at three airports — Bhogapuram (Visakhapatnam), Vijayawada, and Tirupati — as a precautionary measure.
According to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, an official U.S. government website, the outbreak is spreading “substantially faster” than previous Ebola outbreaks and is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record.
In this connection, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare held a video conference on November 5, Thursday, with State governments regarding the precautionary measures to be taken. The Union government officials also reviewed the implementation of the Ebola guidelines.
A.P. Health Secretary G. Veerapandian, who took part in the conference, explained the arrangements being made in the State as part of the preparedness.
Arrangements at 5 govt. hospitals
According to a release from the department on Thursday, isolation beds at five government hospitals, medical personnel, emergency equipment have been readied. Mr. Veerapandian informed the Union government that medical teams had been deputed at three airports to screen passengers arriving from Ebola-affected countries for any symptoms. Similar arrangements are also in place at Visakhapatnam, Kakinada and Nellore ports.
A total of 46 beds, 3,288 personal protective equipment (PPE) kits, 104 sample collection kits and five ambulances had been kept ready to deal with any eventuality, he said.
Mock drill
A mock drill will be conducted on November 12 to assess preparedness at the State and district levels, he said, adding that the departments concerned would be alerted to ensure that the guidelines are followed.
The Central officials have advised that passengers arriving from Ebola-affected countries be screened for symptoms, and those who had direct contact with infected persons be placed under observation. The medical teams should verify travel history of even those who do not exhibit any symptoms, the officials said.
If any person exhibits any symptoms, they should be taken to the hospital where isolation beds have been set up, the officials told the States.
As of October 31, Democratic Republic of the Congo reported 10,467 cases and 5,103 deaths, Kenya nine cases and two deaths, Uganda 20 cases and two deaths, Nigeria one case and France one case. Overall, 10,498 confirmed cases and 5,107 deaths were reported across five countries.

New Delhi: After India's gram (chana) imports fell in FY26 from a record high a year earlier, the government is stepping up efforts to strengthen domestic production of the pulse and further reduce import dependence and keep prices under control.
The Department of Consumer Affairs is identifying rainfed areas that can be brought under chana cultivation, two people aware of the matter said.
It has identified 80 districts across states, including Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, Punjab, Jharkhand and Bihar, where rainfed land could be utilised to grow the crop, the people said.
India imported gram worth $3.63 billion in FY26, down from a record $5.54 billion in FY25. The proposed move aims to build on this reduction by expanding domestic chana supplies.
“The government has a tentative estimate of around 2.38 million hectares of rainfed land across watershed areas in the identified states, and the exact extent of land suitable for chana cultivation will be mapped by the two departments,” said the first among the two officials cited above.
"As part of the plan, the department will approach the agriculture ministry and the Department of Land Resources to identify suitable acreage and assess its additional production potential,” the official added.
The department plans to support farmers with quality seeds and technical assistance, along with procurement assurance, the second official said.
Chana is a relatively less water-intensive crop that can be grown using residual soil moisture after the kharif harvest. The government expects the proposed expansion to strengthen domestic supplies and eventually create scope for chana dal exports, subject to domestic demand and surplus availability.
The average retail price of chana dal rose 10.8% year-on-year to ₹90.27 per kg as on 9 November.
Domestic chana consumption is estimated at 8-8.5 million tonnes annually, according to industry estimates.
The effort also has implications for food price stability. The RBI's October 2026 Monetary Policy Report noted that pulses inflation stood at 3.6% in August, after the category remained in deflation through much of FY26.
Queries sent to the spokespersons of the department of consumer affairs and agriculture ministry remained unanswered till press time.
Self reliance
The initiative is part of the Centre's Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses, which aims to make India self-reliant in pulse production and reduce import dependence. The six-year mission, running from 2025-26 to 2030-31, has a financial outlay of ₹11,440 crore.
Agriculture ministry data show that the gram cultivation area declined from 10.74 million hectares in 2021-22 to 9.12 million hectares in 2024-25, then recovered to 9.66 million hectares in 2025-26.
Chana acreage fell 21.61% in the current rabi sowing as of 6 November to 2.14 million hectares, according to the agriculture ministry's weekly sowing data.
Production fell from 13.54 million tonnes in 2021-22 to 11.03 million tonnes in 2023-24, before recovering to 12.51 million tonnes in 2025-26.
Meanwhile, the area under pulses during the current rabi sowing season declined 14.39% year-on-year to 3.19 million hectares as of 6 November.
“Identifying rainfed land alone will not be enough to expand chana production,” said B.B. Singh, former ADG (oilseeds & pulses), ICAR. “The key is to match the crop variety and its duration with the soil type, available moisture and local weather conditions. If sowing is timed well and farmers have access to varieties suited to their region, they can make better use of land that otherwise remains fallow after the monsoon.”
Expanding chana cultivation in suitable rainfed areas can improve domestic availability, while a more stable supply would also reduce the need for imports to bridge production shortfalls, said Rakesh Arrawatia, professor at the Institute of Rural Management Anand and dean, School of Cooperative Banking and Finance.
Rainfed areas offer significant potential to expand chana cultivation, as the crop can utilize residual soil moisture after the monsoon and with suitable crop planning, improved seeds and better agricultural practices, these areas can help increase production, said K.J. Ramesh, former director general of the India Meteorological Department.

Sports Personality of the Year returns - with five awards decided by public
- Published
The 2026 BBC Sports Personality of the Year show will be held on Sunday, 13 December - with five winners decided by public votes.
Clare Balding, Gabby Logan and Alex Scott will again host the programme, which will be hosted in Salford and broadcast live on BBC One, BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app from 17:45 GMT.
Five of the nine awards to be presented on the night will be decided by public vote.
The show will celebrate another great year of sport, including Team GB's most successful Winter Olympics, England's best finish at a men's Fifa World Cup since 1966, and record-breaking displays at the European Athletics Championships.
There will be two new award categories at the ceremony this year - Men's Footballer of the Year and BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year.
The latter has been a BBC World Service award since 2015 but will now be presented as part of the BBC Sports Personality of the Year awards for the first time. Voting - for global audiences - opens on Tuesday, 10 November.
In addition to crowning the winners of both football awards, fans will also select the winners of the World Sport Star of the Year, Team of the Year and Sports Personality of the Year award itself.
An independent panel made up of industry experts, sports broadcasters, sports journalists and former sportspeople will determine the shortlists for the Sports Personality of the Year, Team of the Year and World Sports Star awards, with the winners chosen by public votes. The independent panel will also determine the winners of Young Sports Personality of the Year and Coach of the Year.
Separate panels of football experts will provide the shortlist of contenders for Men's Footballer of the Year and Women's Footballer of the Year.
Alex Kay-Jelski - director of BBC Sport - said: "What I love about BBC Sports Personality of the Year is that it brings together all those moments that stopped us in our tracks. The goals, the medals, the upsets, the records, the stories that had us talking at work, in the pub and around the dinner table.
"And what a year we've had. This year's shortlists will be packed with athletes and teams who have achieved extraordinary things, but what's especially exciting is that audiences will have a bigger say than ever before in who takes home the trophies."
The nine award categories are:
- BBC Sports Personality of the Year
- Helen Rollason Award
- Young Sports Personality of the Year
- Coach of the Year
- Team of the Year
- Lifetime Achievement award
- Men's Footballer of the Year
- Women's Footballer of the Year
- World Sport Star of the Year
Full voting details, dates and T&Cs will be announced in due course.

ఉత్తరప్రదేశ్లోని ఒక పాఠశాల బయట బాలికలను వేధించినందుకు షెహబాజ్ హుస్సేన్, మహ్మద్ తౌఫీక్ అనే ఇద్దరు వ్యక్తులను పోలీసులు అరెస్టు చేసి వీధుల్లో ఊరేగించారంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ఉత్తరప్రదేశ్లో బాలికలను వేధించినందుకు షెహబాజ్ హుస్సేన్, మహ్మద్ తౌఫీక్ అనే ఇద్దరు ముస్లిం వ్యక్తులను పోలీసులు వీధుల్లో ఊరేగిస్తున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: మహిళలను వేధించినందుకు ఇద్దరు వ్యక్తులను ఉత్తరప్రదేశ్ పోలీసులు వీధుల్లో ఊరేగించిన మాట వాస్తవమే అయినప్పటికీ, నిందితులు హిందువులు, ముస్లింలు కారు. అరెస్టయిన వ్యక్తులను సుభాష్ పాల్, దక్ష్ పాల్గా పోలీసులు అధికారికంగా గుర్తించారు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.

A man who lost over $308,000 making sports wagers on Kalshi is suing the prediction market for violating the state of Washington’s ban on online gambling. He’s trying to turn those losses into an overall victory with a lawsuit seeking a payment of over $580,000.
Bellevue, Washington, resident Scott Bright’s “wagering occurred at a time when it was unlawful in Washington and when the Washington Attorney General had already sued KalshiEX LLC in this Court alleging precisely that,” said the gambler’s lawsuit filed on September 24 in King County Superior Court. Kalshi has since filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit.
While state attorneys general throughout the US are trying to shut down Kalshi for allegedly violating state gambling laws, Bright’s case tests whether unsuccessful gamblers can obtain restitution from the company through individual lawsuits.
“Washington has prohibited Internet gambling since 2006. Washington has also provided, since long before that, a statutory cause of action permitting any person who loses money at illegal gambling to recover it from the proprietor for whose benefit the game was conducted,” Bright’s lawsuit said.
Even if Bright’s lawsuit fails, gamblers who lost on Kalshi could get money back through the lawsuits filed by state governments. For example, Washington’s lawsuit against the company said the attorney general “is entitled to recover all money Washingtonians have lost through Defendant Kalshi’s illegal gambling operation” under the state’s Recovery of Money Lost at Gambling Act. Washington already won a court order restricting the kinds of wagers Kalshi can offer in the state, but it took effect after Bright’s losses.
Kalshi says event contracts aren’t gambling
Kalshi wants Bright’s lawsuit to be moved to US District Court for the Western District of Washington, saying it must be tried in a federal court instead of a state one. In an October 30 motion to dismiss Bright’s case, Kalshi argued that he did not lose any money on “gambling.” Kalshi said he lost money on “event contracts,” which Kalshi says can only be regulated by the federal government.

Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”
Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.
“It’s the men who ask such intrusive questions: Who are you? Where are you from? What does your father do?” she says.
Sheel was recounting these experiences atop Delhi’s oldest fort inside Sanjay Van, a sprawling city forest overlooking a 12th-century minaret. She was one of about 20 women who had gathered on a crisp Sunday morning in October to enjoy nature, safely. Many had never experienced a forest before.
Among the group were a scientist who had stopped birding since she moved to Delhi, a psychiatrist who can’t find a safe place to run, and an environmental planner who cycles everywhere. For many women, simple pleasures such as enjoying nature have become beset by gender crimes.
“The city feels designed to crush any form of freedom, any form of exploration,” says Neha Sinha, who organised the walk. Author of My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital, Sinha has been organising these walks for two years.
During her own walks around the city’s forts, forests and wetlands to observe the diminishing number of fireflies, flying foxes, howling jackals, leopards and hyenas, civets and owls, and groves of 350-year-old trees, she has faced the wrath of men. She has changed her route countless times to mislead stalkers, and been asked by men on the street how much she would charge for sex.
“As has everybody else,” she says. “Nearly every woman I know has called a cop saying ‘I have a stalker.’ In a culture that tells you not to go out … how do you make nature your own?”
Two weeks before the women gathered on the walking trails of Sanjay Van, dotted with ruellias, vajradantis and jaal trees, hundreds of people had joined a protest in Delhi over the gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park.
Their demand was to make public spaces safer for women. The government’s response was to ban entry to public parks after sunset.
For Alankrita Narayan, a wildlife conservation student who often needs to work alone at night, that rule was unhelpful. During an internship, she recalls, her organisation trained her for worst-case scenarios in the jungle: What if something happens to your partner? What if you encounter a man carrying a weapon? What if you encounter a forest officer asking for sexual favours?
“And I was like, where did the animal come in here? What if I’m caught alone and a leopard comes in front of me? And they were like, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into,” she says. Sinha agrees: “Animals have rules.”
Paroma Mukherjee, a photographer, recalls the advice she once got from a well-known photographer: be inconspicuous, wear clothes that blend in, keep your equipment small. “But then, he was a man. So he could blend in,” she adds.
“Men can pee on the road and we can’t even carry a camera,” another woman says. “You know, we had to take a detour today to avoid a lonely stretch on our way here,” says another. “I carry a pepper spray,” another adds.
On group walks, the women pick up and drop off each other at their homes, wait outside the forest gate until everyone has arrived, and stick together in isolated areas. “I always tell women, ‘Don’t go alone’,” Sinha says.
“We started the walk at 7am today, which is late for birdwatching, but everybody could not leave home while it was still dark,” she says.
However, the group agree that many of these measures might not work for women from less privileged backgrounds, who then miss out.
“No woman in the city is fully free,” Sinha says.
Walking as a woman is an act of resistance, as is observing nature. “Because you’re actually slowing down when you do that,” she says. “It’s so different from the instant gratification culture that we have today. It is more of an immersion, rather than conquering. Both are very political acts.”
In the heart of New Delhi, where India’s senior officials and dignitaries live, there are thousands of fruit bats that swarm out of their roosts every evening to feast on mahua trees.
“And on very clear wintry nights, when everything is silent, I even hear jackals crying and laughing from my home. It’s almost like a parallel city,” Sinha says.
Over three hours, the women collect cuttings, peer and marvel at speckle-like flowers through a pocket microscope, discuss the colonial concepts of wild plants labelled as weeds, chat about the drongo, black kite and tailorbird they spotted, and the next walk.
“Can we do it at night?” someone asks. “What would the forest look like at night?”
Sinha describes a previous night walk experience when frogs had put up an orchestral noise, fireflies lit the bushes and jackals were laughing. “It was the most eerie, magical, bewitching atmosphere I have ever experienced,” she says.
Men, she points out, can simply go ahead and enjoy such experiences, but women have to create an ecosystem around them to be able to.
But, she promises her enthusiastic group, she will try to arrange a night walk.

AI unicorn Sarvam has appointed former Google Cloud India managing director Sashikumar Sreedharan as its president and chief business officer (CBO), as it looks to strengthen its enterprise and government business and scale the commercial deployment of its AI technology. In his new role, Sreedharan will lead Sarvam's business across enterprises and government institutions while expanding its engagement with digital-native companies, developers and partners. He will also oversee marketing, finance, forward-deployed engineering, service delivery and commercial operations, the company said in a blog post. Sreedharan will also join the company's board of directors. Before joining Sarvam, Sreedharan served as MD of Google Cloud India for over a year. Across a career spanning about 35 years, he has served across companies like Microsoft India, IBM, Wipro, Happiest Mind Technologies, among others. His appointment comes as Sarvam looks to move beyond developing indigenous AI models and build a larger enterprise business around its technology. The startup said it provides its full-stack AI offerings to over 100 enterprises and government institutions. “The next phase of Sarvam is about advancing our research, developing products loved by people around the world, and building a company that can operate at a much greater scale,” the startup said. Sarvam AI's Push To Build The India Stack Founded in 2023 by Pratyush Kumar and Vivek Raghavan, Sarvam develops foundational AI models, computing infrastructure, and enterprise applications. Its offerings target businesses and government agencies seeking tools tailored to Indian languages, data-security requirements, and local use cases. The new CBO appointment comes shortly after Sarvam expanded its AI portfolio with the launch of Prism. The "System One" decision model built on top of Sarvam AI's Sarvam 105B foundation model. Rather than generating open-ended text token-by-token like a conventional LLM, it evaluates a given context, a question, and a predefined list of options in a single processing pass to return calibrated probabilities for each choice. The startup has also released several other models in recent months, including Sarvam Vision 2.1, a vision-language model for processing documents and recognising text in Indian languages, and Saaras V4, its speech-to-text model. In October, it launched Bulbul V4 Flash, a text-to-speech model for generating natural speech across Indian languages. Earlier this year, Sarvam raised $234 Mn in the first close of its $300 Mn Series B funding round, which valued the company at $1.5 Bn. The unicorn minting round saw participation from investors HCLTech, Bessemer Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners. DR Congo sentences 66 soldiers to death for being 'cowards'
- Published
At least 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in the Democratic Republic of Congo for cowardice, mutiny and refusing to obey orders, local media report.
The sentences followed a trial of 71 soldiers before a military court in Walikale, in North Kivu province, in eastern DR Congo. Four soldiers were acquitted, while another was sentenced to 10 years in prison.
The army said the trial was intended to improve discipline among troops as they battle armed groups in eastern DR Congo.
The region has endured decades of conflict, with fighting continuing between government forces and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), a rebel coalition that includes the M23 group.
The soldiers were reportedly arrested on 20 October in Walikale, where they were accused of abandoning their positions and fleeing during clashes with FRN fighters.
The Congolese army's campaign against armed groups, including the M23, has long been undermined by poor discipline and disorganisation within its ranks.
The government has repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda of supporting the M23, an allegation denied by both Kigali and the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
The army has faced persistent criticism over its lack of professionalism and disciplined, while soldiers have complained of poor pay and inadequate equipment.
Last month, another 27 soldiers were sentenced to death on similar charges of cowardice after reportedly withdrawing from the frontline during clashes with rebels.
In March 2024, DR Congo lifted a 20-year moratorium on the death penalty, citing the need to remove "traitors" within the army.
The government said capital punishment would also apply to people involved in armed groups, insurrection, as well as committing treason and war crimes.
The decision to reinstate the death penalty was widely criticised by rights groups. However, no formal executions have been carried out since the moratorium was lifted.
Since the beginning of 2025, at least 507 soldiers have been convicted, including 381 death sentences, according to figures compiled by French broadcaster RFI.
In October 2025, former Congolese President Joseph Kabila was sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself. He has since been named as the FRN's leader.

Homes and temples glow across India as Diwali celebrations begin
- Published
Millions across India are set to celebrate Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.
The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.
Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.
But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.
Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.
In the capital, Delhi, the air quality index (AQI) reached 391 on Friday morning, placing it in the "very poor" category ahead of the festival. There are fears that pollution levels could rise further after the celebrations.
India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks, with its AQI reaching 322 on 24 October. Although air quality has improved in recent days to reach "moderate" levels of 104 on Friday, there are concerns that Diwali fireworks could trigger another spike.
In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.
These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% less emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are in reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.
Despite the debate over fireworks, Diwali is about much more than firecrackers.
The festival celebrates the return of Lord Ram to Ayodhya after his victory over over Ravan, the main antagonist in the Hindu epic Ramayana, and symbolises the triumph of good over evil.
In the days leading up to the festival, families clean and decorate their homes with flowers, colourful lights and traditional oil lamps known as diyas.
The celebrations also bring families and friends together for prayers, elaborate feasts and the exchange of gifts, and lots of traditional Indian sweets.
Colourful patterns known as rangoli are created at entrances to homes, while markets bustle with shoppers buying festive essentials beneath brightly lit decorations.
The celebrations began on 6 November with Dhanteras, when buying gold, silver or new utensils is considered auspicious and believed to bring good fortune.
The second day, known as Chhoti Diwali, or small Diwali, is marked by the lighting of oil lamps and, in some households, setting off firecrackers.
The third day is the main celebration, when families offer evening prayers to Lakshmi, the Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity, before gathering for festive meals and fireworks.
The fourth day is celebrated differently across India, with family gatherings and New Year festivities in some communities. The fifth and final day, known as Bhai Dooj, celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters.
The festival is also celebrated by Sikhs and Jains along with other important religious observances.
Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, or Prisoner Release Day, commemorating the release of their sixth guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment at Gwalior Fort in the early 17th Century.
For Jains, Diwali marks the attainment of moksha, or liberation from the cycle of rebirth, by Lord Mahavira, the 24th and last Tirthankara, or spiritual teacher, of the current era.
With Indian communities spread across the world, Diwali is also celebrated internationally, with families and friends coming together for festive gatherings and exchanging gifts.
The festival is considered an auspicious time to make new purchases, which many believe bring prosperity and good fortune. India's stock exchanges even hold a special one-hour trading session for investors who consider buying and selling shares on Diwali auspicious. Known as known as Muhurat trading, it will take place on 8 November this year.
Although rooted in Hindu traditions, Diwali is celebrated by people across different faiths and communities.

Malaysia's disgraced former PM leaves jail for house arrest after embezzling millions
- Published
Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest of a jail sentence for corruption under house arrest.
There was a big media presence at his Kuala Lumpur residence to see the 73-year-old return from prison in an SUV late on Tuesday night, escorted by a heavily armed police convoy.
Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund.
The 1MDB scandal brought down his government and made headlines around the world when it came to light a decade ago, embroiling prominent figures from Malaysia to Goldman Sachs and Hollywood.
Investigators estimated that $4.5bn (£3.3bn) was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund, which Najib co-founded, into private pockets, including his own. More than $1bn allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, according to prosecutors.
Najib's lawyers claim he had been misled by his advisers - in particular the financier Jho Low, who has maintained his innocence and remains at large.
Najib's mansion in one of the capital's most exclusive neighbourhoods was declared a federal prison ahead of his homecoming on Tuesday.
Critics said his release from jail undermined efforts to fight corruption and questioned its legal basis, saying Malaysian law made no provision for house arrest.
Najib, who was prime minister from 2009 to 2018, denied wrongdoing but was convicted at two separate trials.
In the first trial he was sentenced in 2020 to 12 years in prison and jailed in 2022. The term was later halved on appeal.
In September, the King of Malaysia granted him a conditional pardon to see out the remaining two years of his sentence at home.
The transfer to his mansion was to take place on Friday but put on hold after the attorney general sought clarification of the royal decree. On Tuesday the high court ruled the house arrest was effective immediately.
Najib's party paid a $12m fine as part of the terms of the royal pardon allowing him to serve the rest of his term at home.
He was sentenced after being convicted of abuse of power, money laundering and breach of trust over 42 million ringgit ($10m; £7.7m) transferred from SRC International - a former unit of 1MDB - into his private accounts.
Najib is appealing against a 15-year prison sentence, handed down at a second trial in December 2025, in a case involving much larger sums of money. In that case he was convicted of misappropriating nearly 2.3 billion Malaysian ringgit ($569m; £422m) from the nation's sovereign wealth fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
He is due to start serving that sentence after his house arrest ends, which is expected in August 2028.

Judoka determined to prove refugees belong at Dakar 2026
- Published
Arno Yafunga Botay was six when his family fled the Democratic Republic of Congo after threats to his father's life culminated in an attack on their home which claimed the life of his seven-month-old sibling.
Following a spell living in the Kakuma refugee camp in north-west Kenya, the family settled in Nairobi. There, Arno used to watch his father Arnold practising judo and eventually asked him to teach him the sport.
Now, having coming through trials in East Africa, he will compete for the Refugee Olympic Team in the under-55kg category at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games.
"I didn't expect to be selected," the 15-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"I was so excited. I was crying tears of joy."
This is the first time that a team of refugees will appear at a Youth Games.
"It [means] a lot to me to represent other refugees, represent my community," Yafunga Botay added.
The family have been in Kenya since they were forced to leave DR Congo in 2017.
"There were people who wanted to kill me," Arnold said.
"At the time, I was detained somewhere when people came to our house and attacked my family. The situation led to the death of my child."

After finding safety, Yafunga Botay and his elder brother Christian would watch their father training before he headed out to work as a labourer.
Yafunga Botay began receiving instructions in judo rules and techniques at the age of seven.
However, life in their adopted East African nation provided its own challenges.
"I [did] not have the judogi clothes or transport fees for local competitions," he explained.
"It's been difficult going to school. There's no money for school fees.
"My father has no work. He needs to go to work and give us money to go and pay the school fees.
"And here we don't have support. As a refugee, to stay in Kenya, you need to have documents.
"[Thankfully] the IOC (International Olympic Committee) came with this programme of helping refugees achieve their dreams."
An Olympic first for refugees
The Refugee Olympic Team was first introduced at the Rio 2016 Olympics and Cameroon-born boxer Cindy Ngamba won the team's first ever medal at Paris 2024 when she claimed bronze in the women's 75kg category.
In a double first, the team will now make its Youth Olympics debut at Dakar 2026, which is the first Olympic event hosted on African soil.
"As a refugee, we have a right to compete," Yafunga Botay said.
"A refugee is a human being like other people."
Father Arnold says the team serves as a message of hope to people around the world who have been displaced.
"Being a refugee does not mean your life is over," he said.
"Refugees can also do things that surprise people.
"My message to fellow refugees is don't give up. Keep pushing until the end."
The six-strong team competing in Senegal is being mentored by two-time Olympic marathon champion Eliud Kipchoge.
"He teaches us [to] respect the coach, focus on what you are doing," Yafunga Botay said.
"I promised him I'll bring the gold medal [back] so he can see [what] I achieved."
Discipline and respect
Judo has become a central part of life for the family.
Arnold still coaches Yafunga Botay and Christian, now 17, occasionally serves as his younger brother's sparring partner.
The teenager describes his father as "strict" even at home, with a firm focus on the importance of discipline.
"Maintaining his weight is not easy. He [Arno] has to keep training consistently," Arnold said.
"Judo teaches him respect and helps him interact with others, whether at school or at home.
"Those lessons follow him everywhere. In judo, every time you fall you gain the strength to keep going."
The owner of the dojo in the Kenyan capital where Yafunga Botay has trained since 2020 says his selection for Dakar 2026 has "changed perceptions" of judo in the community.
"It is helping parents understand that judo is not just a fighting sport - it has real value," Lawrence Karisa Nyundo told the BBC.
"I have received calls from parents who want to enrol their children.
"It is a big achievement for this club that one of our athletes is going to compete at the Olympics. We are praying that he performs well."
After Dakar, Yafunga Botay hopes other refugees can benefit from his experience in the future.
"In Kakuma, there are good judokas.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins on Friday, with the opening ceremony a day later and judo events running from 1-3 November.

Six members each of two families were killed in separate incidents of fire in Katni and Seoni districts of Madhya Pradesh during Diwali celebrations early on Monday, police said.
In Katni, an earthen lamp triggered a massive blaze inside a three-storey building, killing six people across three generations, including a two-month-old infant who was found dead in his mother’s lap.
According to police, the deceased were identified as Puran Agrawal (77), his wife Chandrakala (74), daughter-in-law Poonam, and granddaughters Arya (14), Anvi (6), and the infant. Two people managed to escape, an official said.

Katni superintendent of police (SP) Abhinav Vishwakarma said the fire broke out on the upper floors, situated above a crockery shop. “Preliminary investigation and survivors informed police that a fire started from an earthen lamp kept near a coffee machine and later spread quickly through the house,” he said.
Meanwhile, a second fire broke out at a gold trader’s house in Seoni, killing six members of his family.
According to police, the fire broke out in a three-storey building, owned by Kundan Lal Soni (75), at 4.30 am in Chhapara town.
The deceased were identified as Kundan Lal Soni (75), his wife Rajkumari Soni (65), daughters-in-law Ritu Soni (42) and Smriti Soni (40), relative Surya Soni (45), and grandson Aditya Soni (16).
Chhapara sub-divisional police officer Apoorv Bhalavi said it took firefighters several hours to bring the fire under control. Soni’s neighbours tried to fight the flames using water buckets before firefighters arrived. Police said the cause of the fire is yet to be determined.

Why Danielle Smith wants to give a subsidy to the oilpatch despite near-record profits
Oil and gas industry forecast to post revenues of more than $200B this year
The Alberta government is preparing to unveil new subsidies later this month for oil companies to ramp up production in order to help fill the province's proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast.
The incentives would come as the largest oil producers are posting billions of dollars in profits in their latest financial results and the industry as a whole is experiencing one of its most lucrative years over the last decade.
Suncor Energy, Cenovus Energy, Canadian Natural Resources and Imperial Oil posted combined profits of more than $12.5 billion in recent quarterly earnings reports. The Canadian oil and gas industry is forecast to post revenues of more than $200 billion in 2026, according to Studio Energy, after oil prices climbed above $100 US per barrel several times this year amid the U.S.-Iran war.
That's why some industry experts question why new subsidies are needed.
"What kind of incentives does the oil and gas sector really need?" said Janet Annesley, a former executive with Husky Energy and Shell Canada, on CBC Radio's Alberta at Noon.
"They've got money, they're buying back shares, they're flowing lots of dividends to shareholders. So what really more do we Albertans have to do to get them to make investments here and have more projects?"
Premier Danielle Smith, Annesley said, will have to "prosecute the case with Albertans about why we should be giving more incentives to oil companies."
Oil production is already at record levels, but with several new and expanded pipeline projects in development, there is uncertainty whether the industry will pump out enough crude to justify beginning construction on the Pacific Link — for which Smith wants construction to begin in fall 2027.
The province is seeking to create an "alternative enhanced royalty structure," according to Smith, to incentivize companies to commit to growing oil production.
"We hope that once that is on the table and they know all of the factors that would go into it, I suspect that you're going to see a lot of interest in being able to fill that pipeline," Smith told journalists in Fort McMurray, Alta., in September.
More oil wanted
The new subsidy is expected to be aimed at the oilsands sector, since that is the source of most oil production in the province and new projects are often large enough to noticeably increase overall production levels.
The Alberta government already provides a financial incentive to oilsands companies to build new projects, since they pay much lower levels of royalties to the government during the first few years of operation.
A view of Suncor's Base Plant oilsands mine. Suncor is one of the companies considering whether to proceed with expanding production in the oilsands. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)
Already, some companies are hinting at potentially moving quicker to build new projects.
Imperial Oil was considering a decision to proceed with its Aspen oilsands project by the end of the decade, but chief executive John Whelan said that could occur sooner.
"We are looking at do we want to bring it forward," he said, during a conference call with analysts on Oct. 30, while acknowledging the company is encouraged by steps taken by the provincial and federal governments to support the sector.
Suncor executives are looking at their growth plans over the next several years and contemplating how they could potentially move faster, if they decide to, said chief executive Rich Kruger.
"We're asking ourselves and doing some preliminary work," he said, during a conference call with analysts on Nov. 4.
"We're all anxiously waiting to hear more from the province on royalties and incentives there. The parties are all sleeves rolled up, meeting endlessly, working hard together."
The Oil Sands Alliance would not comment on the proposed Alberta incentives until an actual announcement is made.
Introducing a deadline
Some oil companies could be hinting at possible growth plans as a way to alert investors and gauge their interest. Despite lucrative oil prices, many investors would rather oil companies continue to produce hefty profits for shareholders, as opposed to spending billions of dollars to invest in new projects.
Many investors are enjoying the robust profits and are reluctant to give up the cash they collect, says Mark Little, the former chief executive of Suncor.
The company leaders are "testing investors' appetite for expansion," said Little, to hear if they will support growth plans or if they warn not to do it.
"To me, the biggest uncertainty on growth isn't the [federal government], it's not the province, it's not money," said Little, "It's whether the investor will support it."
Former Suncor executive Mark Little, pictured in 2022, says the current Alberta royalty system works well. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)
The last large oilsands project to be constructed was nearly a decade ago, which is why Little says it's important for the industry to make investments to ensure the sector's long-term future.
"I almost call it the 'liquidation phase' because all we've been doing is basically producing, spending as little as possible, and handing the cash back to the shareholders," he said.
An aerial view of an oilsands mine north of Fort McMurray, Alta. Oil production continues to increase as companies expand and improve existing facilities. (Bob Grieve/CBC)
The Alberta government's move to introduce a new incentive is "mystifying," said Little, since the current royalty system is already sophisticated, flexible and works well. However, he could see merit in the provincial government introducing a deadline for companies to develop the properties they own.
Production from the oilsands continues to increase as companies invest in expansion projects and find ways to improve existing operations.
Lennie Kaplan, who previously served as a senior manager with the Treasury Board, estimates that some level of incentives are necessary for companies to spend billions of dollars to build new large-scale oilsands projects.
"These projects are very capital intensive," he said, about the level of investment required.

- First Nations challenging Pacific Link pipeline’s national-interest designation
For the Alberta government to reach its goal of doubling oil production, Kaplan's calculations estimate the government would need to provide $115 billion of incentives between 2027 and 2050, which includes $95 billion of royalty relief and $18 billion of additional construction subsidies. Under that scenario of normal oil prices, as forecast by Alberta Energy, the government would collect an additional $250 billion in royalties.
However, in a scenario with low oil prices, the government would need to provide $240 billion of incentives and yet experience a net fiscal loss of $80 billion.
Kaplan's modelling does account for other considerations, including a rising industrial carbon tax, which he said is important considering the Alberta government still pledges to be net-zero by 2050.

The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.
Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN.
 
The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them, but Bangkok appeared to want to avoid upsetting Beijing. The UN has said the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.
Now, two more men fear becoming the latest victims of Beijing’s repressive crackdown against the largely Muslim ethnic group, condemned by the UN as a potential crime against humanity.
The girlfriend of one of the men said her boyfriend, whose name is being withheld for security reasons, told the Guardian he wanted to go “anywhere else but China”.
Human rights groups said two Uyghur men were at risk of deportation after recently being transferred to an immigration detention centre and they feared Thai authorities may once again give in to pressure from Beijing.
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, called for the men to be allowed to travel to a safe third country. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” she said.
The men had been serving a seven-year prison sentence for offences related to an attempted escape from immigration detention in January 2020. They were part of a group of more than 200 Uyghur men, women and children who were apprehended by Thai police in 2014 near the border with Malaysia after they fled from China.
Since 2014, women and children in the group have been released to Turkey, while the men have been deported to China, in separate batches, attracting criticism from the United Nations and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.
Uyghurs, a Turkic minority mainly from the Xinjiang region in China, have been subjected to decades of oppressive and discriminatory treatment from the Chinese authorities. This has included the incarceration of hundreds of thousands of people in detention camps aimed at stamping out their cultural identity.
Beijing has defended its policies in Xinjiang as being aimed at poverty alleviation and counter-terrorism.
In July, Marzeyya Kasem’s (who asked to be referred to by her Islamic alias) boyfriend wrote to her in a letter that he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back to China. “Sometimes I thought why I’m a human being. What I do wrong against China … no want to go back to China,” he wrote. She shared the letter with a Thai rights group.
The two men facing imminent deportation reportedly pleaded their case to Thailand’s office of the National Human Rights Commission on Wednesday.
Relatives of Uyghurs have said the Chinese government was “paranoid about Uyghurs going to a safe country in large numbers and living together”, and preferred to have them deported.
It is not clear whether China has issued a formal extradition request for the two men. But Chaipruak Doungprapat, Thailand’s national security council chief, told reporters that the men, along with three other Uyghurs who are still in prison, had arrest warrants outstanding in China.
Some have questioned whether criminal warrants could be credible considering that at least one of them, Kasem’s boyfriend, was a minor when he left China. “If they are really wanted for a crime in China, why didn’t China immediately issue a [Interpol] red notice [when they were detained in 2014]?” asked Kasem.
Kasem believes that because Thailand was criticised for last year’s mass deportation, this time the authorities were trying to establish a more credible legal basis for the move.
A spokesperson for China’s foreign affairs ministry said: “The cooperation between China and Thailand in combating cross-border illegal and criminal activities such as smuggling is consistent with the laws of the two countries, international law and international practice.”
A spokesperson for Thailand’s foreign affairs ministry declined to comment.
- Additional research by Rebecca Ratcliffe

British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sexual assault
Russell Brand, the raunchy, irreverent British comedian who became a celebrity darling in the early 2000s, has been sentenced to over 10 years in prison after being found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
"The total sentence is one of ten years, six months," said Judge Justice Bennathan on handing down the sentence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday.
Brand, 51, was a career chameleon who went from stand-up comic and MTV host to a political analyst esteemed by Britain's left, only to become a conspiracy theorist and Christian convert beloved by the U.S. right.
But critics of Brand said there was always a clear thread of misogyny running through his comedy routines, and that his mistreatment of women had been an open secret for decades.
Over the past four weeks, six women testified against the comedian in court in London, in a trial that garnered massive media attention.
A jury found Brand guilty last week on four of the seven counts against him. He was found guilty of raping a woman he'd met at one of his shows in 2009 and of sexually assaulting three women — at a bar, a radio station and a TV studio — between 2004 and 2009.
Brand denies all charges and said he never had non-consensual sex.
Before the judge handed down the sentence, four of the women who brought the case against Brand gave victim impact statements to the court. Three of the statements were read out by the prosecution, while one woman appeared in court behind a curtain to read her own.
None of the women have been publicly named and the trial was not televised.
Victim impact statements read
The prosecution read out an impact statement from the one complainant, who Brand was found guilty of anally raping at his home in 2009. In her statement she said: "It's something I carry with me every day and it often feels never-ending."
"I doubt my ability to make good decisions and no longer trust my instinct in the way I did," her statement said, adding that because of Brand's fame she didn't think she'd be believed if she reported him.
Another complainant, who Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting at a bar in 2004 when he grabbed her breasts, said the confusion of what she "should" or "could" do had stayed with her for over 20 years.
The complainant, who spoke in person from behind a curtain in the courtroom, said she felt "physically sick" seeing Brand in the press afterwards as his fame rose.
Another of Brand's victims, who he was found guilty of sexually assaulting in 2005, said the assault had "a lasting impact on her life" and that over the years "hearing his voice on television or seeing his image has made me jump."
A fourth woman, who Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting when they worked together at a TV studio, said she was badly affected and afterwards felt her working environment was unsafe.
Brand holds rosary and prays
British media who were in the court for the sentencing said Brand, who had spent the weekend in prison, was in the suit he was convicted in on Thursday and sat holding a set of white rosary beads as the victim statements were read. Brand's wife Laura, who had supported him throughout the case, was in court, as was his father.
After the victim statements, the defense and prosecution teams had the opportunity to make their last statements.
The prosecution called for a long sentence, saying there were aggravating circumstances in the anal rape case, such as Brand removing a condom. The defence meanwhile said Brand was "a fundamentally different person" from who he was at the time of the crimes.
After considering the victim impact statements and those by the defence and prosecution, the judge handed down the sentence live on camera.
In his remarks, he said Brand had become "a sexual predator" and paused "to pay tribute to the determination and bravery" of the women who'd come forward.
He then ordered Brand to be taken down to the cells.

Since Valve announced its Steam Deck Verified program in 2021, players have found that a game’s “Verified” status doesn’t always match how well it actually runs on the handheld. Now, new Steam Deck frame rate data being shared by Valve itself can help players dig deeper into the performance they can expect from many Steam Deck games.
Valve has been collecting anonymized frame rate data from Steam players who opt in since February. Yesterday evening, the company announced it has started sharing that data on many Steam Store pages as averages and histograms for both the Steam Deck and Steam Deck OLED.
Valve acknowledges that players enabling VSync or frame rate limits can bias the collected data somewhat and that the measurements don’t account for custom in-game settings that Steam Deck users may tinker with to get a game running. Regardless, Valve says it has nonetheless “found that the framerate data consolidates around relatively narrow ranges.”
Beyond the badge
This kind of data can be extremely useful for distinguishing between the wide range of performance levels that can exist among “Verified” Steam Deck games. Both Cyberpunk 2077 and Skyrim: Special Edition earn the same Steam Deck Verified badge, for instance, but the former sees average Deck frame rates in the 30–40 FPS range, while the latter usually achieves 50–60 FPS on the hardware.
Valve’s frame rate data is even more useful for games that the company insists are “Unsupported” on Steam Deck because their “graphics setting cannot be configured to run well” on the hardware or because Valve is “still working on adding support for this game.” Despite warnings like these, games like Starfield, Silent Hill 2, and Assassin’s Creed Syndicate, to name just a few, all show extremely playable frame rates reported by actual Steam Deck users. Assassin’s Creed Syndicate in particular approaches a 60 FPS average on the Steam Deck OLED hardware despite its “Unsupported” status.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began working with a crisis communications firm known for handling public scandals a year before he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The firm, Heller, has handled Huang’s behind-the-scenes communications since at least October 2025, according to two sources familiar with the matter.
Risa Heller, the firm’s founder, has built a reputation as a fixer for powerful men facing allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies, according to a 2023 New York magazine profile. Her past clients and people who have sought her advice include former congressman Anthony Weiner, chef Mario Batali, and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller also handles corporate communications and issues unrelated to personal controversies for its clients.
Heller’s public relations consultants were initially believed to be hired for matters related to Huang’s personal life, including his family’s philanthropic endeavors, according to people familiar with the arrangement. The firm frequently communicated with Huang and his daughter Madison, a product marketing director at Nvidia who has become an increasingly prominent figure within the company, sources tell WIRED. It’s not clear whether Heller’s early work with the Huang family involved Huang’s affair.

In 2024, Huang began appearing in public with a woman who goes by Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed, according to The New York Times. Megaspeed was created when it split off from a Chinese gaming and cloud computing firm in 2023, a few months after the US government began restricting exports of advanced semiconductors to China, including those developed by Nvidia. A subsidiary of Megaspeed later became a major buyer of Nvidia chips.
In early October 2025, Jensen Huang’s business dealings with Megaspeed and his connection to Alice became public in a lengthy New York Times report, which alleged that the US Commerce Department was investigating whether the company was helping Chinese firms evade American export controls through its subsidiaries.
The report caused tensions to rise within Nvidia’s top ranks, and Jensen was rankled by the story, according to sources. By the end of that month, Nvidia’s internal communications teams had been instructed to include Heller’s firm on any press inquiries about Huang, whether personal or professional, according to people familiar with the matter.
When reached by email, a representative for Heller referred WIRED to Nvidia. Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
US intelligence officials have determined that Alice (who has no known relation to Jensen) is a spy working for the Chinese government, according to the Times. Nvidia initially said that Jensen’s interactions with Alice were part of routine business with clients. But on Sunday, Huang acknowledged that his relationship with her was romantic in nature. In an email to Nvidia staff, he said he owed them and his family an apology. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote.
Nvidia’s board of directors announced it is opening an independent investigation into Jensen’s activities. It said it has no reason to believe that national security or confidential Nvidia information has been compromised.
Before founding her firm, Risa Heller worked for Jane Harman, then a Democratic congresswoman from California, and later served as Democratic senator Chuck Schumer’s New York City press secretary. Nvidia’s head of public policy communications, John Rizzo, also previously worked for Schumer, serving as his deputy communications director.

Your iPhone Duo can do more than multitask! These 10 quirky apps turn the foldable into a retro computer, cassette player, Nintendo DS, accordion, instant camera, virtual fridge, and even a grilled cheese toaster. Some are free, others paid, but all make clever, fun use of its folding design.
The iPhone Duo is perhaps the most radically different iPhone since the original iPhone. While its arrival was rumored for over a year, Apple finally launched it this September. The phone can fold in half to become nearly passport-sized and can be unfolded to shape-shift into a bigger, tablet-ish smartphone. Ever since its launch, we have been constantly hearing about its multitasking prowess, its computer-like processing abilities, how well it handles productivity apps, yada yada yada…
But all this is pretty basic, something we expect with all new iPhones, or rather flagship smartphones at this point. With the kind of price and specs these high-end smartphones come with, it hardly is a surprise that they can handle power-hungry tasks with ease. The foldable form-factor and the added display real estate make it a different experience, surely. But surely there is way more to the device than the same old tasks and apps? So, we are on a mission to make your iPhone Duo fun, using all that processing and multitasking magic that it possesses.
The result is these ten apps.
They are not at all useful. But they make the Duo a-not-just-another-serious (read: boring) device out there. They add an element to it that we all so need to survive – they make it fun. Got an iPhone Duo? Download! (Note: relax, all of these are optimized for the iPhone Duo)
