Tiny Computer (USD 3.99): Unfolding Retro computer feels
Imagine getting a vintage PC feel on something as new and pristine as the iPhone Duo? That is exactly what the app Tiny Computer can deliver. Using the half-fold setting of the iPhone Duo, the app turns your phone into a proper vintage computer. The upper half of the screen becomes the display while the lower half becomes the keyboard. You get to choose from ten different computers in total, including the Apple Macintosh, IBM PC, iMac G3, IBM ThinkPad, Windows XP, Amiga 500, and more.
It is not just all show; you can actually use some retro paint apps, run old command-line interfaces, play games like Solitaire, and even type on clicky keyboards. Each machine also hides secret commands and files paired with occasional crashes to make the whole experience even more believable.
Deck Man (USD 4.99): Go cassette crazy!
Another app that brings retro feels to the Duo is the Deck Man. It is one of the most visually appealing apps for the Duo because it essentially turns your iPhone Duo into a 1980s cassette Walkman player. The app uses the unfolded version of the phone as the collection of cassettes in your music library that you can browse. You then “insert” the cassette of your choice into the deck, and once you fold it, the secondary screen mimics the look of a cassette Walkman player.
The app has realistic mechanical clicks, background tape static, and if you fast-forward or rewind it too aggressively, the virtual tape inside can get all tangled and then would have to be untangled manually, just like a retro cassette player. “Tape” this one to your Duo!
MD Vinyl (Free): Spin those discs!
If cassettes are “too” modern for you, then you can go even further back in the music era with the iPhone Duo by installing MD Vinyl. This essentially turns the Duo into a virtual turntable with spinning records and album art. The record design determines the aesthetics of the app. The app allows you to pick and drop the needle to play or pause the tracks. It can pair with music apps like Apple Music and Spotify. It is not a new app and has existed for years, but it attains a whole new dimension on the Duo, adding a vintage touch to the modern audio experience.
Fold Accordion (USD 2.99): Fold and unfold to create music
If there is one app that makes the most use of the iPhone Duo’s form factor, it is the Fold Accordion. It literally turns the hinge of the iPhone Duo into working accordion bellows. When you launch the app, it places the keys on the display, which you can press with your right hand while opening and closing the Duo with the left hand to create music of your own. The app comes with a learning mode which highlights keys you have to press to create something pleasant, instead of getting straight to the chaos of keys. A great way to test that folding mechanism too.
Delta (Nintendo DS) (free): Double screen gaming magic, DS style!
Popular Retro Game emulator Delta has launched an updated version of its app, specifically for the iPhone Duo. The app brings specially designed skins for the iPhone Duo, and the most interesting one of the lot is the Nintendo DS portable gaming console, which interestingly was the world’s first mainstream foldable device. The app uses the inner display of the iPhone Duo to bring a DS-style layout and controls across the displays. The game even enters sleep state when the device is folded, similar to the Nintendo DS. Trust the Duo to bring back the magic of double-screen gaming.
Toastie (USD 2.99): Smartest thing since sliced bread!
Unleash the inner chef in you with the absolutely useless but equally fun app called Toastie. This app turns the iPhone Duo into a – wait for it – virtual grilled cheese toaster. You get 15 seconds to assemble your sandwich, and once you are done, you have to hit the ‘grill’ button and physically close the iPhone Duo shut. You then have to wait, listen to the sizzle, or get a slight peek to ensure your toastie is grilling well. If you open the phone too soon, the cheese won’t be melted; if you wait too long, it might end up getting burned. Once you are done with it, you serve it, and you get a star based on your accuracy, recipe, timing, and so on. Useful? Not. But definitely the smartest thing since sliced bread. Actually, the smartest thing done to sliced bread!
TypeDraw (USD 4.99): Paper-like Moleskine
The iPhone Duo looks like a handy pocket notebook or a passport, and TypeDraw literally converts it into a handy little Moleskine-like notebook. It even comes with a digital thread, just like you find on a notebook, which you have to move or swipe aside to open the notebook (or just open the Duo). You can write anywhere on a page using an Apple Pencil or your finger and can even fiddle and curl up paper corners, as well as choose fonts (you can convert your handwriting into one, if you wish), types of paper, and even plain, ruled, dotted, or grid patterns on paper. And the page turns on the internal display are absolutely paper-like. It is like carrying a real notebook.
Snapshots ($1.99): Unfold to Polaroid
Snapshots is an app that helps your Duo morph into an instant camera. It is one of the very first community-developed apps optimized specifically for the iPhone Duo. When bent in half (90 degrees), the top half of the primary display becomes the viewfinder while the bottom half holds the controls. Once you hit the shutter, the photo captured on the upper half of the viewfinder is virtually printed on the lower half with the same mechanical sound and effect as on an instant camera. Just like with a real instant camera, the photo does not appear right away but takes a few seconds to develop, giving us those Polaroid feels.
Phridge (free): Chill…literally!
This is perhaps the most quirky and our personal favorite app in the list. It turns the iPhone Duo into a – wait for it – refrigerator. When folded, you can decorate the ‘door’ of this fridge with magnets, to-do lists, photographs. And when you open it, you can see groceries and food and drink inside and arrange them. This is when the real fun happens, because you can topple something over, drop a fizzy drink, or break a glass jar or bottle. You can also place your hand in a slingshot to shoot stones at the shelves, or get a sword to slice things in half, if you feel like some chaos. You can only close the fridge when you fold the phone shut, making the hinge integral to its operation. How cool is that? Just chillin…
Chompduo (Free): Jaw-dropping (and closing) stuff!
We all need an app that adds six hungry monsters to your iPhone Duo. Well, we do, anyway. That is exactly what ChompDuo does. When installed, it unleashes six hungry monsters on your Duo that open their huge mouths when the device is unfolded, making the inner display a giant mouth. You can tap on the open mouth to make it bite or drag it to squeeze it shut. When you fold the phone, the jaws close shut with a chomp sound, and a pair of googly eyes appear on the outer display, which can jump when you tap on them. What more does one need on a foldable?

The Enforcement Directorate (ED) conducted searches at three premises linked to crypto exchanges CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India (DEI) over alleged unauthorised cross-border transactions involving crypto derivatives and tokenised foreign stocks. In a statement, the agency said the searches were conducted between November 4 and November 5 across Bengaluru. The crypto trading transactions in question run into thousands of crores of Rupees, as per ED. “ED Bengaluru has conducted search(es) at three premises linked to Neblio Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (CoinDCX parent) and Excelium Technologies Pvt. Ltd.(which operates Delta Exchange India) under FEMA 1999 in the case of large scale unauthorised cross-border financial transactions involving crypto token derivatives and real world asset tokens,” said ED in a statement. As per the directorate, ED began its probe into the matter after receiving information of alleged forex violations by CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India. The agency alleged that CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India facilitated spot trading, futures and options (F&O) trading and trading in tokenised shares of foreign companies – all through cryptocurrencies. ED also claimed CoinDCX advertised these products despite not being authorised to offer them. While CoinDCX is yet to issue a statement on the matter, Delta Exchange India said that it cooperated “fully” with the officials and furnished the information sought. In a post on X, the crypto exchange further claimed that it is not involved in “any cross-border transfer of VDAs (virtual digital assets) in any form or manner”. “We acknowledge the Enforcement Directorate’s statement regarding their visit to our premises on 4th & 5th November… We cooperated fully with the officials and provided the information that they sought. We remain committed to extending our support and cooperation as may be required…,” said Delta Exchange India. CoinDCX's Alleged Modus Operandi According to the ED, user funds (deposited in Rupees) were allegedly converted into stablecoins, primarily USDT, and then transferred to overseas crypto platforms including Binance, KuCoin, Gate.io and Bybit. The agency alleged that these transfers circumvented forex rules governing cross-border money transfers. For spot trades, the ED alleged that CoinDCX used an account, opened in the name of a Costa Rica-based entity, to send the USDT to foreign crypto platforms. Describing the Costa Rican company as a mere “paper entity”, the agency alleged that the transactions were allegedly actually executed directly through CoinDCX APIs. The directorate also made similar allegations for CoinDCX’s F&O product. ED said that the homegrown platform allegedly opened matching positions via APIs on foreign platforms after users placed orders, with settlements occurring overseas when positions were closed. The ED also claimed that tokenised-stock trading on CoinDCX was routed through Hyperliquid, an overseas decentralised crypto trading platform. It said that user funds were converted into USDT to open positions, with settlements completed on the overseas platform. The alleged volumes of spot, derivatives and tokenised-stock transactions were described as running into thousands of crores of rupees. The ED also alleged that CoinDCX paid hundreds of crores in transaction fees to foreign platforms in stablecoins. This, the agency said, contravened forex rules. Delta Exchange India Under ED Radar Just like CoinDCX, the Enforcement Directorate also alleged that Delta Exchange India offered spot trading, crypto derivatives and tokenised foreign stocks via cryptocurrencies. It alleged that a large volume of DEI’s derivatives and tokenised-stock transactions was routed through CoinDCX, which in turn executed them on foreign platforms. The agency alleged that Delta Exchange India also transferred hundreds of crores of Rupees to overseas associate entities. These transfers are under investigation, added the ED. In a statement, the ED said the fintech products offered by both crypto exchanges appear to have prima facie contravened norms under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, the SEBI Act, 1992 and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The investigation remains ongoing. The searches are part of ED’s broader clampdown on forex violations involving crypto platforms. Just days ago, the directorate launched a probe into alleged FEMA violations involving crypto platforms Mudrex and Saber.money as well as decentralised finance (DeFi) protocol Instadapp and its associated platform, Fluid, over alleged unauthorised cross-border fund transfers worth more than ₹4,940 Cr. Prior to this in June this year, the ED had also searched six premises linked to five platforms, namely Transak, Carret, Xpat, Onramp.money and Onmeta, over alleged unauthorised cross-border crypto transfers.

Vote for your greatest all-British boxing fight
- Published
From bitter rivalries to controversial decisions and dramatic knockouts, British boxing has produced some unforgettable nights.
But which all-British fight staged on home soil stands above the rest?
With Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua just over a month away, Stacey Copeland will be joined by 5 Live boxing pundit Steve Bunce and esteemed boxing commentator Mike Costello on BBC Radio 5 Live at 19:30 GMT on Wednesday, 11 November to debate five of the greatest domestic contests.
Take a look at the five fights below and let us know which deserves top spot.
Have your say in our vote, which closes at 12:00 GMT on 11 November, at the bottom of the page. The results will be revealed during Wednesday's show.
Henry Cooper v Joe Bugner - March 1971
It was the end of an era when 21-year-old Joe Bugner faced British boxing favourite Henry Cooper at Wembley's Empire Pool. Cooper, affectionately known as 'Our 'Enry', was 36 and defending his British, European and Commonwealth heavyweight titles against a man 15 years his junior.
After 15 gruelling rounds, Bugner claimed a hugely controversial points victory by just a quarter of a point. The decision was met with boos from the crowd, while BBC commentator Harry Carpenter protested: "How can you take the man's three titles away like that?"
Cooper announced his retirement afterwards, with the result remaining one of the most fiercely debated in British boxing history.
Nigel Benn v Chris Eubank - November 1990
Few rivalries have captured the British public's imagination quite like Nigel Benn and Chris Eubank. The aggressive, hard-hitting Benn and flamboyant, outspoken Eubank were contrasting characters who shared a genuine dislike for one another.
Their first meeting at Birmingham's NEC lived up to the bitter build-up, with the pair trading punishing blows in a ferocious contest.
Benn was ahead on two scorecards when Eubank forced a dramatic ninth-round stoppage to claim the WBO middleweight title. The result launched one of British boxing's defining rivalries, with their 1993 rematch at Old Trafford ending in a draw.
Lennox Lewis v Frank Bruno - October 1993
It was a clash between two of Britain's biggest heavyweight stars, but Lennox Lewis and Frank Bruno arrived in Cardiff with contrasting reputations.
Bruno was a hugely popular figure still chasing his first world title, while Lewis, born in London but raised in Canada, was defending his WBC heavyweight crown.
Bruno made the stronger start and was ahead on one scorecard, with the other two level, before Lewis turned the contest around with a devastating left hook and a flurry of punches in the seventh round.
The victory cemented Lewis' status as world champion, while Bruno would have to wait another two years to finally fulfil his world title dream.
Carl Froch v George Groves - November 2013
Bad blood between Carl Froch and George Groves produced a sensational world super-middleweight title fight in Manchester, with the younger challenger determined to prove he belonged at the highest level.
Groves stunned the champion with a first-round knockdown and was ahead on all three scorecards before Froch fought back.
But referee Howard Foster's decision to stop the contest in the ninth round sparked outrage, with sections of the crowd booing and Groves insisting he had been robbed of victory.
The controversy only intensified their rivalry, setting up a blockbuster rematch at Wembley in front of 80,000 fans six months later.
Fabio Wardley v Daniel Dubois - May 2026
The most recent fight on the list was a remarkable display of heavyweight resilience at Manchester's Co-op Live arena.
Fabio Wardley, whose rise from white-collar boxing to world champion had captured the imagination, floored Daniel Dubois just 10 seconds into their WBO title contest and again in the third round.
But Dubois, whose determination had been questioned after previous defeats, produced an extraordinary comeback, repeatedly hurting a bloodied Wardley before forcing an 11th-round stoppage.
Promoter Frank Warren described it as the best heavyweight fight he had ever put on. The pair met again five months later, with Dubois winning a far more one-sided rematch in the second round.

Stephen Curry, Brandin Podziemski and Yaxel Lendeborg combined for 73 points to give Golden State Warriors its eighth straight win (Warriors 138, Pelicans 87) and cap a 6-0 homestand. The Warriors are the first team in NBA history to start a season 0-3 and then run off eight wins in succession.
Lendeborg, a rookie, had 16 of his 23 points and Podziemski 15 of his 25 in the first half. Curry wound up with 25 points as Golden State posted its fourth-largest winning margin in team history.
Derik Queen accumulated 16 points to go with three blocks for New Orleans, which elected to rest star big man Zion Williamson. The Pelicans have dropped three in a row. The defeat was just the second in New Orleans history by 50 or more points.
Spurs 112, Suns 96
Victor Wembanyama racked up 40 points, 11 rebounds and nine blocked shots in 25 minutes as visiting San Antonio routed Phoenix for its ninth straight win.
Wembanyama went 15 of 19 from the floor in the victory that kept the Spurs perfect on the road this season (5-0). Dylan Harper added 17 points, and Julian Champagnie contributed 11 points in a spot start for Devin Vassell (adductor).
Devin Booker put up 32 points to lead the Suns, who had a two-game winning streak snapped. Khaman Maluach added 11 points off the bench.
Mavericks 125, Pacers 122
Cooper Flagg scored 30 of his season-high 43 points in the second half, and Kyrie Irving added 35 as the Dallas Mavericks overturned a 13-point deficit to post a win over the visiting Indiana Pacers on Monday.
Flagg hit 16 of 25 from the floor and compiled 10 rebounds, six assists and three steals, while Irving drilled 7 of 10 3-point attempts.
Flagg, 19, became the second teenager to post a 40-10-5 game -- after Kevin Durant for the Seattle SuperSonics in the last game of the 2007-08 season.
Pascal Siakam scored 26 of his 29 points in the first half for Indiana and also recorded nine boards and eight assists. Indiana had the ball in the final seconds with a chance to tie, but Caleb Martin’s steal sealed the outcome.
Hornets 124, Cavaliers 112
Grayson Allen’s 27 points and Naz Reid’s 25 points and 13 rebounds carried Charlotte, which ended a six-game losing streak with a win over visiting Cleveland.
The Hornets shot 23-for-46 from 3-point range. Tidjane Salaun and Royce O’Neale, who scored 14 and 10 points, respectively, were part of the team’s 43-point bench production. Ryan Kalkbrenner’s 15 rebounds helped the Hornets control the boards 49-32.
Rookie Meleek Thomas led the Cavaliers with a season-high 18 points off the bench. Donovan Mitchell managed a season-low 11 points on 4-for-11 shooting.
Lakers 124, Hawks 114
Luka Doncic returned to the lineup and scored 32 points as Los Angeles extended its winning streak to six games with a victory at Atlanta.
Doncic missed the Lakers’ Sunday game against Detroit due to lower back tightness but came back to shoot 11-for-22 from the field while adding eight rebounds and 10 assists. The Lakers played without Austin Reaves (illness), who scored 43 points against the Pistons.
CJ McCollum came off the bench to score 21 for the Hawks, whose four-game winning streak ended. Nickeil Alexander-Walker put up 20 points.
Pistons 122, Wizards 111
John Collins had 24 points and 10 rebounds as host Detroit overcame a big performance from Anthony Davis and downed Washington, which has lost four straight.
Daniss Jenkins supplied 22 points, eight assists, six rebounds and four steals for the Pistons. Duncan Robinson also scored 22 points, while Cade Cunningham finished with 17 points and seven assists.
Davis, who had missed the Wizards’ previous two games with a right ankle sprain, poured in 44 points and grabbed 13 rebounds. Rookie AJ Dybantsa had 21 points and eight rebounds, while Trae Young contributed 20 points and seven assists.
Grizzlies 118, Raptors 102
Ty Jerome scored 27 points and made five 3-pointers to help Memphis snap a three-game losing streak and improve to 5-0 on the road. Cameron Boozer added 22 points, seven rebounds and eight assists for the Grizzlies, who shot 16-for-34 (47.1%) on 3-point attempts.
Jamal Shead led Toronto with 20 points and 11 assists, and RJ Barrett put up 19 points. The Raptors have dropped four of their past six.
Rockets 110, Nuggets 100
Kevin Durant and Alperen Sengun posted double-doubles as host Houston held off Denver to snap a two-game skid.
Durant finished with 23 points, 12 rebounds and eight assists, and Sengun added 20 points, 11 rebounds and eight assists. Jabari Smith Jr. finished with 14 points and seven rebounds.
Jamal Murray scored 15 of his game-high 38 points in the fourth quarter to lead the Nuggets, who had won four of their previous five games. Nikola Jokic added 25 points, a game-high 16 rebounds and nine assists.

Cardiologists have called for a review of a recent order issued by the Director General of Health Services (DGHS), strictly prohibiting the sterilisation and re-use of single-use devices and disposable surgical items used in critical specialties like cardiology and cardiothoracic and vascular surgery, citing issues of patient safety
At the annual conference of the Cardiological Society of India (CSI), Kerala chapter, here on Sunday, the CSI Kerala Chapter president Asokan P.K. said the association would seek a review of the order by DGHS as the exorbitant cost of medical devices and accessories would make crucial procedures such as angioplasty unaffordable and inaccessible to many.
Prathap Kumar N., organising chairman of the conference, said the rising cost of complex angioplasty, particularly procedures requiring multiple specialised devices, had become a major concern. Reimbursement package rates under government-funded health insurance schemes were often inadequate to cover the actual cost of advanced cardiac interventions.
With an increasing proportion of the population requiring advanced cardiac interventions, making complex procedures affordable to ordinary patients was a major challenge. Permitting the regulated re-use of select interventional devices, wherever scientifically proven safe, could help reduce treatment costs and extend the benefits of modern cardiac care to a wider section of the population, Dr. Prathap Kumar pointed out
He said cardiologists had sought a review to determine whether selected catheters, guidewires and other equipment could be safely re-processed under scientifically validated protocols and re-used for patients.
“Patient safety must remain paramount. Any proposal for re-use must be supported by scientific evidence, validated sterilisation, functional testing and strict regulatory oversight,” Dr. Prathap Kumar said.
He called for wider consultation among medical specialists, infection-control experts and regulatory authorities to develop an evidence-based policy regarding the sterilisation and re-use of medical devices, balancing affordability with patient safety.
The order by the DGHS said the practice of re-using single-use devices and disposable surgical items was a serious concern from the perspective of patient safety, infection prevention and control, regulatory compliance and healthcare expenditure. It said such re-use may also expose patients to significant risks, including cross-infection, device malfunction, loss of performance and other procedure-related complications
However, it is a fact that sterilisation and re-use of medical devices, ensuring the integrity of the devices and patient safety, is a common practice in both private and public sector hospitals across the country.
The Cardiological Society of India had in 2017 brought out a consensus document, “Guidance on reuse of cardio-vascular catheters and devices in India”, which clearly endorsed re-use, but set out certain requirements which had to be met for re-use to be safe and effective.
The devices, which can be reused, should be clearly defined, a meticulous process for disinfection and sterilisation followed and its functionality ascertained before use. Also, “an appropriate consent should be obtained where necessary” and the cost saving entailed should be directly passed on to the patient, the document said.
The CSI(K) conference also featured discussions on the evolving roles of drug-coated balloons and drug-eluting stents in coronary angioplasty, leadless pacemakers, laser-assisted coronary interventions, invasive coronary function testing, newer cholesterol-lowering therapies, complex valve procedures and advances in heart failure management.

Revised Maximum Retail Prices (MRPs) of 1,364 anti-cancer formulations have come into effect from Monday (November 9, 2026), a move projected to save consumers an estimated ₹3,540.38 crore annually, according to an official release.
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), functioning under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, capped trade margins on the MRP of 137 anti-cancer drugs based on recommendations submitted on October 17, 2026, by an Expert Committee constituted by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.
Also read | Cancer care: Long battle for affordable treatment
According to the Ministry, 85 pharmaceutical companies have reported revised MRPs for 1,364 anti-cancer formulations across 121 drugs as of November 8, 2026.
Price reductions of over 50% have been reported for 679 brands, with the highest price cut recorded at 96.45%, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers: Department of Pharmaceuticals said in the release.
The Ministry stated that no chemist or hospital pharmacy is permitted to charge more than the revised MRP.
Consumers can verify medicine rates via the revised MRP printed on packs, the 'Pharma Sahi Daam' mobile application, or the official NPPA website (nppa.gov.in), it said.
Consumers can lodge complaints against instances of overcharging or other pricing-related issues through the Pharma Jan Samadhan portal or contact the NPPA helpline at 1800-111-255, the release added.

India’s anaemia burden is not in doubt. The fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) found that more than half of women and about two-thirds of young children are anaemic. In this context, double-fortified salt (DFS) — fortified with iodine and iron — is often proposed as a potentially transformative solution. However, the case for DFS rests on convenience: everyone consumes salt, so why not add iron to it? But convenience is not efficacy, and a policy that asks the country to continue consuming salt to deliver iron deserves closer scrutiny.
Iron fortification of salt is a vehicle that cuts against public health. Indians consume, by most estimates, roughly twice the five grams of salt a day recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). About one in three adults has hypertension, and India’s own non-communicable disease (NCD) action plan commits to a 30% relative reduction in salt intake.

Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling
In northern Ethiopia, conflict pushes a strained healthcare system to the brink
"It was a mess, it was chaos, and that continued for almost seven, eight days. Without (cell) network, without electricity," recalls a surgeon in Ethiopia.
On September 24, a two-year ceasefire between rebels and the Ethiopian government began to collapse. As injured people streamed in from the countryside, this surgeon and his colleagues treated as many as they could at a hospital in Mekele, the capital city of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Fearing repercussions for treating rebel fighters, the surgeon asked NPR not to publish his name.
"The whole emergency (room) was flooded with war trauma patients," he recalls. "The floors were all filled up, there was no place to step."
For the past several weeks, the violence has continued at a steady pace, raising concerns that Ethiopia could again face a civil war. The Ethiopian military has accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of backing Tigrayan militants, who have aligned themselves with seven rebel groups in Ethiopia with the goal of ousting Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
After drone strikes in late October killed at least 15 people, including children, the director-general of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, posted on X that the violence in northern Ethiopia "is pushing an already fragile health system closer to collapse."
During the initial outbreak of violence in September, the surgeon in Tigray says he spent days operating on victims of gunfire, drone attacks, and mortar shells. Some were clearly civilians, but others were fighters in uniform. Complicating matters, he recalls, there was no way to know how many patients were coming because cell service and the internet were cut.
"We don't know where they're from — you just go ahead and do whatever you can, you know?" he told NPR.
There had been signs that the war between Ethiopia's federal government and rebel groups could reopen. In May, Tigrayan rebels ousted regional leaders and installed their own. In response, Ethiopia's federal government cut funds to Tigray — including to hospitals run by the regional administration. Doctors, he says, haven't been paid in months.
"It's an open wound, which was never closed, you know. Left for healing and never healed," he says. "I guess now it's infected."
For Tedros of WHO, the situation is deeply personal. He is Tigrayan and previously served as Ethiopia's minister of health. In his social media post, he wrote that hospitals are facing shortages of workers, medicine and ambulances, and that WHO and the U.N. are working to deliver medical supplies to the affected regions.
"As fighting continues, more people are likely to lose access to essential healthcare … civilians must be protected," Tedros wrote. "The most courageous choose peace."
A worldwide worry
Public health experts say targeted attacks on healthcare —– generally considered a war crime —– have become a growing concern in conflict zones around the world.
So far in 2026, attacks on health care facilities and workers in 19 countries led to more than 960 deaths, according to data collected by WHO. While the largest mass casualty event occurred in a Pakistani airstrike on a drug rehabilitation center in Afghanistan, hundreds of people have died in attacks on healthcare settings in Sudan, Lebanon, and Ukraine.
Complicating matters are funding cuts to global health initiatives, including the dismantling of USAID shortly after Donald Trump took office in 2025.
"The continual attack against healthcare is eroding the norm of healthcare being a protected part of conflict," says Lindsey Green, a researcher focused on Ethiopia for the U.S. nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights.
The Tigray war lasted two years, killing an estimated 600,000 people. The majority of Tigray's health facilities were only partially functional, as the Ethiopian government imposed an aid blockade on the region — home to more than 7 million people.
Attacks continued, despite a peace agreement
The government struck a peace agreement with Tigrayan rebels in 2022, ending most hostilities, but attacks on healthcare continued. In August of this year, Physicians for Human Rights worked with the Organization for Justice and Accountability in the Horn of Africa to publish a report detailing these attacks.
Of more than 600 health workers surveyed across three regions of northern Ethiopia, 63% reported attacks on ambulances, some as they tried to reach injured patients, and 57% reported witnessing an armed takeover of their clinic or hospital between 2020 and 2024. One health worker in Mekele recalled Ethiopian forces occupying a hospital and placing the uniforms of Tigrayan rebels on the floor and forcing staff to step on them. "Nonsense stuff," he said.
"Armed groups were occupying facilities to take resources or to destroy resources, to destroy machines and equipment, really with the goal of making healthcare harder to access," Green says.
In the report, researchers confirmed targeted attacks on health care workers perpetrated by both rebels and government forces – often as retribution for a community's perceived alliances or against doctors who treated an enemy. But there has been no way for victims to seek justice from either party.
"It's very clear that this ongoing pattern of attacks on healthcare links back to impunity for these violations," Green says.
NPR reached out to Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry and Office of the Prime Minister, but did not receive a response.
Doctors in northern Ethiopia say the one-two punch of a war that specifically targeted healthcare, followed by foreign aid cuts, have left the region without a chance to recover.
A health worker in Tigray counted more than 100 women who died in childbirth over the past year. He attributed their deaths to the dire state of the health system. He spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity, due to fear of being targeted for speaking out.
"They died during delivery because of a lack of medicine, lack of health care providers, a lack of fuel. So the ambulances are not functional," he said.
An independent review of birth data during the Tigray war from 2020 - 2022 showed that the maternal mortality rate per 100,000 live births increased fivefold, compared to prewar data. Researchers in 2022 found that 83% of clinics and hospitals were no longer able to serve pregnant women. Additionally, systemic rape and sexual violence were regularly used as a weapon of war.
"They told us, the people should be punished, because we are supporters of the TPLF (Tigrayan rebels)," the health worker says.
Ayoda Werede, a California-based physician with the nonprofit, Health Professionals for Tigray, says that since the latest outbreak of violence, the Ethiopian military has not targeted health centers. But other unidentified groups have stolen supplies, "including medication, equipment, even mattresses off of patient's beds," Werede says. "This was just the opportunistic vacuum space that was created because of this conflict."
Her fear is that Ethiopia's healthcare system is already stretched beyond its capacity — and as the conflict reignites, injured people will have nowhere to go. The surgeon in Mekele has similar concerns. Many of Tigray's doctors, he says, have already left the country.
"We've lost our sense of being secure," he says. "It's a repeat of what's happened in the past."
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

The claim referred to a segment from an extended interview with El-Sayed on "60 Minutes," available to view on YouTube. In it, El-Sayed was asked about parental control over education and the interviewer cited one example being the debate over transgender kids playing sports. In response, El-Sayed made the argument that rather than try to shield kids from things they may not understand, it is a parent’s job to guide them through it. There was no mention of locker rooms or male genitalia, nor was there evidence El-Sayed ever made such a statement.
Rumors that Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed allegedly said it was OK for girls or young women to see male genitals in their locker rooms because they could see them just as easily on the internet are circulating.
People on X shared a purported clip of an interview with El-Sayed, with one person claiming, "Abdul El Sayed just embroiled himself in national scandal by saying we should let girls see men in their locker room because they can SEE IT ANYWAY on the internet."
The claim, including different versions of supposed direct quotes from El-Sayed on the matter, circulated online in anticipation of the 2026 midterm elections, in which El-Sayed opposed Republican Mike Rogers.
Can someone please check his hard drive? 😳 "Your daughters are going to see male g***tals anyway…so who cares if they see it in their locker room…" -Abdul El Sayed
— Liz Churchill (@liz_churchill10) November 2, 2026
The clip shared with the claim was authentic, but the alleged quotes on the subject attributed to El-Sayed were fabricated. We reached out to El-Sayed to ask if the alleged quotes accurately reflected his views and will update this article if we hear back.
Neither the clip itself nor the full-length version of the same interview showed El-Sayed made the statement, and there was no evidence he ever made such a statement publicly.
Rather, those sharing the claim were hyperbolizing one of El-Sayed's responses during an interview on "60 Minutes."
On Nov. 1, "60 Minutes" aired a segment about the contentious Michigan Senate race between El-Sayed and Rogers that featured interviews with both candidates. The segment is available to watch on the "60 Minutes" YouTube channel, and a transcript of the segment that aired is available to read on CBS News.
"60 Minutes" also posted extended interviews with the candidates to the show's YouTube page.
Social media users twisted El-Sayed's response to the question at the 44:30 mark of his extended interview into the version of the claim that circulated on social media.
The response came during a conversation about the protection of rights, including rights to religious and sexual preferences, that some individuals might not understand.
Interviewer Ross Douthat asked El-Sayed:
What about the rights of parents to control over their children's education? Because a lot of places where there's tension between Islam and Muslim voters and what I'm calling cultural liberalism are around issues like what is taught in school, what happens with transgender kids on sports teams, and so on, right? These are places where rights are in conflict. What do you think happens there?
El-Sayed did not immediately address the transgender kids in sports specifically. Instead, he explained a broader approach to his thinking behind the issue:
You have a phone in your pocket. You can get access to anything and everything in the whole world. All the world's information in your pocket. The notion, somehow, that you are going to prevent your child from being exposed to something that you may find disagreeable, and that that is going to be because of school, is so profoundly outdated.
Because of course, you have all the information and they have all the information. So here's the thing about it. I think it's really important for us to recognize that the free flow of information is actually a beautiful thing. It's really important. And the most important thing you can do is not try to protect a person from seeing a thing, it's about trying to make sure that as you coach your kids through the world, that you are engaging with them and saying, "Here's what I believe. Here's what you may see in the world."
You get to make your choices about who you're going to be in the world, but that's going to require us to make do with the fact that the internet is a real thing and this debate about "what's taught in a classroom," I think, has been made intro a cultural flashpoint because a lot of the folks who want to make this a topic of conversation don't want to be talking about the real issues that we face in our lives.
It was this part of his response that critics on social media latched onto, turning it from a hypothetical conversation about fundamental rights to a made-up example about male genitals in girls' locker rooms, presumably in an attempt to extend his line of reasoning to that specific scenario despite him not doing so himself.
Regarding transgender kids in sports specifically, El-Sayed said:
A lot of the culture war issues that get fought right now are about trying to distract us from the fact that we can't afford our gas, can't afford our groceries, can't see a doctor, are worried about whether or not our kids are going to have a good life. And instead, we're out here talking about who gets to play what sport. Which should be a question for the people who govern sports. I'm not running to govern sports.
My interest is in making sure people have the ability to live a good life, that they can get the healthcare that they need. That they can breathe clean air, drink clean water. That they've got good schools are well-funded in the first place.
A comprehensive search of Bing, Google, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo about El-Sayed saying a statement such as the one in the claim yielded no credible results.
Given the tumultuous nature of the Michigan Senate race and the national attention it drew, had El-Sayed actually said the statement or one like it, major media outlets would have reported on it.
El-Sayed won election in Michigan on Nov. 3 and said during his victory speech of his opponent, "You chose hate and Michigan chose hope. May we never have to see the likes of you in this state again."

On 4 November 2026, the results of the 2026 US midterm elections were announced, with the Democratic Party winning a majority in the House of Representatives & the Senate. Against this background, a video is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows US President Donald Trump destroying his office following the Republican Party’s defeat in the 2026 US midterm elections. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals showing US President Trump vandalizing his office after the Republican Party’s defeat in the midterm elections of 2026.
Fact: We found no credible reports confirming such an incident. This is an AI-generated video by a creator named Iman Rus. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
We found no credible reports confirming such an incident. A reverse image search using keyframes led us to the original video, which was uploaded on 4 November 2026 by the Iranian Embassy in Lebanon on X. The video clearly carries the label “AI Generated” in the upper-right corner. It also credits the creator, Iman Rus, at the end.
A keyword search based on the information gathered above led us to the same video uploaded on the YouTube channel ‘Iman Rus’ on 4 November 2026. The video title clearly identifies it as AI-generated. Additionally, YouTube’s AI disclosure in the video also confirms that the content was created using AI.
We also analysed the viral video using AI detection tools, Hive AI and SynthID, both of which indicated the video was AI-generated.
To sum up, the viral video claiming that Trump vandalised his office following the Republican Party’s defeat is AI-generated.

There may be 200-300 people at National’s event in Auckland, but the mood is muted, with long stretches of near-silence as the results roll in.
National may scoop up more seats than Labour via an overhang – enough to nudge the coalition back into power. But the results are still precarious. A higher number of National-leaning seats have been counted early, with some Labour strongholds still to come through. Meanwhile, a number of National’s high profile MPs are at risk of not making it back into parliament on the list.
No one here is in celebration mode yet with the vote so tight.
Keep an eye on the inner Auckland suburb of Mt Albert.
It’s been held by two Labour prime ministers, Helen Clark and Jacinda Ardern, but Labour’s Helen White won it by only 20 votes in 2023.
This year, the Greens have been pushing hard as has Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong. That had Labour worried about a potential vote split allowing National’s Melissa Lee to come through the middle and claim the seat.
But so far, with 13% counted, White is ahead of Lee by 465 votes.
Who is the Opportunity Party, this year’s potential kingmaker?
Eva Corlett
Who is the Opportunity Party, this year’s potential kingmaker?
Opinion polls in the lead up the election showed the Opportunity party, led by businesswoman Qiulae Wong, 38, clearing the 5% threshold to become kingmaker.
The centrist minor party, whose policies include a land tax and a $370 a week universal basic income, says it is looking to “market-driven solutions” while being committed to a low-emission future and evidence-based policy.
Opportunity will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of votes.
However, Luxon has ruled out working with Opportunity numerous times, saying its proposed land tax runs contrary to National’s “no new taxes” pledge.
The media outlet Stuff, which is hosting a panel of pundits, has just said it is looking like Opportunity could hold the balance of power by the end of the night, given how things are currently trending.
For anyone tuning in who needs a refresher on the MMP electoral system, here goes:
MMP means voters are asked to vote twice – once for their preferred party and the second time for an electorate MP.
There is a single chamber of parliament which generally has 120 MPs. This is the overhang issue which I think we’re going to be talking about tonight as results come in.
Under MMP it is very uncommon for a single party to form a government.
If there is no majority winner, the major parties will start negotiations after the election and can either form a coalition or confidence-and-supply agreements with minor parties. The party with the largest number of votes does not necessarily win, and negotiations can take days or weeks.
Some senior National heavy hitters will, remarkably, be out of a job if National’s party vote goes badly tonight.
Those most at risk include:
Nicola Willis (finance minister), Chris Bishop (like Willis, is tipped as a potential future leader of the party), Paul Goldsmith (justice minister) and Gerry Brownlee (speaker of the house).
Some background: All the pre-election polls looked bad for any National MP who was relying on the list vote to return them to parliament; such as Willis and Brownlee, who are list-only candidates. Goldsmith (Epsom) and Bishop (Hutt South) are both engaged in tense, marginal electorate battles. If either loses, they are then reliant on winning via the list. We’ll be watching all this closely.
Some of the Labour party candidates are locked in neck and neck races, with tensions high for those at the Labour party event watching the candidates in Hutt South. With more than 20% of the vote counted, Labour’s Ginny Anderson has edged just ahead of the incumbent, National MP Chris Bishop, by just a handful of ballots.
Green MP Julie-Anne Genter is just holding off Labour challenger Craig Renney in Wellington North, while Labour’s Kieran McAnulty is winning against National’s Mike Butterick in Wairarapa.
Elsewhere in Wellington, Labour party MP Ayesha Verrall was hoping to win Wellington North off the incumbent Green MP Tamatha Paul, but early votes suggest this won’t be the case. Paul is leading comfortably, at almost twice Verrall’s count in an electorate where Green is also leading the party vote.
Another key feature of this election has been the possibility of an overhang - where a party wins more electorates than its share of the party vote.
If that occurs, more seats will be added to parliament to make up the difference and could dictate which coalition can form a government.
Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) has been calling on supporters to engineer an overhang for its party - by voting for its candidates in the Māori seats, and not giving them a party vote. This could benefit the left bloc.
Meanwhile, if National holds on to a good portion of its seats but its party vote falls short, that will give the party an edge to form a government but could see some of its most prominent MPs out of parliament.
Elsewhere in the Upper Hutt Cosmopolitan Club, punters were ordering crate bottles of local beer Tui and listening to a band kick up a rendition of Tennessee Whiskey.
For Hutt locals, the Cossie Club is a social hub; karaoke on Thursdays, Bingo on Sundays, and a jug of lager for $14 during happy hour.
While everyone spoken to by The Guardian voted for Hipkins in the Remutaka electorate – “he’s a local boy,” – party votes were otherwise split between Labour, the Opportunity party, and NZ First.
“I’ve always voted Labour, Chris knows that,” said Gladys Cooney, 96. “I haven’t heard anything from them this election, I don’t think anyone has gone deep enough.” The cost of living was appalling, she said. “Everything you touch has gone up.”
Fellow local Paul O’Riley also voted for Hipkins, but party voted NZ First. “I worked for 50 years in this country as a truck driver, Winston [Peters] does the most for us.”
Seven of the seats in New Zealand’s 120-seat parliamentare Māori electorates. Voters of Māori descent can choose to vote on the Māori roll – allowing them to vote for these seats – or the general roll. More than half of Māori voters are on the Māori roll.
They still get two votes; one for the electorate, and one for their preferred political party.
Last election, Te Pāti Māori won six of the seven seats. But internal turmoil has plagued the party since. Tonight, eyes will be on Te Tai Tokerau – covering the geographical area from New Zealand’s most northern point in Cape Reinga to West Auckland – where the Green’s candidate Hūhana Lyndon could help the party nab their first Māori seat.
Latest polls put her leading the race, followed by Labour’s Willow-Jean Prime and Te Pāti Māori candidate Aperahama Edwards.
Te Pāti Māori remain ahead in most other electorates, aside from Ikaroa-Rāwhiti and Te Tai Tonga (the biggest electorate, covering the entirety of the South Island and Stewart Island) where Labour candidates lead polling.
In an election night that has come down to Chris vs Chris, it’s important to know the difference.
Christopher Luxon, 56, the incumbent, leader of the National party and PM since 2023, is the former chief executive of the country’s national airline, Air New Zealand, and previously worked a slew of corporate jobs worldwide. He entered parliament in 2020, winning the Auckland electorate of Botany. A father-of-two, he is Christian but doesn’t discuss his faith, and has emphasised his business credentials — in 2023, his party was elected on its economic pledges.
Chris Hipkins, 48, the career politician who leads the center-left Labour party, is having a second crack at being PM tonight. Following the resignation of Jacinda Ardern in January 2023, Hipkins, also a father of two, took the reins for nine months ahead of that election, which his party lost. He’s held the Remutaka electorate in parliament since 2008. Some voters still associate him with Covid-19 and strict lockdown measures, while others connect with his pledges for better healthcare and improved cost of living.
National party faithful are starting to trickle into its event at the cavernous Viaduct Event Centre on Auckland’s waterfront. The room is awash in blue light.
People are grabbing drinks and milling around. The reaction is flicking between nervousness and excitement as the first numbers show the race is - as predicted - neck and neck.
As the first results of the night flashed up onto the big screen, Labour party volunteer Jasmine, 22, who works in the public service and didn’t want to use her last name, stopped talking mid-sentence.
A hush fell over the room as the first poll results show the main parties neck and neck . “That’s close,” she said, exhaling. “It’s great that Opportunity is over 5%, I’m happy about that. It’s just overwhelming; this is years of work, and that’s real numbers.” She’s been working for the party since she was 16.
Cheers are going up in the room as electorate results begin to come in. About 200 party supporters are expected here tonight.

Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don’t agree on why.
In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate.
The missing electrons
Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there’s these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said.
Over the decades, physicists have put forward two main competing explanations. The first hypothesizes that the electrons get stuck in some sort of structure. In this view, electrons freeze into patterns, such as charge density waves, and superconductivity develops separately. The alternative explanation tightly links this phenomenon to superconductivity. “Other people think they’re missing because they form pairs,” Allan said. Pairs of electrons, called Cooper pairs, are what carry current in a superconductor. If, as the material cools, these pairs appear before the material becomes superconducting, they would be a precondition of superconductivity, a waiting room of sorts, where pairs exist but can’t yet move together in lockstep.
Settling this proved extremely hard. “Lots of different experimental signatures are kind of lumped inside this,” Allan said. Different instruments all see something, but their readings, Allan said, are never conclusive. “It’s always something kind of incoherent, hard to grasp,” he said. What the researchers needed was a way to see pairs directly, and Allan and his colleagues figured it out.

“Before Tuesday, I would have not expected much activity in the 10 remaining states that have not expanded Medicaid,” KFF Executive Vice President for Health Policy Larry Levitt said, referring to the elections. “But I think that dynamic has changed.”

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
- Published
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.
Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."
After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.
But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry.
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.
Huang's position vulnerable unlike other tech bosses
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.
Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.
Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.
Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.
- What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy 
  - Published6 hours ago
Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.
Additional reporter by Samira Hussain, North America business correspondent.

Indian stockbrokers’ combined total active user base shrunk by 0.5% to 4.59 Cr in October, dropping from 4.61 Cr users in September. Despite the broader market plateau, user consolidation accelerated in favour of newer players. Groww continued to cement its market-leading position with 1.38 Cr active users in October, commanding a 30% market share. Notably, it added 3.04 Lakh users in the month, more than any other competitor in the top 10. To note, Groww’s net active client additions in October were approximately 1.5X the combined additions of the next four largest brokers by active client base, Angel One, Zerodha, ICICI Securities and Upstox, which collectively added around 2.02 lakh active clients. But the positions below saw an intriguing shakeup. Zerodha, after losing clients in many months over the past year, slipped from second place. Angel One overtook Zerodha, adding around 2.4 Lakh users to take its active user count to 69.99 Lakh and its market share to 15.3%. It grew at a 3.3% rate over the past month to overtake Zerodha. “During the quarter, Angel One acquired nearly 15 lakh new clients, up 11.6% from the previous quarter, taking its client base to 3.99 Cr by September before it crossed 4 Cr in October. Its wealth management business continued to scale, with assets under management rising 19.1% quarter-on-quarter and 160.5% year-on-year to ₹16,000 Cr,” the company said in a statement. Meanwhile, more than 32K users or around 0.5% of Zerodha’s active user base turned inactive over the previous month. It ended the month with 67.59 Lakh users, compared to 67.92 Lakh users in the previous month, although its market share remained nearly unchanged at 14.7%. ICICI Securities held its fourth place with 21.64 Lakh active users, adding 3.7 Lakh users in October to take its market share to 4.7% market share. In fifth place, Upstox shed 0.6% of its user base as the startup saw 11.3 Lakh users leave to bring its active user count down to 18.43 Lakh with a market share of just 4%. Kotak Securities occupied sixth position with 14.05 Lakh active users while HDFC Securities finished seventh with 13.61 Lakh active users. The two bank-linked brokerages grew their user base by 0.9% and 0.5% respectively. Meanwhile, Dhan, in eighth place, added nearly 26K users over the past, as its user base increased 2.3% to 11.47 Lakh from 11.21 Lakh in September. It was able to match Groww in terms of growth rate to become the second fastest growing brokerage among the top 10 after Angel One. SBI Securities lost the most users after Zerodha, with an exodus of 17K users or 1.7% of its user base. The retail stockbroking subsidiary of SBI Capital Markets saw its active user count decline to 10.04 Lakh compared to 10.21 Lakh in September. Rounding off the top 10, Motilal Oswal’s active user count grew 0.8% to 9.16 Lakh from 9.09 Lakh. Beyond the top 10, Sahi added 34,372 active clients during October, adding to its bid to solidify its name in the discount brokerage space. Markets Recover In The Month Of October October marked a modest recovery for Indian equities after September’s sharp correction, although foreign investor selling remained elevated. The Nifty 50 rose 2.81% while Sensex gained over 3%. The gains ended the benchmarks’ two-month losing streak, but the recovery was not broad-based, with mid- and small-cap stocks continuing to face pressure. As per data shared by Bajaj Broking, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) were net sellers of ₹45,162 Cr in October, while domestic institutional investors (DIIs) bought shares worth ₹62,220 Cr on a net basis. However, foreign selling eased in the second half of the month, with FPIs turning net buyers and investing ₹13,112 Cr between October 16 and 31, after pulling out nearly ₹47,955 Cr in the first fortnight. “Going ahead, the reversal in FII flows is an encouraging signal for sentiment, though elevated crude and global event risk could temper the momentum,” Pabitro Mukherjee, Deputy Vice President-Research, Bajaj Broking had noted.

Popular weight loss drugs including Ozempic and Wegovy will carry a new warning about a possible rare side effect that can sometimes lead to permanent vision loss, U.S. health regulators announced Monday, November 9, 2026.
The Food and Drug Administration said the risk will be added to the labelling of all GLP-1 drugs, the blockbuster medications used to treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The class includes a dozen injectable or pill-based drugs, including widely used brands like Zepbound and Mounjaro.
The eye condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, can cause significant vision loss. The problem, which has been reported with all GLP-1 drugs, is caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve, although the underlying cause isn't understood, the FDA said.
FDA scientists began looking into the problem after the publication of a 2024 medical paper tying the condition to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Eli Lilly's Ozempic.
An FDA analysis of more than 125 clinical trials found that the problem occurred in roughly 6 of every 100,000 patients who took a GLP-1 for at least one year. The comparable rate for people taking a placebo or other types of glucose-lowering medications was less than 4 per 100,000, the FDA said.
The agency also found reports of the problem in its electronic reporting system for drug injuries and side effects.
Symptoms of the problem include blurred vision, blind spots, distorted colors and other visual disturbances, according to the FDA. Patients experiencing such problems should contact a health care professional immediately, the agency said.
