Steven Tan walks along a narrow concourse in the Northern Leaf greenhouse in St Lawrence, Jersey, reading aloud the strains of his cannabis plants: Pink Gasoline, Moon Beam Gelato, Carbon Fibre, Gorilla Kush. Rows of plants stretch off into the distance. To the untrained eye, they look largely the same, with their distinctive jagged-edged, multi-fingered leaf shape and sticky buds like tiny pinecones.
But Tan, the CEO and director of medical cannabis manufacturer Northern Leaf, knows them intimately. “These plants are all different,” he says, stopping next to a mature Carbon Fibre specimen. “Just like humans.”
Northern Leaf is one of the largest licensed medical marijuana producers in Europe. Its 100,000-square-foot growing facility is based in Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands, located between England and France. Previously, this greenhouse was home to Jersey tomatoes, once a famed crop on the island that came close to extinction, thanks to growing fuel costs and cheaper competition from overseas. Now, it is fitted out with all of the technology required for cultivating cannabis that meets strict regulations for medical use, which include: automated irrigation, environmental monitoring, and air purification.
Despite being just 45 square miles in size, with a population of 100,000, Jersey—which lies 14 miles off the coast of the French mainland but is a British Crown Dependency—has emerged as an unlikely player in the medical cannabis industry. Although its total exports (over 9,200 kilograms in 2025) are small compared to UK growers, this represents an enormous amount per capita, and cannabis is fast becoming one of the island’s important new industries. Jersey’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, has previously said that he wants Jersey to be a “centre of excellence” for medical cannabis, and for cannabis production to become a mainstay of the island’s economy.
Currently, 90 percent of Jersey’s cannabis production comes from Northern Leaf. In 2025, the company exported £8.4 million ($11.3 million) worth of medical marijuana to markets including the UK and Germany (regulations mean it is only permitted to grow for export and cannot sell to customers in Jersey). Tan has much greater ambitions. He points to another famous Jersey export, Jersey Royal potatoes. “Jersey’s potato industry did £40 million in 2025,” he said. “I am already doing a quarter of the potato industry on 5 percent of the land. On 20 percent of the land, I could create an industry worth more than the potato industry. That is where it will get interesting.”
Born in Malaysia to a Chinese dad and Irish mother, Tan, 50, wanted to become a vet, but after graduating from university in 1998, ended up developing software for Citibank. He was making good money, but his heart wasn’t in finance. What really interested him was growing weed. “I loved the science of it, the genetics, the seeds, the smells,” Tan says.
The early 2000s were the perfect time for an inquisitive young business grad to get into the cannabis business. Across the world, governments were legalizing medical marijuana and moving towards decriminalization over draconian sentencing.
Tan began bouncing around jurisdictions that were relaxing laws on cannabis, working as a consultant in California, the Netherlands, and Canada. “I started to see these legal frameworks opening up. The minute they existed, I went there,” he says.
Jersey has a somewhat unique regulatory environment. As a Crown Dependency, it has close ties to Britain, but is not a part of the UK. Crucially, it is self-governing: It can make its own laws. Jersey’s main reputation today is as a tax haven, attracting some of the world’s wealthiest individuals and companies, thanks to its lack of capital gains tax and 0 percent corporation tax for most companies. Along its coastline, next to twee beachside cafes and Nazi bunkers (the Channel Islands were the only part of the British Isles to be occupied by Hitler’s forces in World War II), you can find offices of international banks and wealth management firms catering to the super rich.
Although traditionally culturally conservative, Jersey has become something of a trailblazer on cannabis. The island legalized medical cannabis in 2019. Today, five private clinics operate on the island. The latest figures suggest that 6 percent of the population is prescribed cannabis, compared to an estimated 0.4 percent in Germany and 0.1 percent in the UK. Upon legalization, the island’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, laid out ambitious plans for the island to become a hub of the medical cannabis trade, repurposing the horticultural facilities and know-how from its tomato-growing glory days for this new endeavor.
Tan joined Northern Leaf as CEO in 2024, when the company was in dire straits after a failed IPO. That year, it was valued at just £3.7 million, despite having spent as much as £30 million on its weed-growing facility.
Tan nevertheless saw a lot of potential, and over the last two years has seen capacity at the site increase from 25 percent to 75 percent. He believes the £8.4 million of product the company exported last year is just the beginning.
Sarah Clover, a barrister at Kings Chambers who works on cannabis licensing in Jersey, told WIRED the island’s advantage is hard to replicate. Growers are inspected by the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which is known for enforcing rigorous standards on quality. “Anybody buying from Jersey knows that the stuff coming out of it is absolutely gold standard, because the MHRA says it is,” she says. Permits, however, are handled by a small team on the island: “You can make an application for a permit on a Monday and get it on a Tuesday.”
Many within the Jersey medicinal cannabis industry now want to go beyond growing the raw ingredient and package it for export as a final product on the island. Northern Leaf already has the facilities to do so, but Jersey law dictates it can only export bulk amounts of raw cannabis for other companies to process and pack for distribution and sale. The company is waiting to see if Jersey will change its law. “At the minute we’re kind of on this seesaw—which way will the island go?” Clover says. “It could really take off here. Jersey could be a life sciences hub, not just for cannabis but for all sorts of pharmaceuticals.”
But running a cannabis business on a small island poses challenges, and not everyone is enthused about the idea of expansion. Tan has faced off against residents every time that the facility has expanded production. Some locals have complained that they can smell cannabis from their balconies. Others have linked the growing industry to concerns over misuse of cannabis on the island, despite the fact that all of its product is exported. Cannabis is a “contributory factor” in 22 percent of admissions to the island’s acute mental health ward, according to Jersey’s health minister.
One patient, Michael, told WIRED that he was prescribed medical cannabis for 18 months after having tried two other prescribed medications for insomnia and anxiety. “The initial assessment was simple. I had a meeting with the cannabis doctor who was pretty evangelical about its medicinal properties. They check your medical history with your GP, and within 10 days you’re good to go,” he says.
Michael was prescribed 30 grams a month of “unbelievably good” cannabis and told that if he ran out he could back and ask for more. “I stopped because it was seriously affecting my mental health [and] I have since seen a psychiatric professional who said I should never have been prescribed it given my documented mental health history,” he says.
Illegal resale of medical cannabis is also an issue, with a rise in so-called “user-dealers,” who sell their excess medical marijuana to others. Jersey Police told WIRED this “undermines the legal framework and creates opportunities for criminal supply.”
Overall, however, cannabis-related offenses have dropped since Jersey legalized medical cannabis in 2019—from 216 in 2016 to just 12, as of July 2026.
Tan is circumspect about the challenges of operating on Jersey. “Culturally, the people here are harder to convince about cannabis,” he says. “It’s an older society.” But after 25 years working in the industry, he’s used to the pushback.
“It’s a normal challenge,” he says. “And I think when anyone sits down and meets me, they understand. This isn’t a bunch of stoners growing a bit of weed in a plastic greenhouse.”
While Jersey’s medical cannabis industry grows, some people on the island want to go further. In 2024, a vote to decriminalize recreational cannabis was defeated by a single vote in the island’s parliament. When it was brought back for another vote by the island’s then health minister, it was withdrawn before it could be debated. It is expected to be brought back before the parliament in the coming months.
Some individuals on the island have decided not to wait. By exploiting a loophole in current laws, they have made Jersey one of the only places in Europe outside of Amsterdam where THC products can be purchased and consumed legally.
One morning in February 2024, Gary Tucker arrived at work, his weed shop in St Helier, Jersey, to find a dozen customs officers and the local media waiting outside. It was a raid—and not his first. The officers emptied shelves and boxes into bin bags. “They were literally running their arms down the shelves and putting everything into bags. They took everything,” Tucker, a California native and former analyst in the US Army, told WIRED.
Tucker operates outside of Jersey’s medical cannabis industry. His shop, Bailiwick Botanicals, sells products that are clearly recreational: hash cakes, gummies, and other snacks, all infused with tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the psychoactive ingredient in cannabis that gets you high and is heavily controlled.
He’s able to do this owing to a loophole in Jersey law which allows the sale of products containing CBD—another critical ingredient in cannabis, but one that doesn’t get you high. Jersey’s law says that the amount of THC in CBD products cannot exceed 3 percent of the weight of the CBD. So, if you want to sell products with high levels of THC, you just have to boost the CBD. “It’s just a math equation,” Tucker says.
Tucker admits it isn’t an ideal situation: studies suggest that ingesting high levels of CBD can cause liver damage. But he sees that as an issue with the regulation, not his solution. “I’m just following consumer demand,” he says.
Tucker is somewhat evangelical about the properties of cannabis. In his time as a weapons trainer for the military, he struggled with the mental health impacts of hearing that recruits he had trained had been killed in action. “I needed to step back from it. It started to really affect my mind,” Tucker says.
Veterans he knew were turning to cannabis, and Tucker began buying it on the black market. “It was the only thing that helped me,” he says. ”Cannabis gave me my life back.”
Tucker currently manufactures most of his products in the US before shipping them to Sark—a smaller Channel Island best known for having no cars and also its own government—and then to Jersey. New regulations in the US, however, mean Tucker may need to change his approach.
Tucker sees Jersey as a potential export hub for THC products to Europe. He believes Jersey’s budding weed industry should push beyond medical cannabis and into the recreational market. “This isn’t just a bunch of guys in a cellar somewhere. Not only does cannabis help people, but getting it to the shelf creates jobs. From the grower to the retailer. It permeates across all industries. We’re making cosmetics. We’re making gummies. We’re making drinks,” he says.
After the 2024 raid, Bailiwick Botanicals shut its doors for two weeks, and its full stock wasn’t returned until six months later. As of June 2026, Tucker and his team are selling THC-infused fudge, chocolate, and other sweets. His newest product, THC-infused coffee beans, is selling well. The police have stayed away.
In a written statement to WIRED, Jersey’s government said that the “possibility of abuse of our limits to get round the law in other jurisdictions is a matter of concern to the Government of Jersey and we are looking at ways to address it. Work is underway to consider whether Jersey’s existing legal exemptions for CBD products require amendment.”
For his part, Tan is reluctant to be drawn on his views on the so-called “rec” (recreational) market. For now, Jersey still has harsh sentencing rules on recreational cannabis use, with the penalties for possession and possession with intent to supply remaining up to five years and 14 years in jail, respectively. The proposed (and withdrawn) law to decriminalize cannabis notes that, the way the law is currently written, someone who rolled three joints and gave one to a friend would be guilty of supply and receive a criminal record. “Without change, people will continue receiving serious criminal records for small amounts … punishments [that] can result in additional harms greater than the drug itself,” it said.
While Jersey makes its own laws, however, it may not be able to completely legalize cannabis. Jersey is a signatory to the UN Convention on drugs control via the UK, and the UK Home Office would undoubtedly have a view if the island were to set itself up as an “Amsterdam on the Sea.” In 2022, an effort by the government of Bermuda (a British Overseas Territory) to legalize recreational cannabis was blocked after the UK withheld Royal Assent from the bill.
Back at the Northern Leaf warehouse in the Jersey parish of St Lawrence, Tan is flipping the lids off large boxes and rifling through clear plastic bags packed full of cannabis.
This is all weed that will not be sold, either because there were issues with production or the THC levels were too low. Instead, it is taken to a secure area of the facility where it is locked away in a reinforced armored vault. Specialist staff with bodycams take the bags to the island’s incinerator, where it is unceremoniously burned, as required by law.
Tan regularly makes a case to the government for changes to the law and support for the cannabis industry, such as an industrial energy tariff to help with spiraling energy costs.
He has claimed that Jersey could be home to “the Monsanto of cannabis,” alluding to the agricultural giant that was acquired by pharmaceutical company Bayer in 2018 for $66 billion. He’d like to get deeper into the genetics of cannabis, form a tissue-culture lab, and “bring out strains that nobody has ever seen.”
But speaking of himself, he references a different genre of business: He’s Willy Wonka, but for weed. Thirty years ago, when Tan quit corporate finance, his father warned him that he could make a lot more money if he stayed in banking. “And you know what, he was right,” he says. “But I would not have had nearly as much fun.”

Congress' parliamentary party chairperson and former president Sonia Gandhi has opened up about her life in her book, Belonging: A Journey of Love, which went on sale on Tuesday.
Published by HarperCollins in India, the memoir traces her journey from her childhood in post-war Italy to her eventual marriage to Rajiv Gandhi and rise in Indian politics.
In her book, Gandhi talks about why, despite immersing herself in the Indian way of life, she was hesitant to give up her Italian passport.
"Soon a new question arose from the changes in our lives: that of my nationality. I'd kept my Italian passport because it was the part of me that I brought to India, the Italy that my proud and patriotic father had fought for with his comrades. Also, I could visit my parents without filling in many forms, getting sponsorship letters, and so on. But my trips to Italy had become few and far between over time; I didn't relate to the way of life there anymore," she wrote.
Although Gandhi has not specified in her book the exact year in which she decided to renounce her Italian citizenship, ANI says it was 1983, as per the records.
She mentions in her book that once Rajiv Gandhi became the centre of attention after winning an election in 1981, it was fitting that she adopted India as her home, just as she had adapted to its culture, attire, food, and thinking.
"I could see my parents when they visited, and they had come to love India. My family, my friends were here. I had adopted Indian ways in my food and dress habits and in my way of thinking. It was my unquestioned world, and I felt rooted in it. I was, to all intents and purposes, Indian, and formal nationality seemed irrelevant. But now that Rajiv was in public life and had become the focus of attention, it seemed the right time to formalise things," she wrote while speaking of when she decided to get Indian citizenship.
Gandhi also talked about the moment an embassy officer spoke to her about the finality of the decision to renounce her Italian citizenship.
"After I’d filled up the requisite application forms, the procedure took place at the Italian ambassador’s residence. An embassy official handed me a document and directed me to peruse it and understand its contents fully, then read it out before him. In declaring that I was renouncing my nationality and surrendering my passport, in his words, 'I ought to be fully aware of the finality of the action' I was about to take," she wrote in the memoir.
She mentions how once she read the document aloud in front of the Italian ambassador, that a part of her identity, which she had carried to India from back home, was now gone.
"I was a bit taken aback by the emphatic, almost reproachful command of the official. I had taken the decision and was well aware of its meaning, I thought. But then, reading the words aloud before the ambassador, I experienced a strong emotion. My heart began to race, my face was burning, and I could barely hide my agitation. It felt very like the disquiet I’d experienced at the time of my wedding when I had to change my name and let go of one part of my identity. Now the little that had remained of it was going forever," she wrote.

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.
He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.
“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”
Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.
But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.
About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”
For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.
“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.
Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

As Delhiites burst firecrackers well past the 10 p.m. deadline set by the Supreme Court for Deepavali night, air pollution shot up to over 50 times World Health Organisation (WHO) limits in parts of the city, official data showed.
The level of PM2.5 (a major pollutant) in Akshardham was 760.99 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) data. This is about 50.73 times the WHO permissible limit of 15 micrograms per cubic meter for a 24-hour period.
Deepavali 2026: All you need to know about Supreme Court-permitted time slots, green crackers and other directives
PM2.5 (Particulate Matter 2.5) are fine inhalable particles, which can get into lungs and bloodstream and lead to a range of respiratory and other diseases.
The level of PM2.5 in Anand Vihar was 767 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per DPCC data — This is about 51.13 times the WHO permissible limit.
The level of PM2.5 in Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium was 702 micrograms per cubic meter, as per DPCC data, which is about 46.8 times the WHO permissible limit.
The overall air quality of Delhi continued to be in the “very poor” category while many parts of the city continued to reel under “severe” air quality.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

Quick commerce has tilted the balance for India's beauty and personal care (BPC) brands. So much so, that some brands are now entirely reliant on quick commerce for growth and reevaluating how much they should invest in horizontal marketplaces. At roughly $1 Bn in annualised gross merchandise value (GMV), sales of beauty products on quick commerce is growing by about 90% a year, according to Redseer. Separately, Elara Securities estimates the channel will grow to 25-30% of online BPC sales by FY30. Karan Taurani, executive vice president at Elara Capital, says that BPC as a category was a natural progression for quick commerce platforms after they had figured out the grocery supply chain. "Beauty has got a very premium gross margin, and higher EBITDA margin as compared to other categories.That is why quick commerce is also getting on this aggressively,” Taurani said. But while the balance is shifting, the contest between quick commerce and ecommerce marketplaces is far from settled. Marketplaces are still the biggest destinations for shoppers to compare, read reviews and discover new products, especially those with a premium price tag. But the likes of Nykaa, Myntra, Amazon and Flipkart are having to play the game started by Blinkit, Instamart and Zepto to catch up. For D2C brands, this is the time to recalibrate and optimise for both channels. From sizing their SKUs and dividing their marketing budgets to rethinking how shoppers find them, the brands Inc42 spoke to, are adapting to what they call a "tectonic shift" in consumer behaviour. And it all started after the sales on quick commerce channels zoomed over the last couple of years. How Brands Are Recalibrating It’s not that long ago that marketplaces ruled the market. "A year ago, they (quick commerce as a channel) didn't even exist for us. So it's growing very fast. Our largest channel used to be marketplaces, but that’s not the number one any more," skincare brand Asaya cofounder and CEO Neeraj Biyani. Others are reporting a similar boost from quick commerce as consumers splurged during the festive season. At haircare brand Moxie Beauty, whose annualised revenue had crossed ₹100 Cr last December, quick commerce is now the largest channel accounting for more than 30% of sales, cofounder Nikita Khanna told us. Renee Cosmetics, which reported ₹440 Cr in FY26 revenue, has seen quick commerce's share of sales grow from about 3% to over 13% in two years. Typsy Beauty, which raised ₹20 Cr in August to double down on quick commerce and offline retail, is also keeping up with the fast paced trend. "The biggest change has been quick commerce. A year ago it was a single-digit share of our revenue. Today, it has grown about 5x in absolute terms, faster than any other channel," Typsy cofounder and CEO Kairavi Bharat Ram said. That growth has pushed brands to rethink how much they spend on marketplaces vs quick commerce, when it comes to ads as well as in product development. Quick Commerce Gets The Ad Money As sales on quick commerce rose, brands have followed up by allocating more budget for visibility. The likes of Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart have reimagined placement of ads in a bid to grow their average order value and this means brands have more real estate to get that all-important click. "We are spending more on quick commerce since we are selling more on quick commerce. It's not that we spend more on ads and therefore that channel grows, it's that people are choosing to buy there. And so then you want to be easily found on the platform where they're going to be buying their hair care," added Moxie Beauty’s Khanna. Social media spending is still the largest part of ad spends, but At Typsy Beauty founder Bharat Ram believes the share going to quick commerce ads has risen through the year, following the shift in sales. The data also points to a change in how shoppers search. Volumes for 10 generic makeup keywords rose 236% on Blinkit between Q1 2025 and Q2 2026 and fell 76% on Amazon, though Amazon's volume still appears larger, according to a report by 1DigitalStack (1DS), which was accessed by Inc42. Quick commerce has not suddenly eliminated marketplace or social media ad costs, but it is becoming a dedicated channel by itself. Awareness is still built elsewhere. "Most new customers still find us on Instagram, through creator content and reels far more than polished brand ads. A lot of that discovery then converts somewhere else: someone sees a creator video and later searches for us on Nykaa, Blinkit or our website," says Bharat Ram. Brands Rethink Pricing, Packaging The second biggest learning for brands is to customise SKUs and pricing to suit the replenishment cycles and consumption patterns on quick commerce, which typically involves faster stockouts. These are somewhat interlinked because repricing is often forced by SKU resizing. "We realised that the typical consumer habit on quick commerce apps was not to buy full packs. Our product was usually a last minute purchase. Hence, we had curated special packs for Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart. And that really hit the spot,” Renee Cosmetics cofounder Ashutosh Valani said. Brands are also curating a combo of small and full size packs depending on the demand from each one of the quick commerce platforms even as some BPC startups say that it is too early a stage to go full throttle on producing small size SKUs across all quick commerce channels. "Eventually if you find something that works for you, you will continue to purchase that and you will want your regular size. So it's a very healthy mix,” according to Moxie Beauty’s cofounder. Founders like Asaya’s Biyani or Bharat Ram of Typsy Beauty warn that the biggest risk for a beauty brand on quick commerce is stockouts. A few days where the product is out of stock from key dark stores costs more than the lost sales. It hurts rank, visibility and results in poor return on advertising. "Replenishment cycles have gone from monthly to weekly and we had to move from warehouse-level planning to much more frequent, city and SKU-level planning for quick commerce. This requires tighter forecasting around platform sale events,” the Typsy founder said, indicating that brands have had to make changes in their own supply chain operations to meet the rush. Pricing and discount math is also undergoing a change. Quick commerce should not be necessarily regarded as a cheaper shelf, but it is true that brands encounter more value-conscious shoppers there. "We agree that value and entry price points gain on quick commerce. We see it less as people trading down and more as quick commerce being where a first try or a top-up happens," according to Typsy Beauty’s Bharat Ram. While the average order value may be smaller on quick commerce, the frequency of purchases makes up for that. Why Ecommerce Marketplaces Still Matter None of this has, however, made marketplaces optional. The majority of the founders we spoke to say that serious, intent-based shopping is still prevalent in ecommerce. Horizontal as well as vertical marketplaces enjoy a premiumisation moat which is not easy to displace. PAC Cosmetics, the self-funded makeup brand that crossed ₹100 Cr in FY26 revenue, has stayed off quick commerce thus far. "Consumers are evolving, and some of them choose convenience. But for an informed decision, many still prefer to see more in front of them: shades, swatches, reviews, and the full range. Staying off quick commerce is a conscious choice, because we'd rather present the brand with clarity than make it available quickly,” said founder and director Bonish Jain. Elara Capital’s Taurani highlighted that one of the reasons that Nykaa will be tough to beat is the exclusive tie-ups with the niche and international brands, which complements the company’s private label and owned brands business. Nykaa has also shifted to an inventory-led model, which allows the company more flexibility in negotiating procurement. "Marketplaces do have their own value. It is not like they can be completely replaced by quick commerce. If you are just looking for what to try, you will go to an Amazon or a Nykaa where you get to see the user experience and reviews, whereas this is not possible on quick commerce," Moxie Beauty's cofounder says. For the past two years, vertical and horizontal marketplaces have been gradually moving to the quick commerce lane, using the learnings of the industry to enable 10-minute deliveries. Nykaa has hired former Swiggy Instamart COO Ankit Jain to run Nykaa Now, which went to operate from three cities to 13 in a year. Myntra's M-Now, which runs in over 12 cities, now carries 596 beauty brands, while Flipkart says beauty on Flipkart Minutes grew 5X in a year. Taurani reads Nykaa Now as defence. "A Nykaa customer doesn't really want a quick delivery," he said, indicating that it is more of a need for marketplaces. Quick commerce, she said, lacks the depth of product content because it is a platform geared towards faster transactions and fulfilment. "The apps don't want you to get lost in the discovery. They want you to go from home to checkout in 60 seconds or whatever. So that kind of slower discovery, cart building is not happening there. And hence marketplace channels are still quite strong in our category,” Khanna told us. The early trends indicate that quick commerce and 10-minute delivery models have taken over the beauty aisle. But don’t write off the ‘plain jane’ ecommerce marketplace that may still have a trick or two up its sleeves. THE STARTUP SPOTLIGHT | HOW FORMIAL LABS IS TAKING THE GUESSWORK OUT OF SKINCARE Formial Labs aims to address the trial-and-error approach to skincare by offering customised formulations tailored to individual skin concerns, including acne, pigmentation and uneven skin texture. The startup combines dermatological expertise with personalised treatment plans, seeking to simplify skincare decisions and deliver more targeted solutions. As India's beauty market becomes increasingly crowded, Formial is betting on personalisation and professional guidance to differentiate itself from conventional skincare brands and build long-term consumer relationships. ECOMMERCE BUZZ Nykaa’s Q2 Profit More Than Triples: Beauty and fashion ecommerce major Nykaa reported a more than threefold jump in its Q2 profit to ₹101 Cr, while revenue grew 28% YoY. The strong performance reflects the company’s growing scale as it continues to expand its beauty and fashion businesses. Lenskart’s Q2 Profit Surges 125%: Eyewear major Lenskart reported a 125% YoY jump in Q2 profit to ₹233 Cr, while revenue climbed 36%. The numbers highlight the company’s improving profitability alongside its expanding eyewear business. GIVA Bags ₹975 Cr Funding: Jewellery startup GIVA raised ₹975 Cr in a funding round led by Multiples PE as it doubles down on offline expansion. The company plans to open 160 new stores in FY27, signalling its ambitions to scale its omnichannel jewellery business. Blue Ashva Exits iD Fresh In ₹50 Cr Deal: Early investor Blue Ashva Capital exited iD Fresh Food by selling its entire stake for ₹50 Cr in a secondary transaction. The deal, co-led by Upsurge India, Triumph Global Fund and White Whale Ventures, saw around 1% equity change hands as the ready-to-cook food brand continues its growth journey ahead of its IPO ambitions. THE DEEP DIVE THE OPERATOR QUESTION How Should Premium Beauty Brands Choose Between Marketplaces And Quick Commerce Without Compromising Their Positioning? Bonish Jain, founder and director at PAC Cosmetics which targets professional makeup artists and everyday consumers, says these are the five things that matter: Understand Purchase Behaviour: Not every beauty purchase is driven by convenience. Consumers buying foundations, concealers or setting sprays often want to compare shades, explore swatches, read reviews and understand product performance. The channel should support this decision-making process. Protect Positioning: Being available everywhere isn't always the right strategy. Quick commerce screens offer limited room to showcase an extensive portfolio or communicate the brand story. For premium brands, how products are presented matters as much as where they are sold. Look Beyond Transactions: Marketplaces are more than sales channels. They enable discovery, allowing consumers to explore different categories and products. Alongside influencers, makeup artists and tutorials, they help build brand presence, improve product visibility and strengthen consumer engagement. Evaluate Channel Economics: Every additional platform requires investment, inventory planning, marketing support and operational bandwidth. Assess the overall contribution of each channel, including opportunities to improve assortment, understand consumer preferences and strengthen platform partnerships. Prioritise Sustainable Growth: Focus on improving product discovery, online experiences and repeat engagement across existing channels. Evaluate new opportunities, including quick commerce, based on business potential, consumer needs and brand fit. Growth isn't about being present everywhere, but choosing platforms that support long-term scalability.

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.
- This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

Quick Answer
Samsung’s latest Galaxy Z Fold 8 ad mocks Apple’s iPhone Duo at a difficult time. Reports of cracked displays, long delivery delays, and missing features have raised concerns about Apple’s first foldable. With its reputation for hardware excellence at stake, Apple needs more than silence to restore confidence.
Believe it or not, Samsung might finally have landed an ad glove on Apple. While the two brands have been taking digs at each other for years, Apple has kept things subtle, while Samsung has never been shy about being more direct. So when Apple finally decided to join the foldable race with the iPhone Duo, it was hardly surprising to see Samsung going all out against its rival – from Apple’s late arrival to the foldable party, the Duo name, the features, the price, you name it, and Samsung probably has tried to make fun of it. But as in the past, these attempts seemed just that… attempts to ruffle a leading brand on a perceived weakness, and to reassure their own fanbase. But very recently, we think Samsung struck a bit of a serious nerve in the Apple nervous system.
The Samsung Z Fold 8 slices up an apple (no, really!)
Samsung released a 32-second video on Instagram that shows an apple (duh) with a “new” sticker on the open screen of the Galaxy Z Fold8. The phone folds, and the apple gets sliced. This slice rolls down the floor, through all the old versions of the Z Fold in the past to show how many foldables Samsung launched before Apple made its first.
The video also boasts about the Z Fold 8 being thinner and lighter than the iPhone Duo, all while comparing it to a slice of apple. This is not the most clever or cinematic Apple attack we have ever seen, but it is entertaining and thankfully is not over the top (unlike some others). What it also is, is a direct jab at something that Apple rarely has had to face – a perceived hardware problem with the iPhone.
iPhone Duo: from potential elixir to possible albatross
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, we thought it would be just the thing the foldables needed. Foldables have been a regular part of tech news and product portfolios since pre-COVID times (the first Galaxy Z Fold came in 2019), but even after years of iterations and multiple devices from multiple brands, the foldable segment was actually running out of steam.
So, when Apple launched the iPhone Duo, we thought that foldables would finally get some serious momentum. After all, once Apple launches something (even if it has been in the market for some time), it usually becomes more desirable and eminently “inspirational” for the competition: we have seen new features, specs, and design get picked up by the competition from Apple products, and become mainstream. From accepting touch to rejecting 3.5 mm audio jacks, it has all happened. So you could hardly blame many for thinking that Apple would launch a foldable phone, and voila! All foldable phones would start selling like hotcakes.
That scenario, however, does not seem to be playing out.
When Apple launched the iPhone Duo, the tech world went abuzz, which is business as usual when a new iPhone launches. But when the iPhone Duo became available for purchase, all the news that came in was not good. In many markets, due to supply and production issues, consumers had to wait for two months or more to get a device even after paying an advance. The brand’s decision to limit sales to two devices per person was also not well-received in some markets. It would have been understandable in the case of a new brand launching its first product, but from the first trillion-dollar company in the world, it just seemed unusually odd. The fact that it came with a super premium price tag did not help matters.
All those who have got their hands on Apple’s first foldable phone have not been thoroughly impressed with it either. There has been talk of users missing the speed and convenience of Face ID, the lack of app optimization, the new placement of the status bar, and more. And as if that were not enough, there was news that landed Apple in perhaps the hottest soup it has been in a very long time – reports have started coming in of the internal display cracking at the hinge, and a line of dead pixels appearing on it.
Often coming late to the party and rocking it…but perhaps not this time!
Once again, such problems from a new brand’s first product might have been treated with more patience. But imagine spending Rs. 2,99,900 and getting a device whose display has hardware issues. Imagine also being a person who has booked the device and is waiting for their unit, which is two months away. While Apple has acknowledged the issue, insisted that the issues exist in a small number of devices, and has assured users that all devices facing the issue will be replaced, a lot of damage has been done.
Apple’s reputation has, in some ways, worked against it. With Apple, the tech world has become accustomed to waiting for features, functions, and form factors that were seen on other devices. Android users have mocked Apple fans for getting the features that were on Android after years. But while Apple has delayed the addition of a feature or an entry into a segment, it has generally delivered an excellent performance. And that has been the defense of many Apple fans – Apple might not be the first to make a certain kind of device or bring a certain feature, but its implementation (whether it was capacitive touchscreens, Touch ID, App Store, and more) has been excellent and often an industry benchmark.
With Duo, that belief is being rocked. The brand has stepped into the foldable zone almost seven years after others, and launched a device with what seems to be a hardware flaw– not a software bug that can be fixed with an update, but a problem that can only be fixed with replacement.
Is silence golden for the communication wizard?
Apple’s handling of the issue so far has been a little unusual. The brand has found itself in trouble in the past as well with issues such as Antennagate and Bendgate, both of which generated a storm of criticism. But Apple officially addressed those issues publicly – Steve Jobs himself came out with an explanation in the case of the iPhone 4 when its stainless steel band interfered with the phone’s cellular performance, and the company also issued a very detailed statement on BendGate, famously pointing out that the issue had occurred with only nine users.
While there has not been radio silence from Apple with regard to Duo’s screen, no major management figure has come out to explain the issue or build back confidence – even in his first earnings call, new Apple CEO John Ternus limited himself to saying that while the issue existed, it affected a very small percentage of units. This relative silence could be (mis)interpreted by many in the public. To many, it does not seem as if the brand is working out solutions, as it has actually been launching devices left, right, and center since the Duo was launched.
To see management showcasing new products and talking of record earnings, even while complaints trickle in about a high-profile flagship does not make for great optics. We hope that changes soon, or alternatively, Apple comes out with a strong defense of its first foldable – it needs it. The longer it keeps silent, the more space it gives to its competitors to score points off its perceived weakness. And Apple cannot really afford to let cracks develop not just on the Duo, but in its own reputation for hardware excellence. As Samsung has shown, its competitors will not hang back in taking potshots at it. And unless credibly explained, these shots will start to hurt.
Given its potential and the hype around it, the Duo could still prove to be the elixir the foldable sector needs, but Apple needs to address the issues around it swiftly and effectively. This is a challenge unlike any other the brand has faced in recent times. Even the relative failure of the Vision Pro was more about a product being too futuristic (almost a prototype of sorts for an elite audience). The Duo, however, is supposed to redefine how we use foldables in particular and even smartphones in general. Many have even called it Apple’s most radical iPhone since the OG iPhone. How John Ternus tackles the issues surrounding the Duo could well define the tone of his tenure.

Greta Thunberg arrives at UN climate talks saying ‘everything we love is at stake’
Greta Thunberg has arrived at the U.N. climate meeting in Turkey, emphasizing the need to prioritize people and the planet over profits

Prominent climate change activist Greta Thunberg arrived Tuesday at the U.N. climate meeting, where she emphasized the need to protect people and the planet over profits and power.
This year's meeting — called the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes after a year of climate-induced heat waves and other disasters.
As she arrived at the meeting venue in Antalya, Turkey, Thunberg said climate change is “threatening everything" and that “everything and everyone we love is at stake.”
“We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she told reporters.
Thunberg is attending her first U.N. climate summit since she participated in the 2021 COP in Glasgow, Scotland, where she dismissed promises made by global leaders as “blah, blah, blah."
In 2024, Thunberg participated in a protest rally in Georgia against Azerbaijan hosting that year's climate talks. Thunberg accused Azerbaijan of using that summit to "greenwash their crimes and human rights abuses.”
Thunberg is expected to join this year's talks for a few days. She said structural changes are needed across the world to deal with the climate crisis because current political and economic systems “have become incompatible with human nature.”

IPO-bound hospitality chain PRISM, the parent entity of OYO, reported a consolidated profit after tax (PAT) of ₹353 Cr in the first quarter (Q1) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27), up 17.3% from ₹301 Cr in the year-ago period. According to PRISM’s audited financials seen by Inc42, the profitability came largely on the back of a deferred tax credit of nearly ₹244 Cr in the quarter under review. Nevertheless, PRISM continued to grow its top line and generated an operating revenue of ₹2,814 Cr in Q1 FY27. This was nearly 35% higher than ₹2,078 Cr reported in the year ago quarter. The IPO-bound startup also managed to improve its EBITDA by 24.3% to ₹760 Cr in the quarter under review as against ₹611 Cr in Q1 FY26. On the operational front, PRISM’s gross booking value (GBV) stood at nearly ₹9,600 Cr in the quarter ended June 2026, up nearly 30% from ₹7,408 Cr in Q1 FY26. This is largely in line with what PRISM founder and CEO Ritesh Agarwal had said during the company’s extraordinary general meeting (EGM) in October this year. “Our performance (in Q1 FY27) across segments on hotels or on vacation homes has demonstrated improving gross margins, higher operating earnings, even as we invest in expanding our brands and strengthening customer demand,” Agarwal had said then. During the EGM, Agarwal also attributed PRISM’s performance to investments made in technology, brands and distribution capabilities over the past few years. Founded in 2012 by Agarwal, OYO initially operated a budget hotel chain. It has since grown into a hospitality giant that offers holiday homes, coworking spaces, motels and corporate stays in more than 35 countries. The startup’s parent Oravel Stays rebranded to PRISM last year ahead of its initial public offering (IPO). The startup has raised about $3.5 Bn in funding to date and counts the likes of SoftBank, Lightspeed India, Peak XV Partners and Microsoft among its backers. The Q1 FY27 performance comes as PRISM is gearing up to list on the bourses. The hospitality giant first filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in December last year. It then received the market regulator’s approval for its IPO in June this year. Right after, the startup filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for a ₹6,650 Cr IPO, which will comprise entirely of a fresh issue of shares. The Ritesh Agarwal-led startup is said to be eyeing a valuation of $7 Bn to $8 Bn for the public issue.

“My recollection hasn’t changed,” said Mitchell Starc as he rejected former teammate Usman Khawaja’s assertions that the entire Australian team was a part of the 2018 Sandpapergate conspiracy even though only three players ended up being punished for the scandal.
In his soon-to-be-released book, Khawaja has said that then captain Steve Smith, vice captain David Warner and opener Cameron Bancroft were made scapegoats by the game’s administrators even though the entire team was aware of the plan to use sandpaper to alter the ball during the Cape Town Test against South Africa.
In addition to the one-year suspension from playing, Smith and Warner also copped leadership bans from Cricket Australia.
Starc, who was part of that team, said it was not his place to comment on the claims and he stands by a statement of innocence that he made in 2021.
“. . . I guess I won’t speak on behalf of the bowlers but where I stand, my opinion hasn’t changed, my recollection hasn’t changed from what we said in 2021,” Starc said referring to the joint statement he issued along with Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, and Nathan Lyon, denying prior knowledge of the plan.
“That’s obviously in a book. That’s for someone to explain further. As far as our statement said in 2021, we weren’t aware of things being taken on the field. That’s what we will leave it for. I haven’t really paid much attention to be fair,” he added.
Khawaja has found support from Warner, who has described his revelations as “100 per cent accurate”.
However, Cricket Australia has ruled out a fresh inquiry, insisting that there is no “compelling reason” to revisit the scandal that created an image crisis for game’s governing body in the country.

On 02 November 2026, three BSF personnel, including an Assistant Commandant, were injured after a group of people allegedly attacked them during an anti-smuggling operation in Ashabari, Boxanagar, Tripura. The attackers allegedly assaulted the personnel, damaged their vehicle, and snatched a service weapon. By 08 November 2026, police had arrested 21 people, including two key accused, Rabiul Hossain and Mahabul Hossain. Chief Minister Manik Saha also chaired a security review meeting and directed strict action against those involved. Subsequently, authorities launched land demarcation and ownership verification near the Ashabari Border Outpost, while security agencies intensified identity checks and patrols along the India-Bangladesh border (here, here, and here).
Following the incident, several videos are being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming to show BSF personnel retaliating against the attackers by identifying and assaulting them, along with bulldozer action against their properties. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The video shows BSF personnel in Tripura retaliating against those involved in the attack by assaulting them.
Fact: The videos do not show BSF personnel retaliating against those involved in the 2 November 2026 attack in Tripura. The first video dates back to a lathi charge during local election counting in Tripura’s Khowai district on 5 October 2026. The second shows police action against garment workers protesting in Mirpur, Bangladesh, on 1 November 2026. The third is from a protest against a proposed land port in Jaigaon-Gotibari, West Bengal, on 3 November 2026. The fourth shows an eviction drive in Baburhat, Chandpur, Bangladesh, during which illegal structures were demolished. None of these videos are related to the BSF attack in Ashabari, Tripura. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1 & 2
In our investigation, we found that the first video, which shows security personnel lathi-charging people as they run away, dates back to 5 October 2026. It shows an incident during the vote-counting process for local elections in Tripura’s Khowai district. According to local media reports (here, here), the video was recorded near a counting centre in the Champahawar area, where workers from several political parties had gathered to hear the Gram Sabha election results. Tensions escalated during the counting process, prompting security personnel to use lathis to disperse the crowd. One person reportedly died in the ensuing stampede.
The second video, which shows a man being assaulted by security personnel, is also unrelated to the BSF attack in Tripura. We found that it shows police chasing and assaulting garment workers during a protest in Mirpur, Dhaka, Bangladesh (here, here, and here). According to local media reports, garment workers in the Mirpur-10 and Mirpur-11 areas staged protests on 1 November 2026, demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka. Police used batons and tear gas to disperse the protesters, leading to clashes, stone-pelting, and chases between the two sides. A police vehicle was also reportedly set on fire near the Mirpur-11 metro station (here, here, and here).
Video 3
In our investigation, we found (here, here, and here) that the video is from a protest held in the Jaigaon-Gotibari area of Alipurduar district, West Bengal, on 03 November 2026. Local tribal residents were protesting against a proposed land port, demanding rehabilitation and compensation. The situation escalated when police arrived to clear the road blockade, resulting in clashes between the protesters and police. Following the incident, police arrested 11 people.
Video 4
In our investigation, we found that the video shows an eviction drive in Baburhat, Chandpur, Bangladesh, during which more than 200 illegal structures were demolished. According to media reports (here, here, and here), local authorities launched a joint eviction campaign to remove illegal structures along the Chandpur-Comilla highway, between Khajuria and Border Bazar. Officials had issued prior warnings and public announcements before carrying out the demolition drive, which was scheduled to continue for three days, with the possibility of extension. The Roads and Highways Department and district administration also planned to plant trees in the cleared areas and construct a dedicated traffic intersection to ease congestion. Police and administrative personnel were deployed to maintain law and order during the operation.
To sum up, unrelated videos are being shared showing BSF personnel retaliating against attackers in Tripura.
