The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 combines a stylish translucent design with smooth linear switches, a compact 75% layout, multi-device connectivity, and excellent battery life. It’s great for everyday typing, but limited customization, closely packed keys, and a premium price may put some buyers off.
ASUS has a wide range of product categories, and its mechanical keyboards are quite popular among gamers.
ASUS also offers standard mechanical keyboards for regular users. The company recently sent us its recently announced Jelly75 keyboard for review. It features a 75% layout, a unique translucent design, and multi-device connectivity. The keyboard also comes with a slightly higher price tag of Rs 7,999 (US $129.99)
I have been using this keyboard for the past several days, and in this review, you will learn everything about the keyboard, including the good and the bad things, and also learn if this Jelly75 keyboard is worth the price for what it offers.
Table of Contents
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Review: Design, Typing Experience, and Everyday Use
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Unboxing
You get a fairly simple package when you unbox the ASUS Jelly75 KD201. Inside, you find the keyboard, a USB-A to USB-C cable, a 2.4GHz wireless receiver, a quick start guide, and warranty documentation.
However, ASUS doesn’t provide a keycap puller or even a switch puller out of the box.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Design and Build Quality
The ASUS Jelly75 keyboard is available in two colors: Volt Green and Orange Meadow. I received the Volt Green variant of the Jelly75, which comes with a translucent chassis and a combination of white, black, and mint green keys. This color combination makes it very attractive for a vibrant and unique desktop setup.
If you don’t like contrasting looks, the Orange Meadow color variant, which offers muted colors and a retro-looking design, is the best choice, which I personally prefer.
But the Volt Green variant also looks good in person and stands out more than the regular black-and-white finishes on most mechanical keyboards.
The standout feature on both variants is the translucent design, so you can see parts of the internal keyboard structure through the casing.
However, the body and keys are made of polycarbonate, but it’s solidly built, and the weight adds extra rigidity.
The steel plate inside the keyboard adds to its weight, bringing it to about 1.19 kg.
While the weight helps the keyboard stay stable during typing, it can be inconvenient if you plan to carry it often.
Since the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard uses a 75% layout, it measures about 326.2 x 142.1 x 39.5 mm, which takes up less space than traditional full-size keypads but more than smaller percentage keypads.
If you are not familiar with keyboard percentages, here is a detailed visual guide we created to help you understand different keyboard layouts.
The keys are densely packed together, and there is not much space between them; also, there is no gap between functional keys and the regular keys, especially around the arrow key cluster, where, until you get used to this layout, there is a high chance that you can accidentally mispress the other keys.
Also, the keyboard doesn’t have any knobs, which would have been a nice addition for direct volume control. Additionally, the Caps Lock key doesn’t come with any light indication to show it’s active.
The rubber pads on the bottom help it stay stable and in place without sliding on a smooth desk surface.
The keyboard also comes with adjustable kickstands that let you set three typing-angle positions.
While the design is attractive, the translucent, lighter-colored keycaps make dirt more visible. It also supports a wireless receiver, but the keypad doesn’t have a dedicated compartment to store it, which is inconvenient, especially if you plan to carry it between workspaces. It won’t be much of a concern if you plan to connect it via Bluetooth, but it’s something you should know.
Continuing with the design, you will find the ASUS logo on the bottom right, a toggle to switch between connection types on the top, and a USB-C charging port on the top left.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Keyboard Layout and Ergonomics
The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 uses a 75% keyboard layout, which is a sweet spot between portability and functionality.
Unlike smaller 60% or 65% layouts, it includes a function row at the top and navigation keys on the right.
However, it doesn’t include a separate number pad, which full-size keyboards often have.
This compact layout has all essential keys and doesn’t miss anything, especially if you are coming from notebooks or a Mac.
This layout works for writing, programming, office work, and even standard gaming.
Although you get a dedicated number row below the function keys, a dedicated number pad is still more convenient, especially if your work involves entering numbers regularly.
However, the keys are densely packed, with negligible gaps between them.
ASUS has also included a dedicated Copilot key near the arrow key cluster, which could accidentally launch Windows Copilot, especially until you get used to this densely packed layout.
In terms of key design, ASUS used tall, squarish-rounded keycaps instead of the flatter options found on many keyboards.
While this makes them look unique, it may take time to get used to, especially if you are switching from a MacBook or another low-profile keyboard.
Since these keys are taller, I recommend a separate wrist rest, especially if you plan to use the keyboard lying flat.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Switches, Keycaps and Typing Experience
Typing experience is one of the most important things to consider when buying a mechanical keyboard, since you spend several hours every day writing, coding, or working on documents.
The ASUS Jelly75 comes with linear mechanical switches that offer 4mm of total key travel.
However, you won’t get tactile feedback when you press the keys. Unlike tactile switches, which have a noticeable bump when pressed, the Jelly75’s linear mechanism presses the keys gently, creating a smooth typing experience.
I personally prefer tactile feedback because I am used to my MacBook keyboard, but many also prefer smooth switches for longer typing sessions.
ASUS also rates the switches at 50 million keystrokes, which should last longer with regular use.
The keyboard also offers a gasket-mounted structure. ASUS calls it Uni-cushion technology, where it uses cushioning between the internal keyboard layout assembly and the outer body to help absorb vibrations.
This is especially useful if you press the keys harder, as the chassis absorbs vibration and stays steady overall.
The keycaps have a rigid feel. You won’t get rattling, wobbling, or uneven keypresses even on the larger keys like the spacebar.
As a mechanical keyboard, the ASUS Jelly75 offers hot-swappable switches, so you can remove and replace individual switches without soldering.
If you prefer tactile switches, you can also replace linear switches with tactile options.
However, ASUS doesn’t include a switch puller in the box, so you will need to buy it separately if you plan to swap the keys.
The ASUS Jelly75 keyboard comes with a white backlight instead of RGB backlighting. It keeps the keyboard looking cleaner.
You can adjust the white backlighting to four brightness levels using the dedicated keys on your keyboard, including Fn + F9 shortcuts.
You can also turn off the backlight completely, which can help extend battery life further.
However, the backlight illuminates the area around the keys and doesn’t illuminate the letters and symbols printed on the keys; instead, it glows around them.
This won’t be an issue if you are already used to this keyboard layout and type without looking at the keyboard, but if you look at the keys while typing, the lighting may not be as helpful in low light.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Connectivity and Multi-Device Switching
Another big advantage of the ASUS Jelly75 KD201 keyboard is its connectivity. If you use multiple devices, such as a Windows PC, MacBook, or iPad, you can connect this keyboard to all of them wirelessly and switch between them easily.
The Jelly75 keyboard supports three connectivity options: Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless, and a wired USB connection, and it can connect up to five devices using all three connection types.
The Jelly75 keyboard supports Bluetooth 3.0 and 5.0, and it can remember up to three Bluetooth devices.
To pair your devices, switch the keyboard to Bluetooth mode and hold Fn + 1, 2, or 3 for more than three seconds.
Once paired, you can easily switch between devices using the corresponding shortcuts.
You can pair up to three devices via Bluetooth. It also supports a 2.4 GHz wireless connection using the included USB receiver. ASUS says the wireless range is about 10 meters.
You can also connect the keyboard using the USB cable provided in the box.
The USB cable is long and suitable for any desktop layout, and its braided design lets you fold it easily and keeps it tngle-free.
However, as I said before, the main limitation is that it lacks a dedicated compartment for storing the 2.4GHz receiver if you plan to carry the keyboard between workplaces.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Customization
You won’t get much customization on the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard. Instead, ASUS kept it simple with a plug-and-play design.
It supports dedicated shortcuts to switch between Windows and MacBook layouts and offers several function-key shortcuts.
You can use Fn + F1, F2, and F3 to mute or adjust the volume, and F6-F8 to control music playback. It also includes shortcuts for switching between applications, searching, and launching Launchpad on macOS and Windows Search and Spotlight on macOS.
The keyboard also includes a dedicated Microsoft Copilot key, which lets you launch Copilot directly from your keyboard.
However, one noticeable downside is that, unlike other mechanical keyboards, it doesn’t include dedicated software for advanced key-mapping customization, so you can’t set custom shortcuts.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Battery Life
The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 has a 4000mAh rechargeable battery. ASUS rates the keyboard as lasting up to 8500 hours on a single charge with the backlight off, which translates to roughly 354 days.
It can last days without needing to charge. I used this keyboard with the backlight on throughout the entire two-week review period. I didn’t have to charge it once.
Regarding charging, the Jelly75 uses a USB-C port and includes a USB-A to USB-C cable in the box. It supports up to 5W charging. You can also charge the keyboard by connecting it directly to your device. It also includes a useful wired USB mode, which can be convenient if you suddenly run out of battery.
The keyboard uses battery light indicators to show the remaining battery. When the battery level drops to 20%, the status light slowly flashes red and reminds you to charge it. While charging, the indicator flashes, and when it’s fully charged, the light turns solid white. You can also check the remaining battery life in the Bluetooth settings for the connected device.
Asus MD105 Wireless Mouse Review
Along with the Jelly75 keyboard, ASUS also sent the MD105 wireless mouse, which pairs well with it. Interestingly, it comes in two color variants: Volt Green, which perfectly matches your keyboard if you picked up the Volt Green variant, and Milky White, which suits the Orange variant.
In terms of design, the MD105 mouse looks like a conventional mouse with a slightly wider body, and it comes with a dedicated thumb rest designed for right-hand users that offers great support, especially if you are a creator and plan to use the mouse for several hours a day.
It feels very light and weighs just 66 grams without a battery, and although it’s slightly wider, it isn’t as travel-friendly as other compact mice.
One feature I particularly like is the silent-click mechanism, which reduces clicking noise. This can be especially useful in shared offices and libraries, or when you’re working late at night.
The MD105 uses an optical sensor with three adjustable DPI settings, including 1200, 1600, and 2400. You can switch between them using the DPI button. Lower DPI settings offer more controlled cursor movement, while higher settings let you move the cursor faster.
For my big hands, the mouse feels perfectly compact, and my right finger rests comfortably on the support, making it comfortable to use.
Since it is lightweight, it is also quickly responsive and easy to move. For connectivity, the MD105 supports Bluetooth 5.0 and also offers 2.4 GHz wireless through the included USB receiver.
You can pair up to three devices: two via Bluetooth and one via the wireless receiver.
It also offers a wireless compartment in the mouse. If you are planning to use it with Bluetooth, you can safely store the wireless receiver in the compartment.
Since it supports multiple devices like the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard, it is also useful for switching between Windows and Mac computers.
A few months ago, I switched to a mouse with a built-in battery, but the MD105 comes with a single AA battery included in the box.
You need to replace it whenever you want, without waiting for the mouse to recharge. However, I prefer a rechargeable mouse, as mine also comes with a battery level indicator, so I can charge it.
If you can, this MD105 mouse suggests you need to keep an AA battery on hand in case it suddenly runs out of battery
The ASUS MD105 mouse is priced at Rs 1,699, which is a good value considering the ergonomics, comfort, and portability it offers.
It also has dedicated left-side switches for extra shortcuts, and its quiet operation, adjustable sensitivity, and multi-device connectivity make it a great buy if you are planning to get it alongside the Jelly75 keyboard.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Review Verdict
At Rs 8,999 (US$129.99), ASUS faces stiff competition from brands like AULA, Royal Kludge, and Keychron, which offer feature-packed mechanical keyboards with hot-swappable switches, RGB lighting, and dedicated volume knobs.
Some keyboards, like Royal Kludge, also offer a small dedicated display that shows useful information such as battery status and connection mode.
However, ASUS Jelly75 bets on its design, with colorful, translucent, rounded keycaps that make it one of the most distinctive-looking keyboards.
The gasket-mounted construction, linear switches, and multi-device connectivity also make it a great everyday companion with a simple plug-and-play device for a productive and attractive-looking desktop setup. However, if you want a fully customizable keyboard experience with a dedicated knob and customizable software, this might be a limitation.

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has warned of a potential increased risk of a rare eye condition that can cause sudden and permanent vision loss among patients taking glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) medications, widely used to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.
The condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), can cause sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye. The FDA said patients may experience acute vision impairment, including permanent vision loss, and urged those taking these medications to watch for symptoms.
Following a comprehensive safety review, the agency is requiring manufacturers of all GLP-1 RA medications to include information about the potential increased risk of NAION in the 'Warnings and Precautions' section of their product labels.
GLP-1 drugs mimic the action of a natural hormone released by the intestine. The hormone helps regulate blood sugar levels after meals and acts on parts of the brain responsible for controlling appetite and food intake.
These medications are widely prescribed to people with type 2 diabetes and those seeking to reduce excess body weight and maintain long-term weight loss. Certain drugs in the class are also approved to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events, including heart attacks, strokes and death, in eligible adults.
Other approved uses include reducing the risk of worsening kidney disease in certain patients with type 2 diabetes, treating moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnoea in adults with obesity, and treating metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) with moderate-to-advanced liver scarring.
NAION occurs when blood flow to the front portion of the optic nerve, known as the optic disc, is reduced. Although the exact underlying cause is not fully understood, the condition can lead to sudden vision impairment.
According to the FDA, symptoms may include sudden, painless vision loss in one eye, which patients may first notice upon waking up. Other warning signs include blurred vision, blind spots, tunnel vision, distortion of colours and reduced central visual sharpness, including hazy or blurry patches.
The agency has advised patients to contact their healthcare professionals immediately if they experience any of these symptoms.
Patients who have experienced a NAION event should discuss with their doctors whether to continue taking their GLP-1 RA medication or discontinue treatment.
The FDA's analysis of 126 randomised controlled clinical trials involving 134,253 participants found a higher incidence of NAION among patients treated with GLP-1 RAs compared with those receiving a placebo or other non-GLP-1 blood sugar-lowering medications.
The analysis identified 15 probable NAION cases, including 10 among GLP-1 RA users and five among patients receiving a placebo. No cases were identified among participants receiving other non-GLP-1 RA glucose-lowering medications.
The incidence rate was 6.4 cases per 100,000 person-years among GLP-1 RA users, compared with 3.8 cases per 100,000 person-years among those in the comparator group.
For context, the reported incidence of NAION in the general population is between 2.3 and 10.2 cases per 100,000 people annually among adults above the age of 50, based on published literature.
The FDA also conducted a retrospective study using its Sentinel Real-World Evidence Data Enterprise, examining adults with type 2 diabetes who started GLP-1 RAs or other commonly prescribed diabetes medications between 2019 and 2024.
The study found NAION incidence rates of 30-32 cases per 100,000 person-years among GLP-1 RA users, 31 among those taking SGLT-2 inhibitors and 26 among patients receiving DPP-4 inhibitors.
While the study did not find a statistically significant increase in NAION risk among GLP-1 RA users compared with SGLT-2 inhibitor users, it found an increased risk compared with patients taking DPP-4 inhibitors.
The FDA said NAION cases have been reported across all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products. It also noted that people with a history of NAION face an increased risk of recurrence, while those who have experienced the condition in one eye are at greater risk of developing it in the other eye.
Other potential risk factors include smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnoea, anaemia and kidney disease.
The agency has advised healthcare professionals to inform patients about the potential risk and instruct them to immediately report sudden, painless vision loss, visual field defects or other visual disturbances in one eye.
Doctors should promptly refer patients suspected of having NAION to an ophthalmologist for evaluation. They should also consider discontinuing GLP-1 RA treatment in patients who develop the condition, unless the benefits of continuing treatment clearly outweigh the risks.

Earlier this week, people began sharing a rumor claiming the U.S. Space Force took over the Federal Aviation Administration, including air traffic control.
For example, on Nov. 5, a Facebook user posted (archived) the rumor, alleging President Donald Trump and tech entrepreneur Elon Musk were taking the U.S. into World War III. That post read in part:
LOOKS LIKE TRUMP AND MUSK ARE STILL TRYING TO KILL US ALL WITH WW3! Look what just happened LAST NIGHT WHILE WE WERE SLEEPING! WE ARE NOT OUT OF THE WOODS YET WITH THESE CRAZY PSYCHOS! SPACE FORCE JUST TOOK OVER THE FAA. AIR TRAFFIC IS NOW MILITARY.
From Lisa Derry (link at the end of this quote):
The Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control system was transferred to the United States Space Force.
The corporate media is calling it a "temporary integration." A "national security precaution." A "seamless transition."
THEY ARE LYING TO YOU BECAUSE THE FAA WAS NEVER JUST ABOUT AIRPLANES.
What they are hiding in total panic: At exactly 01:00 AM Eastern this morning, the authority over every civilian air traffic control tower in the United States was transferred to Space Force Command. The transfer was signed at 11:47 PM the night before. It was not a budget decision. It was not a security review. It was a takeover.
No congressional hearing. No public announcement. No explanation.
THE SKIES ARE NOW MILITARY AIRSPACE.
Other users shared the same claim on Facebook (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived).
Snopes readers also emailed to inquire about the rumor. For example, one person asked, "Is this true? The Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control system was transferred to the United States Space Force."
Another reader sent, "This is going viral on the internet tonight. Is this true? The Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control system was transferred to the United States Space Force."
In sum, Snopes' research, as well as our correspondence with Air Force and FAA officials, confirmed this rumor was false.
An FAA spokesperson told Snopes via email, "There is absolutely no truth to this rumor." A Space Force spokesperson also said, "These claims are false." (The government organizes Space Force under the Air Force, though both are still considered separate branches of the Armed Forces.)
Searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo, as well as various social media platforms, found no news media outlets credibly reporting Space Force took over the FAA's air traffic control systems.
According to those same search engine queries, X user Mr. Pool, or @looP_rM_3117211, appeared to first post (archived) the fabricated story, minus the World War III mention, on Monday.
(Mr. Pool (@looP_rM_3117211) via X)
The same user, Mr. Pool, also recently shared other false- or unfounded-appearing stories also with the same writing structure resembling artificial intelligence-generated text, both on Telegram and X. For example, on Monday, the user falsely alleged a patent on a "suppressed" cancer cure from 1971 "just expired," adding that a "55-year cancer blockade" was "over."
We attempted to contact the X user, who is also on Telegram, to ask questions, including to confirm the user created the story and used AI to write it. We will update this article if we receive further details.
How we know it's written with AI
A scan of the post's full text with the Pangram AI detection tool returned a result reading, "100% of this text is AI," as well as, "We believe that this entire text is AI."
Snopes doesn't rely solely on AI detection tools to identify AI-produced content. Since some tools appear to vary in reliability, we consider the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging authenticity. For Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as criticisms of the tool.
Outside of AI detection tools, visible signs of AI included the tricolon writing style — which reports have said can be an indicator of AI writing — with the words, "No congressional hearing. No public announcement. No explanation."
Other signs of AI we observed included the post's full text featuring three bullet points with emojis, as well as the following dramatic, forward-thinking conclusion for which we've found AI tools seem to commonly generate:
You don't transfer the FAA to Space Force unless you are ready to take control of the entire airspace above the United States.
They told you the FAA was civilian. They called you crazy for questioning the transfer. They laughed when you said the sky was being militarized.
Look at the flight boards tonight. The planes are still flying. But the system that guides them is no longer civilian. The sky is not falling. It is being claimed.
The airspace was never yours. It was always theirs. And now it is being taken back.
For further reading, we previously reported whether Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired astronaut, said Trump forming the Space Force military branch was a dumb idea.

What to know about the presidential wiretapping scandal rocking Indonesia
- Published
Authorities are investigating possible treason in Indonesia after a bombshell announcement this week that President Prabowo Subianto's phone conversations might have been spied on.
Several senior figures of Prabowo's administration have been embroiled in the wiretapping scandal, including his chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - who is not related to the president despite his name.
It is unfolding against what many have interpreted as a widening rift between Prabowo and his predecessor, Joko Widodo - otherwise know as Jokowi - who had thrown his support behind Prabowo's 2024 presidential campaign.
"Listyo's position, as we know, is actually very close to Jokowi," Made Supriatma, a visiting fellow at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, told BBC Indonesian.
"So now it's practically said that they're going their separate ways."
What happened?
Listyo Sigit Prabowo, the president's chief of staff, was arrested on Tuesday along with two senior police officers for allegedly wiretapping President Prabowo.
The three men are suspected of keying phone numbers, including Prabowo's, into the police's official electronic surveillance system - which allows authorities to intercept communications - without following proper procedures, such as obtaining an investigation warrant or case report.
Authorities say the operation was discovered last week after a tip-off from a police officer. But they believe the alleged wiretapping stretches back to 2025, when Listyo was serving as the national police chief.
This could amount to treason, as it involved "sensitive information" that could "endanger the interests and sovereignty of the nation", a spokesperson for the president told reporters on Wednesday.
In Indonesia, treason is punishable by life imprisonment or even the death penalty - though the country has not executed anyone in a decade.
The spokesperson said the motive behind the alleged wiretapping remained unclear.
It was not just President Prabowo who was targeted in the alleged wiretapping operation, either. Other targets included politicians, journalists, NGO representatives and businesspeople, authorities said.
On Thursday evening, police named a fourth suspect: Slamet Uliandi, from the national police criminal investigation unit. But he was not detained due to his ill health after suffering a stroke, according to authorities.
Listyo, who was appointed the president's chief of staff last month, was sacked from his new position shortly after his arrest.
This is not the first wiretapping scandal to have involved Indonesia's leaders. In 2014, several wiretapping devices were discovered at Jokowi's official residence when he was the governor of Jakarta. Former president Megawati Soekarnoputri claimed in 2024 that she had avoided using her personal mobile phone number because she was the target of wiretapping.
Indonesia's police chief Suyudi Ario Seto told reporters on Thursday that the probe into wiretapping was "purely law enforcement and has nothing to do with rivalries or anything else".
But many see it as the latest blow in a disintegrating alliance between President Prabowo and former president Jokowi, who led the country from 2014 to 2024.
Prabowo vs Jokowi
Jokowi had thrown his support behind Prabowo in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, as part of an alliance that ultimately propelled Prabowo to become Indonesia's next leader.
Riding to victory with him was Gibran Rakabuming Raka, Jokowi's eldest son, who became Indonesia's vice president.
Two years on, that alliance appears to be fracturing - even if neither party has confirmed the rift.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many of Jokowi's allies into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Meanwhile, uncertainty also looms over Gibran, Jokowi's son, who is mired in a growing controversy over the validity of his high school credentials, a pre-requisite to run for vice presidency. He now faces calls to be disqualified from his job, on the grounds that he should not have been eligible as a candidate.
The wiretapping scandal and subsequent arrest of Listyo - who rose to the top of the police force in Jokowi's administration, and is seen as one of the ex-president's longtime allies - is now adding to the tensions between Prabowo and Jokowi.
When asked about the wiretapping incident after the court session on Thursday, Jokowi told reporters that "we should all respect the ongoing legal process".
This latest scandal comes during a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. His flagship free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
Experts, meanwhile, say all this has distracted from the more pressing challenges that Indonesians are facing on the ground - from economic uncertainties to environmental pollution.
In recent months, protesters have taken to the streets to pressure the government on a range of issues such as toxic wildfire haze, corruption, and cost-of-living woes.
"It's like we're living in a country on autopilot," Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Indonesia, told BBC Indonesian.
"Because the way the government operates proves that it's not the people's interests that are being pursued, but rather the interests of individual groups."

More than a decade ago, Peak Design rethought the humble camera strap. This was a necessary development. When you buy a camera, manufacturers almost always toss in a chintzy, uninspired strap with their logo on it. These cheap straps have cheap mounting systems that make it hard to quickly remove the strap from the camera when you need to, like when you're attaching your camera to a tripod or gimbal and you’d rather not have a dangling strap whacking you in the face.
Peak Design solved this with its Anchor Links system, small circular nubs you leave attached to camera eyelets that make detaching or even swapping straps easy. The quick-connect mechanism is now the de facto industry standard and has inspired countless copycats.
Now, Wandrd has outdone that design using magnets.
“We're photographers ourselves, so we're constantly ideating, tinkering, thinking of ways that things can be better,” Ryan Cope, Wandrd cofounder, tells WIRED. “A camera strap like this has been at the back of our minds for a while.”
Wandrd—known for its camera bags—launched its Magnetic Camera Strap system on Thursday. It features a circular anchor similar to Peak Design, called “Torus Links.” The anchors attach to your camera’s eyelets and are rated to carry up to 198 pounds—so unless you're bench-pressing your camera, they'll do the job. If the cord does start to wear down over time, you'll first see yellow under the black fabric—a sign you should replace the Torus Link. If it's red, you should stop using the link immediately—a warning system borrowed from Peak Design. (Wandrd offers a two-year warranty.)
Unlike Peak Design's anchors, the Wandrd anchors look like donuts, with a hole in the middle. When you attach the strap, the embedded magnets guide the Torus Link into the strap's CoreLock mechanism, which pinches into the hole to secure the camera body. The magnets make connecting a strap easier, and they keep the strap fastened to the anchor, but you can’t just pull the strap off like you’re pulling a MagSafe accessory on your phone. You’ll need to use the strap’s dual-pinch mechanism to remove it from the Torus Link, a design that’s more secure.
It’s a much faster way to connect and disconnect a strap, and that speed pays off in the field. This week, I had to photograph a product during a press briefing. Usually, I use Peak Design's Leash and, instead of taking off the strap, I bunch it up in my hand when it's not around my neck. It's not that it's hard to remove—it's just an extra step I have to think about. But Wandrd's magnetic system felt faster to unlock mid-shoot when I wanted to lower the camera for an awkward, low-angle shot, and reattaching the strap was practically instantaneous. I did the whole swap one-handed, with the magnets doing most of the work.
“I love magnets, man,” Cope says. “I love the simplicity they create—guiding things into place. You don't always have a place to put your camera down; I like that magnets help guide them and are a lot more secure, and they're also just fun.”
I have two Torus Links on my camera body, one on the right eyelet and another on the tripod baseplate. But my favorite configuration turns the strap into a single-point sling. The strap has a built-in “Torus Loop” on the buckle—clip one end directly into it to create a closed loop worn across your torso, leaving just a single magnetic connector to snap onto your camera. When you unclip the camera to shoot freely, the strap stays neatly in place across your body instead of sliding off your shoulder.
The nylon felt comfortable across my chest and near my neck—there's no padding, but that's intentional. Cope says Wandrd spent two years developing this custom “liquid nylon” tubular webbing that is softer along the edges, so it won't feel like the strap is cutting into your neck after a long day of wear. The lack of metal throughout the strap system also prevents the strap from scratching up your camera gear.
Best of all, you don't have to replace your strap to use Wandrd's system. If you have a strap you love—maybe a fancy leather strap someone gifted you—Wandrd is selling a DIY kit ($29) that lets you attach its Magnetic CoreLock system to the ends of your preferred strap. Otherwise, the strap kit comes in a 30-mm size ($69), a 15-mm “Lite" ($49), and a wrist strap ($39).
I don't know if Wandrd's system will see the same success as Peak Design's Anchor Links, but I don't see myself switching back anytime soon. Magnets are just too dang cool.

France accuses Iran of cyber 'sabotage' in fridge attacks
France is accusing Iran of having launched a series of destructive cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure in October.
According to the French National Cybersecurity Agency, ANSSI, Iranian military hackers took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites in France, from supermarkets to butcher shops, turning up the temperature in the middle of the night and spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.
They also targeted several small hydroelectric power plants, resulting in "moderate effects," wrote ANSSI in its press release.
The hacking campaign was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," said French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot. He said it "marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people."
The Paris Prosecutor's Office has opened its own investigation into the Iranian cyber unit, Shahid Kaveh, which the French government is linking to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. "The Paris Public Prosecutor's Office is requesting the issuance of international arrest warrants," the office said in a statement.
A trend of attacks on refrigeration systems
The attacks on French industrial controllers are part of a larger trend. In 2026 alone, hackers have targeted refrigeration controllers from Europe to Israel and the United States.
Grocery stores in European countries including Sweden and Ireland were hit in similar attacks last week.
In a separate incident in France, employees at a major French blood bank had to act fast to save blood samples from heating up when their refrigeration system was hit last week, prompting international calls for the health sector to protect its lifesaving products from spoiling.
In Israel in the spring, suspected Iranian hackers going by the name of "Cyber Isnaad Front" claimed responsibility for sabotaging an industrial food processing plant, including infecting its corporate computers with malware, taking over office printers to print out threatening messages and hacking office cameras for use in a propaganda video released in early October. That video included a taunt in French referencing ongoing education-related protests, and came just before the attacks on French supermarket fridges. Cyber incident response firm Profero attributed the Israel attack to a wing of Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Over the summer, commissaries on U.S. military bases also went through something similar, when food spoiled after the temperature shot up inside refrigerators and freezers overnight.
The French government is the first to formally assign blame for the wave of destructive attacks.
They were able to identify the hackers through a series of digital clues, including digital infrastructure used by the hackers, connection to a propaganda outlet, and "traces" of the use of Farsi language in the attack, according to ANSSI.
While NPR and others have reported that U.S. officials suspect Iran may have been behind the attacks on U.S. military bases in August, the Pentagon has not made any official statement, even to conclude that the disruptions were in fact the result of a cyberattack.
"Consistent with our policy and to preserve the integrity of the process, the DOD [Office of Inspector General] Criminal Investigative Service does not discuss ongoing investigations," Mollie Halpern, a spokesperson for the Department of War Office of the Inspector General wrote in an email to NPR.
Attacks fit Iranian hackers' modus operandi
If Iranian hackers are behind the attacks across Europe, the U.S. and Israel, cybersecurity experts say that would fit with what they know about Iranian hackers' strategy and goals.
"Iran's cyberattacks against refrigeration systems likely represents the IRGC attempting to reassert Iranian power abroad through both physically and psychologically disruptive operations," Alex Orleans, the head of threat intelligence at cybersecurity firm Sublime Security, told NPR. "Such activities continue to provide tangible and cost-effect results given how Iran's national resources remain tied down in the war."
"Also, Shahid Kaveh, the IRGC cyber unit that the French specifically attributed the disruptive attacks to, is repeating a pattern here," Orleans says. He referenced a series of cyberattacks on American water treatment plants in August, which most experts believe were linked to Iran, as precedent. The U.S. government has still not officially attributed those attacks.
"This unit has once again refined its tradecraft through attacks on Israeli targets before shifting their targeting to the same systems in the West," Orleans says.
For those tracking Shahid Kaveh and the other Iranian cyber units that operate alongside it, these attacks fit squarely into their modus operandi.
"Shahid Kaveh group is an offensive cyber unit responsible for some of the greatest hits of Iranian offensive cyber [operations]," says Ari Ben Am, an adjunct fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies' Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation.
One group tied to Shahid Kaveh is the Cyber Av3ngers, he explains, which the U.S. government linked to cyberattacks on Israeli-made systems in U.S. water treatment facilities in the winter between 2023 and 2024. The French government also cited other cyberattacks carried out on behalf of the IRGC against French interests, including against the satirical French magazine Charlie Hebdo and another against digital kiosks used at the Paris Olympics in 2024.
Challenges in securing operational technology
Cybersecurity experts say the attacks on refrigeration controllers have highlighted a yearslong difficulty with securing operational technology, the machines that control physical processes in the real world — from water pumps to cooling systems.
These machines are often outdated and riddled with vulnerabilities, and are very difficult to patch because operators can't afford to shut them down and disrupt critical services including healthcare and transportation. Additionally, the machines are often left exposed to the open internet — often at least in part due to contractual requirements with vendors that want to maintain those systems remotely. That combination of factors makes it a complicated problem to solve.
Iran has yet to respond to the accusations. However, Monday's accusation by the French government may lead other affected countries to take action as well.
During Monday's G7 meeting in Paris, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked by journalists whether the U.S. shared information with the French to help with their attribution of the Iranian hacks. Rubio said he couldn't comment, but noted that the "French are quite capable."
"What kind of sickos are these people?" he asked. "They attack refrigerators. France is not even involved in this, really," referring to the war between the U.S. and Iran, which began in February. "[These Iranians] do terrible things around the world … the news today doesn't surprise us," Rubio concluded.
Rebecca Rosman reported from Paris.

An Indian film that nobody would release is finally a hit - 18 awards later
- Published
A film about the tender love and quiet loneliness of an elderly couple, which took two years to reach cinemas after it was completed, is wowing critics and audiences across India.
The 111-minute Pyre, directed by television journalist-turned-filmmaker Vinod Kapri, also explores the pressing issue of outmigration which has left hundreds of picturesque Himalayan hamlets abandoned and turned them into ghost villages. It further reflects on the impact of climate change, which has made the region's weather increasingly harsh.
On social media, many Indians have shared videos showing audiences leaving theatres with tears in their eyes. Others have posted that they have not been so moved by a film in a long time.
The film's lead actors, ordinary villagers who had never faced a camera before, have also won praise from some of Bollywood's most respected figures, including Naseeruddin Shah and Anupam Kher.
Pyre's protagonists - Padam Singh (played by Kapri's uncle, Padam Singh) and Tulsi (played by Heera Devi) - are Bubu and Aama, local terms for grandfather and grandmother. The couple live in a small home in the mountains of the northern state of Uttarakhand .
It's a place where age is measured against momentous events. Singh was born two years before the outbreak of World War II. Tulsi was born in the year atomic bombs were dropped on Japan.
There are no roads and no electricity. Whenever the couple need help – which is often as Tulsi frequently has to be carried to hospital – Padam Singh uses a traditional long-horn instrument to summon neighbours. In return for their kindness, he pays them with goats.
"There's nothing here – just mountains," as one character puts it. So the young leave in search of greener pastures, and those who depart this beautiful, but blighted, land rarely return.
Kapri says his film remains focused on the "soulful love story of the ageing couple in their last days".
"They have shared a life together for 65 years and, for the last 28 years, they've been waiting for their son, Hariya, who's gone to Mumbai in search of work, to come back," Kapri tells the BBC. "It's a story of companionship, of loneliness and of waiting."
Their wait takes on a new urgency when suddenly, after all these years, a letter arrives from Hariya setting a date for his visit.
As Padam Singh and Tulsi count down the days, the handful of villagers around them leave one by one, until the couple find themselves alone in the vast mountain landscape.
"You and Tulsi should also leave as soon as possible. Otherwise, you won't even have four people to carry your body down the mountain to the funeral pyre when you or Tulsi die," one departing villager advises Padam Singh. "Or die before we leave," he adds in jest.
With no one left to call for help, Padam Singh builds two funeral pyres side by side right outside his door – one for his wife and one for himself.
"How will I carry you down the mountain if you die?" he tells Tulsi when she questions the decision.
Despite the bleak setting and the weight of the topics covered, Pyre is suffused with humour. The central couple are delightful. Like many long-married spouses, they seem to treat bickering as a love language.
Kapri, who is from Uttarakhand, got the idea for the film in 2018 after meeting an 84-year-old man in Munsiyari, a scenic hill town in the state.
"I visited him after seeing his photo in a Facebook post. The wrinkles on his face really fascinated me. His face was unique."
Kapri said he asked him and his wife what their biggest worry was.
"He said, 'My biggest worry is, if I die first, who is going to take care of her?' And she said, 'He doesn't know how to cook. So if I die first, I don't know who is going to cook food for him.' That was so heartwarming for me."
Kapri says he initially tried to make his film with "the real couple", but abandoned the idea after a week of shooting, when it became clear it was not working. He then approached actors Naseeruddin Shah and Ratna Pathak - a couple themselves - for the lead roles.
Shah loved the script, Kapri says, but felt that he and Pathak did not belong to the region and would struggle to do justice to the characters.
Kapri finally found his Padam Singh within his own family – his father's younger brother, a retired army soldier who expressed an interest in acting. He found his Tulsi in another village. Heera Devi, an elderly widow, had raised her children through years of farming, cutting grass and tending to her buffalo.
Over the years, Padam Singh and Heera Devi tell the BBC, they have watched stories of ghost villages, of children migrating for work, abandoning the elderly, play out all around them. They say today they are overwhelmed by the attention Pyre has got.
Since 2024, the film has been screened at some of the world's biggest festivals. It has won 18 awards, Kapri says, including three for best feature and 12 audience-choice best film prizes.
Despite its success at festivals, Kapri says, Pyre spent two years without a distributor. Even OTT platforms passed on the film and it finally reached cinemas only when a producer friend of his stepped in to fund a theatrical release.
But, he says, the modest 70-screen release on 30 October sparked favourable word-of-mouth reviews and with the demand for tickets going up, there was an increase in overall screenings too.
Meanwhile, the misgivings that both Padam Singh and Heera Devi say they initially had about stepping in front of the camera and forgetting their lines are gone now.
Heera Devi says she was even concerned about what her children would think - and what would society say?
Today she and Padam Singh are basking in the positive reviews of film critics and the affection of their audiences.
They have met teary-eyed people at multiple screenings - many wanting to touch their feet and hug them, many who said the film reminded them of their own parents and grandparents who are waiting in villages, towns and cities that they had come from.
"We felt immense joy and happiness. We've received so much love and inspiration - something we had never imagined," says Padam Singh.
But the best moment for him came when he met Naseeruddin Shah in Mumbai. "He watched the entire movie and had tears in his eyes. He hugged me. He said, 'Bubu, the role you have performed, I wouldn't be able to pull off even in seven lifetimes.'"
The film's appeal, Heera Devi says, is because "in reality, our village is just like this".
"Across villages in India, the elderly are left alone. No one's children stay at home anymore and it's the same situation for all parents. They keep waiting for their son and daughter-in-law, hoping that their grandchildren would visit and spend a few days with them. The loneliness is simply unbearable."
Padam Singh says he has a message for the younger generation in Uttarakhand and the rest of India.
"I want to tell them they must not abandon their motherland, the land where they were born," he says. "I also appeal to the government to bring education and employment to where people are - so that they don't have to wander away. When that happens, the parents who are being left behind will also be cared for."

One in three students across the globe experiences bullying every month, while one in 10 faces cyber bullying, the UNESCO said, warning that AI is accelerating new forms of technology-facilitated violence (TFV).
UNESCO's new policy brief, ‘Connected and Safe’, shows that nudification apps, voice cloning, automated harassment and AI companion apps used for grooming are now surfacing in school-based incidents across multiple regions.
The United Nations agency has called upon countries to invest in digital safety measures, teacher preparation, and mental health support for students, in coordination with technology companies.
According to Khaled El-Enany, director-general of UNESCO, one in three learners experience bullying every month, while one in ten face cyber bullying. Behind these figures are millions of children whose education, health and well-being are at risk, with consequences that can extend far beyond the classroom.
"Online and technology-facilitated violence (TFV) is no longer a peripheral concern for education systems. It is part of the reality of school life for many learners, with direct consequences for safety, well-being, participation and learning. Around one in ten learners worldwide has experienced cyber bullying, and across 44 countries in Europe, Central Asia and North America, prevalence rose from 12 to 15 per cent between 2018 and 2022, among both boys and girls," the policy brief said.
"Some learners are more exposed than others. Girls, learners with disabilities, learners of diverse sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, and those marginalised by socio-economic status or geography face distinct and often more severe forms of harm," it said.
In the context of bullying, data shows that girls are just as likely as boys to experience bullying, although the types of bullying differ.
"Boys are generally more exposed to physical bullying and violence, while girls are more exposed to psychological bullying, particularly through cyber bullying and appearance-based bullying. Sexual bullying (sexual jokes, comments and gestures) affects boys and girls at similar rates.
"Physical sexual violence (assault, harassment and rape) can affect both boys and girls, but girls are more likely to experience this form of violence. Corporal punishment and all forms of violent discipline are also influenced by gender, with boys more likely to experience physical corporal punishment than girls and learners likely to be punished to reinforce expectations regarding behaviours deemed socially appropriate for each gender," the brief said.
UNESCO argued that responsibility for safer digital environments for students must be shared between governments, technology companies, platforms and regulators, as schools alone cannot face this issue.
"Safer schools require sustained investment in teacher preparation, mental health and psychosocial support, reporting and response systems, digital safety measures, and coordinated action across education, child protection, health and technology sectors.
"UNESCO recently launched the process towards a new global recommendation on young people and digital environments in the age of AI, to ensure that these technologies protect children's rights and well-being, strengthen critical thinking and empower them to shape their own future," it said.
