A team of scientists at the CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB) has identified critical weaknesses in the bacterium that causes Tuberculosis (TB), a finding that could pave the way for the development of new treatments against one of the world’s deadliest infectious diseases.
The discovery is particularly significant for India, which accounts for nearly a quarter of global TB cases and about a third of drug-resistant infections, according to the World Health Organisation’s Global TB Report 2025. Drug-resistant TB remains a major public health challenge, as treatment requires a combination of antibiotics taken over several months and is becoming increasingly difficult due to the emergence of resistant strains.
Led by CCMB Director Vinay Kumar Nandicoori, the research team mapped the protein export machinery of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the bacterium responsible for TB. The study sheds light on how the pathogen transports proteins within and outside its cells, a process essential for its growth, survival and ability to cause disease.
The research was carried out by joint first authors Priyadarshini Sanyal and Jagadeeshwari Uppada in collaboration with scientists from the Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Chennai, led by Areejit Samal, and the Translational Health Science and Technology Institute, Faridabad.
Using a combination of computational modelling and laboratory experiments, the researchers identified 92 key components and nearly 200 molecular reactions involved in the bacterium’s protein transport network. These included the general Sec pathway, the Twin-Arginine Translocation (Tat) system and the specialised ESX secretion systems unique to this group of bacteria.
“Protein secretion acts like a delivery system inside the bacterium and is vital for its survival,” said Dr Uppada. The team focused on two major secretion pathways, SecA1 and Tat, employing CRISPR-based gene-silencing technology to reduce their activity. The results were striking: bacterial growth declined sharply both in laboratory cultures and inside immune cells, demonstrating that both pathways are essential for the pathogen’s survival.
Dr Priyadarshini Sanyal said further analysis revealed that disrupting these systems affected the export of more than 100 proteins in the SecA1 pathway and around 140 proteins linked to the Tat system. Researchers also observed structural damage to the bacterial cell membrane, making it unstable and more permeable. Proteins that normally remain inside the bacterium began leaking into the surrounding environment.
Dr Nandicoori said that these changes highlight the close connection between protein secretion and the maintenance of the bacterial cell envelope, a key factor behind TB’s persistence and resistance to treatment. The findings, published in the peer-reviewed journal Molecular & Cellular Proteomics, could help researchers identify new drug targets, although translating the discovery into effective medicines will require several more years of research.

Norris sparkles in Sao Paulo despite firework mishap
- Published
Showing off on the podium after winning the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, Lando Norris made his first misstep of an afternoon that had challenged the Formula 1 drivers to their very limits.
Norris jumped off the top step, and tried to do his signature move, where he uncorks the champagne bottle by bashing it into the ground.
Except that, not for the first time, the force of his jump pushed things too far, and he smashed the bottle.
Then, holding up the shattered top to the crowd below, he stepped backwards and inadvertently put the side of his head into the sparkles blowing up from the fireworks on the front of the platform.
Red Bull drivers Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar showed no pity, and proceeded to drench him with the contents of their bottles.
In any case, Norris was fine, McLaren team principal Andrea Stella confirmed shortly afterwards, and the Briton showed no ill effects in his post-race interviews.
It was, he said, "one of the hardest races of the year in terms of focus needed every lap and therefore one of the best".

- Norris brilliant in wet & Verstappen recovery extraordinary - driver ratings

Interlagos did what it often can, and threw everything at the drivers. The race started on a wet track, which dried progressively. There was more rain at the end.
Through it all, Norris was virtually impeccable. He made new world champion Kimi Antonelli look fallible for pretty much the first time all year, and then fended off what at one point was threatening to be one of those days when Verstappen appears to have descended from the Gods.
It says a lot for Norris' performance that it overshadowed Verstappen's drive from 21st on the grid to finish second.
Actually, perhaps the race had also started with a small blemish from the man who has had to hand his title of world champion to Antonelli this year without ever really being able to defend it.
Starting from pole, Norris was relatively slow away, at least compared with the Italian, and Antonelli blasted into a lead that for a while looked as if he would not lose.
But after the Mercedes driver had built an eight-second advantage in the first 13 laps, Norris began to come back at him as the track dried.
Stopping for slick tyres a lap before Antonelli cut a seven-second deficit to nothing, and when three laps later the new champion spun at Turn One under pressure from the old, Norris was promoted into a lead that he never again looked like losing.
"A lot was thrown at everyone on a day like today, but it was probably one of our best races in terms of execution and pit stops, timing of things," Norris said.
"We boxed one lap early on to the slicks. I came out and was right behind him and forced him to push a little bit more, and obviously he went into a mistake and I could capitalise on it.
"So, in terms of always being there where we needed to be, being able to put people under pressure was a very good day for that.
"Also, from my side, just not making any mistakes, which is so easy to do on a day like today. So, great performance from the whole team. Certainly up there with one of the best I've ever had."
For both Norris and McLaren, it was a welcome return to form. They started the year slowly, having fallen behind in development on their 2026 car as they diverted resources to ensure they got their title double over the line last year.
By mid-summer, they had caught up, and Norris took two consecutive wins either side of the summer break, and was unlucky not to get another in Madrid in September.
But then other teams overtook them again and McLaren have toiled relatively in recent races, especially in qualifying.
But the combination in Sao Paulo of some new parts, the circuit characteristics suiting them, and Norris excelling in the wet in qualifying and race, put him back in the game.
In so doing, he provided a performance that served as a reminder that he has been one of the drivers of the year, even if his equipment has not always met his exalted standards.
Stella said: "When Lando operates at his best, he's definitely one of the best drivers on the grid.
"We have seen that in these conditions, like yesterday (in qualifying), it's not the first time that when you have mixed variable conditions, he kind of is one of the fastest in finding the limit.
"And you have seen this today as well, when the track was in the middle between dry and wet. It was when he was probably gaining most throughout the races on anybody else.
"He's very sensitive in understanding how much grip is available. And very, I would say, even complete as a driver, despite he's still many years ahead of him, from a technical point of view, in terms of understanding how to deploy his tools to use the grip that is available, or to adapt to the balance of the car, because you're never going to have a really perfect car.
"You're never going to have the perfect conditions. So adaptability is actually probably the most important feature that you may want to possess as a driver. When there's a need to understand what's best, how to operate, he's definitely a master."
Verstappen raced with a car 'not in good shape'
For a time, it looked as if Verstappen might be in the running for a win.
A penalty for using too many engines this year left the four-time champion four places lower than the position from which he had won in similar slippery conditions at Interlagos two years ago.
So when he was up to fifth, and less than 15 seconds behind leader Antonelli, by the time the pit stops for dry tyres were looming on lap 15, with 56 still to go and more rain predicted, it looked ominous.
But once on to the slicks, Verstappen was not a threat to Norris on pace, even when heavy rain returned in the closing laps.
"That first stint went really, really well," Verstappen said. "We got very quickly back into the top 10, and the pace wasn't bad.
"But as soon as I switched to the slicks, I had an extreme amount of oversteer in the car in the high-speed corners, which made it super difficult to drive.
"So, we need to understand if something broke on the car, some kind of aero loss or whatever, because this was not normal.
"I sit here, of course, very happy with second, but at the same time, I know there was more in it if the car had been in good shape.
"Unfortunately, that was not the case. I actually did most of the race with a car that was not in good shape, and to finish second, of course, is fantastic.
"Maybe next year I'd love to start a bit further up front instead of starting from the back or the pit lane."
Mercedes back on top - but Wolff not expecting era of dominance
For a time, Antonelli looked set to celebrate clinching the title and becoming F1's youngest ever champion a week before in Mexico with a win.
But his most uncharacteristic spin ended that hope, and took him out of contention.
"Very disappointing because we were on for the win up to that point," he said.
"Also in this slicks, once I was able to get some temperature, I was getting to the rhythm, but yeah, the spin came, which still is something I need to look at because I don't know why I lost the rear so quickly as well, like no warning, nothing."
It was another bad day for team-mate George Russell, too, who had done excellent work to move up to third place right behind Norris after starting seventh.
He looked the one driver able to threaten Norris for raw pace, but his afternoon unravelled even before Antonelli's, when he spun exiting the pits and turned a 1.2-second deficit to the McLaren into 20. That was it for his hopes of a win.
Still, a fourth and a fifth place for Russell and Antonelli at the end was more than enough for Mercedes to clinch the constructors' championship. It was the team's ninth - but their first since 2021, after a difficult time through the last rule set.
Antonelli said: "I'm going to put all this aside for now because the team, you know, take the title, we take the title for the team and they all deserve it.
"I'm very proud to be part of this group and this team who has done and still does so much for me and I'm very happy for them."
Like Antonelli, team boss Toto Wolff was as focused on the lessons of the day and year as he was on the success.
He reflected on the fact that while Mercedes had dominated the first half of the season, not only have they been caught in the second, but upgrades brought to the car a few races ago did not have the expected effect.
"Look at the last few races," Wolff said. "We haven't won.
"Then today at the beginning of the race, Kimi was just storming away. It looked like this could be ours. But the competition has been getting tougher between Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull and ourselves.
"It's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship. And I have no doubt that this is going to be very difficult for us next year."
Wolff is pleased that Mercedes have found their way back to the front after struggling relatively through what was known as the ground-effect era.
But he says he does not expect this to be the start of another dominant era such as they enjoyed with Lewis Hamilton in the last decade.
"Looking back, those last four years were very difficult between getting it wrong and then kind of understanding why it was wrong and then realising, no, we didn't understand. And that was a bit back and forth," he said.
"It wasn't that bad at all when you look at the sheer numbers, but it felt not good. And the resilience of the team, the people that held together in those tough times is a factor.
"So it feels really good sealing those two titles. Not many sports teams have done that after consecutive run of championships, then a difficult spell and then coming back.
"It looks like the most maybe competitive era that is about to start, because the teams have become so professional in capability, in resource, that this kind of runaway seasons, I don't see them any more, whether it's four in a row or eight in a row. And that is a completely new challenge.
"You can see how quickly it goes from being dominant. And within a few races, you realise that your upgrade doesn't work and you fall back and you're just third on the road.
"It's great for the sport. I wished it was the era of Mercedes and me running away with another few championships. I don't think it's the reality."

Abu Dhabi, Nov 10: The three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States start Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, renewing a push for peace after several rounds of negotiations earlier this year.
The two-day session in Abu Dhabi, the first such meeting since February, will focus on security guarantees. US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner said on X that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were working on a "negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment.”
Russia and Ukraine hold to their divergent demands
Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal to end the full-scale war, now nearing its five-year mark.
Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson — the four regions that Moscow illegally annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.
Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won't agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles. He has warned that Russia will achieve its goals by force if Kyiv refuses to meet its conditions for peace.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejects Putin's demands to voluntarily cede territory that Russia has not been able to take on the battlefield. Zelenskyy also rejects any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.
Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.
Russia and Ukraine send experienced negotiators
The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks.
Russia's chief negotiator is Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who has led Moscow's team since the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul, Turkey, in March 2022. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and deputy chief of the General Staff's operational department Yuri Zhigarlovsky.
Ukraine's delegation is led by Rustem Umerov, head of the country's Foreign Intelligence Service, who also attended earlier talks. It also reportedly includes Zelenskyy's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy Sergiy Kyslytsya and Davyd Arakhamia, the parliamentary faction leader of Zelenskyy's Servant of the People party.
The US says a broader European security deal is in the works
Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as “a big agreement” that is “going to involve more than Ukraine.”
Kushner said Monday on X that a “comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them.” The discussions in Abu Dhabi will set the stage for “that engagement to begin in the near future, as part of a broader multilateral process,” he added.
Moscow has praised the broad approach.
“We can only welcome the (US) negotiators on President Donald Trump's request proposing to put the issue of collective security on top of the agenda of the talks on a Ukrainian settlement,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
Just before Moscow launched the all-out invasion in 2022, it demanded that NATO roll back its deployments in the alliance's member countries in Central and Eastern Europe, seeing their presence as a security threat. Similar demands will likely be part of any comprehensive peace deal proposed by Russia.
Kushner said that before the start of the three-way talks, he and Witkoff will meet separately with envoys from Ukraine, the European Union, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy to “continue the close consultation and coordination we have undertaken on European security and Ukraine's postwar future over the past several weeks.”
Some in the EU see Washington's proposals as too accommodating to Moscow.
Moscow has objected to the Europeans' involvement in the three-way talks but said EU representatives could join at a later stage.
Russia and Ukraine have escalated aerial attacks
While the ground battles have morphed into a war of attrition along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line, Russia and Ukraine have ramped up their long-range strikes with drones and missiles.
Russia has intensified its air campaign against Ukraine's power grid, seeking to weaken the country's resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine's shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has escalated its drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
- Published
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.
Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.
The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.
"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.
Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.
It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.
The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.
But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.
For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.
"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.
I think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.
- Could this be the end of 'Jensanity' 
  - Published1 day ago
The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.
We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.
China denies that she was engaged in espionage.
Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.
China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.
Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.
Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.
He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.
Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.
But can he survive?
At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.
Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.
An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.
And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.
Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.
He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.
While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.
And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) held that laws penalising having more than two children have lost their relevance due to the falling fertility rate in India.
“We are of the strong opinion that laws that penalise having more than two children have lost their relevance. The foundation of such laws, that is, the fear of overpopulation, has crumbled due to demographic changes in the past few decades,” a Bench headed by Justice P.S. Narasimha observed in a 37-page judgment.
The court said its 2003 judgment (in Javed versus State of Haryana) which upheld such penal laws, needed a revisit by a larger Bench. India’s Total Fertility Rate (TFR) had fallen from 3.02 to 1.9. A TFR of 2.1, known as the replacement rate, would allow one generation to completely replace itself.
“Even though India’s population is not yet declining, the TFR falling below the replacement rate will soon result in a demographic transition towards an older population with a declining share of the working-age population. Therefore, laws aimed at limiting population growth have now lost their significance,” Justice Narasimha observed.
The 2003 judgment in the Javed case had referred to the situation that existed in China as of 2000 and drew inspiration from the measures that it had undertaken to control the population.
Justice Narasimha said the decades-old view that population explosion was an impediment for progress was outdated.
Healthy growth
“The earlier perception that population harms development does not hold water anymore. Rather than society and the courts being concerned about the negative consequences of high population, it should instead focus on the need to encourage a healthy growth of population,” the judgment, by a Bench comprising Justice Alok Aradhe, said.
The judgment pointed out that the share of persons aged 60 and above had already risen from about 8.3% in 2014 to 9.7% in 2024, and government projections place that share at nearly 15% by 2036.
India’s falling fertility rate, the court said, would necessarily mean a smaller proportion of younger persons in the future, and, correspondingly, a larger ageing population. It said the issue had been of significant concern in recent years.
The court said the failure to take notice of demographic changes would lead to only serious consequences for India. Failure to adapt not only produced injustice, but was also an abuse of power.
The judgment was based on a petition filed by Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, whose election as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat in Maharashtra was set aside on the ground that she had more than two children. The lower courts and State authorities found that she had given birth to a third child in 2014, but still contested and won the panchayat elections in 2022. They had held that she acted in violation of Section 14(1)(j-1) of the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1959, which upheld the two-child norm.
Justice Narasimha found such laws linking motherhood to political representation a violation of Article 21 (right to life) under the Constitution.
“Allowing such laws to stand excludes an entire class of citizens from political representation on grounds bearing little rational connection to their capacity to hold public office. It compels an unconscionable choice between bearing children and democratic participation, impinging on the right to reproductive autonomy under Article 21,” Justice Narasimha observed.
Seeking an immediate re-visitation of the Javed judgment of 2003, the court permitted the appellant to continue in her elected position as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat while staying any proceedings against her.

Eight people have tested positive for Shigella infection in Malappuram district, with five cases linked to a wedding feast at Korakkuthu in Elamkulam panchayat near Perinthalmanna.
The outbreak has prompted the Health department to step up surveillance and preventive measures in the area.
The five patients attended a wedding held on October 31, 2026, in ward 12 of Elamkulam panchayat. Around 80 people who attended the function have since reported symptoms of diarrhoea. A child from the area is also suspected to have Shigella infection and is under special observation.
The other confirmed cases include a four-year-old girl who ate food from a snack shop at 5th Mile at Amarambalam near Nilambur, and two people who ate mandi rice from a restaurant at Palunda near Chungathara, Nilambur.
The girl and the two patients from Chungathara are undergoing treatment at Government District Hospital, Nilambur. Several others, including the girl’s mother, have also reported similar symptoms.
The Food Safety department has collected samples of food and drinking water served at the wedding and sent them for testing. Stool samples of those affected will be examined at the laboratory at Government Medical College, Manjeri.
A special health team has begun surveillance and field-level interventions. The Health department has advised people to drink boiled and cooled water and eat properly cooked food. Drinking water sources should also be superchlorinated using bleaching powder, said health officials.
The health authorities, in coordination with the panchayat, will intensify inspections at local establishments and public functions. Event organisers have been asked to follow public health guidelines.

Trump's global health strategy is emerging. What will the Democratic Congress say?
By all appearances, it was a classic government ceremony. Officials in suits. Big black chairs around a wooden table. A cluster of microphones. It happened on October 8 in Lusaka, Zambia. Amid applause, U.S. and Zambian officials signed a global health agreement, called a Memorandum of Understanding or MOU.
But Mich Coker — the Chargé d'Affaires at the U.S. Embassy in Zambia — said this agreement was anything but classic.
"This MOU represents a fundamental shift," he said, speaking at the signing ceremony. He explained that the relationship between the two countries was moving "from a traditional donor-recipient model to a true partnership, one grounded in Zambian leadership, in Zambian ownership and in shared accountability."
Global health experts on all sides of the political spectrum and all over the world agree with Coker that there's been a fundamental shift in the U.S. approach to global health.
"The shift that's currently unfolding is very large and it's very rapid," says Janeen Madan Keller, acting co-director of the Global Health Program at the Center for Global Development.
The story of this fundamental shift starts at the beginning of the second Trump Administration with months of global health turmoil — Madan Keller and other experts say — but has given way to a clearer strategy. One with big goals, a short timeline and a lot less transparency than what came before.
Here is a look at where things stand now and how a Congress controlled by the Democratic Party might impact the new landscape.
First, the "chaos"
President Trump's second term started dramatically. When he dismantled USAID (the U.S. Agency for International Development), citing alleged "fraud, waste and abuse," everything changed overnight.
"It is a period that is best described as chaos," says Madan Keller. The repercussions were massive and immediate, she says, "for people and communities in some of the poorest countries of the world."
Clinics shut down suddenly. Patients ran out of HIV medications. In Zambia, as well as a number of other countries, many patients who relied on U.S.-supported clinics and programs faced tons of uncertainty and, often, dire health consequences.
"For the first half of 2025, there was a complete upheaval," says Jennifer Kates, senior vice president and director of global and public health policy at KFF.
A strategy emerged
Next came a new stage in the history of U.S. foreign aid. "Starting over the summer of 2025 and going into September, there actually was a sort of step back to develop an actual strategy and a plan," says Kates.
What emerged from the State Department was the America First Global Health Strategy with the stated goal of making "America safer, stronger, and more prosperous." The main way this strategy is being implemented is through agreements with individual countries. In the past, the U.S. had done more work through large international organizations or local non-governmental organizations.
Experts say one defining feature of these agreements is that they are transactional. For example, in Zambia "there was a massive scandal because activists were able to show that the agreement was planning to condition access to [U.S. global health] funding on access to [Zambia's] copper and rare earth minerals," says Asia Russell, executive director of the HIV/AIDS advocacy organization Health GAP. Her organization helped expose this situation.
While the part of the agreement about minerals was separated from the global health agreement after the public outcry in Zambia, many of the global health agreements do require the recipient country to share data such as pathogen information.
Big (but not new) goals
Speaking at the signing ceremony in Zambia, Coker ticked off some of the top priorities in the new strategy, including that recipient countries increase their financial contributions to health in the years ahead and that they are transitioned off aid in the near future.
He said in the Zambian MOU, the U.S. would pay $1.5 billion over five years "with Zambia simultaneously committing to increase its own domestic health expenditures by $975 million. We are charting a path toward a stronger, more self-reliant health system."
Another priority has been building up a country's own health infrastructure — and not a parallel system run by non-profits and NGOs.
"We are looking to have up to about 40,000 healthcare workers recruited through this support," said Zambian Health Minister Roma Chilengi at the same ceremony.
The priorities in the MOUs — such as recipient countries contributing more and being weaned off aid money — are not new ideas. In the world of global health they have long received bipartisan support. But, up until now, they've been hard to implement. "This approach really does kickstart them in a new way that had not occurred before," says Kates.
But in her view the chaos before this kickstart makes implementing these goals more challenging — as does the fact that everyone's now operating within a greatly diminished U.S. global health system.
The speed of the transition also troubles some. Madan Keller says that the strategy aims to achieve major changes in just a handful of years. "It's happening on a compressed timeline with arguably limited capacity to manage it, and that's where some of the risks and concerns are coming from," she says.
And Russell, for her part, is worried that the main goal of the Trump Administration has been hammering out MOUs rather than setting ambitious health-related goals, such as reducing HIV transmission. The Trump administration is focused on "process indicators — not impact indicators — as its first measure of success, which is basically a loser's gambit when it comes to pandemics," she says. "Rubio crowed about signing documents. That doesn't save lives."
The State Department declined an interview request but said in a statement that most African countries with MOUs now have drawn up implementation plans and "U.S. embassies globally are now focused on operationalizing these implementation plans [and] recipient country governments are also executing on the commitments they have made in the MOUs."
"Very hard to get the information"
Another major challenge in assessing the new strategy has been a lack of information provided to the public, says global health experts.
This represents a big break from past U.S. global health initiatives. For example, the U.S.'s flagship program for HIV/AIDS — called PEPFAR – "was a gold standard for collecting data on a regular basis and sharing it transparently — and then using that data to really inform decision making," Ramona Godbole, the former deputy director of policy, planning and programs at the now-defunct U.S. Agency for International Development, told NPR earlier this year.
"Now it's much more opaque and very hard to get the information. The agreements themselves have not been publicly released by the U.S. government," Kates says. Although, the text for some of the agreements have become available through litigation or Freedom of Information Act requests filed by advocacy groups.
There is even less information on the implementation plans, she says, which are supposed to contain detailed goals and metrics for how the money will be spent and what programs will be supported.
Kates says this is true despite the fact that U.S. taxpayers are underwriting the aid, which totals $16 billion committed across the 36 agreements that have been signed. That money comes from U.S. taxpayer dollars that Congress allocated to foreign aid. KFF has calculated that this represents a 34% drop in U.S. global health aid and it has left some countries without an agreement. For instance, Zimbabwe lost U.S. global health aid since the two governments were not able to agree to MOU terms.
In its statement, the State Department said: "Claims of a lack of accountability and transparency are unfounded….We have and will share every signed MOU with Congress."
A new blue Congress
In the wake of this week's midterms, there are new questions about how this fundamental shift in global health will play out. With the Democratic Party returning to the majority in Congress, many expect that lawmakers will demand more transparency.
"I think 100% they are going to demand: give us the MOUs, show us the implementation plans, come in and tell us more detail about what you're doing," Kates says.
Another question is whether the new Congress might try to resurrect what was dismantled. Kate says there are still a lot of unknowns about what the new Congress will do after it convenes on January 3 and how the Trump Administration will respond, but she expects lawmakers will first push for the public to get more information on what global health work the U.S. is and isn't currently supporting.
Russell says many global health activists are calling for more oversight — and she is one of them. "Congress needs to slam its feet, both feet, on the brakes unless and until it gets this information, gets this accountability," she says.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

EXCLUSIVE: In September, we announced PRƎPPY, the first new film from STX Entertainment in years. And now, there’s a new sign of life at the indie studio, as we’ve learned that Angus Sutherland will lead it as Chief Executive Officer, effective immediately.
Sutherland assumes the reins from Peter Coleman, who was installed when Crown Productions, a subsidiary of insurance and investment platform A-CAP, acquired STX in January. He’ll lead the company while continuing as COO of global completion bond company Film Finances International, which he only joined in July.
Sutherland brings more than two decades of experience across development, acquisitions, financing, production and international sales, with deep expertise in production finance and oversight. At Film Finances, he works with producers, production companies and financiers worldwide on independent film and television projects, from financing through delivery.
Watch on Deadline
Previously, Sutherland served as President of Artesian Wells Pictures, where he launched and ran Omar Sy’s U.S. production company. He has also worked as a producer and held executive roles at New Republic Pictures and MadRiver Pictures, helping build New Republic’s slate, which included Sam Mendes’ Oscar-winning 1917.
Founded in 2014 by film producer Robert Simonds and TPG Growth’s Bill McGlashan, STX Entertainment made its name on star-driven indies like Bad Moms, Hustlers, The Gentlemen, I Feel Pretty, 21 Bridges, Countdown and the Greenland films starring Gerard Butler.
The company is reemerging after a period of inactivity brought on by box-office disappointments and mounting financial pressure. This led to a 2020 all-stock merger with Eros International, an Indian conglomerate, which collapsed in less than two years under financial and regulatory strain. Following a 2022 buyout by global investment firm The Najafi Companies, which left Eros with a 15% non-voting stake, STX sought stability via a North American distribution and library pact with Lionsgate in 2023. In January, Crown Productions acquired 100% of STX, with founder Simonds exiting and Coleman taking over from Noah Fogelson as CEO.
Going forward, STX will look to build on past successes, expanding its slate with a focus on original features, franchise opportunities and collaborations with leading filmmakers and production partners. Since resuming operations, they’ve announced PRƎPPY, a true-crime film co-produced with Aggregate Films that stars Kit Connor and Diana Silvers. Set in the summer of 1986, the film explores the events leading to the murder of recent high school graduate Jennifer Levin by “Preppy Killer” Robert Chambers in New York’s Central Park.

Indonesian VP Gibran’s fate hangs in balance as parliament ponders probe
While Gibran Rakabuming Raka, son of former leader Joko Widodo, helped Prabowo win the 2024 election, questions remain over qualifications
Indonesia’s parliament reconvened on Tuesday with lawmakers weighing the possibility of a probe into the eligibility of Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, amid a widening political rift between his influential father and President Prabowo Subianto.
As son of the hugely popular two-term former President Joko Widodo, Gibran helped Prabowo win the 2024 election by a huge margin, but some lawmakers are seeking to investigate whether his incomplete education documents disqualify him as vice-president.
House Speaker Puan Maharani said many opinions on the issue of Gibran’s eligibility had been received during a one-month recess, and the next steps would be discussed.

The US State Department on Monday served summonses to the Government of India through diplomatic channels in a civil lawsuit filed by Khalistan separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun. The State Department also clarified that it was legally obliged to do so and is not taking a position on the case. Earlier, A court in New York allowed Pannun, who has been declared a terrorist in India, to serve his civil lawsuit on National Security Adviser (NSA) Ajit Doval and former Research and Analysis Wing (RAW) chief Samant Goel through courts in Delhi. The civil lawsuit is linked to the murder for hire investigation in the US by the Department of Justice, in which an Indian national, Nikhil Gupta, was arrested in the Czech Republic in 2023 According to the DoJ, in February 2026, Gupta pleaded guilty in a Manhattan federal court to charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in connection with a failed assassination plot targeting a US citizen and Sikh activist on American soil. Gupta, an alleged drug smuggler, was recruited in May 2023 by Vikash Yadav, an officer with the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), to carry out the murder. Gupta faces a maximum statutory penalty of up to 40 years in prison. In August, Pannun, the general counsel for Sikhs For Justice, which is banned in India as an unlawful association, claimed that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had warned him that he faces a new credible threat to his life. Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen said he was warned by FBI agents who visited him August 12 that he should not travel until the threat is resolved, and, if he does, the agency should be notified in advance of his plans. He said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police warned him by telephone on Tuesday, though neither law enforcement agency gave any details about the plot that was uncovered. Messages seeking comment from both law enforcement agencies were not immediately returned. Pannun said he was warned according to the terms of a “Duty to Warn” law in the United States that obligates U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies to notify individuals when they discover credible and specific threats of murder, severe bodily harm, or kidnapping. NIA court grants default bail to 2 of 12 accused in Vijayawada terror links case
On March 24, the Andhra Pradesh police’s counter-intelligence cell arrested 12 people belonging to Al Malik Islamic Youth
Two of the 12 accused in the Vijayawada terror links case have been released on default bail, four days after a special court hearing for National Investigation Agency (NIA) cases in Visakhapatnam granted them bail, people familiar with the development said on Tuesday.
Defence advocate Abdus Saleem, who represents the accused, said Sayeeda Begum was released from the special women’s prison in Rajamahendravaram on Tuesday, while Shadman Dilkash was released from the same prison on Monday.
On March 24, the Andhra Pradesh police’s counter-intelligence cell arrested 12 people belonging to Al Malik Islamic Youth, who were suspected of having links to banned terrorist outfits such as al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS) and the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS), following a multi-state operation.
Sayeeda Begum is a Hyderabad-based domestic helper, while Shadman Dilkash hails from Patna in Bihar and is a National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) aspirant. Both were named as accused in the NIA chargesheet in the case.
Also Read:Telangana Women’s Commission questions 5 Hyderabad IVF centres over egg racket
Saleem said the NIA court directed both accused to furnish personal bonds of ₹50,000 each, along with two sureties. As part of the bail conditions, Sayeeda Begum must report to the NIA office in Hyderabad once a month, while Shadman Dilkash was directed to appear before the NIA office in Patna, Bihar.
According to Saleem, the NIA court granted default bail to the two accused on October 6 after the statutory investigation period of 180 days expired without the investigating agency filing charge sheets. The defence argued that the NIA filed charge sheets against other accused in the case but had not named the two for want of evidence, claiming that no material evidence existed to establish the alleged offences against them. It argued that their continued detention was not legally sustainable once the prescribed investigation period elapsed.
Those arrested in the case included Mohammed Rahantulla Sharif (A1), Mohammed Danish (A2) and Mirza Sohail Beg (A3), all from Vijayawada; Shadman Dilkash (A4) from Bihar; Sayeeda Begum (A5) from Hyderabad; Shaikh Fayaz Rehman (A6); Lucky Ahmed (A7) from Delhi; Azmanulla Khan (A8); Zeeshan (A9) from Rajasthan; Meer Asif Ali Bankura (A10) from West Bengal; Abdul Salam (A11) from Ballari in Karnataka; and Shah Rukh Khan (A12) from Pune.
Also Read:Andhra local body elections: TDP-led coalition wins two-third of zilla parishad seats
The investigation revealed that Pakistan-based handlers had planned a dedicated women’s wing, Khawateen, allegedly headed by Sayeeda Begum, to train recruits in using sniper rifles, guns, black powder bombs and improvised explosive devices (IEDs) to target non-Muslims and spread terror in India.
According to the police, the accused told investigators that although they had harboured extremist tendencies for some time, their radicalisation intensified only after they came into contact with a foreign handler identified as Al Hakeem Shukur on social media.
The case was initially registered by the II Town Police Station in Vijayawada under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) and the Information Technology Act. The investigation was subsequently transferred to the National Investigation Agency.

Ahead of its long due IPO, adtech unicorn InMobi has bolstered its marketing by securing a naming rights for Bengaluru's Ibbaluru Metro Station for the next 30 years via a ₹65 Cr deal. The partnership will see InMobi support Namma Metro over a 30-year concession, and Ibbaluru Metro Station will be known as InMobi Ibbaluru Metro Station. "Bengaluru is one of the world’s leading technology hubs. InMobi was born here, and over the last 18 years, we’ve grown alongside the city, continuing to build from India for the world. This partnership is our way of giving back to the city that gave us our start," the company said in a statement. The deal will contribute to BMRCL's non-fare revenue, which includes income from commercial activities such as station branding and advertising, alongside its core passenger fare collections. BMRCL said the partnership would support metro infrastructure development and encourage more corporate participation in the city's public transport ecosystem. The naming-rights deal comes as InMobi continues to work towards a public listing in India, a plan first reported over two years ago. In July 2024, reports said the company was targeting a 2025 IPO at a valuation of around $10 Bn. However, the proposed timeline has since slipped, with InMobi yet to file its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP). The delay in the proposed listing has coincided with changes in InMobi's shareholding structure. In December 2025, InMobi's cofounders bought back around 25-30% stake from early investor SoftBank, bringing the latter's holding down from approximately 35% to less than 8%. The transaction was backed by $350 Mn in debt raised from Varde Partners, Elham Credit Partners and SeaTown Holdings. The reshuffle in InMobi's cap table continued in 2026, with private equity firm True North reportedly acquiring a 2-3% stake through a secondary transaction valued at around $50-60 Mn. The deal also provided partial exits to some early investors. Alongside these shareholder transactions, InMobi has been putting the banking team in place for its proposed listing. The company has appointed JPMorgan Chase, Jefferies, Kotak Mahindra Capital and Axis Capital as merchant bankers for the IPO. Earlier reports pegged the proposed issue at around $1 Bn, although subsequent valuation estimates have varied. While the IPO remains a work in progress, InMobi has continued to expand its advertising technology capabilities through acquisitions. In May 2026, the company acquired San Francisco-based mobile app marketing and analytics platform MobileAction to strengthen its capabilities in app discovery, user acquisition and advertising optimisation.

OpenAI will not face criminal penalties over the Medicare data breach, but the prime minister has flagged changes to Australia’s criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies.
Anthony Albanese on Tuesday released the recommendations of a “rapid review” into the June breach of a Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia, but not the findings or the report itself, which he committed to releasing in the future.
A key recommendation is for the Attorney-General’s Department, Australian Federal Police and Department of Home Affairs to consider introducing “penalties for egregious regulatory non-compliance” and a “failure to prevent” offence, which would criminalise developing an AI model that engaged in harmful conduct while failing “to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm”.
The rapid review came in response to an AI agent, developed by OpenAI, accessing data from Services Australia and three other systems in June. The company did not notify the Australian government until mid-September despite becoming aware of the incident itself in August, prompting criticism from Labor and Albanese.
Guardian Australia revealed last month OpenAI used AI to help write the email to notify Australian authorities.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
Albanese said the government would set up a new AI safety regulator and implement six key obligations on AI companies:
- Maintaining security controls across all stages of development and deployment.
- Identifying and managing serious risks associated with their models.
- Providing mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian government rapidly.
- Allowing independent evaluation of their models.
- Maintaining and publishing safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency.
- Responding to updated standards and rules as technologies change.
The review recommended the federal government “consider mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting”, including around AI agents behaving in ways their creators may not have intended.
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, appearing with Albanese, told reporters: “It should never be the case that there’s an argument that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded.
“We need to make sure that our laws and our systems keep pace with the technology and also make sure that we’re able to use the technology to find vulnerabilities before others do,” Burke said.
“The mandatory reporting, when artificial intelligence goes rogue, gives us a chance to be able to make sure that when this happens, the reporting occurs and occurs immediately.”
But despite the government’s earlier public anger at OpenAI, Albanese on Tuesday characterised OpenAI’s breach of Services Australia as “minor” in terms of the implications for personal privacy. Guardian Australia understands OpenAI is unlikely to face further legal proceedings related to the June breach.
While Albanese did not directly answer a question about whether the OpenAI incident in June would have breached the proposed new laws if they were in place, government sources indicated that the new legislation would address similar future incidents.
“The clear indication is that no information was got that involves people’s personal details,” Albanese said.
“All of that was confirmed essentially … but that doesn’t mean that it wasn’t a serious issue and that in other areas there might be more serious implications.”
In a statement, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was reviewing the recommendations and the government’s proposals.
“We have been in close dialogue with the Government and we’ll continue to engage constructively as it develops its proposed legislation,” they said.
A separate OpenAI-led process, which is discussing better coordination between AI developers and the government, is expected to report back by 31 December.
The review made 18 recommendations. Albanese said “we accept all of the recommendations and we’ve commenced work to implement them”.
The AI researcher Toby Walsh said the people in charge of these companies needed to be criminally liable to ensure they did the right thing.
“We’ve tried fining them, and we’re not the only ones. These companies are incredibly wealthy, and it’s almost impossible to fine them enough,” he told Guardian Australia.
But the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, branded the news a “capitulation” to the AI industry, claiming the reforms would not do enough to change the behaviour of those companies. He said the government should have committed to implementing even stronger changes, rather than the review’s recommendation that Labor simply “consider” them.
“Safety keeps coming second to corporate investment, and this review locks that priority in by tying every AI safety effort to bringing in more AI money and more datacentres,” Shoebridge claimed.
“Being a world leader in AI doesn’t mean being a doormat to big tech. It means being prepared to regulate it, to protect Australians and to make sure corporate profits don’t come at the expense of everyone else.”
The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, said the Coalition backed the announcement, and had no criticism of the government. He said “AI is too important to become an unnecessarily partisan political contest”, signalling an “enduring and multi-partisan approach” to the technology.
