G7 attention turns to Ukraine while US-mediated talks get underway in Abu Dhabi
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his counterparts from the Group of 7 developed democracies are turning their attention toward Ukraine and how to support it in its struggle to defend itself from Russia
PARIS -- U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his counterparts from the Group of 7 developed democracies are turning their attention toward Ukraine and how to support it in its struggle to defend itself from Russia. As three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States get underway in the United Arab Emirates, top G7 diplomats are meeting Tuesday with Ukraine’s foreign minister in France.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha will start his day in Paris in talks with Rubio before heading to the French foreign ministry for a larger group meeting with the entire G7. They will discuss defense and security assistance to Ukraine, which President Donald Trump's administration has reduced, causing consternation not only in Kyiv but in capitals across Europe, the largest of which — Paris, Berlin, Rome and London — are G7 members.
It was not immediately clear if the U.S. or any of its G7 partners would announce any new assistance for Ukraine.
Meanwhile in Abu Dhabi, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will be meeting Russian and Ukrainian officials in part to persuade Moscow to agree to broader negotiations that would include key European officials on how to end nearly five years of war.
In Paris, Europeans have been clamoring for a seat at the table in Abu Dhabi, but two U.S. officials said Monday that representatives from Britain, Germany, France, NATO and the European Union would not join the main talks but rather discuss potential security guarantees and the long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe beforehand.
Russia has resisted European participation in negotiations and insisted the talks should proceed strictly as a trilateral format involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States. The three last held talks in February.
But on Monday in Paris, German Foreign Minister Johan Wadephul, who met separately with Rubio on the sidelines of the G7, was emphatic that Europe must be included.
“I am still very grateful to the United States of America for making every effort to get the parties to the conflict to the table,” he said. “But I made clear again here that Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe, only with Europe.”
Rubio said the U.S. has no objection to eventual European involvement in the direct talks, but that it wasn’t yet time.
“Ultimately, it would be a positive, but we’ve got a ways to go,” he told reporters after a full day of group and bilateral meetings with G7 counterparts. “But, no, it’s good that they’re talking, it’s good that the trilateral talks are on again. It’s better than not having talks.”
On the eve of the talks, Russia battered Ukraine’s power grid again on Monday and Ukrainian forces hit another of Russia’s biggest oil refineries.
The two countries remain locked in battle with no sign that either side is ready to budge from their demands. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.

John D. “Jay” Rockefeller IV, the progeny of one of America’s most famous and wealthiest families, who during three decades in the U.S. Senate sought expanded healthcare for the poor and excoriated President George W. Bush’s handling of the Iraq War, died on Friday (November 6, 2026) at his home in Washington, the Washington Post reported. He was 89.
His family did not provide a cause, the newspaper added.
Mr. Rockefeller, a tall, soft-spoken Democrat with liberal views, was elected in 1984 to the first of his five six-year terms representing West Virginia in the Senate after two terms as Governor of the poor coal-mining State.
Mr. Rockefeller voted in 2002 in favour of the Republican Bush’s measure authorising the Iraq war, which began with a U.S.-led invasion in 2003. He later expressed regret over that vote and, as head of the Senate intelligence committee, accused Mr. Bush of taking the nation to war on “false premises.”
He was a great-grandson of oil tycoon John D. Rockefeller and the scion of a family that formed a political dynasty that included his uncle, New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller.
Initiatives in public office
New York-born Jay Rockefeller’s life changed direction after he graduated from Harvard and served in a national service program in impoverished rural West Virginia from 1964 to 1966.
When he was put in public office, he worked to increase healthcare access, fight poverty, provide health benefits to coal miners and assist military veterans. As a senator, he had a role in shaping the programme created in 1997 under which the U.S. government helps States provide medical coverage for millions of uninsured children.
Mr. Rockefeller backed Democratic President Bill Clinton’s failed proposal for near-universal health insurance coverage in the 1990s and then fought for Democratic President Barack Obama’s successful quest for a healthcare overhaul law, signed in 2010.
In the debate over Mr. Obama’s measure, Mr. Rockefeller unsuccessfully sought to have the federal government offer a medical insurance program to the general population — in addition to existing programs for the poor and elderly — as an alternative to private insurance plans that could be costly and exclusive.
“Championing those most in need has been my life’s calling and I will never stop fighting to make a difference for the people who mean so much to me,” Mr. Rockefeller said in 2013 when he announced at age 75 he would not seek a sixth Senate term.
On the Iraq war
Before the Iraq invasion, Mr. Bush’s administration built the case for war by touting intelligence indicating Iraq owned an arsenal of weapons of mass destruction — they actually did not exist — and alleged ties between Iraqi leaders and the al Qaeda network responsible for the September 11, 2001, attacks on the U.S.
“If I had known then what I know now, I would have voted against it,” Mr. Rockefeller told the Charleston Gazette newspaper in 2004, referring to the 2002 war authorization measure.
“I think the intelligence was shaped,” he continued. “And I think the interpretation of the intelligence was shaped. You had a president who we now know was determined to go to war.”
‘Fundamentally misleading’
A report from the intelligence committee issued in 2008, when he served as its chairman, asserted that Mr. Bush, Vice President Dick Cheney and other leading officials exaggerated intelligence findings and ignored disputes within U.S. intelligence circles about Iraq’s weapons and the hotly disputed ties to al Qaeda.
The report rejected pre-war statements by Mr. Bush and Cheney that Iraq might give al Qaeda weapons of mass destruction.
“Representing to the American people that the two had an operational partnership and posed a single, indistinguishable threat was fundamentally misleading and led the nation to war on false premises,” Mr. Rockefeller said as the report was released.
During his Senate tenure, he also headed the Commerce, Science, and Transportation and Veterans Affairs committees.
Wealthy family
Mr. Rockefeller was born on June 18, 1937, weeks after the death of his great-grandfather, who had been America’s richest man.
The Rockefeller name came with high expectations. His father was a famous philanthropist. His uncle Nelson served as U.S. vice president, as well as Governor of New York. His uncle David Rockefeller headed Chase Manhattan Bank and uncle Winthrop Rockefeller was governor of Arkansas.
He was elected to West Virginia’s legislature in 1966 before age 30, then elected West Virginia’s Secretary of State in 1968.
He lost a bid to become Governor in 1972, then served as a college president before being elected Governor in 1976. Mr. Rockefeller, who became one of the wealthiest members of the U.S. Congress, spent millions of dollars of his own money to bankroll his successful campaign for the US Senate in 1984.
Mr. Rockefeller sometimes found himself overshadowed by his State’s other senator, Robert Byrd, who died in 2010 at age 92 as the longest-serving member of Congress in U.S. history.
He usually backed his State’s coal and steel industries but angered coal executives in 2012 by fighting Republican efforts to prevent regulation of emissions from coal-fired power plants.
He was married to public television executive Sharon Percy Rockefeller, with whom he had four children.

What do dark circles under a child’s eyes indicate?
Dark circles under a child’s eyes may not always be due to lack of sleep. Genetics, allergies and nasal congestion can also play a role. Paediatricians explain the causes and when parents should seek medical advice
Dark circles alone need not be a cause for concern if the child is otherwise healthy. Parents should, however, consult a paediatrician if the discolouration persists or is accompanied by other symptoms |Image used for representational purpose only
| Photo Credit: File Photo
A child may wake up after a full night’s sleep and still have dark circles under the eyes. For some children, this may simply be a family trait. In others, it could be associated with allergies, persistent nasal congestion or skin conditions. Dark circles, also referred to as periorbital hyperpigmentation, are not a condition in themselves. While parents may immediately associate dark circles with inadequate sleep or nutritional deficiencies, their causes can be more varied.

Record global heat, rising climate risks, finance tensions dominate COP31 day one
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said the world was entering an era of increasingly severe climate extremes
The 12 years from 2015 to 2026 are on course to be the warmest on record, with global average temperatures between January and September this year reaching around 1.47°C above the pre-industrial average, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in an update. The WMO’s State of the Climate Update 2026 was released on the opening day of the 11-day 20th UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Turkey’s Antalya.
The update said the years 2023-2026 were the four hottest on record, and global ocean heat content is on track to record its 10th consecutive annual high. The global mean sea level has reached its highest point in the satellite record, which began in 1993.
The WMO warned that an intensifying El Niño, a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures that affects rainfall and temperature patterns, is expected to reach significant strength by December. It could further raise temperatures and increase the risks of extreme heat, drought and heavy rainfall well into 2027.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said the world was entering an era of increasingly severe climate extremes, with the human and economic costs continuing to rise.
The WMO update underlined the importance of sustained climate observations and early warning systems in helping countries prepare for these growing risks.
Joint presidency, ambitious promise
Australia and Turkey took over the COP31 presidency, marking the beginning of an unusual joint arrangement. Turkey is hosting the summit under COP31 President Murat Kurum. Australia’s Chris Bowen will lead the negotiations.
Kurum and Bowen raised their clasped hands together, signalling a united front, following the ceremonial handover from outgoing COP30 president André Aranha Corrêa do Lago.
Beyond the symbolism, the two countries have their work cut out. Kurum said he wants COP31 to be an “implementation COP,” guided by dialogue, consensus and action.
The emphasis is on moving beyond declarations and ensuring existing climate commitments translate into tangible outcomes on the ground.
Kurum said the 1.5°C goal would continue to guide the presidency. He stressed the need to bridge the gap between countries that have access to finance and technology and those that remain vulnerable.
Kurum outlined Turkey’s 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which seeks to increase electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 through renewables, stronger grids, energy storage and clean transport.
UN climate chief Simon Stiell reinforced the implementation message. He said COP31 must supercharge solutions, including faster deployment of renewables, reducing methane emissions and making committed climate finance easier to access.
Climate finance: a sticking point
The first major test for negotiations arose before substantive discussions could gather momentum. The African Group chair and negotiating team spent much of the night working through disagreements around the agenda. The Climate Finance Work Programme eventually made it onto the agreed agenda.
Finance remains one of the biggest fault lines between developed and developing countries. Vulnerable nations are demanding greater support to deal with the impacts of climate change. But questions remain over how existing commitments will be delivered and whether the money will reach countries that need it.
The tripling of adaptation finance particularly remains contentious. Countries are looking for progress on the commitments made under the new climate finance goal agreed at COP29 in Baku of mobilising at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035. This was to be alongside efforts to scale up overall financing to $1.3 trillion annually.
The negotiations will test whether countries can move from broad commitments to clearer mechanisms for delivering funds.
In his opening address, Bowen noted that the countries needing climate finance most often receive the least.
Mountain-specific adaptation finance
On the opening day of COP31, the Nepalese delegation called attention to the devastating consequences of glacial collapse, floods and other climate-related disasters in the Himalayas. Sagar Dhakal, a Nepalese lawmaker, described the scale of the disaster, which left around 10,000 people dead within 10 minutes following the glacier collapse. He said the damage wiped out around 10% of Nepal’s GDP.
Dhakal’s intervention highlighted concerns that the impacts of global warming are not restricted to rising temperatures or sea levels and that mountain countries have repeatedly raised these concerns at international climate negotiations. The retreat of glaciers, unstable mountain slopes and the growing threat of glacial lake outburst floods pose serious risks to downstream communities, infrastructure and economies.
Nepal demanded mountain-specific adaptation finance, stronger early warning systems and greater international recognition of the risks facing high-altitude regions. The issue featured in the opening remarks of Stiell, who referred to the Himalayan tragedy as an example of the mounting human cost of global heating.
Climate ambition coalition warning
The question of whether the world can still limit global warming to 1.5°C, and what happens if it fails to do so, emerged as a defining theme on the opening day of COP31. Bowen acknowledged that the latest science indicated the world would overshoot the 1.5°C threshold. He said it was still possible to return to that level if countries acted with urgency, solidarity and resolve. Bowen pointed to the progress made since the Paris Agreement. He noted that projected warming had declined from nearly 4°C to around 2.6°C, but stressed that much faster action was needed.
Kurum said the 1.5°C goal remained the guiding principle of Turkey’s presidency.
The High Ambition Coalition, an informal grouping of countries pushing for stronger climate action, said the COP31 success would be judged by how effectively it responded to the looming threat of temperature overshoot.
German climate minister Heike Henn stressed the need to listen to science. She added that support for vulnerable countries remained inadequate.
Pacific envoys warned that overshooting 1.5°C was radically different from simply failing to meet the target. They called on countries to accelerate emissions cuts, scale up renewable energy and increase climate finance through regional mechanisms such as the Pacific Resilience Facility. They demanded that oceans receive greater attention in climate negotiations.
For island nations facing rising seas and increasingly severe climate impacts, the distinction is critical. Their message was that the prospect of overshoot cannot become an excuse for slowing down action.

Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of the climate crisis, as they face big drops in production resulting from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event.
High winds in parts of Colombia, one of the biggest suppliers to the UK market where droughts are predicted in some regions this year, and heavy rainfall in Peru and Ecuador are already affecting production, according to the Fairtrade Foundation ethical trade body. In the Dominican Republic, farmers are expected to face drought conditions, with forecasts of drier and warmer than usual conditions.
Fairtrade research suggests that during the previous El Niño cycle, productivity across its farmers and workers dropped by 13% in the Dominican Republic, 22% in Ecuador, and 6% in Peru compared with the year before. The El Niño event in 1983 – one of the strongest ever recorded – affected 15% of total planted banana area in Ecuador, with a reduction in exports of 36%.
Dr Carley-Jane Stanton, a climate and environment lead at Fairtrade, says this El Niño is expected to lead to more extreme weather, including heavy rainfall and strong winds and “we expect the impacts for producers to be more severe” than in the 23-24 cycle.
Evidence is mounting to fuel those fears. Exports from the Colombian Caribbean region fell 32% to $122m (£91m) between July and September this year, according to the Association of Banana Growers of Magdalena and La Guajira, as reported by the trade publication Fruitnet.
It said that in September alone, shipments were down 42% year on year, with earnings close to halving to $40m from $70m.
“Given the risks threatening the continuity of banana production, we are calling on international markets to foster commercial conditions that recognise actual production costs and contribute to the sector’s sustainability,” the association said.
It said that climate-related productivity losses and a decline in earnings from exports made worse by currency issues was “undermining the economic sustainability of the industry”.
Ever Antonio Flores Muños, a worker at the Agrosiete banana producer in Colombia, told Fairtrade: “Over the past 10 years the climate has changed a lot. It’s been getting much hotter … it’s really intense. Some places have had losses due to the climate, flooding, strong winds. It’s going to affect all of us – our workers, colleagues – everything will be at great risk, and our wages will decrease.”
Fairtrade is calling for legislation in the UK to tackle unfair trading practices, such as low or late payments to farmers and contracts which push risk down the supply chain, so that producers can invest more into improving their crops’ resilience to severe weather and more likelihood of pests and diseases. Worker health is also expected to be affected by more extreme weather.
While some businesses, including Sainsbury’s, the Co-op and Waitrose, have taken voluntary steps by sourcing only Faitrade bananas, which guarantee a minimum price, it says there is more work to do.
Eleanor Harrison, the chief executive of Fairtade, said: “The UK’s banana supply depends on the people growing our bananas having the resources they need to adapt to climate change, and to invest in their future. Fair prices, climate resilience and decent work go hand in hand.”
While bananas are becoming harder and more expensive to produce, supermarket prices have remained unchanged for almost 40 years despite rising costs for fertiliser, fuel and labour.
Caoimhe Buckley, the chief corporate affairs officer at the large supplier Fyffes, said: “The long-term sustainability of the banana sector … cannot be separated from purchasing practices. The price of bananas in the supermarket needs to recognise the real and sustainable cost of production, including labour and decent wages, environmental management, human-rights due diligence and the investment necessary to adapt to climate change.”
Research by the Ethical Trading Initiative found that prices paid to suppliers in 2026 did not even cover basic production costs for 66.7% of them.
It said producers need more help to adapt or mitigate climatic changes, which could mean suitable land for banana cultivation could shrink by an average of 61% across Latin America and the Caribbean by 2050, according to research for the Inter-American Development Bank published in 2020.

Odisha cabinet approves proposal for ₹4,708-crore pumped storage project
Bhubaneswar, The Odisha cabinet on Monday approved 13 proposals, including a ₹4,708-crore 600 MW pumped storage project, free Wi-Fi for college students and unlimited attempts for candidates appearing in the state civil services examination till the prescribed upper age limit.
The proposals were approved at a cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi here.
"The cabinet has approved… the 600 MW Upper Indravati Pumped Storage Project at Ranibahal, Kalahandi district. The state will spend a total of ₹4,708.64 crore, including ₹3,371.88 crore for construction of the project," Chief Secretary Anu Garg told reporters.
Describing it as the first project of its kind in the state, Garg said it is targeted to be commissioned by the 2030-31 financial year. Megha Engineering & Infrastructures Ltd has been selected as the project developer.
The 600 MW facility will generate approximately 1,040 million units of annual peak electricity, officials said.
The project will serve as a grid-scale energy storage system, absorbing surplus electricity during off-peak hours and generating power during periods of peak demand, the chief secretary said.
The cabinet also approved three proposals of the Water Resources Department worth ₹450 crore for in-stream storage projects and mega lift irrigation units.
In another decision, it cleared a proposal of the General Administration and Public Grievance Department to amend the Odisha Civil Services Rules, 1991.
"The key change eliminates all restrictions on the number of attempts for the Odisha Civil Services Examination. A candidate can appear for the examination until his/her upper age limit," Garg said.
The cabinet also approved the Odisha Shikshanet project, worth ₹393.62 crore, to provide free campus Wi-Fi with a daily limit of 1 GB across 601 colleges, benefiting around six lakh students, she said.
Besides, it cleared the Paddy Procurement Policy for the Kharif Marketing Season 2026-27. The government will procure at least 78 lakh metric tonnes of paddy from farmers at ₹3,100 per quintal, with payments transferred directly to their bank accounts within 24-48 hours.
The government also approved a proposal to extend the tenure of around 5,000 private fair price shop dealers by one year, until September 30, 2027.

DST: No INSPIRE grant if student fails, misses exam
Students who fail or miss a university examination will no longer be able to retain their scholarships under the Centre’s flagship INSPIRE-Scholarship for Higher Education (SHE) scheme, and the annual research mentorship grant has been restricted to the third and fourth years, reducing the maximum financial support over five years.
The Department of Science and Technology (DST) has also changed the way scholarships are allocated among school boards, introducing quotas by board, based on the number of Class 12 examinees rather than the number of applications received.
DST announced the changes on November 7, opening applications for the 2025 batch of INSPIRE-SHE, following a delay of more than a year. Experts and students said the revised rules could make it harder for students to retain the scholarship, reduce financial support for research projects and alter the distribution of awards across states, potentially leaving some board quotas unfilled.
The online application window will remain open until December 7, 11.59pm. Only candidates aged 17-22 who cleared their Class 12 examinations in 2025 will be considered.
Every year, around 12,000 INSPIRE-SHE scholarships are awarded to students pursuing undergraduate and postgraduate courses in basic and natural sciences. The scheme provides ₹5,000 a month, or ₹60,000 annually, along with a ₹20,000 annual mentorship grant. Eligible candidates include students in the top 1% of their respective Class 12 board examinations and those qualifying through specified national-level entrance examinations.
The application cycle usually begins around September, after college admissions and competitive examination results, and ends by October-November. However, no application notification was issued in 2025, leaving science aspirants uncertain about the scheme’s future, HT reported on July 15.
In a post on X on the same day, DST, which did not respond to queries from HT at the time, said: “INSPIRE-SHE scheme is not scrapped. It is being redesigned currently. Hence, there has been a delay in announcing the call.”
DST did not respond to HT’s request for comment on the latest changes.
Under the revised financial structure, the monthly scholarship remains ₹5,000, or ₹60,000 annually. However, the ₹20,000 mentorship grant will now be available only in the third and fourth years, instead of every year. This reduces the maximum support over the five-year scholarship period from ₹4 lakh to ₹3.4 lakh.
The academic rules have also been tightened. Under the 2024 guidelines, students who failed an examination or could not appear for it “forfeited” the scholarship for that academic year but could resume receiving support the following year if they met the prescribed requirements.
The 2025 guidelines remove this provision. “If a scholar has failed or secured less than 60% or 7 CGPA (cumulative grade point average) in the first year, he/she will not be eligible to receive even the first-year scholarship, and will be ineligible for the entire SHE scholarship period,” the revised frequently asked questions (FAQs) document says. Failure in subsequent years will mean the “scholarship shall be discontinued with immediate effect”, making the student ineligible for subsequent scholarship and mentorship instalments.
“These are substantial revisions, and not for the better,” said Anindita Bhadra, professor at IISER Kolkata. “The reduction in the fellowship amount is a big setback, as with fees in colleges constantly on the rise, fewer students would be able to support their education with this fellowship. The allocated funds per student should actually increase, not decrease in the revised guidelines.”
Akhil Tripathi, co-founder of Noida-based science education platform SciAstra, said the mentorship grant was particularly important in the initial years. “In the first two years, the ₹20,000 grant is what lets a student take up a proper research project, and that early exposure often decides who stays in science,” he said.
“Since 2008, the PhD fellowship has gone up about three times, but INSPIRE-SHE has stayed at ₹80,000 a year since the start, and now it is being cut. That goes against what INSPIRE was meant to do,” he added.
Tripathi also questioned the stricter academic rules. “In subjects like Maths, a lot of students get a backlog in the first year, and this happens even at institutions like IISc, IISER and NISER. Till now, if someone failed, they lost that year’s scholarship but could get it back the next year. Now one fails in the first year and the student is out of the scholarship completely, and in later years even a missed exam ends it,” he said.
The top-1% eligibility criterion remains unchanged, but the allocation formula has been revised. Under the 2024 guidelines, each board’s share of the total valid scholarship applications determined its allocation. The 2025 guidelines instead link the quota to the proportion of students who appeared for Class 12 examinations from each board. The revised FAQ does not specify whether unfilled board allocations will be redistributed.
“The earlier rule made sense, and was less biased. A state with a higher population is now likely to see more candidates with the fellowship, while more eligible students from other states will lose out,” Bhadra said.
Pranit Sohane, a BSc student at Swargiya Sundar Lal Shivhare Degree College in Hamirpur, affiliated with Bundelkhand University, Jhansi, said the revised formula could leave some board quotas under-utilised while increasing competition in states with larger applicant pools. Sohane scored 87% in the 2025 Uttar Pradesh Board Class 12 examinations, above the state’s 81% top-1% cut-off.
“Earlier, scholarships were allocated based on applications received from different boards. Under the new formula, quotas are linked to the number of students appearing for Class 12, reducing Uttar Pradesh’s share from 6,129 scholarships last year to just 2,095. Boards such as CBSE and Bihar, with fewer applicants for science courses, may fill their quotas with just a few hundred students, leaving seats vacant. If these are not redistributed, the total number of scholarships could fall to around 10,000, while students from Uttar Pradesh will face greater competition for the limited seats,” he said.
The revised guidelines also introduce an explicit course-wise preference order. Students in the top 1% of their boards enrolled in integrated MSc and BS-MS programmes will be considered first. They will be followed by candidates with specified JEE or NEET ranks, NTSE or JBNSTS qualifications, or International Olympiad medals, and then top-1% students enrolled in regular BSc and BS programmes.
The framework also expands the list of eligible undergraduate science subjects from 18 in 2024 to 28 in 2025. Biotechnology, bioinformatics, biostatistics, environmental science, data science, materials science, nanoscience, life sciences and earth sciences are among the subjects included. The postgraduate list has expanded from 30 to 35.
Another change concerns eligibility for the INSPIRE Fellowship for doctoral studies. The revised provisions recognise four-year BSc (Hons.) and BSc with Research degrees of at least eight semesters, alongside MSc/MS qualifications, subject to prescribed academic criteria. This opens a route for eligible graduates to apply for doctoral fellowships without first completing a master’s degree, in line with the four-year undergraduate structure under the National Education Policy (NEP 2020).

For example, last month, an X user reposted (archived) a popular ground-shot photo of the clothes "mountain." The post's text caption began, "There is a mountain of unworn clothes in the driest desert on earth, large enough to be photographed from space."

Others reposted the same image, or in some cases a purported satellite image (archived), on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Reddit (archived) and X (archived).
One satellite image, first reported by the SkyFi satellite imagery company in 2023, was captured in 2022:
In sum, past satellite images indicated more than one clothing dumping spot, or "pile," has existed in Chile's Atacama Desert — which truly is one of the driest places on Earth. Those images were real.
As seen in the ground-shot photo earlier in this article, the real sites looked more like low-lying landfills instead of the ridiculously tall piles visible in other (archived) images (archived) that were generated using artificial intelligence. (The Pangram AI detection tool indicated the latter were created or edited with AI. Miguel Aguirre San Martín, the regional environmental secretary for the Tarapacá region, told the local Expreso Bío Bío radio and TV program in October that the images people most often shared were several years old and showed what he called "mountains" of clothes (possibly using the word after it first appeared on social media and in news articles) that crews have since partially cleared away. He also spoke of legislation aimed at holding the people doing the illegal dumping accountable.
In the absence of capturing of brand-new satellite images or a making a physical visit to each site in the desert, we can't credibly confirm San Martín's statements or determine how many clothes dumping locations remained as of this month.
We contacted San Martín's office and received word back on Oct. 22 that they were awaiting approval to respond to our questions. We will update this article if we receive further information.
This article lays out the known facts, including information about the December 2024 proposed plan by the United Nations to combat the fast-fashion industry's waste problem.
Researching the rumor
Chile is a major importer of secondhand and unsold clothing. After workers in Chile sort through imported garments, a percentage of that clothing has ended up illegally dumped in the country's Atacama Desert, including north of Alto Hospicio, a municipality found within the Iquique Province in the Tarapacá region.
In past years, news outlets and social media users have published real photos (and occasionally videos) showing views of the clothing piling up and lining roads — including the specific clothes dumping area SkyFi highlighted in 2023 with the 2022 satellite image.
Google Earth's satellite images of the region, which display the most recent media publicly available from February 2025, appear to show that crews removed quite a lot of the clothing from the same garment dumping site that SkyFi reported about in 2023. Even so, some clothing or other waste still appeared to line the roads in the lower part of the image.
We located that same SkyFi-reported "pile" north of Alto Hospicio. (Readers can copy and paste these coordinates into Google Earth, Google Maps or another mapping tool to find the same area: -20.2344898,-70.0888835.)
(Google Earth)
Other nearby locations also featured areas of apparent dumped goods. For example, SkyFi provided to Snopes a recent satellite image taken in August that appears to show a volume of waste similar to that of the February 2025 Google Earth capture.
We couldn't match the specific dumping locations shown in a handful of ground-shot photos to those seen in satellite images.
During San Martín's local interview, he specifically spoke of conducting aerial surveys to locate the largest amounts of waste. He also described already having completed the cleanup of 60,000 tons of clothing, coordinating public-private task forces, emphasizing environmental education and looking to the justice system to decide who should be responsible for the garment dumpings.
In our correspondence to San Martín's office, we asked when exactly the clearing of the primary "pile" occurred, where the clothing ended up, whether or not the government planned to clear other dumpings and whether the government had determined which companies or countries dumped the items. We will update this story should we receive answers to these questions.
The United Nations plan
In May 2023, the United Nations announced research to combat the problem, stating, "United Nations will launch a study on global secondhand clothing trade and disposal in Chile."
The announcement mentioned a forthcoming special report identifying Chile as "the world's fourth largest importer of secondhand and unsold clothes," with imports reaching "some 126,000 million tons, originating principally from China, the United States and the Republic of Korea."
Part of the announcement read:
About 40% of these clothes are imported through the Iquique free trade zone in the northern Atacama Desert. As a large share of these clothes have no value in the local secondhand clothing market and cannot be re-exported, they are dumped in the desert. Most of these low-quality clothes, made of synthetic or mixed fibers with chemicals, release pollutants into the air, ground, and water harming the environment and local communities.
The post identified the European Union, U.S. and China as the leading used garment exporters as of 2021, with the U.S. leading per-country exports at 700,000 tons annually. "China has become a prominent player in the last five years, sending clothes to African countries such as Kenya, Angola and Ghana," the report said.
The authors of the report identified an "urgent need for the global fashion market to move from a linear value chain to a genuinely circular one."
In December 2024, the U.N. released its findings from the study, recommending in a special report that changes be made to international trade agreements and domestic policy actions be undertaken regarding importing and exporting countries.
The report's authors stressed that "no single solution can reduce the massive volume of used garments," saying positive steps forward would include a reduction in the volume of new clothes, the ensuring that manufacturers design clothes free of toxic chemicals and the encouraging of using and reusing garments for a longer period of time. Those criteria, if put into practice, would help to foster "a circular economy for fashion."

(Bloomberg) -- US consumers are falling further behind on their debts as they navigate higher costs on fuel, groceries and other goods.
The share of overdue consumer loans rose marginally in the third quarter to 5% from 4.7% the prior quarter, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit released Tuesday. Total household debt balances rose 1.8% to $19.1 trillion.
The share of mortgage balances more than 90 days overdue rose to 1.13%, the highest since the first quarter of 2018. The portion of mortgage debt transitioning into early and severe delinquency ticked up but remained near pre-pandemic norms, New York Fed researchers said.
“Although delinquency transition rates for housing debts have crept up, the overall credit quality of these loans remains strong,” Donghoon Lee, economic research adviser at the New York Fed, said in a press release.
Balances for home equity lines of credit rose by $23 billion, marking the largest increase since 2005 and the 18th straight quarter of growth.
The share of debt becoming newly delinquent also rose for auto loans. Student loan balances increased slightly but loans entered delinquency at a slower pace.
Transition into delinquency also improved for credit cards. In a blog post accompanying the data, New York Fed researchers found delinquency rates for cards opened during the pandemic — when issuance rose for consumers with lower incomes and credit scores — are declining.
“If current patterns hold, the elevated delinquencies of the past few years may prove to be more of a pandemic-era echo than a permanent feature of the credit card market,” they wrote.
Pandemic Delinquencies
Separate data released Tuesday by the Urban Institute, a think tank in Washington, D.C., suggest people have fallen further behind on debts since the pandemic.
About 5.8% of Americans have at least some delinquent credit card debt, with a median amount of $680 debt being late. That’s up from 4.3% who had some credit card delinquency in August 2019, according to the institute’s research. Around 5.5% of consumers have some delinquency in auto and retail loans, compared with 3.9% in August 2019.
Nationwide, about 24% of US consumers with a credit file have debt of any kind in collections, according to the institute. That’s down from the roughly 30% who had debt in collections just before the pandemic, though part of the improvement likely stems from delays in reporting collections to credit bureaus, said Breno Braga, a senior fellow at the institute.
Residents of ZIP codes with a majority of people of color are 50% more likely to have debt in collections than residents of majority white areas, the study found.
The institute tracked the share of people across the US with debt in collections or delinquent by taking a representative sample of credit bureau records from August 2026.
Consumer price data released Tuesday showed underlying inflation excluding food and energy rose 0.3% in October from a month earlier, topping estimates for the third straight month.

Amid ongoing accusations by Opposition parties of increase in crime and deteriorating law and order in Tamil Nadu, MDMK general secretary Vaiko on Tuesday released a catalogue of crimes that occurred over the past 34 years. He also lamented that the TVK-led government was being criticised by two of its coalition partners.
Addressing journalists in Chennai on Tuesday, he said except the IUML and the MDMK, the other parties within the ruling alliance have been criticising the administration.
Mr. Vaiko released a list detailing crimes committed in the State between May 1991 and May 2026. Citing the list compiled by the Madurai-based human rights organisation People’s Watch, he highlighted several major criminal incidents.
Speaking on the subject for over an hour, Vaiko also recounted the backdrop of key moments from his own political journey during this period. In particular, he detailed the circumstances surrounding his arrest under the Prevention of Terrorism Act (POTA) in July 2002. He noted that upon learning of the Tamil Nadu government’s decision to detain him under POTA, he advanced his return from the United States — originally scheduled for July 15 — and arrived in Chennai on July 11 to court arrest. He added while he was meant to be lodged in the Vellore Central Prison, authorities attempted to detain him at the Madurai Central Prison en route, an effort that was abandoned only after his fierce resistance.
He also recalled that it was former Chief Minister M. Karunanidhi who first addressed him as “Vaiko” instead of his full name V. Gopalasamy. He recounted that during the inaugural meeting held in Delhi to form the National Front, M. Karunanidhi had sent him a note on a slip of paper addressed to ‘Thambi Vaikovukku’.
Mr. Vaiko alleged some time after he founded the MDMK, L. Ganesan and Gingee N. Ramachandran attempted to split the party and organise a rival general council meeting on the instructions of the DMK leadership, but those efforts ended in failure.
He further recalled that following his release from prison under POTA, he undertook a padayatra from Tirunelveli to Chennai alongside 1,200 people, demanding an end to caste and communal clashes and the complete eradication of narcotics. Although he was denied entry into Chennai as the march neared the city, he defied the restrictions, entered Chennai, and addressed a public meeting.
Mr. Vaiko also mentioned that when Prime Minister Narendra Modi invited Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa as a special guest to his swearing-in ceremony, he vehemently opposed the move and was arrested after staging a demonstration at Jantar Mantar.
Stating he had opposed the Sterlite plant in Thoothukudi from the very beginning, Mr. Vaiko alleged fresh efforts were under way to reopen the facility under the pretext of producing “Green Copper.” He claimed Vedanta’s Anil Agarwal had sought an appointment with Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay for this purpose; however, following his own appeal urging the Chief Minister not to meet him, the meeting did not take place, and Mr. Agarwal has now approached the court.
Prior to Mr. Vaiko’s address, leaders from his party spoke in detail about his political contributions.

The role of family physicians in ensuring accessible, affordable and patient-centred healthcare came into focus at the premiere of the documentary ‘The Doctor Next Door: A Legacy of Care’, screened at the Indian Heritage Academy in Bengaluru earlier this week.
Through accounts of veteran physicians, patients and young medical professionals, the film examines the decline of neighbourhood family practices and the growing fragmentation of healthcare. It highlights how long-standing doctor-patient relationships built on trust, familiarity and personal attention remain central to effective primary care.
The documentary draws attention to the rising dependence on specialised and corporate hospital-based treatment, making a case for strengthening family medicine as the foundation of India’s healthcare system.
Swetha Reddy, project manager of the documentary, said the film features perspectives from young medical students and practitioners considering careers in general practice, highlighting the need for changes in medical education and healthcare policy to encourage family medicine.
Directed by Ganesh Shankar Raj of Mindia Films and produced in collaboration with the Academy of Family Physicians of India (AFPI), the non-profit documentary explores the enduring relationship between family doctors and patients, and the importance of continuity of care in an increasingly specialised healthcare system.
The screening was followed by a panel discussion featuring scientists, medical professionals, senior family physicians, and community health advocates. The discussion centred on the challenges facing primary healthcare, the need to strengthen family medicine, and the importance of human relationships in medical practice.
Veteran family physician B.C. Rao was among the contributors to the initiative, alongside representatives of AFPI and other healthcare professionals.
The organisers said the documentary was intended to initiate wider conversations on reviving primary healthcare networks in urban and rural communities, and recognising neighbourhood doctors as an integral part of the healthcare system.

Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
- Published
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.
The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.
Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.
The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.
Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.
The Egyptian Red Crescent said it was providing aid and psychological support to victims and their families at the scene.
The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.
The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.
Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.
Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains. The railway authority has not said how long it expects this to take.
The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.
In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.
Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.
There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.
Foreign leaders and dignitaries have shared condolences and support for the victims.
Saudi Arabia's ministry of foreign affairs expressed "solidarity" with Egypt and wished those hurt a speedy recovery.
Turkey's ambassador to Egypt wrote on X that he extended "heartfelt condolences and sincere sympathy" to the victims, their families, and the Egyptian people.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

The Child Development Centre (CDC), Thiruvananthapuram, has received an Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)-approved grant of ₹35 lakh for a three-year research project titled “Development and Validation of a Tool for Assessing Grief among Parents of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.”
The project, led by CDC director Deepa Bhaskaran, aims to develop and validate a culturally relevant tool to assess grief among parents of children with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD).
“The study will use focus group discussions and in-depth interviews involving parents of children with ASD, bereaved parents, professionals working with children with ASD, and members of the general population to understand the dimensions and cultural expressions of grief in the Indian context,” Dr. Bhaskaran said.
According to her, parents commonly experience shock, denial, fear, guilt, anger, sadness, and helplessness following their child’s diagnosis. The grief, described as chronic sorrow or non-finite grief, can recur at different stages of the child’s development, particularly when expected developmental milestones are not attained.
“The findings will help facilitate the identification of grief-related concerns among parents and support the development of appropriate grief counselling protocols and support group interventions, ultimately contributing to improved psychosocial well-being among families of children with ASD,” she said.
Inadequate social support compounds parental distress, she noted.
“There is a need for healthcare professionals to recognise and assess parents’ emotional well-being alongside the rehabilitation needs of children with autism. Early diagnosis, psychological support, and training for professionals to identify grief and help families develop coping strategies are vital,” she added.

At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of Cairo, authorities have said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles (5okm) south of the capital, when a train travelling to the south-western Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. It said one of the trains had derailed.
The health ministry said at least four people had been killed and 88 injured. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.
The president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation into the crash to hold those responsible accountable.
Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.
A train driver and his assistant were injured in September last year when two freight trains collided in the same district.

Ranbir Kapoor has achieved another major box office milestone with Ramayana – Part I. The Nitesh Tiwari-directed mythological epic has crossed the Rs. 300 crore mark at the Indian box office, becoming Ranbir Kapoor's third film to enter the prestigious Rs. 300 crore club. With this achievement, the actor has joined Ranveer Singh and Salman Khan at the top of the all-time rankings for actors with the highest number of films in the club.
According to our data, only three actors have delivered three films collecting more than Rs. 300 crores nett at the Indian box office: Ranveer Singh, Ranbir Kapoor and Salman Khan. The achievement is particularly significant because Ranbir has now moved ahead of Shah Rukh Khan, Aamir Khan and Sunny Deol in terms of the number of films in this coveted club.
Ranbir Kapoor's three Rs. 300 crore grossers are Sanju (2018), Animal (2023) and Ramayana – Part I (2026). What makes Ranbir's achievement interesting is the diversity of these films. Sanju was a biographical drama, Animal an intense action drama and Ramayana a grand mythological spectacle.
Actors with the most Rs. 300 crore films
Ranveer Singh - 3
Ranbir Kapoor - 3
Salman Khan - 3
Shah Rukh Khan - 2
Sunny Deol - 2
Aamir Khan - 2
Another fascinating aspect of Ramayana's performance is the speed with which the film has entered the Rs. 300 crore club. Sanju took 16 days to cross the milestone, while Animal achieved it in six days. Ramayana, meanwhile, has accomplished the feat in just five days, making it Ranbir Kapoor's fastest film to enter the Rs. 300 crore club.

Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied being “obsessed” with Jesse Baird from the start of their relationship, telling a court he would have liked the TV presenter even if he was “a garbage cleaner”.
The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Sitting in the witness box for the fourth day, Lamarre-Condon was grilled by crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC about his relationship with Baird.
The former officer told the NSW supreme court he would meet up with Baird in October and November 2022 for sexual encounters before the pair began going on romantic dates in December of that year.
Under cross-examination on Tuesday, Hatfield asked Lamarre-Condon: “You were obsessed with him right from the start?”
Lamarre-Condon denied this, telling the jury: “I never cared about showing Jesse off. I wanted Jesse to meet my friends because I thought he was genuine”.
“Jesse Baird could have been a garbage cleaner… I liked Jesse for who he was as a person,” Lamarre-Condon said.
Asked by Hatfield if Lamarre-Condon was “obsessed” with Baird in February and March 2023, the accused responded: “I don’t agree with ‘obsessed’. Smitten? Yes. Obsessed? no.”
Hatfield pointed to messages between Lamarre-Condon and his friends sent around the time the pair began going on dates, where the officer says: “it sounds crazy, I love him”.
Lamarre-Condon responded: “I say ‘I love you’ to all my friends and to people like that all the time.”
“That’s different to saying I’m ‘in’ love with him,” he said.
Asked whether he was insecure about the relationship and whether Baird liked him, Lamarre-Condon said his response was “natural” and sometimes occurred when the TV presenter did not reply to his messages straight away.
“I would always joke [with my friends], ‘we’re white girl crazy’,” Lamarre-Condon told the jury.
“It means we should stop being in our head and second-guessing ourselves.”
He told the court he would make jokes and have “banter” with his female friends, not his heterosexual male friends, telling each other things like: “you’re a crazy bitch”.
Hatfield showed screenshots of text messages between Baird and Lamarre-Condon and asked why Baird’s profile photo were low resolution.
“If you’re trying to insinuate any of these are not genuine … we’ve got videos,” the officer said, telling the court Baird’s photo was a screenshot from a video he took of the presenter.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

Israeli forces kill Palestinian boy in West Bank, health ministry says
- Published
Israeli forces have shot dead a 14-year-old Palestinian boy during an operation in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say.
Moataz Daghlas was killed on Monday evening in the village of Burqa, north-west of Nablus, according to the Palestinian health ministry.
The Israeli military said soldiers identified "several terrorists who intended to hurl stones" in an area where stones had previously been thrown at Israeli vehicles. The soldiers fired towards them "to remove the threat", it added.
The Palestinian Red Crescent said its teams treated two people with gunshot wounds, but that Israeli forces blocked their access to a third wounded person and detained three volunteer paramedics.
Moataz Daghlas's relatives said Israeli authorities were withholding his body.
Meanwhile, Palestinian news agency Wafa identified the two Palestinians wounded during the raid as a 17-year-old child, who it said was shot in the abdomen and pelvis, and a 19-year-old man, who was shot in the hand.
According to the UN, at least 98 Palestinians, including 22 children, have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year.
Six Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, it says.
The rules of engagement for Israeli forces were reportedly broadened after the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, allowing soldiers increased discretion to use lethal force against a perceived threat.
In June, the UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory said it had verified the killing of 241 Palestinian children by Israeli security forces and settlers in the West Bank since then.
Most of the children were teenage boys and, in many cases, Israeli authorities accused them of having engaged in stone-throwing as justification, it found.
The UN office said its assessment was that none of the children killed while involved in confrontations with Israeli forces had posed an imminent threat to life, which it said was the only legal justification for the use of lethal force in the West Bank under international law.

The Supreme Court on Friday (November 6, 2026) termed vehicular emissions a major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR and said immediate, medium- and long-term measures were needed to curb the rising air quality index.
Hearing a suo motu case examining the regulatory framework governing air pollution, a Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana also expressed concern over “bumper-to-bumper” traffic in Delhi-NCR.
“We keep talking and sometimes make statements and suggestions, but the point is that AQI is already touching 400,” the CJI said.
The Bench highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad.
“Look at the roads in Delhi and the roads connecting Delhi with the NCR. Take a look at any road and the kind of vehicles moving on it. That is the major problem,” the CJI said.
The Bench said the poor people are the real sufferers, as they are on the roads, and moreover, the festival time is the only period when they earn a livelihood.
On stubble burning, the Bench stressed the need to educate farmers about using machines instead of resorting to farm fires.
On the plea seeking closure of schools or running them in hybrid mode for students of all age groups if the air quality index (AQI) rises above a certain mark, the bench said it will go by experts’ opinion.
Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre and other authorities, referred to the regulatory framework covering five major sectors: industrial emissions, vehicular pollution, construction and demolition dust, road dust and stubble burning.
She told the Bench that several measures had been introduced, including restrictions on the entry of certain vehicles, geo-tagging of pollution under control (PUC) certificates and action against visibly polluting vehicles through complaints received on applications and social media.
Ms. Bhati told the Bench that stubble burning accounted for 14% of Delhi’s pollution on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The Bench said it will pass some orders and take up the plea on November 16 after the court reopens following the Diwali vacation.
A thick layer of smog hung over the national capital on Friday (November 6, 2026) as the air quality deteriorated sharply and edged closer to the ‘severe’ category, with the overall AQI settling at 391.
Of the 59 monitoring stations across the city, 30 recorded ‘severe’ air quality at 9 a.m., while the remaining were in the ‘very poor’ category.
Rohini recorded the worst AQI at 475, followed by IIT Delhi at 472, official data showed.
